0.title: The Acts of the Apostles
0.overview:
Acts is not primarily a history of the early church — it is the history of the risen Christ continuing his work through the Spirit he promised and poured out. Luke begins with a deliberate hinge: the “first book” (his Gospel) recorded all that Jesus “began to do and teach.” The operative word is began. What follows in Acts is what Jesus continued — not in the flesh now, but in the power of the Spirit, through the mouths and feet and wounds of his witnesses.

Luke wrote for Theophilus, likely a Roman official being catechised in the faith. But the scope of the narrative exceeds any single reader. Luke traces the gospel’s movement along the spine of the Roman Empire — Jerusalem to Rome, Jewish synagogue to Gentile household, from a frightened upper room to Caesar’s capital. This is not accident; it is Providence. The same God who told Abraham “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” is the God who compels a tentmaker from Tarsus to stand in the Areopagus and announce that the Unknown God has a name.

The Holy Spirit is the true protagonist of Acts. He falls at Pentecost like a sovereign flame. He speaks through Philip on a desert road. He stops Paul from entering Asia. He binds Paul to go to Jerusalem though chains await. He is not a vague presence but a Person with a will — the third Person of the Trinity, sent by the risen Son at the command of the Father, to accomplish the Father’s eternal purpose: a people for his name drawn from every tongue and tribe and nation.

Reformed readers will find in Acts not an argument for the faith but something far more bracing: the sovereignty of God in mission. The gates of hell do not hold. Persecution only scatters the seed further. Imprisonment opens courts to preach. Shipwreck lands an apostle on the right island. Nothing is accidental; everything is appointed. The book ends with Paul in Rome, under house arrest, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.” The final words are without hindrance. The empire could chain the man but not the Word.

Who wrote Acts, and when? The same author as Luke’s Gospel: both are addressed to Theophilus, and Acts begins by referring back to the first book (1:1). In several passages the story shifts to “we” (16:10–17; 20:5–28:16), so the writer travelled with Paul, and the early church agreed that he was Luke, the beloved physician (Col 4:14; cf. Philem 24; 2 Tim 4:11). Some date Acts in the 80s. The more likely date is the early 60s: the book ends with Paul still awaiting trial in Rome after two years (28:30), and says nothing of his death, Nero’s persecution or the fall of Jerusalem, events Luke could hardly have left out had they already happened.

Should churches copy everything in Acts? Acts is history, the record of what God did as the church was founded. What it describes is not automatically a command. A pattern binds us when the rest of the New Testament teaches it, or when Luke shows it as God’s settled way: preaching Christ, baptizing believers, appointing elders, devotion to the apostles’ teaching and prayer. But the casting of lots (1:26), the sharing of all property (4:32), and the signs that marked the apostles (2:43; 5:12) belonged to that unrepeatable time.

Read Acts with your eyes open to the God who is always working — in the upper room, in the council chambers, in the storm, in the jail at midnight. He is the same God today.

1.title: The Promise and the Wait
1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, <sup>2</sup>until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. <sup>3</sup>He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. <sup>4</sup>And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me; <sup>5</sup>for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” <sup>6</sup>So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” <sup>7</sup>He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. <sup>8</sup>But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” <sup>9</sup>And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. <sup>10</sup>And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes, <sup>11</sup>and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.” <sup>12</sup>Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. <sup>13</sup>And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James. <sup>14</sup>All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. <sup>15</sup>In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said, <sup>16</sup>“Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. <sup>17</sup>For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.” <sup>18</sup>(Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. <sup>19</sup>And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.) <sup>20</sup>“For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it’; and ‘Let another take his office.’ <sup>21</sup>So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, <sup>22</sup>beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us—one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.” <sup>23</sup>And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias. <sup>24</sup>And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen <sup>25</sup>to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.” <sup>26</sup>And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
1.overview:
Acts is the second volume of Luke’s work, written for the same Theophilus as his Gospel. The Gospel told what Jesus “began” to do and teach; Acts tells what the risen Jesus goes on doing by his Spirit through his church, as the gospel spreads from Jerusalem to Rome in about thirty years. Chapter 1 is the hinge between the two volumes. For forty days the risen Jesus shows himself alive and teaches about the kingdom. He tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the promised baptism with the Holy Spirit. When they ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel, he answers that the timing is the Father’s business; their business is to receive power and be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth, a sentence that maps out the whole book. Then he is taken up into heaven, and angels promise he will return in the same way.

The second half of the chapter shows the church waiting: about a hundred and twenty believers, including Jesus’ mother and his once-sceptical brothers, praying together in an upper room. Peter explains from the Psalms that Judas’s betrayal and death fulfilled Scripture and that his place must be filled, so that the Twelve, symbolising the renewed Israel, are complete before the Spirit comes. Two men who had been with Jesus from the beginning and witnessed the resurrection are nominated, the church prays, lots are cast, and Matthias is added to the apostles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Risen Lord Sends His Church
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Luke reminds Theophilus that his first book covered all that Jesus began to do and teach until he was taken up, after giving instructions through the Spirit to the apostles he had chosen. After his suffering Jesus gave them many convincing proofs that he was alive, appearing over forty days and speaking about God’s kingdom. While eating with them he told them not to leave Jerusalem but to wait for the Father’s promised gift: John baptised with water, but in a few days they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit. When they asked whether he was now going to restore the kingdom to Israel, he said it was not for them to know the times the Father has set, but they would receive power when the Spirit came on them, and would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. Then he was taken up before their eyes and a cloud hid him. As they stared into the sky, two men in white told them that this same Jesus would come back in the same way they had seen him go.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Ascension and the Reign of Christ

The ascension is not the absence of Jesus but the exaltation of Jesus. He who died and rose now reigns at the right hand of the Father (Psalm 110:1), exercising all authority in heaven and on earth. The church does not act in the absence of its king; it acts under the authority of its enthroned king. The cloud that received him is the glory-cloud of the Old Testament, and Daniel had already described the scene from the other side: one like a son of man coming with the clouds to the Ancient of Days, to receive a kingdom that shall not pass away (Daniel 7:13-14). The Reformed churches have insisted that the ascension is essential to the gospel and not an epilogue to it: without it Christ does not send the Spirit (John 16:7), does not intercede for his people (Hebrews 7:25), and does not carry our nature into the presence of God, where it now permanently is.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Eleven men were given a promise with no date, a mission far beyond their means, and an order to stay put until God moved. They obeyed the hardest part first, which was the waiting.

Now: The church lives in the same interval, between the cloud that took him and the cloud that brings him back. The temptations at either end are unchanged: to stand looking into heaven, absorbed in timetables the Father reserved to himself, or to rush at the work in a strength that was never promised. The command is the same as it was on the hillside — receive, and then witness.

verseByVerse.quote: In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the first book, O Theophilus, I have dealt with all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day when he was taken up, after he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen.

Meaning first. Acts is the second volume of Luke’s two-part work. The Gospel told what Jesus began to do and teach; Acts tells what he continued to do and teach, from heaven, by the Holy Spirit, through his apostles. It covers about thirty years, from the ascension (around AD 30) to Paul under house arrest in Rome (around AD 62). It is the story of how the gospel went from Jerusalem to Rome, from a handful of Jewish disciples to churches across the empire, and how God kept his promise to bless all nations through Abraham’s offspring. Its hero is not Peter or Paul but the risen Lord, working by his Spirit.

In the first book, O Theophilus. “The first book” is Luke’s Gospel, also written for Theophilus (Luke 1:1–4). His name means “friend of God.” He was probably a real person, perhaps a Roman official (Luke calls him “most excellent,” Luke 1:3), and perhaps Luke’s patron, who paid for copies to be made. Luke, a doctor and Paul’s travelling companion (Colossians 4:14), wrote both books.

All that Jesus began to do and teach. Key words. “Began.” The Gospel was only the beginning. Acts is the continuation of Jesus’ work. He is still the one acting (Acts 2:33, 47; 9:5; 16:7).

Until the day when he was taken up. The ascension, the hinge between the two books (Luke 24:50–51).

After he had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen. Jesus’ own ministry was carried out in the power of the Spirit (Luke 4:18), and so were his final instructions. The apostles are “chosen” by him (Luke 6:13). Their authority comes from him.

In a sentence. Luke told Theophilus that his first book covered all Jesus began to do and teach until the day he was taken up, after giving instructions through the Spirit to his chosen apostles.

For worship. Jesus has not stopped working. He still acts by his Spirit through his people. Expect him to work.
verseByVerse.note: “The first book” is Luke’s Gospel, also written for Theophilus. “Began” implies that Acts records what Jesus continued to do through his Spirit and his church.

verseByVerse.quote: He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, "you heard from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs, appearing to them during forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God. And while staying with them he ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father, which, he said, “you heard from me;

He presented himself alive to them after his suffering by many proofs. Key words. “Proofs” (tekmēria): a technical word for decisive evidence, conclusive proof. Luke the careful historian insists the resurrection was not a vision or a feeling. Jesus ate with them, let them touch him, showed his wounds (Luke 24:39–43; John 20:27). Paul lists over five hundred witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:5–8).

Appearing to them during forty days. Forty days recalls other periods of preparation in Scripture: Moses on the mountain (Exodus 24:18), Elijah’s journey (1 Kings 19:8), Jesus’ temptation in the wilderness (Luke 4:2). A time of preparation for a new stage.

And speaking about the kingdom of God. The theme of Jesus’ ministry continues: God’s reign, which had come in Jesus. Acts ends with Paul still preaching the kingdom (28:31).

He ordered them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to wait for the promise of the Father. The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit (Luke 24:49; Joel 2:28). They must not begin their mission in their own strength. They must wait.

In a sentence. After his suffering Jesus showed himself alive to them with many convincing proofs, appearing over forty days and speaking about the kingdom of God, and told them to stay in Jerusalem and wait for the Father’s promise, which they had heard from him.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection is not wishful thinking; it is backed by many proofs. And before you act, wait on God.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days recalls other periods of preparation in Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.
verseByVerse.commentary:
for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.

For John baptized with water. John the Baptist himself made this contrast (Luke 3:16). His baptism was outward, a sign of repentance.

But you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now. Key words. “Baptized” means immersed, drenched, overwhelmed. They will be plunged into the life of the Spirit. “Not many days”: ten days later, at Pentecost.

Where Christians differ: Spirit baptism. Pentecostal teaching holds that Spirit baptism is a second blessing after conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues, and that every believer should seek it. Verdict: Pentecost was a unique, unrepeatable event in the history of salvation: the Spirit poured out on the church once for all, as the cross and resurrection happened once for all. For believers since, Spirit baptism happens at conversion: all believers have been baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). We are to be filled with the Spirit continually (Ephesians 5:18), but there is no second-class Christian waiting for a second baptism.

In a sentence. John baptised with water, but in a few days they would be baptised with the Holy Spirit.

For worship. If you are in Christ, you have been immersed in the Spirit. Ask him to fill you afresh today.

verseByVerse.quote: So when they had come together, they asked him, "Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?" He said to them, "It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority."
verseByVerse.commentary:
So when they had come together, they asked him, “Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel?” He said to them, “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority.

Lord, will you at this time restore the kingdom to Israel? Setting and background. Many expected the Messiah to restore Israel’s political independence, driving out the Romans and re-establishing David’s kingdom (Luke 24:21). After forty days of teaching, the disciples still think in those terms.

It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has fixed by his own authority. Key words. Jesus doesn’t say the question is foolish, but that the timing is the Father’s secret (Mark 13:32). “Times” (chronous, durations) and “seasons” (kairous, the right moments). Date-setting for the end is forbidden ground.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom and Israel. Dispensationalists read this to mean that a political kingdom will be restored to national Israel in a future millennium, and that Jesus only postponed it. Verdict: Jesus redirects their question from a political kingdom to a worldwide mission (v. 8). The kingdom is restored to Israel as the Messiah reigns from heaven (2:30–36) and gathers a renewed Israel of Jewish and Gentile believers (15:16–17; Galatians 6:16). The Old Testament promises are fulfilled in Christ and his church, and will be completed in the new creation. This is the amillennial view. Paul still hopes for a great turning of the Jewish people to Christ (Romans 11:25–26), and that hope remains.

In a sentence. When they asked if he would now restore the kingdom to Israel, Jesus said it was not for them to know the times and seasons that the Father had set by his own authority.

On a Tuesday. Don’t waste your energy on calculating the end. Spend it on the mission.
verseByVerse.note: Many expected the Messiah to restore Israel’s political independence.

verseByVerse.quote: But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.

But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. Key words. “Power” (dynamis): ability, strength. Not political power but spiritual power, for witness. The Spirit is not given for private experience but for mission.

And you will be my witnesses. A witness tells what he has seen and heard (4:20). The apostles were eyewitnesses of the risen Christ (v. 22). Every believer bears witness to what Christ has done.

In Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth. This verse outlines the book: Jerusalem (chs 1–7), Judea and Samaria (chs 8–12), and the ends of the earth (chs 13–28), ending in Rome, the centre of the world. Samaria, the despised half-breed region, is included. And “the end of the earth” echoes Isaiah 49:6: I will make you a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.

In a sentence. Jesus promised that they would receive power when the Holy Spirit came on them, and would be his witnesses in Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth.

For worship. The Spirit’s power is given for witness. Where is your Jerusalem? Start there.
verseByVerse.note: This verse outlines the book: Jerusalem (chs 1–7), Judea and Samaria (8–12), and the end of the earth (13–28).

parallels.desc: my salvation to the end of the earth

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes,
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when he had said these things, as they were looking on, he was lifted up, and a cloud took him out of their sight. And while they were gazing into heaven as he went, behold, two men stood by them in white robes,

As they were looking on, he was lifted up. Key words. The ascension. A real, bodily event, witnessed by the disciples. Jesus ascended in his resurrected human body, which he still has. It marks his exaltation to the right hand of the Father, where he reigns over all things (2:33; Ephesians 1:20–22) and intercedes for his people (Hebrews 7:25).

And a cloud took him out of their sight. The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s glorious presence: the pillar of cloud in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21), the cloud on Sinai (Exodus 19:16), the cloud that filled the temple (1 Kings 8:10–11), the cloud at the transfiguration (Luke 9:34–35). And Daniel’s Son of Man comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:13). The cloud is not a means of transport, but a sign that he has entered the glory of God.

Two men stood by them in white robes. Angels, as at the tomb (Luke 24:4).

What it does not mean. It does not mean that heaven is a place somewhere above the sky, as if Jesus flew upward through space. The ascension is the visible sign of his passing into God’s presence, into a dimension beyond ours.

In a sentence. After saying this, Jesus was taken up while they watched, and a cloud hid him from their sight, and as they stared into the sky, two men in white stood beside them.

For worship. Christ has ascended. Our Saviour reigns in glory, in our human nature, at the Father’s right hand.
verseByVerse.note: The cloud recalls the cloud of God’s glorious presence.

parallels.desc: two men in dazzling apparel

verseByVerse.quote: and said, "Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
and said, “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven.”

Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? A gentle rebuke. There is work to do.

This Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven. “This Jesus”: the same Jesus, personally. Not some other figure.

Will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven. Key words. The promise of the second coming. Personally, bodily, visibly, with the clouds (Matthew 24:30; Revelation 1:7). Not secretly, not spiritually, but publicly.

Where Christians differ: a secret rapture? Some teach that Christ will return secretly to remove believers before a tribulation, then visibly later. Verdict: the angels promise one return, in the same way he went: visible and bodily. The New Testament knows one second coming, at which believers are gathered, the dead raised, and the world judged (1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 2 Thessalonians 1:7–10). No secret rapture.

In a sentence. The angels asked the men of Galilee why they stood looking into heaven, for this same Jesus would come back in the same way they had seen him go.

On a Tuesday. Don’t stand gazing at the sky. He is coming back. Get on with his work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — The Waiting Church and the Reconstituted Twelve
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The apostles returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, about a kilometre away, and went to the upstairs room where they were staying: Peter, John, James, Andrew, Philip, Thomas, Bartholomew, Matthew, James son of Alphaeus, Simon the Zealot and Judas son of James. They all devoted themselves to prayer together, with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among about a hundred and twenty believers. He said that the Scripture the Holy Spirit spoke through David had to be fulfilled concerning Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus, though he had been one of them and shared in their ministry. Judas had bought a field with the money from his wickedness, and there he fell headlong, burst open and died; everyone in Jerusalem heard of it, and the field became known as Akeldama, Field of Blood. The Psalms say his place should be deserted and someone else should take his office. So one of the men who had been with them throughout Jesus’ ministry, from John’s baptism to the ascension, must become a witness with them to the resurrection. They proposed Joseph called Barsabbas, also known as Justus, and Matthias. They prayed that the Lord, who knows every heart, would show which one he had chosen, then cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, who was added to the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Apostolic College and Its Significance

The reconstitution of the Twelve before Pentecost is deliberate. The Twelve answer to the twelve tribes and represent the reconstituted people of God (Matthew 19:28; Luke 22:30); an incomplete Twelve would be a broken sign at the moment the sign was about to be needed. The qualifications Peter states (v. 22) mark the apostolic circle as a closed and historically anchored group — the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and foundations are laid once. The New Testament does use apostle more widely of sent ones and church messengers, but no one alive can meet the terms stated here, which is why the church has no further foundational word to wait for. Judas, meanwhile, stands as the sober warning at the door of the book: he was numbered among them, sent out with them, and trusted with the money, and nearness to Jesus did not save him.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A hundred and twenty people with no money, no standing and no strategy prayed together for ten days, settled a painful question from Scripture rather than by argument, and appointed a man who is never mentioned again.

Now: The church's preparation for anything God intends to do has not changed shape: gathered, praying, working from the text, willing to be led, and made up very largely of people whose names will appear nowhere. Barsabbas, qualified and passed over in front of everyone, was, so far as we know, still among them when the Spirit fell.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day's journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then they returned to Jerusalem from the mount called Olivet, which is near Jerusalem, a Sabbath day’s journey away. And when they had entered, they went up to the upper room, where they were staying, Peter and John and James and Andrew, Philip and Thomas, Bartholomew and Matthew, James the son of Alphaeus and Simon the Zealot and Judas the son of James.

From the mount called Olivet. The Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem. Luke 24:50 says near Bethany, on its eastern slope. Zechariah 14:4 foretold the Lord standing on the Mount of Olives on the day of the Lord.

A Sabbath day’s journey away. A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance the traditions allowed a person to walk on the Sabbath: 2,000 cubits, about two-thirds of a mile, or a kilometre. Based on the distance between the ark and the people in Joshua 3:4.

They went up to the upper room, where they were staying. Perhaps the room of the Last Supper, or the house of Mary, mother of John Mark (12:12).

Peter and John and James and Andrew... The list of the eleven, matching Luke 6:14–16, minus Judas Iscariot. Simon “the Zealot”: once perhaps a member of the nationalist movement against Rome. Matthew, a former tax collector for Rome, beside him. Christ unites opposites.

In a sentence. They returned to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, a short walk away, and went up to the upper room where the eleven apostles were staying.

For worship. Christ made one company of very different men. He still does.
verseByVerse.note: A Sabbath day’s journey was the distance the traditions allowed on the Sabbath, a little over half a mile. The list of eleven matches the Gospels’ lists; Judas the son of James is probably Thaddaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said,
verseByVerse.commentary:
All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer, together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers. In those days Peter stood up among the brothers (the company of persons was in all about 120) and said,

All these with one accord were devoting themselves to prayer. Key words. “With one accord” (homothymadon): one mind, one purpose, a favourite word of Luke’s (2:46; 4:24; 5:12). “Devoting themselves” (proskarterountes): persisting, holding fast. The church was born in persistent, united prayer. Waiting for the Spirit was not passive.

Together with the women. Probably the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee and witnessed the resurrection (Luke 8:2–3; 24:10).

And Mary the mother of Jesus. Her last mention in Scripture. She is among the believers, praying with them. Not above them, not prayed to, but one of the church, in need of the Spirit like all the rest.

And his brothers. Jesus’ brothers, who had not believed during his ministry (John 7:5), are now among the disciples. The risen Christ had appeared to James (1 Corinthians 15:7). James later led the church in Jerusalem (15:13).

The company of persons was in all about 120. A small beginning. Ten times twelve, perhaps a hint of a renewed Israel.

In a sentence. They all prayed together constantly, with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus and his brothers, and one day Peter stood up among the believers, about 120 of them, and said...

On a Tuesday. Great movements of God begin in prayer meetings. Join one.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ brothers, who had not believed during his ministry, are now among the believers.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry.

Brothers, the Scripture had to be fulfilled. “Had to” (edei): it was necessary. Even Judas’s betrayal was foretold. God was not surprised.

Which the Holy Spirit spoke beforehand by the mouth of David. Key words. A clear statement of inspiration. The Holy Spirit spoke; David was his mouthpiece. Scripture has a divine author and a human author (2 Peter 1:21; 2 Timothy 3:16).

Concerning Judas, who became a guide to those who arrested Jesus. Peter states the facts plainly.

For he was numbered among us and was allotted his share in this ministry. Judas was a real apostle, outwardly. He shared their ministry. Yet he was never truly Christ’s (John 6:70; 17:12). A sobering reminder that office and outward service are not proof of salvation (Matthew 7:22–23).

In a sentence. Peter said Scripture had to be fulfilled, which the Holy Spirit spoke through David about Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus, though he had been one of them and shared their ministry.

On a Tuesday. Having a share in ministry is not the same as belonging to Christ. Examine yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: (Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
(Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness, and falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. And it became known to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so that the field was called in their own language Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood.)

Now this man acquired a field with the reward of his wickedness. Luke’s note in brackets. Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought the field with his returned money (Matthew 27:3–8). The accounts fit together: the priests bought the field with Judas’s money, so in effect he acquired it; and when he hanged himself, perhaps the rope or branch broke, or his body was later cut down after decay had set in, and fell.

Falling headlong he burst open in the middle and all his bowels gushed out. A grim end. Luke the doctor gives the medical detail.

Akeldama, that is, Field of Blood. Aramaic, the local language. “Blood” because it was bought with blood money, and because of Judas’s bloody death. The site is traditionally placed in the Hinnom Valley south of Jerusalem, the valley that gave its name to Gehenna.

In a sentence. Judas bought a field with his wicked reward, and falling headlong burst open, and all Jerusalem heard, so the field was called Akeldama, Field of Blood.

For worship. Sin pays wages, and they are terrible. Thank God for Christ, who took our wages.
verseByVerse.note: Matthew says Judas hanged himself and the priests bought the field; the two accounts are often harmonised as a hanging followed by a fall. Akeldama is Aramaic.

verseByVerse.quote: "For it is written in the Book of Psalms, 'May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it'; and 'Let another take his office.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For it is written in the Book of Psalms, ‘May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it’; and ‘Let another take his office.’

May his camp become desolate, and let there be no one to dwell in it. From Psalm 69:25. Psalm 69 is a lament of the righteous sufferer, often applied to Jesus in the New Testament (John 2:17; 15:25; Romans 15:3). If the righteous sufferer is Christ, his chief enemy is Judas. The psalm’s curse on the persecutor fits him. “Camp” (epaulis): homestead, dwelling. The ESV here translates the Greek of Acts.

Let another take his office. From Psalm 109:8, another psalm against a treacherous friend. “Office” (episkopē): oversight, the position. The word later used for an overseer, or bishop. Judas’s place must be filled.

How Peter reads the Psalms. He reads David’s psalms as speaking ultimately of Christ, David’s greater son, and his enemies. This is how Jesus taught them to read (Luke 24:44). The psalms of the righteous king find their fullest meaning in the true King.

In a sentence. Peter quoted the Psalms: let his dwelling be desolate with no one living there, and let another take his office.

On a Tuesday. Read the Psalms with Christ in view. They speak of him.

parallels.desc: may their camp be a desolation
may another take his office

verseByVerse.quote: So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us — one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.
verseByVerse.commentary:
So one of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us, beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us — one of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection.

One of the men who have accompanied us during all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us. Key words. The qualifications of an apostle: he must have been with Jesus throughout his ministry, from John’s baptism to the ascension, an eyewitness of all.

Beginning from the baptism of John until the day when he was taken up from us. The span of the Gospel story.

One of these men must become with us a witness to his resurrection. Above all, an apostle was a witness to the risen Christ (1 Corinthians 9:1). The heart of their message was the resurrection.

Where Christians differ: apostolic succession. Roman Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican teaching hold that bishops today are successors of the apostles, with their authority passed down. Verdict: by these qualifications, no one after the first generation could be an apostle in this sense. Paul was the exception, as one who saw the risen Lord, “as to one untimely born” (1 Corinthians 15:8). The apostles laid the foundation of the church (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Their authority continues today not in successors but in their writings, the New Testament. When James was killed (12:2), no replacement was chosen.

In a sentence. Peter said that one of the men who had been with them all the time Jesus was among them, from John’s baptism to the ascension, must become with them a witness to his resurrection.

For worship. The apostles’ witness to the risen Christ is the foundation you stand on. It is written in the New Testament for you.

verseByVerse.quote: And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they put forward two, Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus, and Matthias.

And they put forward two. The church does its part, choosing qualified candidates.

Joseph called Barsabbas, who was also called Justus. Three names: Joseph his Hebrew name, Barsabbas (son of the Sabbath, or son of Sabba) his family name, Justus his Latin name. Many Jews had Latin or Greek names too. He was not chosen, and we hear no more of him, but he was a faithful disciple. Tradition says nothing reliable. Not being chosen for office is not failure.

And Matthias. Nothing more is known of him in Scripture.

In a sentence. They nominated two men, Joseph called Barsabbas, also named Justus, and Matthias.

On a Tuesday. Joseph Barsabbas was faithful and passed over, and he is remembered here. God sees the unchosen and the unknown.

parallels.desc: Judas called Barsabbas

verseByVerse.quote: And they prayed and said, "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they prayed and said, “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which one of these two you have chosen to take the place in this ministry and apostleship from which Judas turned aside to go to his own place.”

You, Lord, who know the hearts of all. Key words. “Lord” here probably means Jesus, who chose the apostles (v. 2). He knows hearts (John 2:24–25), a divine attribute (1 Samuel 16:7; Jeremiah 17:10). The first recorded prayer of the church is addressed to the risen Jesus.

Show which one of these two you have chosen. Not “help us choose,” but “show us whom you have already chosen.” Apostles are chosen by Christ.

To take the place in this ministry and apostleship. Literally “to take the place” (topon) in the ministry.

From which Judas turned aside to go to his own place. A different “place.” Judas left his place among the apostles to go to his own place: a solemn way of speaking of his eternal destiny. He went where he belonged.

In a sentence. They prayed to the Lord who knows every heart to show which of the two he had chosen for the apostolic ministry that Judas abandoned to go to his own place.

For worship. The Lord knows every heart, including yours. Pray to him with honesty.

parallels.desc: God, who knows the heart

verseByVerse.quote: And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they cast lots for them, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles.

And they cast lots for them. Setting and background. Casting lots left the choice to God; it is not mentioned again after Pentecost. Stones marked with names were shaken in a container until one fell out. The Old Testament used lots to discern God’s will, for example in dividing the land (Joshua 18:6) and in the Urim and Thummim. Proverbs 16:33: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the Lord.

And the lot fell on Matthias, and he was numbered with the eleven apostles. The Twelve are restored, symbolising the renewed Israel (Luke 22:30), ready for Pentecost.

Where Christians differ: should we cast lots today? Some say the apostles were wrong to do this, and should have waited for Paul. Others use lots or similar methods for guidance today. Verdict: Luke records no disapproval, and the choice was valid. But after Pentecost, the church never cast lots again. With the Spirit given and the Scriptures complete, God guides his people through his word, prayer, wise counsel and the judgment of the church (15:28; Romans 12:2). We don’t need dice.

In a sentence. They cast lots, and the lot fell on Matthias, and he was added to the eleven apostles.

On a Tuesday. God’s guidance is not a lottery for you. Seek it in his word, in prayer, and with wise counsel.
verseByVerse.note: Casting lots left the choice to God; it is not mentioned again after the Spirit is given.

parallels.desc: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD

1.theology: The Ascension and the Reign of Christ. The ascension is the most neglected event in the Christian calendar — and one of the most theologically freighted. It is not simply that Jesus left; it is that he was enthroned. Psalm 110:1 — “The Lord says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool” — is the most-quoted Old Testament text in the New Testament. The early church was obsessed with it because it explained everything: Christ reigns now, at the Father’s right hand, over all things, for his church (Ephesians 1:20–23). He is not waiting to begin his kingdom; his kingdom is already here, hidden but real, advancing through the witness of the Spirit-filled church. Every prayer prayed in his name, every sermon preached, every soul converted is an act of the reigning Christ extending his dominion.
1.examples:
Then: The disciples in Jerusalem, staring at the sky, confused about timing and kingdom, learning that faithfulness in the interval between the ascension and the return looks like prayer and witness. They had no map, no strategy document, no budget — only a promise and an upper room.

Now: We live in the same interval — between the first coming and the second, between the already and the not-yet. The temptation is still to stand looking into heaven, obsessing over the date of the return, while the mission sits unfinished at our feet. The command is unchanged: wait in prayer, go in the Spirit, witness to the ends of the earth. He is coming. In the meantime, there is work.

2.title: The Spirit Poured Out
2.text: <sup>1</sup>When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. <sup>2</sup>And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting. <sup>3</sup>And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. <sup>4</sup>And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. <sup>5</sup>Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. <sup>6</sup>And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language. <sup>7</sup>And they were amazed and astonished, saying, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? <sup>8</sup>And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language? <sup>9</sup>Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, <sup>10</sup>Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome, <sup>11</sup>both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians—we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.” <sup>12</sup>And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?” <sup>13</sup>But others mocking said, “They are filled with new wine.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. <sup>15</sup>For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. <sup>16</sup>But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel: <sup>17</sup>‘And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; <sup>18</sup>even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy. <sup>19</sup>And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; <sup>20</sup>the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day. <sup>21</sup>And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.’ <sup>22</sup>“Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know— <sup>23</sup>this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. <sup>24</sup>God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. <sup>25</sup>For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; <sup>26</sup>therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope. <sup>27</sup>For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. <sup>28</sup>You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.’ <sup>29</sup>“Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. <sup>30</sup>Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne, <sup>31</sup>he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. <sup>32</sup>This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses. <sup>33</sup>Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. <sup>34</sup>For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, <sup>35</sup>until I make your enemies your footstool.’ <sup>36</sup>Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.” <sup>37</sup>Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” <sup>38</sup>And Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. <sup>39</sup>For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.” <sup>40</sup>And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” <sup>41</sup>So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls. <sup>42</sup>And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers. <sup>43</sup>And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. <sup>44</sup>And all who believed were together and had all things in common. <sup>45</sup>And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need. <sup>46</sup>And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, <sup>47</sup>praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
2.overview:
Pentecost (Greek for “fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, when Israel thanked God for the wheat harvest by offering the first loaves of the new crop (Leviticus 23:15–21). By New Testament times some Jews also linked it with the giving of the law at Sinai, which Exodus places in the third month after the exodus. Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims from across the Jewish world. On that day, ten days after the ascension, the Spirit came as Jesus promised: a sound like a rushing wind, flames resting on each believer, and the disciples speaking in the languages of the pilgrims, so that people from Parthia to Rome heard God’s mighty works in their own native tongues. At Babel, God confused human languages to scatter proud rebels; now he speaks in every language to gather a people for himself.

Some mocked, saying the disciples were drunk. Peter stood and preached the first Christian sermon. This, he said, is what Joel promised for the last days: the Spirit poured out on all kinds of people, and salvation for everyone who calls on the Lord’s name. Then he proclaimed Jesus: attested by miracles, handed over by God’s plan and killed by them through lawless men, but raised by God, as David foresaw in Psalm 16. Exalted to God’s right hand, Jesus has poured out the Spirit, and God has made him both Lord and Christ. Cut to the heart, the crowd asked what to do. Repent and be baptised in Jesus’ name, Peter said, and you will receive forgiveness and the gift of the Spirit. About three thousand did. The chapter ends with a portrait of the new community: devoted to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer, sharing generously, meeting in the temple and in homes, praising God, and growing daily as the Lord added to their number.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — The Coming of the Spirit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the day of Pentecost the believers were all together in one place. Suddenly a sound like a violent wind came from heaven and filled the house where they were sitting. They saw what looked like tongues of fire that separated and settled on each of them, and all of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit enabled them. Devout Jews from every nation were staying in Jerusalem, and when they heard the sound a crowd gathered, bewildered, because each one heard the believers speaking in his own language. Amazed, they asked how these Galileans could be speaking in their native languages: Parthians, Medes, Elamites, people from Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya near Cyrene, visitors from Rome, Jews and converts to Judaism, Cretans and Arabs. All heard God’s wonderful works declared in their own tongues. Amazed and perplexed, they asked what it meant, while others mocked and said the believers had drunk too much wine.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit and the Age He Opens

The Old Testament had promised a day when God would put his Spirit not on a handful of officeholders but on his whole people — Joel 2, Ezekiel 36–37 and Jeremiah 31 all say it, and Moses had wished for it out loud some fourteen centuries earlier (Numbers 11:29). Pentecost is that day arriving. This governs how the event should be read. The Spirit's coming is not a private enrichment handed to a hundred and twenty people who happened to pray hard enough; it is a public, datable, once-for-all act in the history of salvation, standing alongside the birth, the cross and the empty tomb. Christ was born once, died once, rose once, and poured out his Spirit once. What is repeated afterwards is not the outpouring but the filling — and Luke will use that second word again of Peter and the company (4:8, 4:31), and later of Paul (13:9), which is a mercy, because it means what happened to them is not sealed inside one morning in the first century.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Parthians, Medes, Elamites, residents of Mesopotamia — the first four names on Luke's list are exile addresses. Assyria deported the northern tribes and placed them in Halah, and on the Habor, the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes (2 Kings 17:6), and seven centuries later the descendants of the deported are standing in a Jerusalem street hearing the mighty works of God in the language of the country their forefathers were carried off to. Now: The same thing happens every time the Bible is put into a language that has never had it. The God who gave the church its first sermon in fifteen languages at once has never shown the slightest interest in making anyone learn a holy one first.

verseByVerse.quote: When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the day of Pentecost arrived, they were all together in one place. And suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind, and it filled the entire house where they were sitting.

Meaning first. Acts 2 is the birthday of the church as the Spirit-filled people of the new covenant. The risen and exalted Christ pours out the Holy Spirit, as promised. The disciples speak in languages they never learned, Peter preaches the first Christian sermon, three thousand believe and are baptised, and a new community is formed. Pentecost is a once-for-all event in the history of salvation, like the cross and the resurrection: the Spirit comes to dwell in God’s people for ever.

When the day of Pentecost arrived. Setting and background. Pentecost (“fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover (Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12). It was a harvest festival, when the first fruits of the wheat harvest were offered. Later Jewish tradition linked it with the giving of the law at Sinai. Now the first fruits of the gospel harvest are gathered, and the Spirit writes the law on hearts (Jeremiah 31:33; 2 Corinthians 3:3). Jews from across the world were in Jerusalem for it.

They were all together in one place. Probably the 120 (1:15), perhaps in the upper room, or in the temple courts.

Suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind. Key words. Not wind, but a sound “like” wind. In both Hebrew (ruach) and Greek (pneuma), the same word means wind, breath and spirit. Jesus compared the Spirit to the wind (John 3:8). Ezekiel saw the wind breathe life into dry bones (Ezekiel 37:9–14). “From heaven”: the Spirit comes from the exalted Christ (v. 33).

And it filled the entire house where they were sitting. As the glory cloud filled the tabernacle and the temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:10–11). God’s presence fills his new temple, his people.

In a sentence. On the day of Pentecost, when they were all together, a sound like a violent wind suddenly came from heaven and filled the whole house where they were sitting.

For worship. The wind of the Spirit came from heaven, and it still blows where it wills. Pray for him to fill your church.
verseByVerse.note: Pentecost (“fiftieth”) was the Feast of Weeks, fifty days after Passover, celebrating the wheat harvest. Wind and breath picture the Spirit.

parallels.desc: the Feast of Weeks

verseByVerse.quote: And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And divided tongues as of fire appeared to them and rested on each one of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.

Divided tongues as of fire appeared to them. Key words. Fire often signals God’s presence: the burning bush (Exodus 3:2), the fire on Sinai (Exodus 19:18), the pillar of fire. John the Baptist promised that Jesus would baptise with the Spirit and fire (Luke 3:16). The fire is “as of” fire, like fire, in the shape of tongues. Tongues for speaking.

And rested on each one of them. Not one great flame on the group, but one on each. Every believer receives the Spirit (v. 38). In the old covenant, the Spirit rested on chosen individuals: prophets, kings, judges. Now on all God’s people. Moses’ wish is fulfilled: would that all the Lord’s people were prophets (Numbers 11:29).

And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit. “Filled”: controlled, empowered. Luke uses it often for being empowered to speak (4:8, 31; 13:9).

And began to speak in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance. Key words. “Other tongues” (heterais glōssais): other languages. Verses 6–11 make clear these were real human languages, understood by the hearers, not ecstatic speech. The reversal of Babel (Genesis 11:1–9): there, God confused languages and scattered people in judgment; here, he gives languages to gather the nations in grace.

Where Christians differ: tongues today. Pentecostals and charismatics teach that tongues continue today, often as a prayer language, and some that it is the sign of Spirit baptism. Verdict: the tongues of Pentecost were known languages, a sign that the gospel was for every nation. Tongues and other sign gifts served to confirm the apostolic message in the founding era (Hebrews 2:3–4; 1 Corinthians 14:22), and the church’s historic testimony is that they ceased. This is the cessationist position, held charitably: we gladly acknowledge that many charismatic believers love Christ deeply. The Spirit himself, and his saving and sanctifying work, continue in full.

In a sentence. Tongues like fire appeared and rested on each of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages as the Spirit enabled them.

On a Tuesday. The Spirit gives speech for Christ. Ask him to fill your mouth with the gospel today.
verseByVerse.note: Fire often signals God’s presence.

parallels.desc: the LORD descended on it in fire

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And at this sound the multitude came together, and they were bewildered, because each one was hearing them speak in his own language.

Now there were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. Setting and background. Many Jews born abroad settled in Jerusalem, and huge numbers came for the pilgrim feasts. The Jewish population outside Israel, the Dispersion, may have numbered several million across the Roman and Parthian empires. “Devout” (eulabeis): God-fearing, pious.

At this sound the multitude came together. The sound drew a crowd.

Because each one was hearing them speak in his own language. “Language” (dialektos): native dialect. A miracle of speaking, not of hearing: the disciples spoke the languages.

In a sentence. Devout Jews from every nation were living in Jerusalem, and when they heard the sound, a crowd gathered, bewildered because each heard the disciples speaking his own language.

For worship. From the first day, the gospel spoke every language. God wants worshippers from every tongue (Revelation 7:9).
verseByVerse.note: Many Jews born abroad settled in Jerusalem, and huge numbers came as pilgrims for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were amazed and astonished, saying, "Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were amazed and astonished, saying, “Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? And how is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language?”

Are not all these who are speaking Galileans? Galileans spoke with a recognisable accent (Matthew 26:73). Northern country people, not educated linguists. That makes it all the more astonishing.

How is it that we hear, each of us in his own native language? “Native language”: literally, the language in which we were born. Most of them would have understood Greek or Aramaic, but they hear the gospel in their mother tongue, the language of the heart. God speaks to people in their own language. This is the root of the long Christian work of Bible translation.

In a sentence. Amazed, they asked how these Galileans could be speaking, so that each heard in his own native language.

On a Tuesday. Support Bible translation. Every people deserves to hear God’s word in its heart language.
verseByVerse.note: Galileans spoke with a recognisable accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia, Judea and Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia, Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene, and visitors from Rome,

Parthians and Medes and Elamites and residents of Mesopotamia. The list runs roughly from east (Parthia, beyond the Euphrates, in modern Iran) to west (Rome). Parthia, Media and Elam were east of the Roman empire, where Jews had lived since the exile to Babylon. Mesopotamia, between the rivers, was ancient Babylon.

Judea. Perhaps meaning greater Judea, from Egypt to the Euphrates. Or Luke includes it to say that even the locals heard their own speech.

Cappadocia, Pontus and Asia, Phrygia and Pamphylia. Regions of Asia Minor, modern Turkey. Peter later writes to Christians in Pontus, Cappadocia and Asia (1 Peter 1:1). Some of them may have been converted here.

Egypt and the parts of Libya belonging to Cyrene. North Africa. Alexandria in Egypt had a huge Jewish community. Simon who carried Jesus’ cross was from Cyrene (Luke 23:26).

And visitors from Rome. Perhaps the beginnings of the church in Rome, to which Paul later wrote.

In a sentence. They came from Parthia, Media, Elam, Mesopotamia, Judea, Cappadocia, Pontus, Asia, Phrygia, Pamphylia, Egypt, Libya near Cyrene, and Rome.

For worship. The nations of the known world heard the gospel on the church’s first day. Pray for the nations today.
verseByVerse.note: The list runs roughly from east (Parthia, beyond the Euphrates) to west (Rome): the whole Jewish world scattered among the nations.

parallels.desc: the table of nations
Babel, where languages were confused

verseByVerse.quote: both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians — we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
both Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabians — we hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God.

Both Jews and proselytes. Proselytes were Gentiles who had converted to Judaism, being circumcised, baptised and offering sacrifice. So even on this day, Gentile-born believers in Israel’s God were present.

Cretans and Arabians. Island and desert, west and east. Paul later worked in Crete (Titus 1:5) and went to Arabia (Galatians 1:17).

We hear them telling in our own tongues the mighty works of God. Key words. The content of the tongues: “the mighty works of God” (ta megaleia), the great things God has done, above all in Christ. Tongues were not gibberish but praise and proclamation.

In a sentence. Jews and proselytes, Cretans and Arabs, all heard them telling in their own languages the mighty works of God.

On a Tuesday. Tell someone today, in plain words, the mighty works of God.
verseByVerse.note: Proselytes were Gentiles who had converted to Judaism.

parallels.desc: Nicolaus, a proselyte of Antioch

verseByVerse.quote: And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, "What does this mean?" But others mocking said, "They are filled with new wine."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all were amazed and perplexed, saying to one another, “What does this mean?” But others mocking said, “They are filled with new wine.”

What does this mean? The right question. Peter will answer it.

But others mocking said, “They are filled with new wine.” “New wine” (gleukous): sweet wine. Perhaps those who heard only languages they didn’t understand thought it was drunken babble. Paul later warns that tongues without interpretation make outsiders think believers mad (1 Corinthians 14:23). As always, God’s work divides: some wonder, some mock.

In a sentence. All were amazed and asked what this meant, but some mocked that they were drunk on new wine.

For worship. Some will always mock God’s work. Let it not stop you asking, “What does this mean?”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–36 — Peter's Sermon: The Risen Christ Proclaimed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Peter stood up with the Eleven and addressed the crowd. These men are not drunk, he said; it is only nine in the morning. This is what the prophet Joel foretold: in the last days God will pour out his Spirit on all people; sons and daughters will prophesy, young men see visions and old men dream dreams, and even slaves, men and women, will receive the Spirit and prophesy. There will be wonders above and signs below, blood, fire and smoke; the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood before the great day of the Lord. And everyone who calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. Peter then spoke of Jesus of Nazareth, whom God had clearly approved by miracles, wonders and signs done among them, as they knew. This man was handed over according to God’s settled plan and foreknowledge, and they killed him by having lawless men nail him to a cross. But God raised him, freeing him from death’s agony, because death could not keep its hold on him.
verseByVerse.theology:
How Peter Reads the Psalms

Peter's argument from Psalm 16 is not proof-texting; it is a method, and he shows his working. David wrote you will not let your Holy One see corruption. David died, was buried, and his tomb was a landmark a short walk from where Peter was standing. Therefore the words say more than David's own life could pay, and they are prophecy — and the man they fit is the one whose tomb is empty. He does the same with Psalm 110: David did not ascend into the heavens, so the psalm in which David hears the LORD speak to my Lord must be about somebody else. This is the way the risen Christ himself had taught them to read on the road to Emmaus, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets (Luke 24:27, 44). The Reformed tradition has taken this sermon as the pattern for reading the whole Old Testament — not squeezing Christ out of texts that will not hold him, but recognising that the Scriptures were written by a Spirit who knew where the story was going and left the shape of it in the words.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who were personally implicated — this Jesus whom you crucified — and he said it to their faces in the seventh week after they had done it. He did not soften the charge in order to get a hearing, and three thousand of them were baptised before dark. Now: A gospel that never implicates the hearer never has anything to forgive him for. The reason this crowd asked what shall we do is that Peter had left them with something that needed doing. Preaching which manages to be about sin in general, committed by people in general, will produce interest, and will not produce that question.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: "Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter, standing with the eleven, lifted up his voice and addressed them: “Men of Judea and all who dwell in Jerusalem, let this be known to you, and give ear to my words. For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day.

But Peter, standing with the eleven. Key words. The man who denied Jesus to a servant girl seven weeks earlier now stands before thousands. The Spirit has made the difference. The eleven stand with him: one voice for the twelve.

Lifted up his voice and addressed them. “Addressed” (apephthenxato): spoke out boldly, as one inspired (the same word as “utterance” in v. 4).

For these people are not drunk, as you suppose, since it is only the third hour of the day. The ESV notes that the third hour was about 9 a.m., far too early for drunkenness. Devout Jews would not eat or drink before the morning prayer on a feast day.

In a sentence. Peter stood with the eleven and spoke to the crowd, telling them to listen, for these people were not drunk, since it was only nine in the morning.

For worship. The Spirit makes cowards bold. If you’re timid about Christ, ask him to fill you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour was about 9 a.m. — far too early for drunkenness.

parallels.desc: do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit

verseByVerse.quote: "But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel:

But this is what was uttered through the prophet Joel. Key words. “This is that.” Peter explains the present by the Scripture. Pentecost is not a strange new thing, but the fulfilment of what God promised through Joel, about 400 years earlier or more. The Spirit’s work is always in line with Scripture.

In a sentence. Peter declared that this was what the prophet Joel had foretold.

On a Tuesday. Test every spiritual experience by Scripture. Peter’s first move was to open the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy."
verseByVerse.commentary:
‘And in the last days it shall be, God declares, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams; even on my male servants and female servants in those days I will pour out my Spirit, and they shall prophesy.

And in the last days it shall be. Key words. Joel 2:28 has “afterward”; Peter interprets it as “the last days.” The last days began with the coming of Christ and the Spirit (Hebrews 1:2; 1 Corinthians 10:11; 1 John 2:18). We live in the last days now, the age between Christ’s first and second comings.

I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh. “All flesh”: not every individual, but all kinds of people, without distinction. Young and old, men and women, slave and free. Not only prophets and kings, but all God’s people. And soon Gentiles too (10:45).

Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. In the Old Testament, prophecy was rare. Now the Spirit-given knowledge of God and the ability to speak his truth is spread among all believers. Prophecy here means speaking God’s word, declaring his mighty works (v. 11).

Your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams. Poetic parallelism: all will know God directly (Jeremiah 31:34).

Even on my male servants and female servants. Even slaves. No social barrier keeps anyone from the Spirit (Galatians 3:28).

Where Christians differ: prophecy today. Charismatic Christians see ongoing prophecy as new words from God. Verdict: Joel’s promise is fulfilled in the Spirit given to all believers, who all know God and declare his word. In the apostolic era this included revelatory prophecy, which laid the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20; 3:5). With the canon complete, the prophetic word continues in the Spirit-empowered proclamation of Scripture. Women as well as men proclaim God’s mighty works, while the office of elder and preaching in the gathered church belongs to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7).

In a sentence. Joel said that in the last days God would pour out his Spirit on all people: sons and daughters would prophesy, young men see visions, old men dream dreams, and even on slaves, men and women, he would pour out his Spirit.

For worship. You live in the last days, and the Spirit has been poured out on you. Speak of God’s mighty works.

parallels.desc: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh
would that all the LORD’s people were prophets!
Philip’s four daughters prophesied

verseByVerse.quote: "And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below, blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day.

I will show wonders in the heavens above and signs on the earth below. Peter adds “above,” “signs” and “below” to Joel’s words, linking them to the signs Jesus did (v. 22).

Blood, and fire, and vapor of smoke; the sun shall be turned to darkness and the moon to blood. Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God in history: the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:10), the fall of Egypt (Ezekiel 32:7). They describe the shaking of the world when God intervenes. Some of it may already have been fulfilled in the darkness at the crucifixion (Luke 23:44–45). The rest awaits the final day.

Before the day of the Lord comes, the great and magnificent day. The day of the Lord: the day of God’s judgment and salvation. With Christ’s first coming it has begun; with his return it will be complete. The whole age of the church lies between the outpouring of the Spirit and that great day.

In a sentence. God said he would show wonders in heaven and signs on earth, blood, fire and smoke, with the sun darkened and the moon turned to blood, before the great day of the Lord.

On a Tuesday. The day of the Lord is coming. Live today in the light of it.
verseByVerse.note: Prophets used cosmic images like these for great acts of God’s judgment.

parallels.desc: darkness at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it shall come to pass that everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.’

Everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved. Key words. The climax of the quotation and the point of Peter’s sermon. In Joel “the Lord” is the LORD, Yahweh; Peter applies the name to Jesus (v. 36). So does Paul (Romans 10:9–13). To call on Jesus is to call on Yahweh. The early church prayed to Jesus as God.

Everyone. The offer is wide open, to anyone, from any nation.

Calls upon. To call on the Lord’s name is to appeal to him, trusting him for rescue. It is faith expressed in prayer.

In a sentence. Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

For worship. Call on the name of the Lord Jesus. Everyone who does is saved.
verseByVerse.note: In Joel “the Lord” is the LORD; Peter applies the name to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Men of Israel, hear these words: Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God with mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know — this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men.

Jesus of Nazareth, a man attested to you by God. Peter starts with what they know. Jesus was a real man, and God showed his approval of him publicly.

With mighty works and wonders and signs that God did through him in your midst, as you yourselves know. No one denied the miracles. They were public knowledge.

This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God. Key words. The cross was not an accident or a tragedy that took God by surprise. It was God’s “definite plan” (hōrismenē boulē, fixed purpose) and “foreknowledge” (prognōsei). God planned it from eternity (4:27–28; 1 Peter 1:20; Revelation 13:8).

You crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. Lawless men are the Romans, who did not have God’s law. And yet: “you” crucified him. God’s plan does not cancel human guilt. They did it freely and wickedly; God planned it for good. Both stand together (Genesis 50:20). This is the clearest statement in Scripture of how divine sovereignty and human responsibility relate.
