What it does not mean. It does not mean that God forced anyone to sin, or that the Jews are uniquely guilty. All of us, by our sins, put Christ there. Gentiles (the Romans) and Jews together crucified him (4:27).

In a sentence. Peter told the men of Israel that Jesus of Nazareth was approved by God through miracles they knew of, and was handed over by God’s fixed plan and foreknowledge, and they killed him by nailing him to a cross through lawless men.

For worship. The worst sin in history was in God’s hands, and he used it for the greatest good. He is sovereign over your trials too.
verseByVerse.note: Lawless men are the Romans, who did not have God’s law.

verseByVerse.quote: "God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it.

God raised him up. Key words. The heart of the apostolic preaching. You killed him; God raised him. God reversed their verdict.

Loosing the pangs of death. “Pangs” (ōdinas): birth pains. Death is pictured as a woman in labour, unable to hold her child. Death had to give him up. The resurrection is a birth into new life (Colossians 1:18: firstborn from the dead).

Because it was not possible for him to be held by it. Why not possible? Because he is the sinless one, over whom death had no claim (John 14:30); because he is the author of life (3:15); because Scripture foretold it (vv. 25–28); because God’s plan required it.

In a sentence. God raised him, freeing him from the pains of death, because death could not keep its hold on him.

For worship. Death could not hold him, and in him it cannot hold you.

verseByVerse.quote: "For David says concerning him, 'I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For David says concerning him, ‘I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken; therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced; my flesh also will dwell in hope.

For David says concerning him. Psalm 16:8–11. Peter says David spoke “concerning him,” Christ.

I saw the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand that I may not be shaken. The speaker trusts God completely. Perfect communion with God, never shaken. True of David in part, but fully true only of Christ.

Therefore my heart was glad, and my tongue rejoiced. Joy in God.

My flesh also will dwell in hope. Even his body will rest in hope, in the grave.

In a sentence. David spoke of Christ when he said that he always saw the Lord before him at his right hand, so that he would not be shaken, and so his heart was glad and his body would rest in hope.

On a Tuesday. Set the Lord always before you. With him at your right hand, you will not be shaken.

parallels.desc: I have set the LORD always before me

verseByVerse.quote: "For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption. You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence.’

For you will not abandon my soul to Hades. Hades (Sheol) is the realm of the dead. Not hell, but the grave, the place of the dead. God would not leave him there.

Or let your Holy One see corruption. Key words. “Corruption” (diaphthoran): decay. His body would not rot in the grave. Jesus was raised on the third day, before decay could set in (compare Lazarus, John 11:39).

You have made known to me the paths of life; you will make me full of gladness with your presence. The path through death to life, and the joy of God’s presence. Fulfilled in Christ’s resurrection and ascension.

In a sentence. David continued that God would not leave his soul in the grave or let his Holy One decay, but had shown him the paths of life and would fill him with joy in his presence.

For worship. The path of life runs through Christ’s empty tomb. Walk it with joy.
verseByVerse.note: Hades (Sheol) is the realm of the dead.

parallels.desc: you will not let your holy one see corruption

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Brothers, I may say to you with confidence about the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. Being therefore a prophet, and knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne,

About the patriarch David that he both died and was buried, and his tomb is with us to this day. David’s tomb was a known landmark in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 3:16; Josephus mentions it). David’s body did see decay. So Psalm 16 can’t be fully about David.

Being therefore a prophet. Key words. David was a prophet, speaking by the Spirit (1:16; 2 Samuel 23:2).

And knowing that God had sworn with an oath to him that he would set one of his descendants on his throne. The covenant with David (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 132:11): God promised that David’s offspring would reign for ever. David knew that his greater son would come.

In a sentence. Peter said David died and was buried and his tomb is still there, but as a prophet he knew God had sworn to set one of his descendants on his throne.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his oaths. Every promise of his is yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).
verseByVerse.note: David’s tomb was a known landmark in Jerusalem.

parallels.desc: the LORD swore to David a sure oath

verseByVerse.quote: "he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
he foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ, that he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses.

He foresaw and spoke about the resurrection of the Christ. Key words. David looked ahead and wrote of the Messiah’s resurrection. Jesus taught the apostles to read the Old Testament this way (Luke 24:44–47).

That he was not abandoned to Hades, nor did his flesh see corruption. Fulfilled in Jesus.

This Jesus God raised up, and of that we all are witnesses. The apostles’ testimony: we saw him alive. Scripture foretold it; eyewitnesses confirm it.

In a sentence. David foresaw and spoke of the Christ’s resurrection, that he was not left in the grave and his body did not decay, and God raised this Jesus, as they all witnessed.

For worship. Scripture and eyewitnesses agree: Jesus is risen. Rest your faith on that rock.

verseByVerse.quote: "Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God, and having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,

Being therefore exalted at the right hand of God. Key words. The place of highest honour and power. The risen Jesus now reigns with the Father.

And having received from the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit. The Trinity in action: the Son receives the Spirit from the Father.

He has poured out this that you yourselves are seeing and hearing. The exalted Jesus pours out the Spirit. Pentecost is proof that Jesus is alive and reigning. Only God pours out God’s Spirit (Joel 2:28).

For David did not ascend into the heavens, but he himself says, “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand.” From Psalm 110:1, the Old Testament text most quoted in the New. Jesus used it himself (Luke 20:41–44). “The Lord” (Yahweh) said to “my Lord” (David’s Lord, the Messiah): sit at my right hand. David calls his own descendant his Lord. David didn’t ascend; Jesus did.

In a sentence. Peter said that Jesus, exalted to God’s right hand and receiving the promised Spirit from the Father, had poured out what they saw and heard, for David did not ascend to heaven, but said the Lord told his Lord to sit at his right hand.

For worship. The Spirit in you is the gift of the exalted Christ. He reigns, and he gives.

parallels.desc: “Sit at my right hand”

verseByVerse.quote: until I make your enemies your footstool.' Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
until I make your enemies your footstool.’ Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.

Until I make your enemies your footstool. The footstool picture: ancient kings put their feet on the necks of defeated enemies (Joshua 10:24). Christ reigns now, until every enemy is subdued, the last being death (1 Corinthians 15:25–26).

Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain. The conclusion of the sermon. “For certain” (asphalōs): beyond doubt. Luke wrote his Gospel so that Theophilus might have certainty (Luke 1:4, same root).

That God has made him both Lord and Christ. Key words. “Lord” was the title used in the Greek Old Testament for God, translating Yahweh. “Christ”: the Messiah, the anointed king. Not that Jesus became God at his exaltation, but that God has publicly installed him as Lord and Messiah, declared him so by raising him (Romans 1:4). The eternal Son, who humbled himself, is exalted in his human nature to the highest place (Philippians 2:9–11).

This Jesus whom you crucified. The sermon ends with a dagger. You crucified God’s Messiah, the Lord.

In a sentence. God will make his enemies his footstool, so all Israel should know for certain that God has made this Jesus, whom they crucified, both Lord and Christ.

For worship. Jesus is Lord and Christ. Bow to him now, before every enemy becomes his footstool.
verseByVerse.note: “Lord” was the title used in the Greek Old Testament for God’s name; “Christ” means the Messiah.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the people heard this, they were deeply moved and asked Peter and the other apostles what they should do. Peter replied that every one of them should repent and be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of their sins, and they would receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The promise is for them and their children and for all who are far off, as many as the Lord God will call. With many other words he warned them and pleaded with them to save themselves from this corrupt generation. Those who accepted his message were baptised, and about three thousand were added that day. They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. Everyone was filled with awe at the many wonders and signs the apostles performed. All the believers were together and shared everything; they sold property and possessions to give to anyone who had need. Every day they kept meeting together in the temple courts and broke bread in their homes, eating together with glad and sincere hearts, praising God and enjoying the favour of all the people. And the Lord added to their number daily those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Four Marks of the Apostolic Church

Verse 42 gives the church four practices, and each is named with its definite article: the apostles' teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, the prayers. These are not four vague virtues but four definite things a visitor to Jerusalem that summer could have been taken to and shown. Reformed ecclesiology has read them as the permanent shape of church life. The apostles' teaching — which is now the New Testament — norms everything else, so that no experience, however vivid, is permitted to correct it. The fellowship is not sociability but a shared life the Spirit creates, and in this chapter it costs people money within three verses. The breaking of bread is the Supper in which his death is proclaimed until he comes. And the prayers are the church's dependence made audible. A congregation strong in all four will be healthy in almost any circumstances; a congregation that quietly lets one go will be impoverished in ways it may take a generation to notice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Where do you baptise three thousand people in a city with no river? Jerusalem was already equipped. The southern approach to the temple mount was honeycombed with stepped immersion pools cut into the bedrock, so that pilgrims could purify themselves before going up; dozens have been excavated and can still be walked into. The infrastructure of the old covenant was standing ready on the morning the new one needed it. Now: God is not in the habit of waiting for ideal conditions, and he has a long record of using whatever is already lying about — a borrowed upper room, a set of ritual baths, and a preacher with a provincial accent.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, "Brothers, what shall we do?" And Peter said to them, "Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when they heard this they were cut to the heart, and said to Peter and the rest of the apostles, “Brothers, what shall we do?” And Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.”

They were cut to the heart. Key words. “Cut” (katenygēsan): pierced, stabbed. Conviction of sin, the Spirit’s work (John 16:8). They had crucified the Messiah. What hope could there be?

Brothers, what shall we do? The right question.

Repent. Key words. “Repent” (metanoēsate): change your mind, turn around. A change of mind about Jesus, and about sin, leading to a change of life. They had rejected him; now they must turn to him.

And be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ. Baptism publicly marks the turn, identifying with Jesus. “In the name of Jesus Christ”: by his authority, into union with him. Not a different formula from Matthew 28:19, but showing whose disciple one becomes.

For the forgiveness of your sins. The promise: sins forgiven, even the sin of crucifying the Messiah.

And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. The same Spirit poured out on the apostles, given to every believer.

Where Christians differ: does baptism save? Some read this to mean that baptism itself brings forgiveness (baptismal regeneration), so that forgiveness depends on baptism. Verdict: the preposition “for” (eis) can mean “with a view to” or “in connection with.” Throughout Acts forgiveness is received by faith (10:43; 13:38–39; 26:18), and Cornelius received the Spirit before baptism (10:44–48). Repentance and faith receive forgiveness; baptism is the God-given sign and seal of it, closely linked, normally following at once. It is commanded, and no believer should neglect it, but it is not the cause of salvation.

In a sentence. Cut to the heart, they asked what to do, and Peter told them to repent and each be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of their sins, and they would receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. No sin is too great to be forgiven. Even those who crucified Christ were offered pardon. Repent and believe.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the promise is for you and for your children and for all who are far off, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.

For the promise is for you and for your children. The promise of forgiveness and the Spirit. “Your children”: the next generation, their descendants.

And for all who are far off. “All who are far off” came to include the Gentiles (Ephesians 2:13, 17; Isaiah 57:19). Peter may not yet have understood this fully (10:28, 34).

Everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself. Key words. The promise is wide (everyone), and it is grounded in God’s effectual call. Those who receive the promise are those whom God calls. Notice the balance: Peter commands all to repent (v. 38) and assures them that the promise rests on God’s call. Human response and divine calling stand together (13:48).

Where Christians differ: baptism and children. Paedobaptists read “for you and your children” as a covenant promise to believers’ infants, supporting infant baptism. Verdict: the promise is to children as to everyone, “whom the Lord calls”: it is received by those who repent (v. 38), and those baptised were those who received the word (v. 41). Believer’s baptism is the New Testament pattern. Children of believers are in a place of great privilege, and the promise is for them as they come to faith. Paedobaptist brothers and sisters hold their view in good conscience, and we hold ours charitably.

In a sentence. The promise is for them, their children, and all who are far away, everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself.

For worship. The promise reached you, far off as you were, because the Lord called you. Praise him.
verseByVerse.note: “All who are far off” came to include the Gentiles.

parallels.desc: peace, peace, to the far and to the near

verseByVerse.quote: And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, "Save yourselves from this crooked generation." So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And with many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them, saying, “Save yourselves from this crooked generation.” So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls.

With many other words he bore witness and continued to exhort them. Luke gives us a summary; Peter said much more.

Save yourselves from this crooked generation. “Crooked” (skolias): twisted, perverse (Deuteronomy 32:5; Philippians 2:15). Break with the generation that rejected the Messiah. “Save yourselves” is not self-salvation, but “let yourselves be saved,” “escape.”

So those who received his word were baptized. Receiving the word, then baptism. Faith first.

And there were added that day about three thousand souls. Three thousand died when Israel worshipped the golden calf at Sinai, the first Pentecost, as later tradition reckoned it (Exodus 32:28). Here three thousand live. The letter kills, the Spirit gives life (2 Corinthians 3:6). The greater works Jesus promised (John 14:12).

In a sentence. With many more words Peter urged them to be saved from this crooked generation, and those who accepted his message were baptised, about three thousand that day.

For worship. One sermon, three thousand souls. God can do great things through the simple preaching of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Three thousand died when Israel worshipped the golden calf at Sinai; now three thousand receive life.

parallels.desc: a crooked and twisted generation

verseByVerse.quote: And they devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.

And they devoted themselves. Key words. “Devoted” (proskarterountes): persisted, kept at it, gave themselves. The marks of a true church, from its first day.

To the apostles’ teaching. First, teaching. The apostles taught what Jesus taught them. We have it in the New Testament. A church devoted to the apostles’ teaching today is a church devoted to Scripture.

And the fellowship. “Fellowship” (koinōnia): sharing, partnership, common life. Not just friendliness, but shared life in Christ, including practical sharing (v. 44).

To the breaking of bread. “The breaking of bread” likely included the Lord’s Supper within a shared meal (20:7; 1 Corinthians 11:20–26).

And the prayers. “The prayers”: probably set times of prayer, including at the temple (3:1), as well as their own gatherings.

In a sentence. They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer.

On a Tuesday. Measure your church life by these four: the word, fellowship, the Supper, prayer. Devote yourself to them.
verseByVerse.note: “The breaking of bread” likely included the Lord’s Supper within a shared meal.

verseByVerse.quote: And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And awe came upon every soul, and many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. And all who believed were together and had all things in common.

And awe came upon every soul. “Awe” (phobos): fear, reverence. A sense of God’s presence.

And many wonders and signs were being done through the apostles. Through the apostles specifically. Signs marked them as Christ’s authorised messengers (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4).

And all who believed were together and had all things in common. Key words. “In common” (koina): shared. They treated their possessions as available to one another.

In a sentence. Awe came over everyone, many wonders and signs were done by the apostles, and all the believers were together and shared everything.

For worship. The Spirit makes believers one family, with open hearts and open hands.

verseByVerse.quote: And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they were selling their possessions and belongings and distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need.

And they were selling their possessions and belongings. The Greek tense: they kept doing it, as needs arose.

And distributing the proceeds to all, as any had need. Key words. Selling was voluntary and as needs arose, not the abolition of private property. Peter tells Ananias that his property was his own to keep (5:4). Believers still owned homes (v. 46; 12:12).

Where Christians differ: was this communism? Some have seen here a model for Christian communism, or a rule that all Christians must give up private property. Verdict: it was a spontaneous, voluntary expression of love, not a compulsory system imposed by any authority. It met real needs, perhaps of pilgrims who stayed on in Jerusalem. The abiding principle is generous, sacrificial sharing with fellow believers in need (2 Corinthians 8:13–15; 1 John 3:17), not a particular economic model.

In a sentence. They were selling their property and possessions and giving to anyone who had need.

On a Tuesday. Is anyone in your church in need? What could you give?
verseByVerse.note: Selling was voluntary and as needs arose, not the abolition of property.

parallels.desc: there will be no poor among you

verseByVerse.quote: And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And day by day, attending the temple together and breaking bread in their homes, they received their food with glad and generous hearts, praising God and having favor with all the people. And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved.

And day by day, attending the temple together. The believers still worshipped at the temple while meeting in homes. They didn’t think they had left Judaism. They had found its fulfilment in the Messiah. They met in Solomon’s Porch (5:12).

And breaking bread in their homes. Meals together, including the Lord’s Supper. The house church was the basic unit.

They received their food with glad and generous hearts. “Glad” (agalliasei): exultant joy. “Generous” (aphelotēti): simplicity, sincerity, single-heartedness.

Praising God and having favor with all the people. At first, the ordinary people respected them. Persecution would come from the leaders.

And the Lord added to their number day by day those who were being saved. Key words. “The Lord added”: church growth is God’s work. The apostles preached and the church lived out its life; the Lord saved. “Being saved” (present tense): a continual stream.

In a sentence. Every day they met together in the temple and broke bread in their homes, eating with joyful, sincere hearts, praising God and enjoying the people’s goodwill, and every day the Lord added to them those who were being saved.

For worship. The Lord adds to his church. Pray for him to do it in yours, and live in joy that draws others.
verseByVerse.note: The believers still worshipped at the temple while meeting in homes.

2.theology: The Sovereignty of God at the Cross. Acts 2:23 is the Reformed doctrine of divine sovereignty distilled to a sentence. The cross happened “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God.” The “definite plan” is God’s eternal counsel, his settled, unalterable purpose. This is not foreknowledge in the Arminian sense of God merely looking ahead and seeing what humans would choose. This is foreordination: God planned the cross before the world began (1 Peter 1:20, Revelation 13:8). Total depravity and sovereign grace appear in one verse: the guilt is wholly human, the purpose is wholly divine. The cross is the intersection of man’s worst deed and God’s greatest gift.
2.examples:
Then: The feast of Pentecost was transformed on this day from an agricultural harvest festival into the birthday of the church. Devout Jews from fifteen regions of the empire heard the mighty works of God proclaimed in their mother tongues and were cut to the heart. The harvest that day was three thousand souls.

Now: Every Lord’s Day is a Pentecost echo. The same Spirit, the same Word, the same call to repentance — and the same Lord who adds to his church those who are being saved. The question for every preacher and every congregation is whether we are as devoted to the apostles’ teaching, the fellowship, the breaking of bread, and the prayers as that first gathering was. The form has not changed. The power has not diminished.

3.title: The Lame Man and the Living Lord
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. <sup>2</sup>And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple. <sup>3</sup>Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms. <sup>4</sup>And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.” <sup>5</sup>And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them. <sup>6</sup>But Peter said, “I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!” <sup>7</sup>And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. <sup>8</sup>And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God. <sup>9</sup>And all the people saw him walking and praising God, <sup>10</sup>and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him. <sup>11</sup>While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s. <sup>12</sup>And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk? <sup>13</sup>The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. <sup>14</sup>But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, <sup>15</sup>and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses. <sup>16</sup>And his name—by faith in his name—has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all. <sup>17</sup>“And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. <sup>18</sup>But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. <sup>19</sup>Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out, <sup>20</sup>that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, <sup>21</sup>whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago. <sup>22</sup>Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you. <sup>23</sup>And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people.’ <sup>24</sup>And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days. <sup>25</sup>You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ <sup>26</sup>God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.”
3.overview:
Luke now shows one of the “wonders and signs” of 2:43 in detail. Peter and John go up to the temple for the afternoon prayer, at three o’clock, when the evening sacrifice was offered. At the gate called Beautiful sits a man lame from birth, over forty years old (4:22), carried there daily to beg. Peter has no money, but in the name of Jesus of Nazareth tells him to walk, and the man leaps up and goes into the temple courts walking, leaping and praising God, a living fulfilment of Isaiah’s promise that the lame would leap like a deer when God came to save.

A crowd gathers at Solomon’s Portico, and Peter preaches his second sermon. The healing was not their power but Jesus’ name. The God of Abraham has glorified his Servant Jesus, whom they handed over and disowned before Pilate, asking for a murderer instead and killing the Author of life; but God raised him. They acted in ignorance, yet God used it to fulfil what the prophets foretold, that the Messiah would suffer. So they must repent and turn back, so that their sins may be wiped out, refreshing may come from the Lord, and he may send the Messiah, who must remain in heaven until the time when God restores everything. Jesus is the prophet like Moses whom everyone must hear, and the offspring of Abraham through whom all nations will be blessed; God sent him first to Israel, to bless them by turning them from their wickedness.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Healing at the Beautiful Gate
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One afternoon at three, the hour of prayer, Peter and John were going up to the temple. A man lame from birth was being carried to the temple gate called Beautiful, where he was put every day to beg from those going into the temple courts. When he saw Peter and John about to enter, he asked them for money. Peter looked straight at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us!” The man gave them his attention, expecting a gift. Peter said he had no silver or gold, but what he had he would give: “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, walk.” Taking him by the right hand, Peter helped him up, and at once his feet and ankles became strong. He jumped to his feet, began to walk, and went with them into the temple courts, walking, jumping and praising God. All the people saw him and recognised him as the man who used to sit begging at the Beautiful Gate, and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened.
verseByVerse.theology:
Signs, and What They Are Signs Of

The healings in Acts are called signs, and a sign is not the destination; it is a board at the roadside with the name of the destination written on it. These are not displays of power for their own sake, and they are certainly not the working of impersonal forces — Luke will show us in this same book what happens when men try to use the name as a technique (19:13–16). They are the personal act of a risen King through men he has authorised, and what they point to is the repair of a world that has been broken since Eden. A man's ankles are made whole in the middle of Jerusalem, and the thing being said is about everything: a day is coming when the whole creation will be put right, and here is a down payment on it, walking about in the temple courts and making a good deal of noise. Reformed theology has also read the apostolic signs as authenticating the apostolic message, which is why Scripture ties them so closely to the apostles themselves, and why the long argument over whether such things continue is an argument about their function and never about whether God is able.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The man asked for alms and got his legs. But Luke is careful about what else he got: he went into the temple, through the gate that had been the limit of his days. The gate he sat at was the boundary of his whole life, and he had spent forty years on the wrong side of it with his hand out. He received his body back, and his place with it. Now: The church still meets people asking for the small thing because it is the only thing they know how to ask for, and it still has no silver worth mentioning. What it has is a name. The temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by that and to offer something more respectable instead.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. And a man lame from birth was being carried, whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate to ask alms of those entering the temple.

Meaning first. Acts 3 gives one example of the “wonders and signs” done through the apostles (2:43). A man lame from birth is healed in Jesus’ name, a crowd gathers, and Peter preaches his second sermon. The healing is a sign of what Jesus does for all who believe: those who could never walk into God’s presence are made whole and enter, praising God. And it sets off the first persecution (chapter 4).

Now Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour. The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the time of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer. The first Christians kept Jewish hours of prayer. Peter and John, partners in fishing (Luke 5:10), in preparing the Passover (Luke 22:8), and now in ministry.

A man lame from birth. Over forty years old (4:22). Hopeless by any human measure, like the man born blind (John 9).

Whom they laid daily at the gate of the temple that is called the Beautiful Gate. Probably the Nicanor Gate, of Corinthian bronze, between the Court of the Gentiles and the Court of the Women, so costly that Josephus said it far exceeded gates plated with silver and gold. The irony: a broken man at the beautiful gate, unable to go in. The lame were excluded from priestly service (Leviticus 21:18), and some thought from the temple itself (2 Samuel 5:8).

To ask alms of those entering the temple. A good spot for begging.

In a sentence. Peter and John were going up to the temple for the three o’clock prayer, as a man lame from birth was being carried to the Beautiful Gate, where he was laid each day to beg from those going in.

On a Tuesday. Notice the people at the gate, who can’t get in. Christ came for them.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the time of the afternoon sacrifice and prayer. The Beautiful Gate is not named elsewhere; it was probably a great bronze gate into the temple courts.

parallels.desc: the evening offering

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing Peter and John about to go into the temple, he asked to receive alms.

He asked to receive alms. Beggars sat where worshippers passed, since giving alms was a religious duty, especially on the way to prayer (Matthew 6:2). He asked for what he expected: money. He got far more.

In a sentence. When he saw Peter and John about to enter the temple, he asked them for money.

For worship. We often ask God for small things, when he wants to give us great ones (Ephesians 3:20).
verseByVerse.note: Beggars sat where worshippers passed, since giving alms was a religious duty.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, "Look at us." And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John, and said, “Look at us.” And he fixed his attention on them, expecting to receive something from them.

And Peter directed his gaze at him, as did John. “Directed his gaze” (atenisas): looked intently. Most people avoided looking at beggars. Peter looks him in the eye.

Look at us. Not for attention, but to direct his expectation.

Expecting to receive something from them. Expectation is the first step.

In a sentence. Peter and John looked straight at him, and Peter told him to look at them, and he gave them his attention, expecting to receive something.

On a Tuesday. Look people in the eye. Treat the overlooked as people, made in God’s image.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said, "I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!" And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But Peter said, “I have no silver and gold, but what I do have I give to you. In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk!” And he took him by the right hand and raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles were made strong.

I have no silver and gold. The apostles were poor. What money was given went to the needy (2:45; 4:35).

But what I do have I give to you. Something better than money.

In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk! Key words. “In the name of” means by his authority and power. Peter has no power of his own (v. 12). He acts as Jesus’ representative. Jesus is the healer, from heaven. “Of Nazareth”: the despised man from the despised town is the Lord of all.

And he took him by the right hand and raised him up. Peter does what Jesus did (Mark 1:31; 5:41). “Raised him up” (ēgeiren): the word used of resurrection.

And immediately his feet and ankles were made strong. Luke the doctor notes the medical detail. Instant, complete healing, of a condition from birth. Muscles that had never been used, and he had never learned to walk.

In a sentence. Peter said he had no silver or gold, but gave what he had, commanding him in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth to get up and walk, and taking his right hand he raised him up, and immediately his feet and ankles grew strong.

For worship. What the church has to give is better than silver and gold: the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.note: “In the name of” means by his authority and power.

verseByVerse.quote: And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And leaping up, he stood and began to walk, and entered the temple with them, walking and leaping and praising God.

And leaping up, he stood and began to walk. Key words. Isaiah promised: then shall the lame man leap like a deer (Isaiah 35:6), a sign of the messianic age. The prophecy is fulfilled before their eyes.

And entered the temple with them. The man who sat outside for forty years goes in. A picture of salvation: Christ brings those who were shut out into the presence of God (Ephesians 2:13, 18).

Walking and leaping and praising God. Not praising Peter, but God. Joy overflows.

In a sentence. He jumped up, stood and started walking, and went into the temple with them, walking, leaping and praising God.

For worship. Walk, leap, praise. Christ has brought you in, too.

parallels.desc: then shall the lame man leap like a deer

verseByVerse.quote: And all the people saw him walking and praising God, and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And all the people saw him walking and praising God, and recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. And they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.

And all the people saw him walking and praising God. A public miracle.

And recognized him as the one who sat at the Beautiful Gate of the temple, asking for alms. Everyone knew him. There could be no fraud. Even the council couldn’t deny it (4:16).

They were filled with wonder and amazement. The sign draws a crowd, and opens the way for the word.

In a sentence. All the people saw him walking and praising God and recognised him as the beggar from the Beautiful Gate, and were filled with wonder and amazement.

On a Tuesday. A changed life opens doors for the gospel. Let yours be seen.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While the man held on to Peter and John, the astonished crowd ran to them at Solomon’s Colonnade. Peter asked why they were surprised and why they stared as if he and John had made the man walk by their own power or godliness. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had glorified his servant Jesus, whom they handed over and rejected before Pilate when Pilate had decided to release him. They disowned the Holy and Righteous One and asked for a murderer instead; they killed the author of life, but God raised him from the dead, and the apostles are witnesses. By faith in Jesus’ name this man, whom they know, has been made strong; the faith that comes through Jesus has given him complete healing. Peter knows they acted in ignorance, as their leaders did, but this is how God fulfilled what all the prophets had said, that his Messiah would suffer. So they must repent and turn to God, so that their sins may be wiped out, times of refreshing may come from the Lord, and he may send the Messiah appointed for them, Jesus. Heaven must receive him until the time comes for God to restore everything, as he promised long ago through the prophets. Moses said God would raise up a prophet like him, whom they must listen to in everything, and anyone who will not listen will be cut off. All the prophets from Samuel on foretold these days. They are heirs of the prophets and of the covenant God made with Abraham, when he said that through Abraham’s offspring all peoples on earth would be blessed. God raised up his servant and sent him first to them, to bless them by turning each of them from their wicked ways.
verseByVerse.theology:
Jesus as the Fulfilment of the Covenant with Abraham

Peter closes on the promise to Abraham — in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed (v. 25; cf. Genesis 22:18; 28:14) — and it matters a great deal where that promise was sworn. It is repeated on the mountain, after the knife is stopped and the ram is found caught in the thicket: the promise that the whole world would be blessed through Abraham's line is given at the exact moment God provides a substitute for a beloved son. Peter quotes it in a sermon about a beloved Son for whom no substitute was provided. The gospel, on this reading, is not the abandonment of God's promises to Israel but their arrival — not a second plan drawn up after the first failed, but the first plan reaching the date it had been set for. Reformed biblical theology insists that the covenant of grace runs unbroken from Genesis to Revelation and finds its definitive form in Christ, which is why Peter can preach this to Jews in the temple courts without once suggesting that they should change religion.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter preached to people who bore the most direct responsibility there was — you denied the Holy and Righteous One — and then called them brothers three verses later and told them the blessing was coming to them first. Now: The order has never changed. A gospel that cannot name what a man has actually done has nothing to forgive him for; a gospel that names it and leaves him standing there is not the gospel at all. Peter does both in one sermon, and the second half is longer than the first.

verseByVerse.quote: While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon's. And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: "Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he clung to Peter and John, all the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s. And when Peter saw it he addressed the people: “Men of Israel, why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or piety we have made him walk?

While he clung to Peter and John. He won’t let go of them.

All the people, utterly astounded, ran together to them in the portico called Solomon’s. Solomon’s portico was a covered colonnade along the east side of the temple court, where Jesus had walked (John 10:23). The early church met there (5:12).

Why do you wonder at this, or why do you stare at us? Peter refuses the attention.

As though by our own power or piety we have made him walk? Key words. Not by our power, nor by our godliness. Miracles were not rewards for holiness. Peter deflects all glory to Christ. A test of true ministry: whom does it make much of?

In a sentence. As the man held on to Peter and John, the astounded crowd ran to them at Solomon’s portico, and Peter asked why they stared, as if the apostles had made him walk by their own power or godliness.

For worship. All glory to Christ. When God uses you, point away from yourself.
verseByVerse.note: Solomon’s portico was a covered colonnade along the east side of the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers, glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him.

The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our fathers. The name God gave Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:6, 15). Peter is not preaching a new religion. The God of Israel has acted in Jesus.

Glorified his servant Jesus. Key words. “His servant” echoes Isaiah’s Servant, who would be “lifted up” and greatly exalted (Isaiah 52:13), after suffering for the sins of many (Isaiah 53). Jesus is the Suffering Servant, now glorified by God in resurrection and the healing done in his name.

Whom you delivered over and denied in the presence of Pilate, when he had decided to release him. The contrast: God glorified him; you denied him. Even the pagan Pilate wanted to let him go (Luke 23:4, 14–16, 22).

In a sentence. Peter said the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob had glorified his servant Jesus, whom they handed over and rejected before Pilate, though Pilate had decided to release him.

On a Tuesday. The God of the Old Testament is the God who raised Jesus. Read your whole Bible as one story.
verseByVerse.note: “His servant” echoes Isaiah’s Servant, who would be “lifted up” and glorified.

parallels.desc: my servant shall be high and lifted up

verseByVerse.quote: "But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But you denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderer to be granted to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses.

But you denied the Holy and Righteous One. Key words. Titles of the Messiah. The Holy One (Psalm 16:10; Mark 1:24); “the Righteous One” (Isaiah 53:11; Acts 7:52; 22:14). They rejected the only sinless man who ever lived.

And asked for a murderer to be granted to you. Barabbas (Luke 23:18–19, 25).

And you killed the Author of life. Key words. “Author” (archēgos): founder, originator, pioneer, prince. The one through whom all life came, and who leads his people into life (Hebrews 2:10; 12:2). The terrible paradox: they killed the source of life. Spared the murderer, killed the life-giver.

Whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses. Again, eyewitness testimony.

In a sentence. Peter said they rejected the Holy and Righteous One, asked for a murderer instead, and killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead, as the apostles had witnessed.

For worship. The Author of life died, so that you might live. Wonder at it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong whom you see and know, and the faith that is through Jesus has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all.

And his name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong. Key words. The name of Jesus, his person and power, made the man strong. And faith in his name was the means. Whose faith? Probably the apostles’, and perhaps the man’s as he responded. The power is Christ’s; faith is the hand that receives it.

And the faith that is through Jesus. Even the faith comes through Jesus. It is his gift (Ephesians 2:8; Philippians 1:29).

Has given the man this perfect health in the presence of you all. “Perfect health” (holoklērian): complete soundness, wholeness. Public and undeniable.

In a sentence. Peter said it was Jesus’ name, through faith in his name, that made this man strong, and the faith that comes through Jesus gave him complete health in front of them all.

On a Tuesday. Even your faith is Christ’s gift. Thank him for it, and use it.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And now, brothers, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled.

And now, brothers. Peter’s tone softens. Brothers, fellow Jews.

I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers. Key words. Not that they were innocent, but that they did not know who Jesus truly was (Luke 23:34; 1 Corinthians 2:8). The law distinguished sins of ignorance from defiant sins (Numbers 15:27–31). There is hope for those who sinned in ignorance, if they repent. Paul said the same of himself (1 Timothy 1:13).

But what God foretold by the mouth of all the prophets, that his Christ would suffer, he thus fulfilled. “All the prophets”: the whole Old Testament points to a suffering Messiah (Luke 24:25–27; 1 Peter 1:10–11). God fulfilled his own word through their ignorant wickedness.

In a sentence. Peter acknowledged that they and their rulers had acted in ignorance, but God had fulfilled what all the prophets foretold, that his Christ would suffer.

For worship. God’s plan includes even our worst sins, turned to good. There is mercy for those who acted in ignorance.

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repent therefore, and turn back, that your sins may be blotted out,

Repent therefore, and turn back. Key words. Two verbs. “Repent” (metanoēsate): change your mind. “Turn back” (epistrepsate): turn around, return, convert. A change of mind that leads to a change of direction: away from sin and towards God in Christ.

That your sins may be blotted out. “Blotted out” (exaleiphthēnai): wiped away, erased, as ink was washed off papyrus. The record of sin is completely erased (Psalm 51:1, 9; Isaiah 43:25; Colossians 2:14).

In a sentence. Peter told them to repent and turn back so that their sins would be wiped out.

On a Tuesday. Your sins can be wiped out, completely. Repent and turn to Christ, and the slate is clean.

parallels.desc: I am he who blots out your transgressions

verseByVerse.quote: "that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago."
verseByVerse.commentary:
that times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord, and that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus, whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things about which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago.

That times of refreshing may come from the presence of the Lord. “Refreshing” (anapsyxeōs): relief, breathing space, revival. The blessings of salvation, now and finally at Christ’s return.

And that he may send the Christ appointed for you, Jesus. The second coming.

Whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things. Key words. Jesus remains in heaven until the final restoration, the renewal of all creation (Matthew 19:28; Romans 8:19–21; Revelation 21:5). “Restoring” (apokatastaseōs): putting back to right, the new heavens and new earth.

About which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets long ago. Isaiah 65:17; 66:22, among many.

Where Christians differ: restoration of all things. Some (universalists) take “restoring all things” to mean that every person will eventually be saved. Others (dispensationalists) take it as an earthly millennial kingdom for Israel. Verdict: the restoration is of “all things about which God spoke by the prophets,” the renewal of creation, which the prophets also say includes judgment on the wicked (Isaiah 66:24). And the next verses warn that those who refuse Christ will be destroyed (v. 23). It is the new creation at Christ’s single return, not the salvation of all, nor an interim kingdom.

In a sentence. Repentance would bring times of refreshing from the Lord, and he would send Jesus, the appointed Christ, who must remain in heaven until the time when God restores everything, as the prophets foretold long ago.

For worship. Christ will return and make all things new. Lift up your head.

parallels.desc: new heavens and a new earth

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses said, 'The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers. You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you.’

Moses said, “The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet like me from your brothers.” Key words. Deuteronomy 18:15–19. Israel waited for a prophet like Moses (John 1:21; 6:14; 7:40). Peter says Jesus is that prophet. Like Moses, he delivered his people, gave them God’s word, mediated a covenant, and performed signs. But greater than Moses (Hebrews 3:1–6).

You shall listen to him in whatever he tells you. The Father said the same at the transfiguration: listen to him (Luke 9:35).

In a sentence. Moses said God would raise up a prophet like him from among their brothers, to whom they must listen in everything.

On a Tuesday. Listen to Jesus, in whatever he tells you. Not selectively, but in everything.

parallels.desc: a prophet like me from among you

verseByVerse.quote: "And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And it shall be that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days.

Every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be destroyed from the people. Key words. A combination of Deuteronomy 18:19 and Leviticus 23:29. A solemn warning. Rejecting Jesus is not a neutral option. Those who refuse him are cut off from God’s people. The true Israel is defined by response to Jesus.

And all the prophets who have spoken, from Samuel and those who came after him, also proclaimed these days. Samuel anointed David, and through Nathan came the promise of David’s eternal son (2 Samuel 7). All the prophets pointed to the messianic age.

In a sentence. Everyone who would not listen to that prophet would be cut off from the people, and all the prophets from Samuel on foretold these days.

For worship. The whole of Scripture points to these days, the days of Christ. Live in them with gratitude.

parallels.desc: Nathan’s prophecy in Samuel’s days

verseByVerse.quote: "You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, 'And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.' God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers, saying to Abraham, ‘And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.’ God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first, to bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness.

You are the sons of the prophets and of the covenant that God made with your fathers. They are heirs of the promise. It was given to them.

And in your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed. Key words. Genesis 22:18 (12:3). The promise to Abraham: blessing for all nations through his offspring. Paul says the offspring is Christ (Galatians 3:16). The gospel to the Gentiles is no departure from the Old Testament; it is its fulfilment.

God, having raised up his servant, sent him to you first. “First”: to Israel first, then to the nations (13:46; Romans 1:16).

To bless you by turning every one of you from your wickedness. Key words. The blessing of Abraham is not first prosperity but forgiveness and transformation: being turned from sin. Jesus saves his people from their sins (Matthew 1:21), not in them.

In a sentence. Peter said they were heirs of the prophets and of God’s covenant with Abraham, that all families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring, and God raised up his servant and sent him first to them, to bless them by turning each of them from wickedness.

On a Tuesday. The greatest blessing God can give you is to turn you from your sin. Pray for it.

parallels.desc: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed

3.theology: The Name of Jesus. “His name — by faith in his name — has made this man strong” (v. 16). This verse is not about a formula but about a person. The name in the ancient world carried the authority and presence of the one who bore it. When Peter speaks the name of Jesus, he is not invoking magic; he is acting in the delegated authority of the reigning Christ. The healing is an act of the risen Lord performed through his servant. Faith is the hand that reaches for what the name offers. And what the name offers is the full power of the one who conquered death — resurrection life, flowing through a living faith, into a broken body and a guilty conscience alike.
3.examples:
Then: A man lame from birth, set daily at the gate of the temple he could not enter, excluded by his condition from the presence he longed for. His whole life had been one long reaching-out of an empty hand. And then, in the name of Jesus, he entered the temple walking.

Now: The church still carries what the world cannot give. No program, no therapy, no government initiative can do what the name of Jesus does — not because those things are worthless, but because they cannot raise the dead. The church’s temptation in every generation is to be embarrassed by its true wealth and to offer silver and gold instead. The world has plenty of silver and gold. It has only one name by which it can be saved.

4.title: Boldness Before the Council
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, <sup>2</sup>greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. <sup>3</sup>And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. <sup>4</sup>But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand. <sup>5</sup>On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, <sup>6</sup>with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family. <sup>7</sup>And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, “By what power or by what name did you do this?” <sup>8</sup>Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders, <sup>9</sup>if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed, <sup>10</sup>let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead—by him this man is standing before you well. <sup>11</sup>This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone. <sup>12</sup>And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” <sup>13</sup>Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. <sup>14</sup>But seeing the man who was healed standing beside them, they had nothing to say in opposition. <sup>15</sup>But when they had commanded them to leave the council, they conferred with one another, <sup>16</sup>saying, “What shall we do with these men? For that a notable sign has been performed through them is evident to all the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and we cannot deny it. <sup>17</sup>But in order that it may spread no further among the people, let us warn them to speak no more to anyone in this name.” <sup>18</sup>So they called them and charged them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. <sup>19</sup>But Peter and John answered them, “Whether it is right in the sight of God to listen to you rather than to God, you must judge, <sup>20</sup>for we cannot but speak of what we have seen and heard.” <sup>21</sup>And when they had further threatened them, they let them go, finding no way to punish them, because of the people, for all were praising God for what had happened. <sup>22</sup>For the man on whom this sign of healing was performed was more than forty years old. <sup>23</sup>When they were released, they went to their friends and reported what the chief priests and the elders had said to them. <sup>24</sup>And when they heard it, they lifted their voices together to God and said, “Sovereign Lord, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and everything in them, <sup>25</sup>who through the mouth of our father David, your servant, said by the Holy Spirit, ‘Why did the Gentiles rage, and the peoples plot in vain? <sup>26</sup>The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed’— <sup>27</sup>for truly in this city there were gathered together against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed, both Herod and Pontius Pilate, along with the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, <sup>28</sup>to do whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place. <sup>29</sup>And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness, <sup>30</sup>while you stretch out your hand to heal, and signs and wonders are performed through the name of your holy servant Jesus.” <sup>31</sup>And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness. <sup>32</sup>Now the full number of those who believed were of one heart and soul, and no one said that any of the things that belonged to him was his own, but they had everything in common. <sup>33</sup>And with great power the apostles were giving their testimony to the resurrection of the Lord Jesus, and great grace was upon them all. <sup>34</sup>There was not a needy person among them, for as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what was sold <sup>35</sup>and laid it at the apostles’ feet, and it was distributed to each as any had need. <sup>36</sup>Thus Joseph, who was also called by the apostles Barnabas (which means son of encouragement), a Levite, a native of Cyprus, <sup>37</sup>sold a field that belonged to him and brought the money and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
4.overview:
The healing and Peter’s sermon bring the first persecution. The temple authorities were dominated by the Sadducees, the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple, cooperated with Rome to keep order, and denied the resurrection of the dead. Two Galileans proclaiming in the temple courts that Jesus had been raised were a threat on every count. Peter and John are arrested and brought before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council, with the former high priest Annas, his son-in-law Caiaphas and the high priestly family, the very men who had condemned Jesus weeks earlier. Filled with the Spirit, Peter tells them the man was healed by the name of Jesus, the stone they rejected who has become the cornerstone, and that there is salvation in no other name.

The council is astonished at the boldness of these untrained men, recognises that they had been with Jesus, and cannot deny the miracle, so it orders them to stop speaking in his name. Peter and John reply that they must obey God and cannot stop speaking of what they have seen and heard. Released, they return to the believers, who pray using Psalm 2: the nations and rulers raged against the Lord’s Anointed, just as Herod and Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel had done, but only to carry out what God had planned. They do not ask for safety but for boldness and for God to stretch out his hand to heal. The place shakes, they are filled with the Spirit and speak boldly. The chapter ends with the church’s generosity: no one in need, owners selling property for the poor, and a Levite from Cyprus, Joseph, nicknamed Barnabas, “son of encouragement”, selling a field and laying the money at the apostles’ feet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Peter and John were speaking to the people, the priests, the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up, greatly disturbed that the apostles were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead. They seized them and, since it was evening, put them in jail until the next day. But many who heard the message believed, and the number of men grew to about five thousand. The next day the rulers, elders and teachers of the law met in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander and others of the high priest’s family. They had Peter and John brought before them and asked by what power or name they had done this. Filled with the Spirit, Peter replied that if they were being questioned about an act of kindness to a disabled man, everyone in Israel should know it was by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom they crucified and God raised, that this man stood there healed. Jesus is the stone the builders rejected, now the cornerstone, and salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven by which people must be saved. Seeing the courage of Peter and John and realising they were ordinary men with no formal training, the council was astonished and recognised that they had been with Jesus. With the healed man standing there, they had nothing to say. They sent them out, conferred, and admitted that an undeniable miracle had happened which everyone in Jerusalem knew about. To stop it spreading, they warned the apostles not to speak or teach in Jesus’ name. Peter and John answered that the council must judge whether it is right before God to obey them rather than God; as for themselves, they could not help speaking about what they had seen and heard. After further threats the council let them go, because they could find no way to punish them without upsetting the people, who were all praising God for the healing of a man over forty years old.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Exclusivity of Christ

Peter's declaration in v. 12 — there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved — is among the clearest statements of Christ's exclusive lordship in salvation anywhere in Scripture, and it is worth noticing that it is spoken in a courtroom, to men who could imprison him for it. Reformed theology has always held this exclusivity to follow from the incarnation itself: if God became flesh in one particular person, in one particular place, at one particular hour of history, then salvation is tied to that person and cannot be detached from him. A plurality of saviours would require a plurality of incarnations, which is not a thing the gospel can be stretched to accommodate. And the same logic that makes the claim exclusive makes it universal: the name is given among men, offered, held out — the door is single and it is not shut.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter and John were laymen without rabbinic training, standing in the middle of the supreme court of Israel, and their boldness astonished the men trying them — parresia, a word that in Greek public life meant the free speech of a citizen in the assembly, the very thing a slave did not have. Now: The same Spirit who supplied it is given to every believer, and the church prays for more of it in this very chapter (v. 29). Boldness in the New Testament is not a temperament. It is a gift, asked for and granted, and it is perfectly compatible with being frightened.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And as they were speaking to the people, the priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them, greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people and proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead.

Meaning first. Acts 4 tells of the first persecution of the church. Peter and John are arrested, tried before the same council that condemned Jesus, and forbidden to speak in his name. They refuse, are released, and the church prays not for safety but for boldness. The chapter shows the pattern of the whole book: opposition cannot stop the word of God; it only spreads it.

The priests and the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came upon them. Setting and background. The captain of the temple commanded the temple police and ranked next to the high priest. The Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple. They accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative, denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (23:8), and cooperated with Rome to keep their power.

Greatly annoyed because they were teaching the people. Unauthorised teachers in the temple, drawing crowds.

And proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection from the dead. Key words. The doctrine the Sadducees denied, proven in the person of Jesus. “In Jesus”: his resurrection is the proof and the guarantee of the general resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20–23).

In a sentence. While they were speaking, the priests, the captain of the temple and the Sadducees came to them, angered that they were teaching the people and proclaiming the resurrection of the dead in Jesus.

On a Tuesday. The resurrection offends those whose power depends on this world. Proclaim it anyway.
verseByVerse.note: The captain of the temple commanded the temple police and ranked next to the high priest. The Sadducees, the priestly party, denied the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. But many of those who had heard the word believed, and the number of the men came to about five thousand.

And they arrested them and put them in custody until the next day, for it was already evening. Hearings were not normally held at night. (Jesus’ trial had been an exception, and illegal.)

But many of those who had heard the word believed. Key words. “But.” The apostles are locked up; the word is not (2 Timothy 2:9).

And the number of the men came to about five thousand. “Men” (andrōn): males, perhaps heads of households, so the total was larger. From 120, to 3,000, to over 5,000.

In a sentence. They arrested them and held them overnight, but many who heard the message believed, and the number of men grew to about five thousand.

For worship. You can chain the preacher, but not the word. Thank God for it.
verseByVerse.note: Hearings were not normally held at night.

verseByVerse.quote: On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the next day their rulers and elders and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander, and all who were of the high-priestly family.

Their rulers and elders and scribes. The rulers, elders and scribes made up the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish council of seventy-one. Rulers were the chief priests; elders, leading lay aristocrats; scribes, experts in the law.

With Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander. Annas had been deposed by Rome but was still called high priest by many; Caiaphas held the office. John and Alexander were probably family members; one John (Jonathan) son of Annas later became high priest. The same men who tried Jesus (John 18:13, 24).

In a sentence. The next day the rulers, elders and scribes gathered in Jerusalem, with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander and the whole high-priestly family.

For worship. The same council that condemned Jesus now faces his apostles. His story continues in his people.
verseByVerse.note: The rulers, elders and scribes made up the Sanhedrin. Annas had been high priest earlier and remained head of the family; Caiaphas was the serving high priest.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, "By what power or by what name did you do this?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they had set them in the midst, they inquired, “By what power or by what name did you do this?”

When they had set them in the midst. The council sat in a semicircle, with the accused in the middle.

By what power or by what name did you do this? They don’t deny the miracle. They want to know its source, perhaps hoping to find magic or false prophecy (Deuteronomy 13:1–5). “You” is emphatic and contemptuous: people like you?

In a sentence. They stood them in the middle and asked by what power or in whose name they had done this.

On a Tuesday. When asked about the source of your hope, be ready to answer (1 Peter 3:15).

parallels.desc: by what authority?

verseByVerse.quote: Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, "Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them, “Rulers of the people and elders, if we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man, by what means this man has been healed,

Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit. Key words. Jesus promised that when they were brought before rulers, the Holy Spirit would teach them what to say (Luke 12:11–12; 21:12–15). The promise is kept. A fresh filling for a fresh need.

If we are being examined today concerning a good deed done to a crippled man. A touch of irony. They are on trial for an act of kindness.

By what means this man has been healed. “Healed” (sesōstai): literally “saved.” The same word as in v. 12. Physical healing points to the greater salvation.

In a sentence. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, answered that if they were being questioned about a good deed to a crippled man and how he was healed...

For worship. The Spirit gives words in the hour of need. Trust him when you are put on the spot for Christ.

parallels.desc: I will give you a mouth and wisdom

verseByVerse.quote: "let it be known to all of you and to all the people of Israel that by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified, whom God raised from the dead — by him this man is standing before you well. This Jesus is the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone."
