Jesus had said the witness would go from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the end of the earth (1:8), and for perhaps two years nothing had moved; the church was large, joyful, generous and entirely stationary. It took a murder and a persecution to get it out of the city. The point is not that God needed the persecution, nor that the suffering was anything other than real — Luke records men weeping loudly over a grave in the same breath. It is that the machinery of opposition turned out to be the machinery of expansion, and that the man superintending the destruction was, without the faintest idea of it, dispersing the gospel across two provinces. The kingdom advanced that year in the shape of a defeat.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Jews had no dealings with Samaritans, and the quarrel was not a misunderstanding — it had a ruined temple on Mount Gerizim in it, pulled down by a Jewish army. The gospel crossed that line before anybody had written a word of argument about whether it should. Now: The barrier a congregation is least likely to cross is never the one it debates. It is the one it has stopped noticing, because everyone it knows is on the same side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And Saul approved of his execution. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, and they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles. Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Stephen’s death unleashes persecution that scatters the church beyond Jerusalem, as Jesus’ plan required.

Saul approved. Syneudokōn: he heartily agreed. Later he confessed it (22:20).

Scattered. Diesparēsan, from which we get “diaspora”: sown like seed. Persecution scattered the seed of the gospel.

Except the apostles. Perhaps the persecution targeted especially the Greek-speaking believers associated with Stephen’s views on the temple.

Great lamentation. Grief is right. Christians mourn their dead, though not as those without hope.

On a Tuesday. When hardship scatters you, through a job loss or a move, ask where God wants you to sow the gospel in the new place.
verseByVerse.note: The scattering fulfils Jesus’ plan in 1:8: Judea and Samaria come next.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul was ravaging the church, and entering house after house, he dragged off men and women and committed them to prison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul’s campaign is violent and thorough, reaching into homes and sparing no one.

Ravaging. Elymaineto: used of wild animals tearing prey. Paul later admitted, “I persecuted this Way to the death” (22:4), and called himself the least of the apostles because of it (1 Corinthians 15:9).

House after house. The church met in homes, so the homes were raided.

Men and women. Women were persecuted equally.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who persecute Christians today, and for house churches facing raids in countries such as China and Iran.

verseByVerse.quote: Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The scattered believers become missionaries, and Philip takes the gospel to Samaria.

Preaching. Euangelizomenoi: announcing the good news. Ordinary believers, not just apostles, spread the gospel.

Philip. The evangelist, one of the seven (6:5; 21:8), not the apostle Philip.

Samaria. Samaritans were descended from the northern Israelites and the foreign settlers brought in by the Assyrians after 722 BC (2 Kings 17:24–41). They accepted only the five books of Moses and worshipped on Mount Gerizim. Jews and Samaritans despised each other: “Jews have no dealings with Samaritans” (John 4:9). Yet the Samaritans too expected a Messiah (John 4:25), whom they called the Taheb, “the Restorer”.

A textual note. Manuscripts vary between “the city of Samaria” (the capital, then called Sebaste) and “a city of Samaria”. The meaning is unaffected.

On a Tuesday. Who are your Samaritans, the people your community dislikes? The gospel is for them.
verseByVerse.note: This Philip is one of the seven, not the apostle. Samaritans were a mixed people despised by Jews; they also expected a coming deliverer.

parallels.desc: Philip the evangelist

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip, when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Samaritans listen eagerly as Philip’s words are confirmed by healings and deliverances.

One accord. United attention.

Signs. Like those of Jesus and the apostles. Philip had been commissioned by the apostles (6:6).

On a Tuesday. The gospel brings freedom from spiritual bondage. Pray for those trapped in the occult.

verseByVerse.quote: So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel brings great joy to a city long held in the grip of a famous magician.

Much joy. The fruit of the gospel (8:39; 13:52).

Simon. Later Christian writers (Justin Martyr, Irenaeus) called him Simon Magus and saw him as the father of Gnostic heresy, claiming he went to Rome and was honoured as a god. These traditions mix fact and legend.

Magic. Mageuōn: sorcery, the practice of manipulating spiritual powers. Widespread in the ancient world (19:19).

On a Tuesday. Fascination with magic, astrology and the occult is still common. The gospel brings something far greater.
verseByVerse.note: Later Christian writers regarded this Simon (often called Simon Magus) as an early false teacher; from his name comes “simony,” the buying of church office.

verseByVerse.quote: They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, "This man is the power of God that is called Great." And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon had won everyone’s attention by claiming to be the great power of God.

The Great Power. Perhaps Simon claimed to be a divine being, an emanation of God.

Amazed. Simon amazed people; Philip’s miracles amazed Simon (v. 13).

On a Tuesday. Charismatic personalities can captivate whole communities. Test claims of spiritual power by Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they believed Philip as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the Samaritans believe the good news of the kingdom and of Jesus, they are baptised, and even Simon professes faith.

The kingdom and the name. Philip’s message: God’s reign has arrived in Jesus.

Men and women. Baptism followed belief. No infants are mentioned here.

Simon believed. Was his faith genuine? The rest of the story suggests not: Peter says his heart is not right with God and he is in the bond of iniquity (vv. 21–23). His “faith” was fascination with power. Jesus warned of those who say “Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name” but whom he never knew (Matthew 7:22–23). Baptism does not guarantee new birth.

On a Tuesday. Being impressed by Christianity is not the same as trusting Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles send Peter and John to confirm and join this new work to the church.

Sent Peter and John. The apostles confirm the new work. John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village: “Lord, do you want us to tell fire to come down from heaven and consume them?” (Luke 9:54). Now he prays for the Samaritans to receive the Spirit.

On a Tuesday. God can change our prejudices. Whom did you once despise that you now pray for?
verseByVerse.note: John had once wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village.

verseByVerse.quote: for he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them and they received the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit is given through the apostles so that Samaritan and Jewish believers are seen to be one church.

Not yet received. Unusual: elsewhere the Spirit is given at faith (2:38; 10:44; Romans 8:9). Why the delay?

Pentecostals see a pattern: conversion first, Spirit baptism later.

Roman Catholics see the origin of confirmation: the bishop’s laying on of hands confers the Spirit.

Some say the Samaritans’ faith was defective until the apostles came.

Most Reformed and evangelical interpreters see a unique moment in salvation history: the first time the gospel crossed the Jew–Samaritan divide.

Verdict: the last. God withheld the Spirit until the apostles came, so that the Samaritans would not form a rival church, and so that the Jerusalem apostles would see with their own eyes that God accepted Samaritans. It was a “Samaritan Pentecost”, as there will be a Gentile Pentecost in chapter 10. It was not meant as a pattern for all believers.

On a Tuesday. God cares about the unity of his church across ethnic and historic divides. So should we.
verseByVerse.note: The apostles’ presence tied the Samaritan believers to the church in Jerusalem, with one Spirit in one church.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, "Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon tries to buy the power to give the Spirit, treating God’s gift as a trade.

Simon saw. Something visible happened, perhaps tongues or prophecy.

Offered money. Simon saw spiritual power as a technique to acquire, like a trade secret magicians bought and sold. From his name comes “simony”, the medieval sin of buying church offices.

On a Tuesday. Watch out for any thinking that treats God’s gifts as products to purchase: paying for blessings, healing or position.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money! You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter declares that God’s gift cannot be bought, and that Simon’s heart is not right with God.

Perish with you. Literally “to destruction”. J. B. Phillips once translated it, “To hell with you and your money!” Peter is not cursing casually but declaring that Simon is on the road to ruin.

The gift of God. The Spirit is a gift, not for sale.

No part. Simon had no share in the kingdom. His baptism was empty.

On a Tuesday. No amount of money can buy God’s favour, and no amount of giving earns it.

parallels.desc: Gehazi takes silver for Elisha’s healing
give without pay

verseByVerse.quote: "Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter calls Simon to repent and pray, for he is still bound by bitterness and sin.

Repent. Even after so severe a rebuke, Peter offers hope.

If possible. Not doubt about God’s mercy, but about whether Simon will truly repent.

The gall of bitterness. Echoing Moses’ warning against “a root bearing poisonous and bitter fruit” in Israel: someone who turns to other gods while thinking himself safe (Deuteronomy 29:18).

The bond of iniquity. Chained by sin. Simon was still a slave.

On a Tuesday. Bitterness poisons. If it is growing in you, bring it to God today.
verseByVerse.note: “Gall of bitterness” echoes Moses’ warning about a root bearing poisonous fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: And Simon answered, "Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me." Now when they had testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simon asks for prayer to escape punishment, and the apostles preach in many Samaritan villages on their way home.

Pray for me. Simon asks for prayer to avoid punishment, not for a new heart. Fear of consequences is not repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10).

Many villages. Peter and John themselves now preach to Samaritans on their way home.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself: am I sorry for sin, or sorry for its consequences?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 26–40 — Philip and the Ethiopian Eunuch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: An angel of the Lord told Philip to go south to the desert road that runs from Jerusalem down to Gaza. On the way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, a senior official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake, queen of the Ethiopians. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and on his way home was sitting in his chariot reading the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit told Philip to go to that chariot and stay near it. Philip ran up, heard the man reading Isaiah and asked whether he understood it. He replied that he could not unless someone explained it, and invited Philip to sit with him. He was reading the passage about one led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent like a lamb before its shearer, humiliated and denied justice, whose life was taken from the earth. The eunuch asked whom the prophet meant, himself or someone else. Philip began with that very passage and told him the good news about Jesus. As they travelled they came to some water, and the eunuch asked what stood in the way of his being baptised. He ordered the chariot to stop, and both went down into the water and Philip baptised him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. Philip appeared at Azotus and preached the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.
verseByVerse.theology:
Isaiah 53 and the Death of the Servant

Philip began with this Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus, and the Scripture was the last of Isaiah's Servant Songs. It is the passage in the Old Testament that comes nearest to explaining what a cross is for: the Servant is pierced for our transgressions and crushed for our iniquities, the chastisement that brought us peace was upon him, and with his wounds we are healed. Notice the grammar, because the Reformed tradition has always insisted that everything turns on it: the transgressions are ours, the wounds are his, and the exchange is the entire point. He is not merely an instance of innocent suffering, of which the world has always had an ample supply. He is a substitute — the guiltless one bearing what the guilty had coming, so that the guilty go free. That is what Philip preached from. And it is worth noticing that he did not have to argue his way to Christ across a long distance. He started at Isaiah 53 and the road was short.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: A man barred from the assembly by Deuteronomy 23:1 was reading a scroll which, three chapters past where he had it open, promised eunuchs a name in God's house better than sons and daughters. He was reading his own exclusion, and without knowing it his own invitation. Now: The people most certain the door is shut to them are usually the ones who know the rules best. It was not a careless man who needed telling that nothing prevented him. It was the man who had read the regulation and accepted it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, "Rise and go toward the south to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza." This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends Philip from a city revival to a desert road, for one man: a royal official of Ethiopia.

From a revival to a desert. Philip leaves a city-wide awakening for one man on a lonely road.

Gaza. The last town before the desert route to Egypt.

Ethiopia. Not modern Ethiopia, but the ancient kingdom of Kush or Meroë, on the Nile in what is now Sudan. To Greeks and Romans it was the edge of the known world. “Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm 68:31).

Candace. A title, not a name: Kandake, the queen mother who ruled in Meroë.

A eunuch. Castrated men often served royal courts. Under the law a eunuch could not enter the assembly of the LORD (Deuteronomy 23:1), so this man, though he worshipped Israel’s God, was kept at a distance in the temple. But Isaiah promised eunuchs who keep God’s covenant, “I will give in my house and within my walls a monument and a name better than sons and daughters” (Isaiah 56:4–5). Now that promise is fulfilled.

On a Tuesday. God may send you away from a busy, fruitful place to meet one person. Be ready to go.
verseByVerse.note: Gaza was the last town on the road to Egypt. “Ethiopia” here is the kingdom south of Egypt (in modern Sudan); Candace was the title of its ruling queen. The law barred eunuchs from the assembly, but Isaiah promised them a place.

parallels.desc: to the eunuchs … a name better than sons and daughters
Cush shall hasten to stretch out her hands to God

verseByVerse.quote: and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, "Go over and join this chariot."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit leads Philip to a seeker already reading Isaiah.

Reading Isaiah. A scroll was expensive; he had probably bought it in Jerusalem. People read aloud in the ancient world.

The Spirit said. The angel started Philip on the road; the Spirit guided him to the chariot.

On a Tuesday. God prepares people before we arrive. Pray for God to lead you to someone already searching.
verseByVerse.note: People usually read aloud. A scroll of Isaiah was a costly possession.

verseByVerse.quote: So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, "Do you understand what you are reading?" And he said, "How can I, unless someone guides me?" And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip begins with a simple question, and the Ethiopian admits he needs someone to explain.

Philip ran. Eager obedience.

Do you understand? A wordplay in Greek: ginōskeis ha anaginōskeis, “do you know what you are reading?”

Someone to guide. Scripture is clear in its central message, but God uses teachers to help us understand (Ephesians 4:11). Humility asks for help.

On a Tuesday. Offer to read the Bible with someone. Many want to understand but need a guide.
verseByVerse.note: A wordplay in Greek: “Do you understand (ginōskeis) what you are reading (anaginōskeis)?”

verseByVerse.quote: Now the passage of the Scripture that he was reading was this: "Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The passage is Isaiah 53: the servant led silently to slaughter.

Isaiah 53:7–8. The heart of the fourth Servant Song (Isaiah 52:13–53:12), about a Servant who suffers silently for the sins of others and is then exalted.

The Greek version. The quotation follows the Greek Old Testament, which differs slightly from the Hebrew.

His generation. “Who can describe his descendants?” Perhaps: he died without children. Fitting words for a eunuch to read. But Isaiah 53:10 says “he shall see his offspring”: the Servant will have spiritual descendants, and the eunuch was about to become one.

On a Tuesday. Read Isaiah 53 this week, slowly, thinking of Jesus.

parallels.desc: like a sheep he was led to the slaughter

verseByVerse.quote: And the eunuch said to Philip, "About whom, I ask you, does the prophet say this, about himself or about someone else?" Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this Scripture he told him the good news about Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great question, who is the prophet speaking of, opens the way for Philip to tell him about Jesus.

The great question. Jewish interpreters had various answers: the prophet himself, Israel as a nation, or the Messiah. Philip says: Jesus.

Beginning with this Scripture. Philip started where the man was. Jesus did the same on the Emmaus road: “beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke 24:27).

On a Tuesday. Start where people are, with their questions, and lead them to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, "See, here is water! What prevents me from being baptized?" And Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." And he answered and said, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith leads straight to a request for baptism.

What prevents me? Philip must have explained baptism. Perhaps the eunuch wondered whether, as a eunuch and a foreigner, he would be excluded again, as he had been from the temple. Nothing prevents him.

A textual note. Verse 37 (“And Philip said, ‘If you believe with all your heart, you may.’ And he replied, ‘I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God’”) is in the KJV but absent from the earliest and best manuscripts. It was probably added from early baptismal practice, where a confession of faith was required. Its content is true, but it was not part of what Luke wrote, which is why modern translations put it in a footnote.

On a Tuesday. No barrier of race, disability or past can keep anyone from Christ who believes.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 37: Philip says “If you believe with all your heart, you may,” and the eunuch replies, “I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God.”

parallels.desc: can anyone withhold water for baptizing?

verseByVerse.quote: And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him. And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip baptises him, then is taken away, and the Ethiopian goes home rejoicing.

Down into the water. Both went down into the water. This suggests immersion, the earliest practice, though the phrase could describe stepping into water for pouring. Baptists and many others see immersion as the clearest picture of burial and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:4). Verdict: immersion is the most likely New Testament practice, though the validity of baptism does not depend on the amount of water.

Carried away. A miraculous removal, like the prophet Elijah: “the Spirit of the LORD will carry you I know not where” (1 Kings 18:12).

Rejoicing. The eunuch went home alone, with no church nearby, but with Christ, Scripture and joy. Ethiopian Christians traditionally trace their faith to him.

A textual note. Some Western manuscripts expand: “the Holy Spirit fell on the eunuch, and an angel of the Lord caught up Philip”. The shorter reading is original.

For worship. Thank God that the gospel reached the ends of the earth, and reached you.

parallels.desc: the Spirit of the LORD caught him up

verseByVerse.quote: But Philip found himself at Azotus, and as he passed through he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip continues preaching through the coastal towns until he settles in Caesarea.

Azotus. The old Philistine city of Ashdod, on the coast.

Caesarea. Caesarea Maritima, the Roman capital of Judea, built by Herod the Great. Philip settled there, and twenty years later Paul stayed in his home, where his four unmarried daughters prophesied (21:8–9).

All the towns. Philip kept preaching wherever he went.

On a Tuesday. Whatever town you are in this week, you can share the gospel there.
verseByVerse.note: Azotus is Ashdod, on the coast. Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, became Philip’s home.

8.theology: The Gospel Breaks Every Barrier. Acts 8 is the chapter in which the gospel crosses its first major boundary — from Jews to Samaritans, and then from Israel to Africa. This is not accidental; it is the working out of Acts 1:8: Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, ends of the earth. The Ethiopian eunuch is the first representative of the “ends of the earth” in the book — geographically distant, ethnically foreign, ritually excluded. And the gospel reaches him on a desert road through a text he happened to be reading. This is the Reformed doctrine of effectual calling in action: the Spirit directs the preacher, opens the Scriptures, and draws the seeker. Nothing is left to chance. The God who elects a people from every tongue and tribe and nation uses the ordinary means — a man, a chariot, a scroll — to accomplish his extraordinary purposes.
8.examples:
Then: Scattered believers, fleeing for their lives, who could not stop preaching. A deacon pulled off a city-wide revival and then redirected to one man on a road. An African official who came to Jerusalem seeking God and left having found him in the most unexpected way. The gospel in chapter 8 is gloriously uncontrollable.

Now: The church tends to think of mission in terms of programs and strategies. Acts 8 shows God doing his best work through disruption — persecution that scatters, divine direction that redirects, a Scripture passage that raises exactly the right question. The lesson is not that we should abandon planning, but that we must hold our plans loosely enough that we can hear “go over and join this chariot” when the Spirit speaks it.

9.title: The Road to Damascus
9.text: <sup>1</sup>But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest <sup>2</sup>and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem. <sup>3</sup>Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. <sup>4</sup>And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” <sup>5</sup>And he said, “Who are you, Lord?” And he said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. <sup>6</sup>But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do.” <sup>7</sup>The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. <sup>8</sup>Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus. <sup>9</sup>And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank. <sup>10</sup>Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” And he said, “Here I am, Lord.” <sup>11</sup>And the Lord said to him, “Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying, <sup>12</sup>and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight.” <sup>13</sup>But Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. <sup>14</sup>And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name.” <sup>15</sup>But the Lord said to him, “Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. <sup>16</sup>For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name.” <sup>17</sup>So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” <sup>18</sup>And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized; <sup>19</sup>and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. <sup>20</sup>And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.” <sup>21</sup>And all who heard him were amazed and said, “Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?” <sup>22</sup>But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ. <sup>23</sup>When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, <sup>24</sup>but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him, <sup>25</sup>but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket. <sup>26</sup>And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. <sup>27</sup>But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus. <sup>28</sup>So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. <sup>29</sup>And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him. <sup>30</sup>And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. <sup>31</sup>So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied. <sup>32</sup>Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. <sup>33</sup>There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed. <sup>34</sup>And Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed.” And immediately he rose. <sup>35</sup>And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord. <sup>36</sup>Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. <sup>37</sup>In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room. <sup>38</sup>Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, “Please come to us without delay.” <sup>39</sup>So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. <sup>40</sup>But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, “Tabitha, arise.” And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up. <sup>41</sup>And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive. <sup>42</sup>And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. <sup>43</sup>And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
9.overview:
The chapter tells the most important conversion in church history; Luke tells it three times in Acts (here, 22:3–16 and 26:9–18). Saul of Tarsus, a brilliant young Pharisee, is so zealous against “the Way”, as the Christian movement was called, that he obtains letters from the high priest to arrest believers in the synagogues of Damascus, about 135 miles to the north-east. Near the city a blinding light flashes from heaven and a voice asks, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” It is Jesus. Blind, Saul is led into Damascus and fasts for three days. The Lord sends a frightened disciple named Ananias to lay hands on him, calling Saul his chosen instrument to carry his name to Gentiles, kings and Israel, and to suffer for it. Saul’s sight returns, he is filled with the Spirit and baptised, and at once he preaches in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

The persecutor becomes the persecuted. After some time, including a period in Arabia (Galatians 1:17), plots in Damascus force him to escape in a basket over the wall. In Jerusalem the believers are afraid of him until Barnabas vouches for him; when Greek-speaking Jews try to kill him, the church sends him home to Tarsus. The church enjoys a season of peace and growth. Luke then returns to Peter, who heals a paralysed man named Aeneas at Lydda and raises a beloved disciple named Tabitha (Dorcas) from death at Joppa, and stays there in the house of a tanner, setting the scene for chapter 10.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Saul, still breathing murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples, went to the high priest and asked for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, men or women, he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem. As he neared Damascus, a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He asked who it was, and the reply came: “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” His companions stood speechless; they heard the sound but saw no one. Saul got up, but when he opened his eyes he could see nothing, so they led him by the hand into Damascus. For three days he was blind and did not eat or drink. In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias, whom the Lord called in a vision and sent to the house of Judas on Straight Street to ask for Saul of Tarsus, who was praying and had seen in a vision a man named Ananias come and lay hands on him to restore his sight. Ananias protested that he had heard how much harm this man had done to the Lord’s people in Jerusalem, and that he had come with authority to arrest everyone who called on the Lord’s name. But the Lord told him to go, for this man was his chosen instrument to proclaim his name to the Gentiles, their kings and the people of Israel, and the Lord would show him how much he must suffer for his name. So Ananias went, laid his hands on Saul and called him brother, saying the Lord Jesus who appeared to him on the road had sent him so that Saul might see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Immediately something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes and he could see. He got up and was baptised, and after eating he regained his strength. He spent several days with the disciples in Damascus and at once began to preach in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. All who heard him were astonished, asking whether this was not the man who had caused havoc among those who call on this name in Jerusalem, and had come to take them as prisoners. Yet Saul grew more and more powerful and baffled the Jews in Damascus by proving that Jesus is the Messiah. After many days the Jews conspired to kill him, watching the city gates day and night, but Saul learned of their plan, and his followers lowered him in a basket through an opening in the wall. When he came to Jerusalem he tried to join the disciples, but they were all afraid of him, not believing he was really a disciple. Barnabas took him to the apostles and told them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road and how he had preached fearlessly in Damascus in Jesus’ name. So Saul stayed with them, moving freely in Jerusalem and speaking boldly in the Lord’s name. He talked and debated with the Greek-speaking Jews, but they tried to kill him. When the believers learned of this, they took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus. Then the church throughout Judea, Galilee and Samaria enjoyed peace and was strengthened. Living in the fear of the Lord and encouraged by the Holy Spirit, it increased in numbers.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Sovereignty of Grace in Conversion

Saul's conversion is the purest demonstration in the New Testament of grace that does not wait to be wanted. He was not seeking Christ; he was hunting Christians. He was not wavering, not quietly troubled, not secretly drawn — he was riding to Damascus with an arrest warrant in his bag. Nothing in the account suggests any prior movement toward faith, and Paul himself, looking back, never once describes his conversion as a search that ended. He describes it as being laid hold of. Reformed theology has read it as the pattern rather than the exception: everybody who comes to Christ was, in one degree or another, going the other way when God stopped them, and the difference between Saul and a quieter case is a matter of speed and lighting rather than of mechanism. It is also the passage that makes despair about anybody unreasonable. The church's most violent enemy would go on to write a great part of its Scriptures, and not one person in Jerusalem could have guessed it.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Ananias was told to go to the man who had done much evil to the saints in Jerusalem and who was carrying a warrant that covered Ananias himself. He said what he thought about it, out loud, to God — and then he went, and the first word out of his mouth was brother. Now: The church's most persuasive argument has always been the existence of people in it who ought, by every reasonable calculation, to be enemies. That is not an argument anybody constructs. It is one a congregation either exhibits or does not.

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, still breathing threats and murder against the disciples of the Lord, went to the high priest and asked him for letters to the synagogues at Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, men or women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul, still raging, seeks authority to arrest followers of the Way as far away as Damascus.

Breathing threats. Persecution was his very breath.

Letters. The high priest had authority over Jewish communities in religious matters, and the Romans tolerated it. The letters would ask the synagogue leaders in Damascus to hand over Christian Jews.

Damascus. An ancient city in Syria, about 135 miles (220 km) north-east of Jerusalem, a week’s journey, with a large Jewish community. Believers had fled there.

The Way. An early name for the Christian movement (19:9, 23; 22:4; 24:14), perhaps from Jesus’ words, “I am the way” (John 14:6).

Saul’s zeal. He later said, “as to zeal, a persecutor of the church” (Philippians 3:6). He thought he was serving God (John 16:2).

On a Tuesday. Zeal is not the same as being right. Sincere people can be sincerely wrong.
verseByVerse.note: Damascus lay about 135 miles north-east of Jerusalem and had a large Jewish community. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian movement.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as he went on his way, he approached Damascus, and suddenly a light from heaven shone around him. And falling to the ground, he heard a voice saying to him, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The risen Jesus confronts Saul on the road, identifying himself with the people Saul is persecuting.

A light from heaven. At midday, brighter than the sun (26:13). The glory of the risen Christ.

Saul, Saul. The doubled name, as God called Abraham, Jacob, Moses and Samuel (Genesis 22:11; 46:2; Exodus 3:4; 1 Samuel 3:10).

Persecuting me. Not “my followers” but “me”. Christ is so united with his people that what is done to them is done to him (Matthew 25:40). Paul’s later teaching on the church as Christ’s body may have its roots in this moment.

Converted or called? Some scholars (Krister Stendahl) argue that Paul was not converted from one religion to another, but called, like a prophet, to a new task within Judaism. Verdict: both. Paul himself speaks of a prophetic call (Galatians 1:15–16; Jeremiah 1:5), but also of a radical turning from his old righteousness to Christ (Philippians 3:4–9). He was a sinner saved by grace (1 Timothy 1:13–16), and an apostle sent.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond the reach of Christ. Pray for the most hostile opponent of the gospel you know.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said, "I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting. But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you are to do."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The persecutor learns that the Lord he serves is Jesus, and he is told to wait for instructions.

Who are you, Lord? “Lord” may at first be a respectful address, but Saul knows he is facing a heavenly being.

I am Jesus. The shattering answer. The crucified man Saul hated is alive and Lord of glory. Everything Saul believed was overturned in a moment.

Go into the city. Christ uses an ordinary disciple to complete the work.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add here: “it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks. And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” These words were borrowed from Paul’s later accounts (26:14; 22:10) and are not in the earliest manuscripts of chapter 9.

On a Tuesday. Every Christian’s story has this moment, quiet or dramatic: discovering that Jesus is Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: The men who were traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one. Saul rose from the ground, and although his eyes were opened, he saw nothing. So they led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His companions witness something, but only Saul sees the Lord, and he is led blind into the city.

Hearing but not seeing. In 22:9 Paul says his companions “did not understand the voice”. Not a contradiction. The Greek verb “hear” can mean “hear a sound” or “understand words”. They heard a noise but did not understand the words; only Saul did. Compare John 12:28–29, where a voice from heaven sounded to some like thunder.

Led by the hand. The proud persecutor, who came to lead prisoners, is led like a child.

On a Tuesday. God sometimes humbles us before he uses us.
verseByVerse.note: In 22:9 Paul says his companions did not understand the voice; they heard a sound but not the words.

verseByVerse.quote: And for three days he was without sight, and neither ate nor drank.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three days of blindness and fasting mark the death of the old Saul.

Three days. A period of darkness before light, like Jesus’ three days in the tomb. Saul’s old life was dying.

Fasting. Shock, repentance and prayer (v. 11).

On a Tuesday. If you are in a time of darkness after a great change, God is still at work.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a disciple at Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, "Ananias." And he said, "Here I am, Lord." And the Lord said to him, "Rise and go to the street called Straight, and at the house of Judas look for a man of Tarsus named Saul, for behold, he is praying,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord calls an ordinary disciple, Ananias, to go to the persecutor.

Ananias. An ordinary disciple, “a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews” (22:12). Not the Ananias of chapter 5.

Here I am, Lord. Like Samuel (1 Samuel 3:10). Ready to listen.

Straight Street. The main east–west street of Damascus, still there today, called Via Recta by the Romans.

Tarsus. A major city in Cilicia, famous for its university and philosophers: “no obscure city” (21:39).

He is praying. The persecutor has become a man of prayer.

On a Tuesday. God uses ordinary believers at key moments. You may be someone’s Ananias.
verseByVerse.note: Straight Street still runs east–west through the old city of Damascus. Tarsus was a major city in Cilicia, known for learning.

verseByVerse.quote: and he has seen in a vision a man named Ananias come in and lay his hands on him so that he might regain his sight."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has already prepared Saul to receive Ananias.

Two visions. God prepared both men. When God brings two people together for his purposes, he often works on both sides.

On a Tuesday. When you feel prompted to speak to someone about Christ, God may already be preparing them.

verseByVerse.quote: But Ananias answered, "Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to your saints at Jerusalem. And here he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call on your name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ananias’s fear is understandable: Saul came to arrest people like him.

Ananias’s fear. Natural and honest. He tells the Lord what the Lord already knows.

Your saints. All believers are “holy ones”, set apart for God.

Call on your name. A definition of Christians: those who pray to Jesus as Lord (1 Corinthians 1:2).

On a Tuesday. It is fine to tell God honestly that you are afraid of what he asks. Then obey.
verseByVerse.note: “Saints” means those set apart as God’s holy people — all believers.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord said to him, "Go, for he is a chosen instrument of mine to carry my name before the Gentiles and kings and the children of Israel. For I will show him how much he must suffer for the sake of my name."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord has chosen Saul as his instrument to carry his name to Gentiles, kings and Israel, and to suffer for it.

A chosen instrument. Skeuos eklogēs: a vessel of election. Saul did not choose Christ; Christ chose him. Paul later wrote that God “set me apart before I was born, and … called me by his grace” (Galatians 1:15). A clear example of God’s sovereign, effectual call: Saul was not seeking Christ but fighting him.

Gentiles, kings, Israel. A summary of Paul’s future ministry: to the nations, before rulers (Agrippa, Festus, Caesar), and to Jews.

How much he must suffer. The persecutor will be persecuted. Suffering was part of the calling (2 Corinthians 11:23–28).

On a Tuesday. If God has saved you, he has a purpose for you. Ask him what it is.

verseByVerse.quote: So Ananias departed and entered the house. And laying his hands on him he said, "Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus who appeared to you on the road by which you came has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit." And immediately something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. Then he rose and was baptized;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ananias calls Saul brother, his sight is restored, he is filled with the Spirit and he is baptised.

Brother Saul. The first word Saul hears from a Christian is “brother”. The man he came to arrest welcomes him into the family.

Filled with the Spirit. Through a non-apostle. Paul’s apostleship came directly from Christ, not from the Twelve (Galatians 1:1, 12).

Scales. Luke the doctor describes it precisely. Physical and spiritual sight restored together.

Baptised. At once, as the outward sign of his new life (22:16, “Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name”).

On a Tuesday. Welcome new believers warmly, whatever their past. Call them “brother” and “sister”.

verseByVerse.quote: and taking food, he was strengthened. For some days he was with the disciples at Damascus. And immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, "He is the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul immediately preaches in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God.

With the disciples. Saul joined the people he had come to destroy.

Immediately. No long delay before witness.

The Son of God. The only use of this title in Acts. Saul’s message from the beginning: Jesus is divine.

Arabia. At some point in this period Saul went to Arabia, the Nabataean kingdom south and east of Damascus, perhaps to preach or to reflect, before returning (Galatians 1:17, “I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus”). Luke does not mention it.

On a Tuesday. New Christians can witness straight away. Their story of change is powerful.
verseByVerse.note: Paul says he also went to Arabia (the Nabataean kingdom) before returning to Damascus.

verseByVerse.quote: And all who heard him were amazed and said, "Is not this the man who made havoc in Jerusalem of those who called upon this name? And has he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?" But Saul increased all the more in strength, and confounded the Jews who lived in Damascus by proving that Jesus was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone is amazed at the change, and Saul grows stronger in proving that Jesus is the Christ.

Amazed. The change was undeniable.

Proving. Symbibazōn: putting together, showing by comparing Scriptures. Saul used his training in the Old Testament to show that Jesus fulfilled it.

On a Tuesday. Use your gifts and training, now redeemed, for Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: When many days had passed, the Jews plotted to kill him, but their plot became known to Saul. They were watching the gates day and night in order to kill him,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The persecutor becomes the persecuted: his former allies plot to kill him.

Many days. Probably about three years, including the time in Arabia (Galatians 1:18).

The plot. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas of the Nabataeans was also guarding the city to arrest him (2 Corinthians 11:32). Saul had made enemies among Jews and Nabataean officials alike.

On a Tuesday. Faithfulness can bring opposition quickly. Do not be surprised.
verseByVerse.note: “Many days” probably covers about three years. Paul adds that the governor under King Aretas was guarding the city.

verseByVerse.quote: but his disciples took him by night and let him down through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The new disciples help him escape over the wall in a basket.

His disciples. Saul already had followers who believed through him.

A basket. A large rope basket, used for goods. Paul later boasted of this humiliating escape as a sign of weakness (2 Corinthians 11:32–33, “I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall”).

On a Tuesday. Sometimes the wise course is to escape danger, not to stay and die. Jesus also withdrew at times (Luke 4:30).

parallels.desc: let down in a basket through a window in the wall

verseByVerse.quote: And when he had come to Jerusalem, he attempted to join the disciples. And they were all afraid of him, for they did not believe that he was a disciple. But Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles and declared to them how on the road he had seen the Lord, who spoke to him, and how at Damascus he had preached boldly in the name of Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Jerusalem the disciples fear him until Barnabas vouches for him.

Afraid. Understandable: they suspected a trick.

Barnabas. The “son of encouragement” (4:36) lives up to his name. He took a risk on Saul when no one else would. Paul says he saw only Peter and James on this visit, which lasted fifteen days (Galatians 1:18–19).

On a Tuesday. Is there a new believer, or someone with a bad reputation, whom you could take under your wing?
verseByVerse.note: Barnabas was a respected believer from Cyprus.

parallels.desc: Paul visits Cephas and James

verseByVerse.quote: So he went in and out among them at Jerusalem, preaching boldly in the name of the Lord. And he spoke and disputed against the Hellenists. But they were seeking to kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Saul preaches boldly in Jerusalem and debates the Greek-speaking Jews, as Stephen had.

Boldly. The same courage as the apostles (4:13, 31).

The Hellenists. The Greek-speaking Jews who had opposed Stephen (6:9). Saul had been one of them. Now he takes up Stephen’s argument, and they try to kill him as they killed Stephen.

On a Tuesday. God can make a former opponent of the gospel its most effective advocate.
verseByVerse.note: The Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jews — the group that had opposed Stephen.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When his life is in danger, the believers send him home to Tarsus.

The brothers. The church protected Saul.

Tarsus. Saul’s home town. He spent several years there, probably preaching in Cilicia and Syria (Galatians 1:21), until Barnabas fetched him to Antioch (11:25–26). These are sometimes called Paul’s “silent years”, perhaps when he had the vision of 2 Corinthians 12:2.

On a Tuesday. God sometimes sends his servants into a quiet season before a great work. Do not despise yours.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea was the port; Tarsus was Paul’s home city.

parallels.desc: the regions of Syria and Cilicia

verseByVerse.quote: So the church throughout all Judea and Galilee and Samaria had peace and was being built up. And walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church throughout the land has peace, grows, and lives in the fear of the Lord and the comfort of the Spirit.

The church. Singular, spread across three regions. One church in many places.

Peace. The persecutor had become a preacher. Perhaps also because the Roman emperor Caligula’s attempt to put his statue in the temple (around AD 40) distracted the Jewish authorities.

Fear and comfort. Reverence for the Lord and the Spirit’s encouragement together. A healthy church has both.

Galilee. The only mention in Acts of churches in Galilee, where Jesus ministered.

For worship. Thank God for seasons of peace in your church. Use them for growth.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 32–43 — Peter's Ministry in Lydda and Joppa
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As Peter travelled about the country, he went to visit the Lord’s people in Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, paralysed and bedridden for eight years. Peter told him that Jesus Christ was healing him and to get up and roll up his mat, and Aeneas got up at once. Everyone in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord. In Joppa there was a disciple named Tabitha (in Greek, Dorcas), always doing good and helping the poor. She became ill and died, and her body was washed and laid in an upstairs room. Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples sent two men to urge Peter to come at once. When he arrived he was taken upstairs, where all the widows stood around him crying and showing him the robes and other clothing Dorcas had made while she was with them. Peter sent them all out, knelt and prayed. Turning to the body, he said, “Tabitha, get up.” She opened her eyes, saw Peter and sat up. He took her hand and helped her to her feet, then called the believers, especially the widows, and presented her to them alive. This became known all over Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. Peter stayed in Joppa for some time with a tanner named Simon.
verseByVerse.theology:
Resurrection as the Power Behind Healing and New Life

The raising of Tabitha is told in a way that deliberately recalls the raising of Jairus's daughter — the mourners put outside, the taking of the hand, the command to rise, the girl presented back to her people. Peter is not improvising, and he is not exercising a power of his own; he is doing what he had watched being done, in the name of the one who did it and who was himself raised afterwards. That is why he kneels first. Reformed theology has read every healing and raising in Acts as a sign rather than a policy: a working sample of the new creation, offered in advance and on a small scale, of the day when everything sin and death have broken is put right permanently. Which is also why these events are rare rather than routine even in Acts. A sign that happened every time would not be a sign; it would be the arrangement, and the arrangement is still to come.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: When Tabitha died, the widows stood in the room holding up the coats and the dresses she had made, and Luke notes that she had made them while she was with them. That is what her ministry consisted of, and it is what the church had to show for her. Now: It is worth asking what would be held up. Not what would be said at the service, which is a different question and easier — but what could be carried into the room and shown.

verseByVerse.quote: Now as Peter went here and there among them all, he came down also to the saints who lived at Lydda. There he found a man named Aeneas, bedridden for eight years, who was paralyzed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter’s travels bring him to Lydda, where a man has been paralysed for eight years.

Lydda. Modern Lod, near Tel Aviv’s airport, about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem. The church there probably began through believers scattered after Stephen’s death, or through Philip (8:40).

Aeneas. A Greek name (the hero of Virgil’s epic of Rome’s founding).

Eight years. A chronic, hopeless case.

On a Tuesday. Visit believers who are housebound. They are often forgotten.
verseByVerse.note: Lydda (modern Lod) lay about 25 miles north-west of Jerusalem, on the road to the coast.

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you; rise and make your bed." And immediately he rose. And all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus Christ heals Aeneas through Peter, and the region turns to the Lord.

Jesus Christ heals you. Present tense: Jesus is healing you now. Peter is clear that it is not his power.

Make your bed. Or “get yourself something to eat”; the phrase is uncertain. Either way, a practical sign of restored strength.

Sharon. The fertile coastal plain from Joppa to Caesarea.

Turned to the Lord. The purpose of the miracle: not spectacle, but conversion.

On a Tuesday. When God answers prayer, tell others so that they too may turn to the Lord.
verseByVerse.note: Sharon was the fertile coastal plain.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was in Joppa a disciple named Tabitha, which, translated, means Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity. In those days she became ill and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tabitha, known for her kindness to the poor, dies, and the church mourns.

Joppa. Modern Jaffa, the ancient port of Jerusalem. The port from which Jonah fled to avoid going to the Gentiles (Jonah 1:3, “went down to Joppa”). Here Peter will be sent to the Gentiles.

Tabitha, Dorcas. Both mean “gazelle”, in Aramaic and Greek. The only woman in the New Testament explicitly called a “disciple” (mathētria).

Good works and charity. Like the woman of Proverbs: “She opens her hand to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy” (Proverbs 31:20).

Washed. Jewish burial preparation. She was clearly dead.

On a Tuesday. Tabitha’s ministry was making clothes for widows. Practical kindness is a great ministry.
verseByVerse.note: Joppa (modern Jaffa) was the port from which Jonah sailed. Tabitha (Aramaic) and Dorcas (Greek) both mean “gazelle.”

verseByVerse.quote: Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging him, "Please come to us without delay."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The disciples send urgently for Peter, hoping for more than comfort.

Near. About 11 miles, a few hours’ walk.

Please come. The disciples had faith that something could be done, though she was dead.

On a Tuesday. In a crisis, call for your church’s elders and pray (James 5:14).
verseByVerse.note: Lydda was about 11 miles from Joppa.

verseByVerse.quote: So Peter rose and went with them. And when he arrived, they took him to the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing tunics and other garments that Dorcas made while she was with them. But Peter put them all outside, and knelt down and prayed; and turning to the body he said, "Tabitha, arise." And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter she sat up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Peter prays alone and, in the name of the Lord, calls the dead woman to rise.

The widows. The poor women she had clothed. Their grief and her garments are her memorial.

Put them outside. Exactly as Jesus did when he raised Jairus’s daughter, which Peter had witnessed (Mark 5:40).

Knelt and prayed. Peter had no power of his own.

Tabitha, arise. In Aramaic, Tabitha qumi, one letter different from Jesus’ words to Jairus’s daughter, Talitha cumi, “Little girl, I say to you, arise” (Mark 5:41). Peter does what he saw his Lord do.

On a Tuesday. Your good works may be remembered more than you know, by the people you helped.

parallels.desc: “Talitha cumi”

verseByVerse.quote: And he gave her his hand and raised her up. Then, calling the saints and widows, he presented her alive.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tabitha is restored to the widows she served, a sign of the Lord of life.

Gave her his hand. As Peter had raised the lame man (3:7).

Presented her alive. To the widows who loved her. A foretaste of the resurrection reunion.

What it does not mean. Tabitha was raised to mortal life and died again later. Resurrection to immortal life awaits the last day (1 Corinthians 15:52).

For worship. Thank God that death will not have the last word over those you love in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: And it became known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord. And he stayed in Joppa for many days with one Simon, a tanner.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many in Joppa believe, and Peter stays with a tanner, a hint of the barriers about to fall.

Many believed. Again the miracle leads to faith.

A tanner. Tanners worked with the hides of dead animals, which made them ritually unclean under Jewish law, and the smell of their trade meant they often lived on the edge of town. That Peter stayed with one shows he was already loosening his scruples, preparing for the vision of chapter 10, where God tells him not to call unclean what God has made clean.

On a Tuesday. Where you stay and with whom you eat can be a witness. Do not avoid people others consider unclean.
verseByVerse.note: Tanners handled the skins of dead animals, a trade many Jews regarded as unclean — a hint of the lesson Peter is about to learn.

9.theology: Sovereign Grace in Conversion. The conversion of Saul is the New Testament’s clearest portrait of unconditional election and effectual calling. There is nothing in Saul that would attract God’s grace — he is actively persecuting the church, violently opposed to Christ, supremely confident in his own righteousness (Philippians 3:4–6). God chose him anyway. Not because of anything foreseen in him, but according to his own sovereign purpose — to display the fullness of his grace in the most unlikely vessel imaginable. Paul himself will later write that his conversion was designed to be a pattern, “an example to those who were to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:16). If God can save Saul of Tarsus, he can save anyone. That is the point. The doctrine of election is not a closed door; it is the foundation of missionary confidence.
9.examples:
Then: A church that had watched Saul drag their brothers and sisters to prison now had to welcome him as a brother. Understandably, they were afraid. It took Barnabas — son of encouragement — to stand between the suspicious church and the new apostle and vouch for the reality of his conversion. The church that had prayed for boldness now needed faith to receive the answer.

Now: No one is beyond the reach of sovereign grace. The person who seems most violently opposed to the gospel may be the one God is about to apprehend. This is not a reason for naivety; it is a reason for prayer — the kind of prayer that believes God can stop any Saul on any road at any time. The church’s task is to be ready, like Ananias, to say “brother” when the moment comes.

10.title: The Gospel to the Gentiles
10.text: <sup>1</sup>At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, <sup>2</sup>a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. <sup>3</sup>About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, “Cornelius.” <sup>4</sup>And he stared at him in terror and said, “What is it, Lord?” And he said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God. <sup>5</sup>And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. <sup>6</sup>He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea.” <sup>7</sup>When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, <sup>8</sup>and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa. <sup>9</sup>The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. <sup>10</sup>And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance <sup>11</sup>and saw the heavens opened and something like a great sheet descending, being let down by its four corners upon the earth. <sup>12</sup>In it were all kinds of animals and reptiles and birds of the air. <sup>13</sup>And there came a voice to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.” <sup>14</sup>But Peter said, “By no means, Lord; for I have never eaten anything that is common or unclean.” <sup>15</sup>And the voice came to him again a second time, “What God has made clean, do not call common.” <sup>16</sup>This happened three times, and the thing was taken up at once to heaven. <sup>17</sup>Now while Peter was inwardly perplexed as to what the vision that he had seen might mean, behold, the men who were sent by Cornelius, having made inquiry for Simon’s house, stood at the gate <sup>18</sup>and called out to ask whether Simon who was called Peter was lodging there. <sup>19</sup>And while Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Behold, three men are looking for you. <sup>20</sup>Rise and go down and accompany them without hesitation, for I have sent them.” <sup>21</sup>And Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are looking for. What is the reason for your coming?” <sup>22</sup>And they said, “Cornelius, a centurion, an upright and God-fearing man, who is well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to send for you to come to his house and to hear what you have to say.” <sup>23</sup>So he invited them in to be his guests. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him. <sup>24</sup>And on the following day they entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends. <sup>25</sup>When Peter entered, Cornelius met him and fell down at his feet and worshiped him. <sup>26</sup>But Peter lifted him up, saying, “Stand up; I too am a man.” <sup>27</sup>And as he talked with him, he went in and found many persons gathered. <sup>28</sup>And he said to them, “You yourselves know how unlawful it is for a Jew to associate with or to visit anyone of another nation, but God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. <sup>29</sup>So when I was sent for, I came without objection. I ask then why you sent for me.” <sup>30</sup>And Cornelius said, “Four days ago, about this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and behold, a man stood before me in bright clothing <sup>31</sup>and said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard and your alms have been remembered before God. <sup>32</sup>Send therefore to Joppa and ask for Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging in the house of Simon, a tanner, by the sea.’ <sup>33</sup>So I sent for you at once, and you have been kind enough to come. Now therefore we are all here in the presence of God to hear all that you have been commanded by the Lord.” <sup>34</sup>So Peter opened his mouth and said: “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality, <sup>35</sup>but in every nation anyone who fears him and does what is right is acceptable to him. <sup>36</sup>As for the word that he sent to Israel, preaching good news of peace through Jesus Christ (he is Lord of all), <sup>37</sup>you yourselves know what happened throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism that John proclaimed: <sup>38</sup>how God anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him. <sup>39</sup>And we are witnesses of all that he did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They put him to death by hanging him on a tree, <sup>40</sup>but God raised him on the third day and made him to appear, <sup>41</sup>not to all the people but to us who had been chosen by God as witnesses, who ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead. <sup>42</sup>And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that he is the one appointed by God to be judge of the living and the dead. <sup>43</sup>To him all the prophets bear witness that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through his name.” <sup>44</sup>While Peter was still saying these things, the Holy Spirit fell on all who heard the word. <sup>45</sup>And the believers from among the circumcised who had come with Peter were amazed, because the gift of the Holy Spirit was poured out even on the Gentiles. <sup>46</sup>For they were hearing them speaking in tongues and extolling God. Then Peter declared, <sup>47</sup>“Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” <sup>48</sup>And he commanded them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to remain for some days.
10.overview:
This is one of the turning points of Acts, so important that Luke tells it twice (again in chapter 11) and Peter retells it at the Jerusalem council (15:7–11). The gospel has reached Samaritans and one Ethiopian; now it reaches Gentiles as Gentiles. Cornelius is a Roman centurion stationed at Caesarea, the Roman capital of Judea, a “God-fearer”: a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God, prayed at the Jewish hours of prayer and gave generously to Jewish causes, but had not become a Jew by circumcision. In a vision at three in the afternoon an angel tells him that God has noticed his prayers and gifts, and that he should send to Joppa for Simon Peter.

The next day at noon, on a flat rooftop in Joppa, Peter sees a sheet let down from heaven full of animals the law of Moses called unclean, and hears a voice telling him to kill and eat. He refuses, and the voice answers: “What God has made clean, do not call common.” This happens three times. As he puzzles over it, Cornelius’s messengers arrive, and the Spirit tells him to go with them. Peter, who earlier would never have entered a Gentile’s house, goes to Caesarea, finds a house full of Cornelius’s relatives and friends, and declares that God shows no partiality. He preaches Jesus: anointed with the Spirit, doing good and healing, killed on a tree, raised on the third day, appointed judge of the living and the dead, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on the Gentiles, they speak in tongues and praise God, and Peter’s Jewish companions are astonished. Peter asks who could refuse them water for baptism, and they are baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–48 — Cornelius and the Gentile Pentecost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Cornelius, a God-fearing Roman centurion at Caesarea, is told by an angel to send for Peter in Joppa. The next day Peter, praying on a rooftop at noon, sees a sheet full of animals the law called unclean and hears a voice telling him to eat; when he refuses, the voice says three times that he must not call unclean what God has made clean. Cornelius’s messengers arrive, the Spirit tells Peter to go with them, and he travels to Caesarea, where he enters a Gentile home full of people waiting to hear him. Peter declares that God shows no favouritism and accepts people from every nation who fear him. He tells them about Jesus: anointed by the Spirit, doing good and healing, put to death on a cross, raised on the third day, seen by chosen witnesses, appointed judge of all, and the one through whom everyone who believes receives forgiveness. While he is still speaking, the Spirit falls on all the Gentiles listening, to the astonishment of Peter’s Jewish companions, and Peter has them baptised in the name of Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Clean and the Unclean, and What the Food Laws Were For

The sheet is full of animals and the argument is about people, and Peter himself makes the translation at verse 28: God has shown me that I should not call any person common or unclean. The food laws had never been about digestion. They were about difference — a daily, three-times-a-day mechanism for keeping Israel visibly distinct from the nations around it, and they worked, which is why a devout Jew could not eat at a Gentile table without the whole arrangement collapsing. Reformed theology has read the vision as the retirement of a shadow rather than the repeal of a word: the separation was always temporary, always pointing forward, and its purpose was fulfilled the moment the dividing wall of hostility came down in Christ (Ephesians 2:14). What is striking is the order in which Peter learned it. He did not reason his way from Christology to table fellowship. He was given a command he found repellent, obeyed it under protest, and worked out the theology afterwards — which is worth remembering by anyone who assumes conviction always precedes obedience.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Peter needed a vision repeated three times, a direct instruction from the Spirit, three men at the gate and the Spirit falling in front of witnesses before he would accept what he had been told plainly at the ascension. And even then the church argued about it for a chapter and a half. Now: The instinct to take the gospel to people like ourselves is not usually held as a conviction; it is held as an assumption, which is why it survives so much preaching against it. Peter did not have an opinion about Gentiles that could be corrected. He had a lifetime of habit, and it took God three goes.

verseByVerse.quote: At Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of what was known as the Italian Cohort, a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is about to open the door to the Gentiles, and he begins with a devout Roman officer in Caesarea.

Caesarea. Caesarea Maritima, built by Herod the Great as a Roman-style city with a huge artificial harbour, theatre and temple to Augustus. The Roman governors of Judea lived there. An inscription naming Pontius Pilate was found in its theatre.

A centurion. Commander of about eighty men, a career soldier and a respected figure. Every centurion in the New Testament is presented favourably (Luke 7:2–10; 23:47; Acts 27:43).

The Italian Cohort. A unit originally raised in Italy. Inscriptions mention a “second Italian cohort” in Syria in this period.

Devout and God-fearing. A “God-fearer”: a Gentile who worshipped the God of Israel, attended synagogue, kept some Jewish customs, but was not circumcised. Many such people were drawn to the gospel.

His household. His family, servants and perhaps soldiers.

On a Tuesday. Pray for soldiers, police and officials. God can reach people in every profession.
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea. A centurion commanded a company of about eighty soldiers. “God-fearers” were Gentiles who worshipped Israel’s God without becoming full converts.

parallels.desc: another centurion who loved the Jewish nation

verseByVerse.quote: About the ninth hour of the day he saw clearly in a vision an angel of God come in and say to him, "Cornelius." And he stared at him in terror and said, "What is it, Lord?" And he said to him, "Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has heard Cornelius’s prayers and gifts, and sends an angel to tell him so.

The ninth hour. 3 p.m., the Jewish hour of afternoon prayer (3:1). Cornelius kept Jewish prayer times.

A memorial. Language of sacrifice: part of the grain offering burned on the altar was called a “memorial portion” (Leviticus 2:2). Cornelius’s prayers and alms rose to God like an offering.

Was Cornelius already saved? Some (inclusivists) argue that Cornelius shows God accepts devout people of other faiths before they hear of Christ. Verdict: no. Peter later reports the angel’s words: Peter would “declare to you a message by which you will be saved” (11:14). Cornelius was seeking God, and God answered by sending the gospel. His prayers were heard, not as earning salvation, but as the cry of a seeker God was drawing.

On a Tuesday. Pray for seekers you know: people interested in God but not yet trusting Christ. God hears their prayers and may send you.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the ninth hour was about 3 p.m., the hour of afternoon prayer. A “memorial” offering was one that brought the worshipper to God’s remembrance.

parallels.desc: the memorial portion

verseByVerse.quote: "And now send men to Joppa and bring one Simon who is called Peter. He is lodging with one Simon, a tanner, whose house is by the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius must send for Peter: salvation will come through hearing the gospel from a messenger.

Why Peter? The angel could have explained the gospel himself. God has chosen to spread the gospel through human messengers (Romans 10:14).

By the sea. Tanners worked near water, and away from town because of the smell.

On a Tuesday. God has given the job of telling the gospel to people, not angels. That means you.

parallels.desc: Simon the tanner

verseByVerse.quote: When the angel who spoke to him had departed, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him, and having related everything to them, he sent them to Joppa.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Cornelius obeys at once, sending servants and a devout soldier to Joppa.

A devout soldier. Cornelius’s faith had spread to his men.

Immediate obedience. He acted at once.

On a Tuesday. When God speaks through his word, respond promptly.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day, as they were on their journey and approaching the city, Peter went up on the housetop about the sixth hour to pray. And he became hungry and wanted something to eat, but while they were preparing it, he fell into a trance
verseByVerse.commentary:
As the messengers approach, God prepares Peter while he prays on the roof at noon.

The sixth hour. Noon. Not an official Jewish hour of prayer, but devout Jews often prayed three times a day (Psalm 55:17; Daniel 6:10).

The roof. Flat roofs were used for rest, work and prayer, private and cool.
