The Lord’s hand was against him, and he would be blind for a time. Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about for someone to lead him by the hand. When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was amazed at the teaching about the Lord.
verseByVerse.theology:
Missionary Call and Corporate Discernment

The Spirit does not speak to Barnabas and Saul privately and send them to inform the church. He speaks in the assembly, to the assembly, about two men who are standing in it — and the church then fasts, prays, and lays hands on them before letting them go. Reformed ecclesiology has taken this as the pattern: an individual sense of call confirmed by a congregation, and a congregation's judgement confirmed by the Spirit, with neither operating alone. Notice also what the sending cost. Barnabas had been sent to build up that church and Saul was its finest teacher, and Antioch gave away both on the strength of one sentence in a prayer meeting. A church's seriousness about mission is not measured by what it collects for it but by whom it is willing to lose.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The list in verse 1 is the most cosmopolitan leadership team in the New Testament, and it was assembled by a persecution. Every man on it was in Antioch because something had gone wrong somewhere else. Now: Congregations tend to produce leaders who resemble each other, and to regard that as normal rather than as a symptom. Antioch did not set out to be diverse; it set out to preach to whoever was in front of it, and this is what the room looked like a few years later.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there were in the church at Antioch prophets and teachers, Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen a lifelong friend of Herod the tetrarch, and Saul. While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While a diverse church worships and fasts, the Spirit calls Barnabas and Saul to a new work: the first mission to the nations.

A diverse leadership. Barnabas, a Levite from Cyprus; Simeon “Niger” (Latin for “black”), perhaps African; Lucius from Cyrene in north Africa; Manaen, raised at court as a foster-brother of Herod Antipas, the ruler who killed John the Baptist; and Saul, a Pharisee from Tarsus. The church reflected the gospel’s reach.

Worshipping and fasting. The mission began in worship, not in a strategy meeting.

The Spirit said. Probably through one of the prophets. The Spirit speaks as a person, with his own will (“for me”, “I have called”).

Set apart. Their best leaders were sent away. A generous church gives its best for mission.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church to be willing to send its best people into mission, even if it costs.
verseByVerse.note: Niger is Latin for “black,” so Simeon may have been from Africa, like Lucius of Cyrene. Manaen had been brought up with Herod Antipas. Here begins Paul’s first missionary journey (13–14).

parallels.desc: set apart for the gospel of God

verseByVerse.quote: Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church confirms the Spirit’s call with fasting, prayer and the laying on of hands, and sends them.

Laying on hands. Commissioning for a specific task, with the church’s blessing. Not making them apostles, which Christ had already done.

Sent them off. Literally “released them”. The church released them; the Spirit sent them (v. 4).

On a Tuesday. Pray and fast before big decisions in your church.
verseByVerse.note: Laying on hands commissioned them for the task.

verseByVerse.quote: So, being sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia, and from there they sailed to Cyprus. When they arrived at Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the synagogues of the Jews. And they had John to assist them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sent by the Spirit, they begin in Cyprus, preaching first in the synagogues.

Seleucia. The port of Antioch, 16 miles west.

Cyprus. Barnabas’s home (4:36), famous for its copper (its name may come from the Greek word for copper). A large Jewish population.

Salamis. The main city in the east of the island.

Synagogues first. Paul’s regular method: start with Jews and God-fearers, who knew the Scriptures.

John. John Mark, as assistant (hypēretēs), perhaps handling practical arrangements, or teaching.

On a Tuesday. Start sharing the gospel with people who already know something of God.
verseByVerse.note: Seleucia was Antioch’s port. Cyprus was Barnabas’s home island; Salamis was its main city in the east. John is John Mark.

parallels.desc: to the Jew first

verseByVerse.quote: When they had gone through the whole island as far as Paphos, they came upon a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus. He was with the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence, who summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Paphos they meet the Roman governor and a Jewish sorcerer who serves him.

Paphos. The Roman capital of Cyprus, at the western end, famous for its temple of Aphrodite, who was said to have been born from the sea nearby.

Proconsul. Luke uses the correct title: Cyprus was a senatorial province governed by a proconsul. Luke’s precision with titles is one reason historians trust him.

Sergius Paulus. Inscriptions mention men of this family, including one Sergius Paulus who was a curator of the Tiber in Rome under Claudius, and family members in Pisidian Antioch, where Paul went next. Perhaps the proconsul suggested the destination.

Bar-Jesus. “Son of Joshua”, an ironic name for an enemy of Jesus. Roman officials often kept astrologers and seers.

On a Tuesday. Pray for intelligent, powerful people in your nation to want to hear God’s word.
verseByVerse.note: Paphos was the Roman capital of Cyprus, at the western end. A proconsul governed a province for the Roman Senate. Bar-Jesus means “son of Joshua.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Elymas the magician (for that is the meaning of his name) opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sorcerer opposes them, trying to keep the governor from faith.

Elymas. Perhaps from an Arabic or Aramaic word for “wise man” or “sorcerer”.

Opposed. He feared losing his influence. Spiritual warfare is real (Ephesians 6:12).

On a Tuesday. When someone is near faith, expect opposition. Pray.

parallels.desc: the magicians of Egypt oppose Moses

verseByVerse.quote: But Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him and said, "You son of the devil, you enemy of all righteousness, full of all deceit and villainy, will you not stop making crooked the straight paths of the Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Full of the Spirit, Paul exposes Elymas as an enemy of righteousness who twists the Lord’s ways.

Saul, also called Paul. Not a new name at conversion. As a Roman citizen, he probably had both from birth: Saul, his Jewish name (after the king from his tribe of Benjamin), and Paulus, his Roman family name, meaning “small”. From here, in the Gentile world, Luke calls him Paul. And from here Paul, not Barnabas, takes the lead.

Son of the devil. The “son of Jesus” is really a son of the devil (John 8:44).

Making crooked the straight paths. Echoing John the Baptist’s call to make the Lord’s paths straight (Luke 3:4–5).

On a Tuesday. There is a time for strong words against those who deliberately twist the truth to keep others from Christ. It is rare, and needs the Spirit.
verseByVerse.note: Saul was his Jewish name, Paul (Paulus) his Roman one; from here on, in the Gentile world, Luke calls him Paul.

parallels.desc: the ways of the LORD are right

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, behold, the hand of the Lord is upon you, and you will be blind and unable to see the sun for a time." Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand. Then the proconsul believed, when he saw what had occurred, for he was astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God strikes the sorcerer blind for a time, and the governor believes, astonished at the Lord’s teaching.

For a time. Temporary blindness, with mercy: a chance to repent, as Paul himself had been blinded and led by the hand on the Damascus road (9:8).

The proconsul believed. The first recorded conversion of a high Roman official.

The teaching. He was astonished not chiefly by the miracle but by the teaching.

On a Tuesday. Signs may get attention, but it is the teaching about the Lord that converts.

parallels.desc: Paul himself led by the hand

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–52 — Paul's Sermon in Pisidian Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The missionaries sail to Perga, where John Mark leaves them, and go inland to Pisidian Antioch. Invited to speak in the synagogue after the Scripture readings, Paul retells Israel’s story from the exodus to King David, and announces that from David’s line God has brought the promised Saviour, Jesus. Jerusalem’s leaders condemned him, unknowingly fulfilling the prophets, but God raised him, as the psalms foretold, and through him forgiveness is offered: everyone who believes is set free from everything the law could not free them from. Many want to hear more, and the next Sabbath almost the whole city comes. Jealous Jewish leaders oppose Paul, and he and Barnabas declare that, since the word has been rejected, they now turn to the Gentiles, as Isaiah’s words about a light for the nations require. The Gentiles rejoice, those appointed for eternal life believe, and the word spreads, until opponents stir up the city’s leading people and expel the missionaries. They shake the dust from their feet and go on, leaving disciples full of joy and the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith in Paul's First Sermon

Paul's climactic statement in vv. 38–39 is the first explicit statement of justification by faith in Acts: let it be known to you that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses. The ESV notes that freed can be rendered justified — a courtroom word, the word for a judge declaring a man to be in the right. The law cannot issue that verdict; faith in the crucified and risen Jesus receives it. This is the heart of Paul's theology, already fully formed in his first recorded sermon — the gospel that will generate the letters to the Galatians and Romans. And it is not preached softly: the same sermon that announces the amnesty ends on Habakkuk's word to scoffers, be astounded and perish (vv. 40–41).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.' The widespread hunger for the gospel was met with jealousy from the Jewish leaders, who spoke against Paul. Their opposition drove the explicit turn to the Gentiles. Now: The pattern repeats whenever the gospel meets institutional religion: those who should be most receptive are sometimes least so, while those outside the religious establishment respond with open hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Paul and his companions set sail from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. And John left them and returned to Jerusalem, but they went on from Perga and came to Antioch in Pisidia. And on the Sabbath day they went into the synagogue and sat down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They sail to Perga, where John Mark leaves them, and then travel inland to Pisidian Antioch.

Paul and his companions. Now Paul leads; Luke names him first.

Perga. On the south coast of modern Turkey.

Why did Mark leave? Luke does not say. Suggestions: homesickness, fear of the dangerous road inland, unhappiness that Paul had replaced his cousin Barnabas as leader, or doubts about the mission to Gentiles. Paul saw it as desertion (15:38). Later Mark was restored and became “very useful” to Paul (2 Timothy 4:11).

Pisidian Antioch. A Roman colony on the high plateau, about 3,600 feet above sea level and 100 miles inland over the Taurus mountains, notorious for bandits (2 Corinthians 11:26). Some think Paul fell ill with malaria in the lowlands of Pamphylia and went up to the healthier highlands, which would explain Galatians 4:13: “it was because of a bodily ailment that I preached the gospel to you at first”.

On a Tuesday. People who fail in ministry can be restored, as Mark was. Do not write anyone off.
verseByVerse.note: Perga was in Pamphylia on the south coast of Asia Minor; Pisidian Antioch lay about 100 miles north, up in the mountains. Mark’s departure later divided Paul and Barnabas.

parallels.desc: Mark is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: After the reading from the Law and the Prophets, the rulers of the synagogue sent a message to them, saying, "Brothers, if you have any word of encouragement for the people, say it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the synagogue the leaders invite the visitors to speak a word of encouragement.

The synagogue service. It included the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4–9), prayers, a reading from the Law, a reading from the Prophets, and a sermon, often by a visiting teacher.

A word of encouragement. The same phrase is used for the letter to the Hebrews (Hebrews 13:22).

On a Tuesday. Christian worship grew out of the synagogue: reading Scripture, prayer and preaching. Keep them at the centre.
verseByVerse.note: A synagogue service included readings from the Law and the Prophets; a visiting teacher could be invited to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: So Paul stood up, and motioning with his hand said: "Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen. The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and made the people great during their stay in the land of Egypt, and with uplifted arm he led them out of it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul addresses Jews and God-fearers, beginning with God’s choice of Israel and the exodus.

Two audiences. Jews and God-fearing Gentiles.

God chose. Paul begins with God’s sovereign election of Israel (Deuteronomy 7:6–8).

Uplifted arm. Literally “with a high arm”, the language of the exodus (Exodus 6:6).

On a Tuesday. When sharing the gospel, start with God’s actions, not ours.
verseByVerse.note: “You who fear God” are Gentile worshippers of Israel’s God.

parallels.desc: with an outstretched arm

verseByVerse.quote: "And for about forty years he put up with them in the wilderness. And after destroying seven nations in the land of Canaan, he gave them their land as an inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God bore with Israel in the wilderness and gave them the land as their inheritance.

Put up with them. God’s patience with a grumbling people.

A textual note. Manuscripts differ by one letter: “put up with them” (etropophorēsen) or “cared for them like a nurse” (etrophophorēsen), echoing Deuteronomy 1:31, where God carried Israel as a father carries his son. Both are true of God.

Seven nations. Deuteronomy 7:1.

On a Tuesday. God has been patient with you too. Thank him.

parallels.desc: seven nations greater than you

verseByVerse.quote: "All this took about 450 years. And after that he gave them judges until Samuel the prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God then gave them judges until Samuel.

450 years. Probably the 400 years in Egypt, the 40 in the wilderness and some years of conquest, before the judges.

A textual note. In later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) the 450 years are attached to the period of the judges, which would conflict with 1 Kings 6:1. The earliest manuscripts place it before the judges, as the ESV does, which fits the chronology.

On a Tuesday. God works patiently over centuries.
verseByVerse.note: The 450 years probably cover the stay in Egypt, the wilderness and the conquest.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul the son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years. And when he had removed him, he raised up David to be their king, of whom he testified and said, 'I have found in David the son of Jesse a man after my heart, who will do all my will.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gave Israel kings: first Saul, then David, the man after his own heart.

Saul of Benjamin. Paul, also a Benjamite named Saul, mentions his namesake.

Forty years. The Old Testament does not state Saul’s reign clearly (1 Samuel 13:1 is uncertain in the Hebrew); Josephus also gives forty.

A man after my heart. Combining 1 Samuel 13:14 (“a man after his own heart”) and Psalm 89:20 (“I have found David, my servant”).

On a Tuesday. David was no perfect man, yet God called him a man after his heart. God looks for a heart turned to him.
verseByVerse.note: The Old Testament does not state Saul’s reign clearly; the historian Josephus also gives forty years.

parallels.desc: a man after his own heart

verseByVerse.quote: "Of this man's offspring God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From David’s line God has brought Israel the promised Saviour, Jesus.

The promise. To David, of an everlasting dynasty (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Isaiah 11:1).

A Saviour. The climax of the history: all of it was leading to Jesus.

For worship. Thank God that his promises across centuries met in Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Before his coming, John had proclaimed a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. And as John was finishing his course, he said, 'What do you suppose that I am? I am not he. No, but behold, after me one is coming, the sandals of whose feet I am not worthy to untie.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John prepared the way, insisting that he was not the one they were waiting for.

John. Even in Asia Minor, people had heard of John the Baptist (19:3).

Not worthy. Untying sandals was a slave’s job. John put himself below a slave compared with Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Like John, point away from yourself to Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "Brothers, sons of the family of Abraham, and those among you who fear God, to us has been sent the message of this salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message of salvation is sent to every descendant of Abraham and every God-fearer.

To us. Paul includes himself and his hearers. The good news is for them.

On a Tuesday. The message of salvation is addressed to you personally.

verseByVerse.quote: "For those who live in Jerusalem and their rulers, because they did not recognize him nor understand the utterances of the prophets, which are read every Sabbath, fulfilled them by condemning him. And though they found in him no guilt worthy of death, they asked Pilate to have him executed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jerusalem’s rulers condemned Jesus without cause, and so fulfilled the prophets they read every Sabbath.

Did not recognise him. Ignorance (3:17).

Fulfilled the prophets. The irony: the people who read the prophets every Sabbath fulfilled them by condemning the one the prophets described.

No guilt. Jesus was innocent (Luke 23:4, 14, 22).

On a Tuesday. It is possible to read the Bible every week and miss Christ. Ask him to open your eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had carried out all that was written of him, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything written of him was fulfilled, and he was laid in a tomb.

All that was written. Every detail of the cross fulfilled Scripture.

The tree. The cross (5:30; 10:39).

A tomb. Joseph of Arimathea’s (Luke 23:50–53). A real burial, a real death.

On a Tuesday. Jesus was really dead and buried. That is why his resurrection matters.

verseByVerse.quote: "But God raised him from the dead, and for many days he appeared to those who had come up with him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now his witnesses to the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raised him, and he appeared to many witnesses.

But God. The great reversal again.

Many days. Forty (1:3).

Witnesses. Paul refers to the original apostles, though he himself saw the risen Lord too (1 Corinthians 15:8).

On a Tuesday. Our faith rests on eyewitness testimony, preserved in the Gospels.

verseByVerse.quote: "And we bring you the good news that what God promised to the fathers, this he has fulfilled to us their children by raising Jesus, as also it is written in the second Psalm, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The resurrection is the fulfilment of God’s promise to the fathers, as Psalm 2 foretold.

The good news. The promise is fulfilled.

Psalm 2:7. “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.” Spoken at a king’s coronation. Paul applies it to the resurrection, when God publicly declared Jesus his Son and King (Romans 1:4, “declared to be the Son of God in power … by his resurrection from the dead”).

Did Jesus become God’s Son at the resurrection? Adoptionists (an early heresy) taught that Jesus was a man adopted as God’s Son. Verdict: no. Jesus is the eternal Son (John 1:1, 18; Hebrews 1:2–3). The resurrection was his public installation as the Son in power, not the beginning of his Sonship.

A textual note. Manuscripts vary between “to us their children” and “to our children”. Some Western manuscripts call it “the first psalm”, since Psalms 1 and 2 were sometimes counted as one.

For worship. Worship Jesus as the eternal Son, crowned at the resurrection.

parallels.desc: you are my Son; today I have begotten you

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the fact that he raised him from the dead, no more to return to corruption, he has spoken in this way, 'I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.' Therefore he says also in another psalm, 'You will not let your Holy One see corruption.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God raised Jesus never to decay, fulfilling the sure blessings promised to David.

No more to return. Unlike Lazarus or Tabitha, who died again, Jesus rose to immortal life.

Isaiah 55:3. “My steadfast, sure love for David.” The promises to David are secured through the risen Christ, and offered to all who come (Isaiah 55:1).

Psalm 16:10. As in Peter’s sermon (2:27).

On a Tuesday. The blessings promised to David are yours in Christ: sure, and lasting.

parallels.desc: the steadfast, sure love for David

verseByVerse.quote: "For David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep and was laid with his fathers and saw corruption, but he whom God raised up did not see corruption."
verseByVerse.commentary:
David served his generation and died; the promise must speak of someone else.

Served his generation. A beautiful epitaph. David did God’s will in his own time.

Saw corruption. David’s body decayed; the psalm must be about someone else.

On a Tuesday. Ask how you can serve God’s purpose in your generation, then rest in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let it be known to you therefore, brothers, that through this man forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you, and by him everyone who believes is freed from everything from which you could not be freed by the law of Moses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Jesus forgiveness is proclaimed, and everyone who believes is freed from all that the law could not free them from.

Forgiveness through this man. The heart of the gospel.

Freed. Literally “justified”: declared righteous. The first use of Paul’s great word in Acts.

Everyone who believes. The only condition.

What the law could not do. Does this mean the law justifies from some sins and Christ from the rest? Verdict: no. Paul means that the law could not justify from any sin, but Christ justifies from all. “By works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight” (Romans 3:20).

On a Tuesday. Whatever you have done, there is forgiveness through Jesus for everyone who believes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Beware, therefore, lest what is said in the Prophets should come about: 'Look, you scoffers, be astounded and perish; for I am doing a work in your days, a work that you will not believe, even if one tells it to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul warns that scoffers who refuse God’s work will perish, as Habakkuk said.

Habakkuk 1:5. “Look among the nations, and see; wonder and be astounded.” God warned Judah that he was raising up the Babylonians as his instrument of judgement. Paul applies it: God’s astonishing work now is the gospel, and rejecting it is dangerous.

Scoffers. The Greek version reads “despisers”.

On a Tuesday. The gospel comes with a warning as well as an invitation. Do not shrug it off.
verseByVerse.note: Habakkuk warned of God’s astonishing judgment by the Babylonians.

parallels.desc: I am doing a work in your days that you would not believe

verseByVerse.quote: As they went out, the people begged that these things might be told them the next Sabbath. And after the meeting of the synagogue broke up, many Jews and devout converts to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas, who, as they spoke with them, urged them to continue in the grace of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Many are eager to hear more, and Paul and Barnabas urge them to continue in God’s grace.

Interest. The sermon stirred real curiosity.

Proselytes. Gentiles who had become Jews.

Continue in grace. The Christian life begins and continues by grace.

On a Tuesday. Follow up with people who show interest. Talk with them after church.
verseByVerse.note: Converts to Judaism are proselytes.

verseByVerse.quote: The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. But when the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and began to contradict what was spoken by Paul, reviling him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When almost the whole city gathers to hear the word, jealous opponents contradict and slander Paul.

The whole city. Gentiles came in large numbers to the synagogue.

Jealousy. The leaders resented Gentiles flocking to hear a message that welcomed them on equal terms, without circumcision.

Reviled. Literally “blasphemed”: abusive speech against Paul, and so against Christ.

On a Tuesday. Success in ministry can provoke jealousy, even among religious people.

verseByVerse.quote: And Paul and Barnabas spoke out boldly, saying, "It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you. Since you thrust it aside and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we are turning to the Gentiles. For so the Lord has commanded us, saying, 'I have made you a light for the Gentiles, that you may bring salvation to the ends of the earth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejected by those who heard first, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, as Isaiah foretold.

To you first. God’s plan: “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Romans 1:16).

Judge yourselves unworthy. By rejecting the gospel, they passed sentence on themselves.

We turn to the Gentiles. A pattern repeated in Acts (18:6; 28:28). Paul kept going to synagogues in each new city, though.

Isaiah 49:6. “I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.” Spoken to the Servant, who is Christ (Luke 2:32), and now carried out through his apostles.

On a Tuesday. When some reject the gospel, take it to others. God’s plan is for all nations.
verseByVerse.note: The Servant’s calling to be a light to the nations is now carried out through the apostles.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: And when the Gentiles heard this, they began rejoicing and glorifying the word of the Lord, and as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. And the word of the Lord was spreading throughout the whole region.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Gentiles rejoice, and all who were appointed to eternal life believe.

Glorifying the word. Joy and praise.

As many as were appointed. One of the clearest statements of election in Acts. Tetagmenoi is a perfect passive: “had been appointed, ordained, enrolled”. Those whom God had appointed to eternal life believed.

Christians differ. Some Arminian interpreters read the verb as middle, “as many as had disposed themselves to eternal life”, meaning those who were already inclined to believe. Verdict: the passive reading is the natural one; Luke uses the verb of appointment by authority (22:10; 28:23). Faith is the result of God’s appointment, not its cause (Romans 8:30, “those whom he predestined he also called”; John 6:37). Yet election never makes preaching unnecessary: those appointed came to believe through hearing Paul.

For worship. If you believe, it is because God appointed you to eternal life. Thank him, humbly.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Jews incited the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, stirred up persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their district. But they shook off the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Opponents stir up the city’s leading people to drive the missionaries out, and they shake off the dust.

Devout women of high standing. Wealthy God-fearing women, influential in Roman society, often married to officials.

Shook the dust. As Jesus instructed: “Even the dust of your town that clings to our feet we wipe off against you” (Luke 10:11). A sign that they had done their part and the town must answer to God.

Iconium. Modern Konya, about 80 miles east.

On a Tuesday. When doors close, move on to the next open one.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking off the dust was a sign that a town was being left to God’s judgment. Iconium lay about 80 miles to the east.

parallels.desc: persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples were filled with joy and with the Holy Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even in persecution the new disciples are filled with joy and the Spirit.

Despite persecution. The missionaries were expelled, but the new believers were full of joy.

The disciples. A church had been born, left behind with the Spirit.

For worship. Pray for new believers left without leaders in hard places, that they may be filled with joy and the Spirit.

parallels.desc: joy of the Holy Spirit in much affliction

13.theology: Election and Evangelism. Acts 13:48 is the Reformed doctrine of election stated with apostolic directness: the believing of the Gentiles in Pisidian Antioch is grounded in their prior appointment to eternal life. This is not fatalism — it does not prevent preaching; it undergirds it. Paul and Barnabas preach with everything they have, to everyone who will listen, in the synagogue and in the streets. They do not know who is appointed; they preach to all. And God, through the preaching, brings to faith those he has appointed. Election is the guarantee that the mission will not ultimately fail: there are sheep in every flock that God is calling, and the voice of the gospel will reach them. This is the ground of missionary confidence in every hostile city.
13.examples:
Then: Barnabas and Saul, sent out from a worshipping, fasting, praying church, arriving in city after city with nothing but the word and the Spirit — and the word going out, and the appointed ones believing, and the disciples filled with joy even when expelled. The first missionary journey is a portrait of how the kingdom advances: through weakness and proclamation and sovereign grace.

Now: The church sends when it worships. Mission flows from the presence of God, not from strategic planning. The Antioch church was not looking for a missionary project; they were seeking God — and God spoke. The question for every congregation is not “what is our mission strategy?” but “are we in the kind of sustained, attentive, fasting prayer in which the Spirit can speak?” When he speaks, we must be ready to send our best.

14.title: Suffering and Strengthening
14.text: <sup>1</sup>Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. <sup>2</sup>But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers. <sup>3</sup>So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands. <sup>4</sup>But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. <sup>5</sup>When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them, <sup>6</sup>they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, <sup>7</sup>and there they continued to preach the gospel. <sup>8</sup>Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. <sup>9</sup>He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well, <sup>10</sup>said in a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” And he sprang up and began walking. <sup>11</sup>And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!” <sup>12</sup>Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker. <sup>13</sup>And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds. <sup>14</sup>But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, <sup>15</sup>“Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them. <sup>16</sup>In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways. <sup>17</sup>Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness.” <sup>18</sup>Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them. <sup>19</sup>But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. <sup>20</sup>But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe. <sup>21</sup>When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, <sup>22</sup>strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God. <sup>23</sup>And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed. <sup>24</sup>Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. <sup>25</sup>And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia, <sup>26</sup>and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled. <sup>27</sup>And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. <sup>28</sup>And they remained no little time with the disciples.
14.overview:
The first missionary journey continues through the cities of southern Galatia, in the heart of modern Turkey, and the pattern of chapter 13 repeats: preaching in the synagogue, many believing, opposition, and moving on. At Iconium a great number of Jews and Greeks believe, and the Lord confirms the message with signs, but the city divides and a plot to stone the apostles drives them to Lystra and Derbe, small towns in the district of Lycaonia. At Lystra Paul heals a man lame from birth, and the crowd, shouting in their local language, decide that the gods Zeus and Hermes have come down in human form. A Roman poet, Ovid, tells a local legend that the two gods once visited this region in disguise and were turned away by everyone except an old couple; the people of Lystra were not going to make that mistake again. The priest of Zeus brings bulls and garlands to sacrifice, and Paul and Barnabas tear their clothes in horror and rush into the crowd. In a short sermon Paul tells these pagans about the living God, Creator of heaven and earth, who in past ages let the nations go their own way but left evidence of his goodness in rain, harvests and gladness.

Opponents arrive from Antioch and Iconium, turn the crowd, and Paul is stoned and dragged out of the city as dead, but he gets up and goes back in, and the next day leaves for Derbe. After making many disciples there, Paul and Barnabas courageously retrace their steps through the cities that had persecuted them, strengthening the believers, warning that we must enter God’s kingdom through many hardships, and appointing elders in every church with prayer and fasting. Finally they sail back to Syrian Antioch and report to the church all that God had done, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–28 — The First Journey Continues and Returns
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Iconium Paul and Barnabas spoke so effectively in the synagogue that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed. But Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the believers. The apostles stayed a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who confirmed his message of grace by enabling them to do signs and wonders. The city was divided, and when Gentiles and Jews with their leaders plotted to mistreat and stone them, they fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and the surrounding country, and kept preaching the gospel. At Lystra sat a man lame from birth who had never walked. He listened to Paul, who looked at him, saw he had faith to be healed, and called out to him to stand up on his feet. He jumped up and began to walk. When the crowd saw this, they shouted in Lycaonian that the gods had come down in human form. They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, because he did the speaking. The priest of Zeus, whose temple was just outside the city, brought bulls and wreaths to the gates, wanting to offer sacrifices with the crowd. When Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their clothes and rushed into the crowd, shouting that they were only human, like them, bringing good news that they should turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven, earth, sea and everything in them. In the past he let all nations go their own way, yet he did not leave himself without testimony: he showed kindness by giving rain and crops in their seasons, and filled them with food and joy. Even with these words they had difficulty stopping the crowd from sacrificing to them. Then Jews came from Antioch and Iconium and won the crowd over. They stoned Paul and dragged him outside the city, thinking he was dead. But after the disciples gathered round him, he got up and went back into the city, and the next day left with Barnabas for Derbe. They preached there and made many disciples, then returned to Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, strengthening the disciples, urging them to remain true to the faith, and telling them that we must go through many hardships to enter God’s kingdom. They appointed elders for them in each church and, with prayer and fasting, committed them to the Lord in whom they had put their trust. After passing through Pisidia they came into Pamphylia, preached in Perga, went down to Attalia and sailed back to Antioch, where they had been commended to God’s grace for the work they had now completed. On arriving they gathered the church and reported all that God had done through them and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they stayed there a long time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.theology:
Suffering as the Path into the Kingdom

Paul and Barnabas's declaration in v. 22 — 'through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God' — is not pessimism but theology: the path of the crucified Lord is the path of his followers. Reformed theology insists that suffering is not a sign of God's absence but often a sign of his presence and approval: the servant who shares his Lord's cross shares his Lord's resurrection. The 'must' (dei) is the divine necessity — the same 'must' applied to Christ's suffering in Luke 24:26. The pattern of dying and rising is the pattern of life in the kingdom.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul was stoned and dragged out of Lystra for dead, then got up and went back into the city, and left for Derbe the next day. The courage required to re-enter the city where you were nearly killed is the courage of the man who has nothing to fear from death. Now: The willingness to re-enter dangerous territory — to continue faithful witness after suffering for it — is the distinctive quality of those whose security is not in this world's preservation of their lives but in Christ's resurrection that awaits them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Iconium they entered together into the Jewish synagogue and spoke in such a way that a great number of both Jews and Greeks believed. But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Iconium the gospel wins Jews and Greeks alike, and unbelievers stir up hostility.

Iconium. Modern Konya, a prosperous city on the plateau, in the Roman province of Galatia. Many think Paul’s letter to the Galatians was written to these churches (the “South Galatian” view).

Spoke in such a way. Clear, persuasive preaching is used by God.

Poisoned their minds. Ekakōsan: embittered. Opposition works by turning people against messengers.

On a Tuesday. Expect both fruit and opposition when you speak of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Iconium (modern Konya) was a city in the Roman province of Galatia; Paul’s letter to the Galatians may be to these churches.

verseByVerse.quote: So they remained for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who bore witness to the word of his grace, granting signs and wonders to be done by their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The missionaries stay long and speak boldly, and the Lord confirms his word of grace with signs.

A long time. They did not leave at the first opposition.

The word of his grace. A lovely name for the gospel (20:24, 32).

Bore witness. The signs confirmed the message, as at the beginning (Hebrews 2:3–4).

On a Tuesday. Stay faithful through opposition. God confirms his word.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of the city were divided; some sided with the Jews and some with the apostles. When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, to mistreat them and to stone them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city divides, and when a plot to stone them forms, they move on.

Divided. The gospel divides (Luke 12:51).

The apostles. Paul and Barnabas are both called apostles (also v. 14). Here the word means “those sent out” by the church, as missionaries. Barnabas was not one of the Twelve, and had not been commissioned by the risen Christ as Paul had. So the New Testament uses “apostle” in a narrow sense (the Twelve and Paul, with unique authority) and a broader sense (missionaries).

Apostles today? Some modern movements appoint “apostles” with authority over churches. Verdict: missionary church-planters may be called apostles in the broad sense, but no one today holds the foundational authority of the Twelve and Paul (Ephesians 2:20).

On a Tuesday. Pray for missionaries and church planters, the “sent ones” of today.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Barnabas are both called apostles — men sent out on mission.

verseByVerse.quote: they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and to the surrounding country, and there they continued to preach the gospel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fleeing danger is not cowardice: they go on to preach in Lycaonia.

Fled. Jesus told his disciples, “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next” (Matthew 10:23).

Lycaonia. A rural district with its own language.

Lystra. A Roman colony, Timothy’s home town (16:1).

Derbe. A small town on the eastern frontier of the province.

On a Tuesday. Fleeing persecution is not cowardice if you keep preaching where you go.
verseByVerse.note: Lystra and Derbe were smaller towns to the south and south-east, in the region of Lycaonia.

parallels.desc: Timothy of Lystra

verseByVerse.quote: Now at Lystra there was a man sitting who could not use his feet. He was crippled from birth and had never walked. He listened to Paul speaking. And Paul, looking intently at him and seeing that he had faith to be made well,
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Lystra a man lame from birth listens to Paul, and Paul sees that he has faith to be healed.

Lame from birth. Like the man at the temple gate (3:2). Luke deliberately parallels Paul and Peter: the same miracles, the same Lord.

Faith to be made well. The Greek is “faith to be saved”, a word meaning both healing and salvation. Faith came through listening.

Does healing depend on faith? Sometimes Jesus and the apostles responded to faith (Mark 5:34); sometimes they healed people who had no faith at all (Luke 7:11–15; Acts 3:1–8). Verdict: faith is not a power that compels God to heal. A sick believer who is not healed should never be told that their faith is too weak (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).

On a Tuesday. Look at people when you speak to them, as Paul did.
verseByVerse.note: The healing closely resembles Peter’s healing of the lame man at the temple.

verseByVerse.quote: said in a loud voice, "Stand upright on your feet." And he sprang up and began walking.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Paul’s command the man leaps up and walks.

A loud voice. So everyone could hear.

Sprang up. Instant, complete healing, as Isaiah promised: the lame shall leap (Isaiah 35:6).

A textual note. Some Western manuscripts add “I say to you in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ”, matching 3:6. The shorter text is original.

On a Tuesday. Pray for disabled people in your church, and treat them with dignity whether or not God heals them.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowds saw what Paul had done, they lifted up their voices, saying in Lycaonian, "The gods have come down to us in the likeness of men!" Barnabas they called Zeus, and Paul, Hermes, because he was the chief speaker.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pagan crowd decides that the gods have come down in human form.

In Lycaonian. Their local language, which Paul and Barnabas did not understand, which is why they did not react at once.

Zeus and Hermes. The Roman poet Ovid tells a legend set in this region: Zeus (Jupiter) and Hermes (Mercury) visited in disguise, were refused hospitality by a thousand homes, and were welcomed only by an old couple, Philemon and Baucis, who were rewarded while everyone else was drowned in a flood. Inscriptions from near Lystra show that Zeus and Hermes were worshipped together there. The people did not want to make the same mistake twice.

Barnabas as Zeus. Perhaps the more dignified, silent one; Hermes was the messenger of the gods and god of eloquence.

On a Tuesday. People often interpret the gospel through their existing beliefs. Be ready to explain clearly what you do and do not mean.
verseByVerse.note: A local legend told of Zeus and Hermes visiting the region in human form unrecognised. Hermes was messenger of the gods, so the speaker, Paul, was taken for him.

parallels.desc: they said that he was a god

verseByVerse.quote: And the priest of Zeus, whose temple was at the entrance to the city, brought oxen and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The priest of Zeus prepares to offer sacrifice to the missionaries.

Zeus before the city. A title for the patron god whose temple stood at the city entrance.

Garlands. Woollen wreaths placed on sacrificial animals.

On a Tuesday. Popularity can be more dangerous than persecution. Watch out when people start treating you as more than you are.
verseByVerse.note: Garlands were wreaths placed on sacrificial animals.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard of it, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out, "Men, why are you doing these things? We also are men, of like nature with you, and we bring you good news, that you should turn from these vain things to a living God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all that is in them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Horrified, Barnabas and Paul insist they are mere men, calling the crowd from idols to the living God, the Creator.

Tore their clothes. A Jewish sign of horror at blasphemy (Mark 14:63).

Of like nature. “The same feelings as you.” Ordinary, mortal men.

Vain things. Mataia: empty, futile. The Old Testament word for idols (Jeremiah 10:15).

The living God, Creator. To pagans with no Bible, Paul starts with creation, not with Israel’s history (compare 13:16–41). He echoes Exodus 20:11. This is the first example of preaching to pure pagans in Acts (compare 17:22–31).

On a Tuesday. When talking with someone who knows nothing of the Bible, you may need to start with the God who made everything.
verseByVerse.note: Tearing one’s garments was a sign of horror or grief.

parallels.desc: turned to God from idols

verseByVerse.quote: "In past generations he allowed all the nations to walk in their own ways."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In past generations God allowed the nations to go their own way.

Allowed. God did not send prophets to the nations as he did to Israel. He let them go their way, which was a form of judgement (Romans 1:24).

What it does not mean. Not that the nations were innocent or saved by their ignorance. Paul says in Athens: “The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent” (17:30).

On a Tuesday. Now is the time when God calls all nations to turn to him.

parallels.desc: the times of ignorance God overlooked

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet he did not leave himself without witness, for he did good by giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, satisfying your hearts with food and gladness." Even with these words they scarcely restrained the people from offering sacrifice to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet God never left himself without witness: his kindness in rain, harvest and gladness speaks of him.

A witness. General revelation: creation and providence point to the Creator (Romans 1:19–20, “his invisible attributes, namely, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly perceived”).

Rain and fruitful seasons. Lystra was a farming region; Zeus was thought to send rain. Paul says the true God sends it.

Common grace. God gives good gifts to all people, believers and unbelievers: “he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:45; Psalm 145:15–16). This is what Reformed theology calls common grace.

Gladness. Joy in food, harvest and life is a gift from God, pointing to the Giver.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for your food and the joy of a good meal. Use such gifts to point others to the Giver.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, and having persuaded the crowds, they stoned Paul and dragged him out of the city, supposing that he was dead. But when the disciples gathered about him, he rose up and entered the city, and on the next day he went on with Barnabas to Derbe.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The fickle crowd that wanted to worship Paul now stones him, but he gets up and goes back into the city.

Opponents travelled. Antioch was about 100 miles away. Their hostility was determined.

Fickle crowds. One day they worshipped Paul; the next they stoned him.

Stoned. Paul remembered it: “Once I was stoned” (2 Corinthians 11:25). Perhaps some of the scars he called “the marks of Jesus” (Galatians 6:17) came from this day. Timothy, from Lystra, probably saw it (2 Timothy 3:11, “my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra”).

He rose up. Perhaps a miraculous recovery. And he went back into the city that had stoned him.

On a Tuesday. When you have been badly hurt in serving Christ, the disciples gathering round you matters. Gather round those who are suffering.
verseByVerse.note: Antioch was about 100 miles from Lystra.

parallels.desc: once I was stoned

verseByVerse.quote: When they had preached the gospel to that city and had made many disciples, they returned to Lystra and to Iconium and to Antioch, strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to continue in the faith, and saying that through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The missionaries return through the cities where they suffered, strengthening the disciples: entry to the kingdom is through many troubles.

Returned. The shortest way home from Derbe was east through the Cilician Gates to Tarsus. Instead they went back through the very cities where they had been persecuted. Courageous pastoral care.

Strengthening. New believers need follow-up.

Through many tribulations. Not that suffering earns the kingdom, but that the road to it runs through hardship. “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

The kingdom. Here, its future fullness.

On a Tuesday. If you teach new believers, tell them honestly that following Christ will involve hardship.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They appoint elders in every church and entrust them to the Lord with prayer and fasting.

Elders. Presbyteroi: older, mature men, leaders of the local church, as synagogues had elders. Plural in every church. Paul later told Titus to “appoint elders in every town as I directed you” (Titus 1:5).

Appointed. Cheirotonēsantes: literally “stretching out the hand”, which could mean electing by a show of hands or simply appointing. Congregationalists see a congregational vote; Presbyterians and Episcopalians see appointment by the apostles. Verdict: the word had come to mean simply “appoint”, and here Paul and Barnabas do it; but the wider New Testament pattern includes the church’s involvement (6:3).

Committed them to the Lord. Paul and Barnabas left. The churches were in the Lord’s hands.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your elders. Their task is heavy.
verseByVerse.note: Elders were leaders appointed in each church, as in the synagogues.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. And when they had spoken the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia,
verseByVerse.commentary:
They preach on the way home and sail from Attalia.

Perga. On the way out they had passed through quickly; now they preached there.

Attalia. The port, modern Antalya.

On a Tuesday. Go back to places where you missed an opportunity before.
verseByVerse.note: Attalia was the port on the south coast.

verseByVerse.quote: and from there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been commended to the grace of God for the work that they had fulfilled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They return to the church that had entrusted them to God’s grace, their work completed.

Commended to grace. The church at Antioch had sent them out in prayer (13:3).

Fulfilled. The first journey was complete, about two years and over a thousand miles.

On a Tuesday. Missionaries need a home church that sends them in prayer and welcomes them back.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they arrived and gathered the church together, they declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles. And they remained no little time with the disciples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They report all that God has done, and how he has opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.

All that God had done. Not what they had done. God gets the credit.

A door of faith. God opened the way for Gentiles to believe (1 Corinthians 16:9; Colossians 4:3). But this open door would soon cause controversy (chapter 15).

A long time. Rest and fellowship after hard work.

For worship. When missionaries report, listen and praise God for what he has done.

parallels.desc: a wide door for effective work

14.theology: Suffering as the Path of the Kingdom. Acts 14:22 is the New Testament’s clearest statement that suffering is the appointed means by which the people of God enter the kingdom. This is not peripheral; it is structural. The cross was not a detour on the way to the resurrection; it was the way. And the church that follows a crucified Lord is called to the same road. Paul writes later that he fills up in his flesh “what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the sake of his body” (Colossians 1:24) — not that Christ’s atoning work was incomplete, but that the suffering of Christ is reproduced in his body, the church, as the gospel goes forth into the world. The church that suffers for the name is the church that looks most like its Lord. And it is the church that the watching world cannot ultimately explain away.
14.examples:
Then: Paul, stoned and left for dead outside Lystra, rising and walking back into the city, going on to Derbe the next morning. Returning through Lystra and Iconium and Antioch — the cities that had tried to kill him — to strengthen the believers he left behind. Appointing elders, committing them to God with prayer and fasting, and sailing home to report everything God had done. This is what faithful looks like.

Now: The Western church has largely lost the theology of suffering. We expect the Christian life to be comfortable, and when it is not, we assume something has gone wrong. Acts 14 says the opposite: tribulation is the appointed road, and the God who walked it first walks it with his people. The suffering church is not the failing church; it is often the most faithful church — and, in God’s strange economy, the most fruitful.

15.title: The Jerusalem Council
15.text: <sup>1</sup>But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” <sup>2</sup>And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question. <sup>3</sup>So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. <sup>4</sup>When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them. <sup>5</sup>But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.” <sup>6</sup>The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. <sup>7</sup>And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, “Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe. <sup>8</sup>And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, <sup>9</sup>and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith. <sup>10</sup>Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? <sup>11</sup>But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.” <sup>12</sup>And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. <sup>13</sup>After they finished speaking, James replied, “Brothers, listen to me. <sup>14</sup>Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name. <sup>15</sup>And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, <sup>16</sup>‘After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it, <sup>17</sup>that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things <sup>18</sup>known from of old.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, <sup>20</sup>but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood. <sup>21</sup>For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.” <sup>22</sup>Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, <sup>23</sup>with the following letter: “The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings. <sup>24</sup>Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, <sup>25</sup>it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul, <sup>26</sup>men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>27</sup>We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth. <sup>28</sup>For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: <sup>29</sup>that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.” <sup>30</sup>So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. <sup>31</sup>And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement. <sup>32</sup>And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. <sup>33</sup>And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them. <sup>35</sup>But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also. <sup>36</sup>And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.” <sup>37</sup>Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. <sup>38</sup>But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work. <sup>39</sup>And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, <sup>40</sup>but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord. <sup>41</sup>And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
15.overview:
The success of the Gentile mission raises the most important question the early church faced. Some Jewish believers from Judea arrive in Antioch teaching that Gentile converts cannot be saved unless they are circumcised and keep the law of Moses: in effect, Gentiles must become Jews to become Christians. This was not an odd idea. Circumcision was the covenant sign God gave Abraham, and for centuries any Gentile who wanted to join God’s people had done exactly that. Paul and Barnabas dispute it fiercely, and the church sends them to Jerusalem to settle it with the apostles and elders.

At the council, believers from the Pharisee party insist on circumcision. Peter reminds everyone how God gave the Spirit to Cornelius’s household, cleansing their hearts by faith, and asks why they would put on Gentiles a yoke that neither they nor their ancestors could bear, since Jews and Gentiles alike are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus. Paul and Barnabas tell of the signs God did among the Gentiles. Then James, the Lord’s brother and leader of the Jerusalem church, shows from the prophet Amos that God always planned to gather Gentiles to rebuild David’s fallen house, and proposes that Gentile believers should not be burdened with the law, but asked to avoid food offered to idols, sexual immorality, the meat of strangled animals and blood, practices especially offensive to Jews, so that Jewish and Gentile believers could share fellowship. A letter is sent with Judas and Silas, and Antioch rejoices. The chapter ends with a painful disagreement: Paul and Barnabas part company over whether to take John Mark on a second journey, so Barnabas sails with Mark to Cyprus and Paul sets out with Silas.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Teachers from Judea tell the Gentile believers in Antioch that they cannot be saved without circumcision and the law of Moses. Paul and Barnabas oppose them, and the church sends them to Jerusalem. There believers from the Pharisee party press the same demand. After long debate Peter reminds the council that God gave the Spirit to Gentiles who believed, making no distinction and cleansing their hearts by faith, and that Jews and Gentiles alike are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus, not by a yoke no one could carry. Paul and Barnabas describe God’s signs among the Gentiles. James then shows from Amos that God planned to gather Gentiles into the restored house of David, and proposes that they be asked only to avoid idol food, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood. The apostles, elders and whole church agree, and send a letter with Judas and Silas declaring that it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to them to lay no greater burden on the Gentiles. The church in Antioch rejoices.
verseByVerse.theology:
Justification by Faith Alone — the Council's Theological Verdict

Peter's speech in vv. 8–11 is the clearest statement of justification by faith alone in the book of Acts: 'God made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith... we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.' The Gentiles are saved the same way the Jews are — by grace through faith, not by law observance. This is the verdict that Paul will develop in Galatians and Romans. The Jerusalem Council is the communal confirmation of what the Spirit had demonstrated in Cornelius's house.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Jerusalem Council produced a letter of pastoral decision rather than a theological treatise — practical guidance that allowed Jew and Gentile to live together in one community. Now: The church continues to face questions about what is required for full membership in the people of God. The council's method — testimony, Scripture, deliberation, pastoral wisdom — remains the model for ecclesial discernment on divisive questions.

verseByVerse.quote: But some men came down from Judea and were teaching the brothers, "Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved." And after Paul and Barnabas had no small dissension and debate with them, Paul and Barnabas and some of the others were appointed to go up to Jerusalem to the apostles and the elders about this question.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Teachers from Judea insist that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved, and Antioch is thrown into dispute.

The teaching. Circumcision was the sign of God’s covenant with Abraham: “Every male among you shall be circumcised” (Genesis 17:10). For centuries Gentiles who joined Israel were circumcised. These teachers held that faith in Jesus was necessary but not sufficient: Gentiles must also become Jews.

Cannot be saved. The issue is salvation itself. Paul saw at once that this destroyed the gospel: “if you accept circumcision, Christ will be of no advantage to you” (Galatians 5:2).

Galatians. Paul’s letter to the Galatians may have been written around this time, against the same teaching (Galatians 2:11–14 describes a related crisis in Antioch involving Peter).

No small dissension. Paul would not compromise on the gospel. Some issues are worth fighting over.

On a Tuesday. Watch for any teaching that says “Jesus plus something” is needed for salvation: a ritual, a church membership, a set of rules.
verseByVerse.note: Circumcision was the covenant sign given to Abraham; the question was whether Gentiles must become Jews to be saved. This meeting in Jerusalem, about AD 49, is often called the Jerusalem Council.

parallels.desc: Paul’s account of a Jerusalem meeting

verseByVerse.quote: "So, being sent on their way by the church, they passed through both Phoenicia and Samaria, describing in detail the conversion of the Gentiles, and brought great joy to all the brothers. When they came to Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the church and the apostles and the elders, and they declared all that God had done with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the way to Jerusalem Paul and Barnabas bring joy to the churches with news of Gentile conversions.

Great joy. In Phoenicia and Samaria, with their many non-Jewish believers, the news delighted the churches.

Welcomed. The Jerusalem church received them warmly, before any debate.

On a Tuesday. Share good news of what God is doing. It encourages the whole church.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some believers who belonged to the party of the Pharisees rose up and said, 'It is necessary to circumcise them and to order them to keep the law of Moses.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believing Pharisees demand that Gentiles keep the law of Moses.

Believing Pharisees. Pharisees who had become Christians but still held that the law must be kept by all believers. Paul himself had been a Pharisee.

It is necessary. The heart of the issue: is law-keeping necessary for Gentile believers?

On a Tuesday. Sincere believers can hold wrong views on the gospel. Debate them with Scripture and charity.

parallels.desc: as to the law, a Pharisee

verseByVerse.quote: The apostles and the elders were gathered together to consider this matter. And after there had been much debate, Peter stood up and said to them, "Brothers, you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles and elders meet to settle the question, and after much debate Peter speaks.

The council. Apostles and elders together, with the whole church present (v. 12, 22).

Much debate. They did not rush. Issues were argued out.

How should churches decide disputes? Roman Catholic teaching sees the council, with Peter speaking first, as a model for councils led by the pope. Presbyterian churches see it as the model for church courts of elders, above the local congregation (Westminster Confession 31). Congregationalists see the whole church’s involvement. Verdict: the council shows elders and apostles deciding together, under Scripture, with the whole church’s agreement. Notably, James, not Peter, gives the final judgement. Councils can err (Westminster Confession 31.4); their decisions are binding as they agree with Scripture.

Peter. His last appearance in Acts. He points back to Cornelius (chapter 10).

On a Tuesday. When your church faces a hard question, pray, study Scripture, discuss patiently, and seek agreement.

verseByVerse.quote: "And God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us, and he made no distinction between us and them, having cleansed their hearts by faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God, who knows hearts, gave Gentiles the Spirit and cleansed their hearts by faith, making no distinction.

Knows the heart. God saw their faith (1:24).

Gave the Spirit. God’s own testimony that he accepted uncircumcised believers.

No distinction. The barrier is down (Ephesians 2:14).

Cleansed by faith. Not by circumcision, food laws or ritual washing, but by faith. Inner purity, not outward ceremony.

On a Tuesday. Faith in Christ cleanses the heart. You do not need to add rituals to be clean before God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now, therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing a yoke on the neck of the disciples that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why test God by imposing a yoke no one could bear? Jews and Gentiles alike are saved by grace.

Testing God. Demanding more than he demands.

A yoke. A wooden frame on the neck of oxen. Rabbis spoke of “taking the yoke of the law”. Peter says it was too heavy: no one kept it perfectly. Jesus offered a different yoke: “my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:29–30).

Saved by grace. Jews too, not only Gentiles. Remarkably, Peter does not say “they are saved as we are”, but “we are saved as they are”. Jewish believers are saved the same way as Gentiles: by grace alone. “By grace you have been saved through faith” (Ephesians 2:8).

On a Tuesday. If you feel weighed down by religious rules, hear Peter: salvation is by grace, for everyone.
verseByVerse.note: A yoke joined animals together for work; teachers spoke of the “yoke” of the law.

verseByVerse.quote: "And all the assembly fell silent, and they listened to Barnabas and Paul as they related what signs and wonders God had done through them among the Gentiles. After they finished speaking, James replied, 'Brothers, listen to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The assembly listens as Barnabas and Paul tell of God’s signs among the Gentiles, and James responds.

Silent. The testimony quieted the debate.

Barnabas first. In Jerusalem Barnabas, the trusted local man, is named first.

James. The Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church, known for strict Jewish piety (later called “James the Just”). His support was crucial. If the most respected Jewish believer agreed, the circumcision party would have to accept it.

On a Tuesday. Respected, conservative leaders who support necessary change can unite a church.
verseByVerse.note: This James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles, to take from them a people for his name.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
James sums up: God has taken a people for his name from among the Gentiles.

Simeon. The Hebrew form of Simon, Peter’s original name. James speaks as a Jew.

A people for his name. A striking phrase. In the Old Testament, Israel was the people God chose “for his treasured possession out of all the peoples” (Deuteronomy 14:2). Now God takes a people from the nations.

On a Tuesday. God is gathering a people from every nation. Your church is part of it.
verseByVerse.note: Simeon is the Hebrew form of Simon (Peter).

verseByVerse.quote: "And with this the words of the prophets agree, just as it is written, "'After this I will return, and I will rebuild the tent of David that has fallen; I will rebuild its ruins, and I will restore it,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prophets agree: Amos foretold the rebuilding of David’s fallen tent.

Amos 9:11–12. “In that day I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen.” David’s dynasty had collapsed into a shelter in ruins. God promised to restore it.

Fulfilled how? Dispensationalists read this as a future restoration of the Davidic kingdom in Jerusalem after the church age. Verdict: James says the prophecy is being fulfilled now, as Gentiles are brought in. The house of David is rebuilt in the risen Messiah, Jesus, son of David, reigning and gathering Jews and Gentiles into one people.

On a Tuesday. When you read Old Testament promises of restoration, look for their fulfilment in Christ and his church.
verseByVerse.note: James quotes Amos in its Greek form. “The tent of David” is David’s fallen royal house.

parallels.desc: I will raise up the booth of David that is fallen

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the remnant of mankind may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by my name, says the Lord, who makes these things'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God promised that the nations called by his name would seek him.

The Greek version. James quotes the Greek Old Testament. The Hebrew reads “that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations who are called by my name”. The Greek translators read “Edom” as “Adam” (mankind) and “possess” as “seek”, the words differing slightly in Hebrew. Both forms of the text promise the inclusion of the nations under God’s name.

Called by my name. Owned by God. Gentiles as Gentiles bear God’s name, without becoming Jews.

On a Tuesday. If you trust Christ, you bear God’s name. Live worthily of it.

parallels.desc: all the nations who are called by my name

verseByVerse.quote: "'known from of old.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the work of the God who made it known long ago.

Known from of old. God’s plan to include the Gentiles was not an afterthought. It was his purpose from the beginning (Genesis 12:3; Ephesians 3:4–6).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) expand this: “Known unto God are all his works from the beginning of the world.” The shorter text is original.

For worship. Praise God that he planned your salvation long ago.

parallels.desc: who told this long ago?

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore my judgment is that we should not trouble those of the Gentiles who turn to God, but should write to them to abstain from the things polluted by idols, and from sexual immorality, and from what has been strangled, and from blood.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
James judges that Gentile converts should not be burdened, but asked to avoid practices most offensive to Jewish believers.

Do not trouble them. No circumcision, no full law-keeping.

Four requests. They echo the laws for foreigners living in Israel (Leviticus 17–18): no sacrifice to idols, no eating blood, no eating animals not properly drained of blood, no forbidden sexual unions. “If any one of the house of Israel or of the strangers who sojourn among them eats any blood” (Leviticus 17:10). These were the practices most offensive to Jews, and avoiding them made shared meals between Jewish and Gentile believers possible.

Binding today? Most Christians see the food requirements as a temporary measure for fellowship in mixed churches, like Paul’s advice about idol food (1 Corinthians 8–10). The prohibition of sexual immorality is moral and permanent. Jehovah’s Witnesses use the ban on “blood” to refuse blood transfusions. Verdict: the ban concerned eating blood, as in Genesis 9:4 (“you shall not eat flesh with its life, that is, its blood”), not medical transfusions, which save life rather than consume it.
