A textual note. The Western text omits “what is strangled” and adds “not to do to others what they would not want done to themselves”, turning the decree into purely moral rules. The shorter, food-related text is original.

On a Tuesday. Freedom in Christ should be used with consideration for others in the church who have different backgrounds and sensitivities.
verseByVerse.note: The four requirements probably echo rules the law gave for foreigners living in Israel (Lev 17–18), and would let Jewish and Gentile believers eat together.

parallels.desc: sacrifices, blood, and what dies of itself
sexual relations

verseByVerse.quote: "'For from ancient generations Moses has had in every city those who proclaim him, for he is read every Sabbath in the synagogues.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moses is read in every synagogue, so sensitivity to Jewish neighbours matters.

Why this? Probably: there are Jews in every city who are sensitive to these things, so Gentile believers should be considerate. Or: Gentiles who want to learn about the law can do so in the synagogue.

On a Tuesday. Consider how your behaviour looks to people of other backgrounds whom you want to reach.

verseByVerse.quote: Then it seemed good to the apostles and the elders, with the whole church, to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas. They sent Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers, with the following letter: "The brothers, both the apostles and the elders, to the brothers who are of the Gentiles in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia, greetings."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The apostles, elders and whole church choose envoys, Judas and Silas, to carry their letter.

The whole church. The decision had the agreement of the whole church.

Judas Barsabbas. Perhaps related to Joseph Barsabbas (1:23).

Silas. Silvanus in Paul’s letters (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 1 Peter 5:12). A Roman citizen (16:37), he became Paul’s partner on the second journey.

Brothers. The Jerusalem leaders address Gentile believers as brothers.

On a Tuesday. Send trusted people to explain hard decisions, not just a letter.
verseByVerse.note: Silas is the Silvanus of Paul’s letters; he became Paul’s travelling companion.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Since we have heard that some persons have gone out from us and troubled you with words, unsettling your minds, although we gave them no instructions, it has seemed good to us, having come to one accord, to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter disowns the troublemakers who unsettled the Gentile believers.

Without instructions. The Jerusalem church disowns the teachers who caused the trouble. They had no authority.

Unsettling. Anaskeuazontes: tearing down, a word used of plundering a house. False teaching wrecks souls.

Beloved. Warm words for Paul and Barnabas.

On a Tuesday. When someone has caused confusion in your name, put it right publicly.

parallels.desc: some who trouble you

verseByVerse.quote: "'men who have risked their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who themselves will tell you the same things by word of mouth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
It commends Barnabas and Paul, who have risked their lives for Christ, and sends Judas and Silas to confirm it in person.

Risked their lives. Recalling Lystra (14:19).

By word of mouth. The letter and the messengers together.

On a Tuesday. Honour those who have suffered for Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay on you no greater burden than these requirements: that you abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Holy Spirit and the council agree to lay no burden on Gentiles beyond a few necessary requests.

The Holy Spirit and us. A remarkable phrase. The church’s decision, reached by debate, Scripture and testimony, was also the Spirit’s guidance. God guides through his word and his people deliberating together.

No greater burden. Minimal requirements, for fellowship.

On a Tuesday. When facing decisions with others in church, seek both the Spirit’s guidance and wise agreement.

verseByVerse.quote: "So when they were sent off, they went down to Antioch, and having gathered the congregation together, they delivered the letter. And when they had read it, they rejoiced because of its encouragement."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church at Antioch rejoices at the letter’s encouragement.

Rejoiced. Freedom from the law’s burden brought joy.

Encouragement. Paraklēsis: comfort, strengthening.

On a Tuesday. The gospel of grace brings joy. Legalism brings anxiety.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Judas and Silas, who were themselves prophets, encouraged and strengthened the brothers with many words. And after they had spent some time, they were sent off in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judas and Silas, themselves prophets, strengthen the believers before returning.

Prophets. Their gift strengthened the church (1 Corinthians 14:3).

In peace. The crisis ended in peace.

A textual note. Some manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add verse 34: “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there.” It is absent from the earliest and was probably added to explain how Silas was in Antioch in verse 40.

On a Tuesday. Encourage someone this week with words that strengthen.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 34: “But it seemed good to Silas to remain there.”

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and preaching the word of the Lord, with many others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul and Barnabas, with many others, keep teaching and preaching in Antioch.

Many others. Antioch had many teachers. Ministry was shared.

Peter’s visit? Perhaps during this period Peter visited Antioch and withdrew from eating with Gentiles, and Paul rebuked him (Galatians 2:11–14). Others date that incident before the council.

For worship. Thank God that the gospel of grace was defended for us at Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 36–41 — The Parting of Paul and Barnabas
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Some time later Paul suggested to Barnabas that they go back and visit the believers in every town where they had preached, to see how they were doing. Barnabas wanted to take John, also called Mark, but Paul thought it unwise to take someone who had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not continued in the work. They had such a sharp disagreement that they parted company. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas and left, commended by the believers to the grace of the Lord. He went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.
verseByVerse.theology:
God's Sovereignty Over Human Conflict

Reformed theology sees in the Paul-Barnabas conflict the characteristic pattern of God's providence: working through human failure and disagreement to accomplish more than perfect human unity might have achieved. The separation produces two missionary teams instead of one. John Mark, the subject of the dispute, will prove his worth — Paul himself will later commend him (2 Timothy 4:11; Colossians 4:10). God does not waste the failures of his servants; he works through them, around them, and despite them.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus — his home, the place that knows him — to restore the man he believes in. Paul took Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches. Both were faithful; both bore fruit. Now: The church's disagreements, when they do not touch the gospel itself, can produce multiplication rather than division if those who disagree remain committed to the mission rather than to winning the argument.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after some days Paul said to Barnabas, 'Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, and see how they are.' Now Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul proposes revisiting the churches they planted; Barnabas wants to take John Mark again.

Pastoral care. The second journey began with concern for existing believers.

Barnabas and Mark. Mark was Barnabas’s cousin (Colossians 4:10). The “son of encouragement” wanted to give him a second chance.

On a Tuesday. Check on people you once helped to faith.

parallels.desc: Mark the cousin of Barnabas

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul refuses to take Mark, who had abandoned them.

Paul’s view. The work was dangerous and demanding; a man who had left before might leave again.

Who was right? Both, in different ways. Paul was concerned for the mission; Barnabas for the man. God used both.

On a Tuesday. Mission needs both: Paul’s seriousness and Barnabas’s grace.

verseByVerse.quote: "And there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed away to Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and departed, having been commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their sharp disagreement divides the team, but God multiplies the mission.

Sharp disagreement. Paroxysmos, from which “paroxysm” comes. Godly men can disagree strongly. Luke does not hide it.

Two teams. God turned the split into two missions.

Reconciliation. Later Paul spoke warmly of Barnabas (1 Corinthians 9:6) and of Mark: “Mark the cousin of Barnabas” (Colossians 4:10); “Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11).

Barnabas. His last appearance in Acts. Barnabas’s investment in Mark gave the church the Gospel of Mark.

On a Tuesday. If you have parted ways with a fellow Christian, pray for reconciliation in time.
verseByVerse.note: Paul and Mark were later reconciled.

parallels.desc: get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me

verseByVerse.quote: "And he went through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul and Silas strengthen the churches of Syria and Cilicia.

Syria and Cilicia. Overland, through Paul’s home region, where he had probably planted churches during his silent years.

Strengthening. Delivering the council’s decree (16:4).

For worship. Thank God that he works through imperfect people and even their disagreements.

15.theology: Justification by Grace Alone through Faith Alone. Acts 15 is the original council on justification. Peter’s summary — “we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will” — is the thesis of the Reformation stated by an apostle. The Judaizers were not wicked men; they were sincere believers who thought obedience to the law was necessary for salvation. But sincerity does not make a false gospel true. The council’s verdict is decisive and irreversible: the Gentiles are saved through grace, and so are the Jews. The law cannot save. It never could. The law was given to demonstrate the need for grace, not to provide an alternative to it. The cross of Christ is sufficient, complete, and alone — and any addition to it, however well-intentioned, is a subtraction from it.
15.examples:
Then: A church divided over the most fundamental question imaginable: what must a person do to be saved? The answer came not from compromise but from clarity, grounded in Scripture (James’s citation of Amos) and confirmed by experience (Peter’s witness to Cornelius, Barnabas and Paul’s report from the Gentile mission). The church that settles this question rightly can face every other challenge. The church that gets it wrong has nothing left to offer.

Now: The Judaizer error never stays buried. It reappears in every generation dressed in different clothes: the idea that grace plus something — baptism, church membership, moral effort, liturgical compliance — constitutes salvation. The Jerusalem Council’s answer is permanent and non-negotiable: the grace of the Lord Jesus alone. The church’s task in every generation is to say it clearly, defend it stubbornly, and live it joyfully.

16.title: Into Macedonia
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. <sup>2</sup>He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium. <sup>3</sup>Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek. <sup>4</sup>As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily. <sup>6</sup>And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. <sup>7</sup>And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them. <sup>8</sup>So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas. <sup>9</sup>And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, “Come over to Macedonia and help us.” <sup>10</sup>And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. <sup>11</sup>So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, <sup>12</sup>and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days. <sup>13</sup>And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together. <sup>14</sup>One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. <sup>15</sup>And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us. <sup>16</sup>As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. <sup>17</sup>She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.” <sup>18</sup>And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” And it came out that very hour. <sup>19</sup>But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. <sup>20</sup>And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, “These men are Jews, and they are disturbing our city. <sup>21</sup>They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.” <sup>22</sup>The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. <sup>23</sup>And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely. <sup>24</sup>Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks. <sup>25</sup>About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, <sup>26</sup>and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone’s bonds were unfastened. <sup>27</sup>When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. <sup>28</sup>But Paul cried with a loud voice, “Do not harm yourself, for we are all here.” <sup>29</sup>And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. <sup>30</sup>Then he brought them out and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” <sup>31</sup>And they said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” <sup>32</sup>And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. <sup>33</sup>And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds, and he was baptized at once, he and all his family. <sup>34</sup>Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God. <sup>35</sup>But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, “Let those men go.” <sup>36</sup>And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, “The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.” <sup>37</sup>But Paul said to them, “They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.” <sup>38</sup>The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. <sup>39</sup>So they came and apologized to them. And they took them out and asked them to leave the city. <sup>40</sup>So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed.
16.overview:
Paul’s second journey begins by revisiting the churches of the first. At Lystra he recruits Timothy, a young believer with a Jewish mother and Greek father, and circumcises him so that his ministry among Jews will not be hindered. Then the Spirit repeatedly blocks their plans: they are kept from preaching in the province of Asia and stopped from entering Bithynia, until at Troas, on the Aegean coast, Paul sees a vision of a man of Macedonia begging, “Come over and help us.” Here Luke slips into “we”: he has joined the team. They cross into Europe and go to Philippi, a Roman colony settled with army veterans, proud of its Roman status, where there were too few Jews even for a synagogue. By the river on the Sabbath they find women praying, and the Lord opens the heart of Lydia, a businesswoman who traded in expensive purple cloth, who is baptised with her household and opens her home to them.

Then trouble. Paul casts a spirit of divination out of a slave girl whose fortune-telling made money for her owners, who drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, accusing them, as Jews, of disturbing the city with un-Roman customs. They are stripped, beaten with rods and put in the stocks in the inner prison. At midnight, as they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens the doors and loosens everyone’s chains. The jailer, about to kill himself, cries out, “What must I do to be saved?” and is told, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.” He washes their wounds, he and his household are baptised, and he rejoices that he has come to believe in God. In the morning, when the magistrates order their release, Paul reveals that they are Roman citizens, beaten without trial, and insists that the officials come and escort them out, protecting the young church before he leaves.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — Timothy, the Macedonian Call, and Lydia
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Lystra Paul found a disciple named Timothy, son of a Jewish believer and a Greek father, well spoken of by the believers there and in Iconium. Paul wanted to take him on the journey, so he circumcised him because of the Jews in the area, who all knew his father was Greek. As they travelled from town to town, they delivered the decisions of the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, and the churches were strengthened in faith and grew daily in numbers. They travelled through Phrygia and Galatia, having been kept by the Holy Spirit from preaching the word in the province of Asia. When they reached the border of Mysia and tried to enter Bithynia, the Spirit of Jesus would not allow them, so they passed by Mysia and went down to Troas. During the night Paul had a vision of a man of Macedonia standing and begging him to come over and help them. After the vision, Luke writes, we got ready at once to leave for Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them. From Troas we sailed straight to Samothrace, the next day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, a Roman colony and leading city of that district of Macedonia, and stayed there several days. On the Sabbath we went outside the city gate to the river, where we expected to find a place of prayer, and sat down to speak to the women who had gathered. One of them was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira, a worshipper of God. The Lord opened her heart to respond to Paul’s message. When she and her household had been baptised, she invited us to stay at her house if we considered her a believer in the Lord, and she persuaded us.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Spirit's Direction of Mission

The second missionary journey is notable for the Spirit's specific prevention and redirection: 'they were forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia... the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them' to go to Bithynia. The door to Europe opens only because two Asian doors close. Reformed missiology sees here the sovereignty of the Spirit over missional geography: the Spirit is not merely the empowerer of human initiative but the director of the mission's course. The church's task is to be obedient to both open doors and closed ones.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Lydia's household was the first European church — gathered in a businesswoman's home around the word of God and the Lord's Supper. Now: The church continues to be built wherever the Lord opens hearts — in homes as often as in purpose-built buildings, through business relationships as often as through formal religious programs.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul came also to Derbe and to Lystra. A disciple was there, named Timothy, the son of a Jewish woman who was a believer, but his father was a Greek. He was well spoken of by the brothers at Lystra and Iconium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Lystra Paul finds Timothy, a young disciple of mixed Jewish and Greek parentage, well regarded by the churches.

Timothy. Probably converted on the first journey. His mother Eunice and grandmother Lois were believers: “your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” (2 Timothy 1:5). He had known the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 3:15).

A mixed marriage. A Jewish mother and a Greek father. Under later Jewish law the child of a Jewish mother was Jewish, though it is uncertain whether that rule applied yet.

Well spoken of. A good reputation was required before Paul took him on.

Paul’s closest co-worker. “I have no one like him, who will be genuinely concerned for your welfare” (Philippians 2:20).

On a Tuesday. Grandparents and mothers: your faithful teaching of children may raise a future Timothy.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s mother was Eunice and his grandmother Lois. He became Paul’s closest co-worker.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul wanted Timothy to accompany him, and he took him and circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul circumcises Timothy not for salvation but to remove a barrier to his ministry among Jews.

Why circumcise Timothy, but not Titus? Paul refused to circumcise Titus, a Gentile, when false brothers demanded it as necessary for salvation (Galatians 2:3–5). Timothy, with a Jewish mother, would have been seen as a Jew who had abandoned the covenant, and his presence would have closed every synagogue door. Paul circumcised him not for salvation but for mission: “To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews” (1 Corinthians 9:20).

The principle. When a practice is demanded as necessary for salvation, refuse it. When it is a matter of freedom, use it in love for others.

On a Tuesday. Are there freedoms you could give up to remove a barrier for someone hearing the gospel?
verseByVerse.note: Paul would not circumcise Titus when it was demanded as necessary for salvation; Timothy, with a Jewish mother, was circumcised to remove an obstacle among Jews.

parallels.desc: to the Jews I became as a Jew

verseByVerse.quote: As they went on their way through the cities, they delivered to them for observance the decisions that had been reached by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem. So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and they increased in numbers daily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The churches receive the Jerusalem decisions and grow stronger in faith and number.

The decisions. The decree of chapter 15.

Strengthened and increased. Clarity about the gospel led to growth.

On a Tuesday. Clear teaching on grace strengthens churches.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they went through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia. And when they had come up to Mysia, they attempted to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit closes doors in Asia and Bithynia, guiding by prevention.

Asia. The Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its capital. Paul would preach there later (chapter 19).

Forbidden. How? Luke does not say: perhaps a prophecy, a circumstance, an illness, or an inner conviction.

The Spirit of Jesus. A rare phrase. The Spirit is the Spirit of the risen Jesus, who directs his mission.

How does God guide today? Some Christians seek guidance through inner impressions, signs or visions. Verdict: God guides his people chiefly through his word, wise counsel and providence, the opening and closing of doors. He can guide in extraordinary ways, but we should not demand them. Paul himself did not wait in Antioch for a vision; he set out with a plan and let God redirect him. “The heart of man plans his way, but the LORD establishes his steps” (Proverbs 16:9).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “the Spirit suffered them not”) omit “of Jesus”. The earliest include it.

On a Tuesday. When your plans are blocked, do not despair. God may be redirecting you to something better.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province on the west coast of Asia Minor, with Ephesus its chief city. Mysia and Bithynia lay in the north-west.

parallels.desc: all the residents of Asia heard the word

verseByVerse.quote: "So, passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their path leads them to Troas, on the edge of Asia.

Troas. Alexandria Troas, a Roman colony and port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy. The gateway to Europe.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes God leads you to the edge before he shows the next step.
verseByVerse.note: Troas was a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy.

verseByVerse.quote: And a vision appeared to Paul in the night: a man of Macedonia was standing there, urging him and saying, "Come over to Macedonia and help us." And when Paul had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go on into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A vision of a Macedonian calling for help shows them that God is calling them to Europe.

A man of Macedonia. Some have suggested it was Luke himself, perhaps a Macedonian; we cannot know.

Macedonia. The Roman province of northern Greece, homeland of Alexander the Great. The gospel’s first step into Europe.

We. Here the first of the “we” passages begins (16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16). Luke the author has joined the team, and writes as an eyewitness.

Concluding. Symbibazontes: putting it together. The team discussed the vision and reached a shared conclusion. Guidance involved reasoning as well as revelation.

On a Tuesday. Discuss important decisions with trusted believers. Guidance is often confirmed together.
verseByVerse.note: Macedonia was the Roman province of northern Greece — the gospel’s first step into Europe. Here “we” appears: Luke, the author, joins the journey.

parallels.desc: further “we” passages

verseByVerse.quote: "So, setting sail from Troas, we made a direct voyage to Samothrace, and the following day to Neapolis, and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia and a Roman colony. We remained in this city some days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A swift voyage brings them to Philippi, a Roman colony and leading city of Macedonia.

A direct voyage. A favourable wind: two days. The reverse journey later took five (20:6).

Samothrace. A mountainous island, halfway across.

Neapolis. “New City”, modern Kavala, Philippi’s port, on the Via Egnatia, the great Roman road across Macedonia.

Philippi. Named after Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander. In 42 BC Antony and Octavian defeated Brutus and Cassius, Caesar’s assassins, there, and Rome settled veterans in the city; Octavian (Augustus) settled more after 31 BC. As a Roman colony it had Roman law, Latin as its official language, and citizens proud of being Roman (16:21; Philippians 3:20).

A textual note. The phrase “a leading city of the district” is uncertain in the Greek; manuscripts differ, and some scholars propose “a city of the first district of Macedonia”, since Macedonia was divided into four districts. The meaning is not affected.

On a Tuesday. God sends the gospel to places of power and pride, too.
verseByVerse.note: Neapolis was Philippi’s port. Philippi was a Roman colony, settled with army veterans, governed like a little Rome.

parallels.desc: our citizenship is in heaven

verseByVerse.quote: "And on the Sabbath day we went outside the gate to the riverside, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and we sat down and spoke to the women who had come together."
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no synagogue in Philippi, they find a group of praying women by the river.

No synagogue. Jewish tradition required ten Jewish men to form a synagogue. Philippi apparently did not have them, so Jews and God-fearers met outside by the river Gangites, perhaps for ritual washing.

Women. Paul sat down with a group of women, which many rabbis would not have done. The European church began with women at prayer.

On a Tuesday. Go where people already gather to seek God, and join them.
verseByVerse.note: There was apparently no synagogue; Jews met to pray in the open, by the river.

verseByVerse.quote: One who heard us was a woman named Lydia, from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods, who was a worshiper of God. The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul. And after she was baptized, and her household as well, she urged us, saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come to my house and stay." And she prevailed upon us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord opens the heart of Lydia, a God-fearing businesswoman, and she and her household are baptised.

Lydia. Perhaps her name (“the Lydian woman”) came from her home region of Lydia, where Thyatira lay.

Thyatira. In the province of Asia, famous for its purple dye. Inscriptions there mention a guild of dyers. Purple dye, made from shellfish or from the madder root, was very expensive; purple cloth was worn by the wealthy and by officials. Lydia was a businesswoman of means, with a household and a house large enough for guests.

A worshipper of God. A God-fearing Gentile.

The Lord opened her heart. Conversion is God’s work. She listened; but it was the Lord who opened her heart to respond. “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44). This is effectual calling.

Her household. Paedobaptists see household baptisms as evidence for baptising infants. Credobaptists reply that nothing is said about children, Lydia may have been unmarried or widowed, and her household probably meant servants or workers who also heard. Verdict: the text does not settle it; elsewhere in Acts baptism follows hearing and believing.

Hospitality. Her first act as a believer was to open her home. It became the first church in Europe (v. 40).

On a Tuesday. Pray for God to open the hearts of people you speak to. And use your home for his work.
verseByVerse.note: Thyatira, in Asia, was famous for its purple dye; purple cloth was a luxury. A “worshiper of God” was a Gentile who worshipped Israel’s God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–40 — Prison and Earthquake in Philippi
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A slave girl whose fortune-telling earned money for her owners follows the missionaries for days, shouting that they are servants of the Most High God, until Paul casts the spirit out of her in Jesus’ name. Her owners, robbed of their profit, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, accusing them as Jews of promoting un-Roman customs. They are stripped, beaten with rods and fastened in the stocks. At midnight, as they pray and sing hymns, an earthquake opens every door and loosens every chain. The jailer, about to kill himself, is stopped by Paul, falls before them and asks what he must do to be saved. They tell him to believe in the Lord Jesus, and speak the word to his whole household. He washes their wounds, he and his household are baptised, and they rejoice together over a meal. In the morning Paul reveals that he and Silas are Roman citizens beaten without trial, and the alarmed magistrates come in person to escort them out. After encouraging the believers at Lydia’s house, they leave.
verseByVerse.theology:
Midnight Praise and the Ministry of Suffering

Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight — after being stripped and beaten with rods — and the other prisoners listen. The praise is not despite the suffering but in it: the same Spirit who fills the church for witness fills the suffering church for worship. Reformed theology sees in this midnight scene the confirmation of what Paul will later write: 'we rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance' (Romans 5:3). The songs at midnight are the most powerful proclamation the prisoners that night will ever hear.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The jailer asked 'What must I do to be saved?' — the question of Pentecost (2:37) repeated in a Philippian prison. The answer is the same: 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.' Now: The gospel's answer to the question of salvation is always the same: not circumcision, not ritual, not moral achievement, but faith in the Lord Jesus Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "As we were going to the place of prayer, we were met by a slave girl who had a spirit of divination and brought her owners much gain by fortune-telling. She followed Paul and us, crying out, 'These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A slave girl possessed by a spirit of divination, exploited by her owners, follows them shouting the truth about them.

A python spirit. The Greek says she had “a spirit, a python”. The python was the serpent associated with the oracle of Apollo at Delphi, where the priestess, the Pythia, gave prophecies in a trance. The Greek writer Plutarch says ventriloquist fortune-tellers were called “pythons”.

Exploited. A slave girl owned and used for profit. Her owners made money from her bondage.

Servants of the Most High God. True words. In the pagan world, “the Most High God” could mean Zeus, and “salvation” could mean physical safety. Demons sometimes spoke truth about Jesus (Mark 1:24), but their testimony confused people and was not wanted.

On a Tuesday. Not every spiritual voice that says the right words is from God. Test the source.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the Greek reads “a spirit, a python” — linked to the oracle at Delphi, where Apollo was said to have slain a serpent called Python.

parallels.desc: no one who practises divination

verseByVerse.quote: "And this she kept doing for many days. Paul, having become greatly annoyed, turned and said to the spirit, 'I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.' And it came out that very hour."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the name of Jesus Paul commands the spirit to leave her, and it does.

Greatly annoyed. Perhaps troubled for the girl, or by the confusion she caused.

In the name of Jesus Christ. Paul’s authority came from Jesus, as Jesus cast out demons with a word.

That very hour. Instant deliverance.

What happened to her? Luke does not say. Perhaps she joined the church at Lydia’s house.

On a Tuesday. Pray for people trapped in occult practices, and for those exploited for profit, such as victims of trafficking.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when her owners saw that their hope of gain was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers. And when they had brought them to the magistrates, they said, 'These men are Jews and they are disturbing our city.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her owners, robbed of their profit, drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates.

Their hope of gain. The real motive. The same Greek word “went out” is used of the spirit leaving and of their profit leaving.

The marketplace. The forum, where the magistrates sat. Its remains can be seen at Philippi today.

The magistrates. Stratēgoi: the two chief magistrates of a Roman colony (duoviri), who liked to call themselves praetors. Luke uses the local title.

Being Jews. Antisemitism: the emperor Claudius had recently expelled Jews from Rome (18:2). Luke (a Gentile, and likely Timothy, half-Greek) are not accused.

On a Tuesday. When the gospel threatens someone’s income, expect fierce opposition. Ask whether any of your income depends on exploiting others.

parallels.desc: profits threatened again at Ephesus

verseByVerse.quote: "'They advocate customs that are not lawful for us as Romans to accept or practice.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge is that these Jews are teaching un-Roman customs.

Customs. Roman law allowed Judaism as a legal religion, but forbade proselytising Roman citizens into foreign cults.

Us Romans. Colonists’ pride. Paul later wrote to this church, “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20).

On a Tuesday. Christians may be accused of being un-national, un-British or un-American. Our first citizenship is in heaven.

verseByVerse.quote: "The crowd joined in attacking them, and the magistrates tore the garments off them and gave orders to beat them with rods. And when they had inflicted many blows upon them, they threw them into prison, ordering the jailer to keep them safely."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Without trial, the missionaries are stripped, beaten with rods and imprisoned.

Beaten with rods. By the lictors, officers who carried bundles of rods (the fasces) as a symbol of the magistrates’ authority. Paul remembers: “Three times I was beaten with rods” (2 Corinthians 11:25), and later recalled how they had been “shamefully treated at Philippi” (1 Thessalonians 2:2).

No trial. Mob justice.

On a Tuesday. Pray for Christians beaten for their faith today.
verseByVerse.note: Beating with rods was done by the magistrates’ officers, the lictors.

parallels.desc: three times I was beaten with rods
shamefully treated at Philippi

verseByVerse.quote: "Having received this order, he put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The jailer secures them in the inner cell with their feet in stocks.

The inner prison. The darkest, most secure cell.

Stocks. Wooden blocks clamping the feet, sometimes spread wide to cause pain. With backs raw from the beating, they could not lie down.

On a Tuesday. When you feel locked in, remember Paul and Silas in the inner cell. God was there too.
verseByVerse.note: Stocks were wooden blocks that clamped the feet.

verseByVerse.quote: About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them, and suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken. And immediately all the doors were opened, and everyone's bonds were unfastened.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At midnight, bleeding, they pray and sing, and God answers with an earthquake that opens every door.

Singing at midnight. In pain, in the dark, in stocks, they sang. “At night his song is with me” (Psalm 42:8). Paul later wrote to this church: “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4).

The prisoners listening. Worship in suffering is a witness.

An earthquake. The region is prone to earthquakes; the timing was God’s. Chains fastened to walls could come loose as the walls shook.

On a Tuesday. When life is darkest, try praying and singing to God. Others may be listening.

parallels.desc: at night his song is with me

verseByVerse.quote: When the jailer woke and saw that the prison doors were open, he drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped. But Paul cried with a loud voice, "Do not harm yourself, for we are all here."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The jailer, about to kill himself, is stopped by Paul: they are all still there.

Suicide. A Roman guard who lost prisoners faced their penalty (12:19). Suicide seemed more honourable than execution. Philippi was the city where Brutus and Cassius had killed themselves after their defeat.

Do not harm yourself. Paul cared about the man who had locked him in the stocks.

We are all here. Remarkably, no one escaped. Perhaps the prisoners were awed by the singing and the earthquake.

On a Tuesday. If you know someone in despair, speak to them as Paul did. Life is precious. In the UK you can call Samaritans on 116 123; in the US, 988.
verseByVerse.note: A guard who let prisoners escape could face their penalty.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the jailer called for lights and rushed in, and trembling with fear he fell down before Paul and Silas. Then he brought them out and said, 'Sirs, what must I do to be saved?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The terrified jailer asks the most important question there is: what must I do to be saved?

Trembling. Fear of God after the earthquake and the singing.

What must I do to be saved? The greatest question anyone can ask. Did he mean spiritual salvation? He had heard the slave girl’s cry about “the way of salvation” (v. 17), and probably the prisoners’ hymns.

On a Tuesday. When someone asks a question like this, be ready to answer simply.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they said, 'Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer is simple: believe in the Lord Jesus, and his household too will be saved as they believe.

Believe. The simplest statement of the gospel: trust Jesus as Lord. Not “do” anything, but believe. “If you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:9).

And your household. Not that his family would be saved by his faith, but that the same offer was for them on the same terms (v. 32, 34): each must believe.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add “Christ”: “Believe on the Lord Jesus Christ”. The earliest have “the Lord Jesus”.

For worship. Thank God that the way of salvation is this simple: believe in the Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they spoke the word of the Lord to him and to all who were in his house. And he took them the same hour of the night and washed their wounds; and he was baptized at once, he and all his family."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They teach the whole household, the jailer washes their wounds, and the household is baptised that night.

Spoke the word. The whole household heard the gospel explained.

Washed their wounds. The first fruit of faith: kindness to those he had hurt. He washed them; they baptised him.

Immediately. No delay. In Acts, baptism followed faith quickly.

His household. Again, paedobaptists see a household baptism including any children; credobaptists note that the word was spoken to all, and all rejoiced in believing (v. 34). Verdict: the household heard and believed, then was baptised; the text supports believer’s baptism, while not settling every question.

On a Tuesday. A real conversion changes how you treat people. Is there someone you need to make amends to?

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he brought them up into his house and set food before them. And he rejoiced along with his entire household that he had believed in God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The jailer’s home becomes a place of joy and hospitality, for they have come to believe in God.

A meal. Hospitality, perhaps the first Lord’s Supper in his home.

Rejoiced. Joy is a mark of salvation.

Believed in God. A Gentile who had worshipped Rome’s gods now believed in the true God.

On a Tuesday. Share a meal with new believers. It builds fellowship.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when it was day, the magistrates sent the police, saying, 'Let those men go.' And the jailer reported these words to Paul, saying, 'The magistrates have sent to let you go. Therefore come out now and go in peace.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the morning the magistrates send word to release them quietly.

The police. The lictors, the rod-bearers who had beaten them.

Release them. Perhaps the magistrates thought the beating was enough, or the earthquake frightened them.

On a Tuesday. God can change the minds of rulers overnight.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said to them, 'They have beaten us publicly, uncondemned, men who are Roman citizens, and have thrown us into prison; and do they now throw us out secretly? No! Let them come themselves and take us out.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul insists on his rights as a Roman citizen, to protect the young church.

Roman citizens. Roman law (the Valerian and Porcian laws) forbade beating a citizen, and certainly without trial. Cicero described the outrage of a citizen being flogged in public while crying out “I am a Roman citizen.”

Why not say so earlier? Perhaps he did, but was not heard in the uproar. Or he chose to suffer, then used his rights later to protect the young church.

Using legal rights. Christians may and sometimes should use their legal rights, especially to protect others. Paul did so again (22:25; 25:11).

On a Tuesday. If you or other Christians are treated unjustly, it is right to use lawful means to seek justice, especially for the sake of the vulnerable.
verseByVerse.note: Roman law forbade beating a citizen, still more without a trial.

verseByVerse.quote: "The police reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Roman citizens. So they came and apologized to them, and they took them out and asked them to leave the city."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The alarmed magistrates come in person, apologise and ask them to leave.

Afraid. The magistrates could lose their office, or worse, for abusing citizens.

Apologised. A public vindication that would protect the church.

On a Tuesday. Justice protects the weak. Pray for just rulers.

verseByVerse.quote: "So they went out of the prison and visited Lydia. And when they had seen the brothers, they encouraged them and departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before leaving they encourage the believers gathered at Lydia’s house.

Lydia’s house. The first church in Europe.

The church at Philippi. A businesswoman, a freed slave girl perhaps, a Roman jailer: rich and poor, women and men. It became Paul’s most generous partner (Philippians 4:15–16), and he wrote it his warmest letter.

Encouraged them. The missionaries, beaten and bruised, comforted the believers.

Luke stays. The “we” stops here and resumes at Philippi in 20:5; Luke may have stayed behind to lead the church.

For worship. Thank God for the church at Philippi, and pray for the church in Greece today.

parallels.desc: your partnership in the gospel from the first day

16.theology: Effectual Calling and the Opened Heart. Acts 16:14 is one of the clearest statements in Scripture of what the Reformed tradition calls effectual calling: “The Lord opened her heart to pay attention to what was said by Paul.” The Word is preached by Paul; the heart is opened by the Lord. Both acts are real and necessary. Without Paul’s preaching, Lydia has no content to respond to. Without the Lord’s opening of her heart, Paul’s words remain external noise. The Spirit works through the Word, but the Spirit’s work is the decisive one — the inward illumination that turns external proclamation into saving faith. This is why prayer for the lost must accompany every act of evangelism: we can preach; only God can open hearts.
16.examples:
Then: A purple-goods merchant, a slave girl, a Roman jailer — three people who could not have been more different in status, ethnicity, or circumstance — all met by one gospel in one city. The Philippian church is born from this unlikely trio, and Paul will write his most joyful letter to it from a prison cell a dozen years later.

Now: The Lord who opened Lydia’s heart still opens hearts today. The Spirit who directed Paul away from Asia and toward Macedonia still directs his church. The closed doors are guidance; the midnight songs are witness; the simplest answer is still the truest: believe in the Lord Jesus. The gospel has not grown more complicated. We have.

17.title: Athens and the Unknown God
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. <sup>2</sup>And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures, <sup>3</sup>explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.” <sup>4</sup>And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. <sup>5</sup>But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar, and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd. <sup>6</sup>And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, “These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, <sup>7</sup>and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.” <sup>8</sup>And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things. <sup>9</sup>And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. <sup>10</sup>The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue. <sup>11</sup>Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. <sup>12</sup>Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men. <sup>13</sup>But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. <sup>14</sup>Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there. <sup>15</sup>Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed. <sup>16</sup>Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. <sup>17</sup>So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there. <sup>18</sup>Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, “What does this babbler wish to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities”—because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. <sup>19</sup>And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting? <sup>20</sup>For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.” <sup>21</sup>Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new. <sup>22</sup>So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. <sup>23</sup>For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: ‘To the unknown god.’ What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you. <sup>24</sup>The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, <sup>25</sup>nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything. <sup>26</sup>And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, <sup>27</sup>that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us, <sup>28</sup>for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring.’ <sup>29</sup>Being then God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. <sup>30</sup>The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent, <sup>31</sup>because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.” <sup>32</sup>Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, “We will hear you again about this.” <sup>33</sup>So Paul went out from their midst. <sup>34</sup>But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them.
17.overview:
Leaving Philippi, Paul and Silas travel west along the Via Egnatia, the great Roman highway, to Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia and a busy port. For three Sabbaths Paul reasons in the synagogue from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Messiah. Some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and a number of leading women believe. Jealous opponents gather a mob, and when they cannot find Paul they drag his host Jason before the city officials, accusing the believers of turning the world upside down and defying Caesar by proclaiming another king, Jesus. Paul and Silas slip away by night to Berea, where the Jews receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to check what Paul says. Opponents from Thessalonica follow, and Paul is sent on to Athens.

Athens was no longer politically powerful, but it was still the intellectual capital of the Greek world, the city of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, crowded with temples and statues. Paul is distressed at so many idols. He reasons in the synagogue and in the marketplace, where Epicurean and Stoic philosophers dismiss him as a babbler, and is brought before the Areopagus, the ancient council that met on the Hill of Ares. His speech is a model of preaching to people without the Bible. He begins from an altar inscribed “to an unknown god”: the God they do not know is the Creator of everything, who does not live in temples or need anything from us, who made all nations from one man and set their times and places so that they would seek him, and who is not far from any of us; even their own poets said we are his offspring. So God cannot be like an image of gold or stone. He overlooked their ignorance in the past, but now commands everyone everywhere to repent, because he has fixed a day to judge the world by a man he has appointed, and has proved it by raising him from the dead. At the mention of resurrection some laugh, some want to hear more, and a few believe, including a member of the council, Dionysius, and a woman named Damaris.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In Thessalonica Paul spends three Sabbaths in the synagogue showing from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Messiah. Some Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and leading women believe, but jealous opponents start a riot, drag Paul’s host Jason before the city officials and accuse the believers of defying Caesar by proclaiming another king, Jesus. Released on bond, the believers send Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, where the Jews are more open-minded, receiving the message eagerly and checking it daily against the Scriptures, and many believe. When opponents arrive from Thessalonica, Paul is sent on to Athens, while Silas and Timothy stay behind for a time.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Berean Standard for Scripture Engagement

The Bereans 'received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.' Reformed theology has always prized this as the model of how the gospel should be received: not credulity (accepting whatever the preacher says without examination) and not skepticism (dismissing the gospel without engagement), but eager reception combined with rigorous scriptural testing. The Berean standard is the Protestant hermeneutical ideal: sola Scriptura applied in the actual practice of hearing and evaluating proclamation.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: 'These men who have turned the world upside down' — the Thessalonian accusation is the most accurate description of the gospel's social effect in Acts. Now: The gospel still turns every human order that opposes the kingdom upside down. The question for the church is not whether the gospel is socially disruptive but whether it is disrupting the right things — the powers of sin, death, and injustice — rather than merely producing comfortable religious experience.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they had passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a synagogue of the Jews. And Paul went in, as was his custom, and on three Sabbath days he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Thessalonica Paul goes first to the synagogue and reasons from the Scriptures for three Sabbaths.

The Via Egnatia. The Roman road across Macedonia linked these towns, a day’s journey apart.

Thessalonica. Modern Thessaloniki, capital of the province and a free city with its own government, a major port, perhaps 100,000 people. Paul’s two letters to this church are among his earliest.

As was his custom. Synagogue first.

Three Sabbaths. He may have stayed longer: the Philippians sent him help there more than once (Philippians 4:16), and he worked night and day at his trade (1 Thessalonians 2:9).

Reasoned. Dielexato, from which “dialogue” comes: discussion, question and answer.

On a Tuesday. Reasoning from the Bible with people, patiently, is still a good way to share the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a port on the great Roman road, the Via Egnatia. Amphipolis and Apollonia were stops along that road.

verseByVerse.quote: "explaining and proving that it was necessary for the Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead, and saying, 'This Jesus, whom I proclaim to you, is the Christ.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His case is that the Scriptures required a suffering and rising Messiah, and that Jesus is he.

Explaining. Literally “opening” the Scriptures (Luke 24:32, 45).

Proving. Literally “placing alongside”: setting texts beside the events.

Necessary. The Messiah had to suffer: “Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and enter into his glory?” (Luke 24:26). The hardest point for Jews, who expected a conquering Messiah.

On a Tuesday. Learn some key Old Testament passages about the suffering Messiah: Isaiah 53, Psalm 22.

verseByVerse.quote: And some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great many of the devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women. But the Jews were jealous, and taking some wicked men of the rabble, they formed a mob, set the city in an uproar and attacked the house of Jason, seeking to bring them out to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jews, many God-fearing Greeks and leading women believe, but jealous opponents stir up a mob against Jason’s house.

Converts. Mostly Gentiles: “you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1 Thessalonians 1:9).

Leading women. As in Philippi, influential women were drawn to the gospel.

Wicked men of the rabble. Literally “market loungers”: hired troublemakers.

Jason. Probably Paul’s host, perhaps a Jewish believer (a Greek name often used by Jews named Joshua). Possibly the Jason of Romans 16:21.

On a Tuesday. Pray for those who host Christian workers. Hospitality can be costly.
verseByVerse.note: Jason was probably Paul’s host.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some of the brothers before the city authorities, shouting, 'These men who have turned the world upside down have come here also, and Jason has received them, and they are all acting against the decrees of Caesar, saying that there is another king, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The believers are accused of turning the world upside down and proclaiming another king, Jesus.

City authorities. Politarchai, “politarchs”. Critics once doubted this title, unknown in classical literature, but more than thirty inscriptions with it have been found in Macedonia, several from Thessalonica, including one from the Vardar Gate now in the British Museum. Luke’s accuracy confirmed again.

Turned the world upside down. An accusation that is also a compliment. The gospel does turn things upside down.

Another king. A dangerous political charge. Treason against Caesar. Paul had probably preached about Christ’s kingdom and return (1 Thessalonians 4:13–5:11; 2 Thessalonians 2).

On a Tuesday. Jesus is King, above every government. That gives Christians courage, and also humility about political loyalties.
verseByVerse.note: The “city authorities” were called politarchs, a title found in inscriptions from Thessalonica. Claiming another king could be treated as treason against Caesar.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the people and the city authorities were disturbed when they heard these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge alarms the crowd and the city officials.

Disturbed. Officials feared Roman displeasure; a free city could lose its privileges if it tolerated sedition.

On a Tuesday. Christians should be good citizens, so that false charges have no basis (1 Peter 2:12–15).

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had taken money as security from Jason and the rest, they let them go. The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea, and when they arrived they went into the Jewish synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jason is bound over to keep the peace, and Paul and Silas move on to Berea by night.

Security. A bond guaranteeing that there would be no more trouble, probably meaning Paul had to leave. Perhaps this is what Paul meant by Satan hindering his return (1 Thessalonians 2:18).

Berea. Modern Veria, about 50 miles west, off the main road.

Synagogue again. Undeterred.

On a Tuesday. Keep going after setbacks.
verseByVerse.note: Berea lay about 50 miles west of Thessalonica.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now these Jews were more noble than those in Thessalonica; they received the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so. Many of them therefore believed, with not a few Greek women of high standing as well as men."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Bereans receive the word eagerly and test it daily against the Scriptures, and many believe.

More noble. Eugenesteroi: originally “well born”, then “open-minded, generous”.

Eagerness and examination. Both: open to hear, careful to check. Not gullible, not closed.

Examining the Scriptures. Even an apostle’s teaching was tested by Scripture. This is the principle of sola Scriptura: every teaching, from any teacher, must be measured by God’s written word.

Daily. Regular, serious study.

On a Tuesday. Be a Berean. When you hear a sermon, check it against the Bible.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God was proclaimed by Paul at Berea also, they came there too, agitating and stirring up the crowds. Then the brothers immediately sent Paul off on his way to the sea, but Silas and Timothy remained there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Opponents follow from Thessalonica, and Paul is sent on while Silas and Timothy stay.

Followed him. Persistent opponents, as at Lystra (14:19).

Paul sent away. Paul was the main target; Silas and Timothy could stay to strengthen the new believers.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes a leader must step aside for the good of the church.

verseByVerse.quote: "Those who conducted Paul brought him as far as Athens, and after receiving a command for Silas and Timothy to come to him as soon as possible, they departed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is taken to Athens, where he waits alone.

Athens. The most famous city of the Greek world: home of Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, the Parthenon, the great schools of philosophy. Politically it had declined into a small university town under Rome, but its intellectual prestige remained.

Alone. Paul waited for his companions (1 Thessalonians 3:1, “we were willing to be left behind at Athens alone”).

On a Tuesday. Pray for Christians alone in hard places, such as students far from home and workers in hostile cities.
verseByVerse.note: Athens had long been the intellectual centre of the Greek world, though no longer politically powerful.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Waiting in Athens, Paul is distressed by the city’s idols and reasons daily in the synagogue and the marketplace. Epicurean and Stoic philosophers mock him as a babbler of foreign gods, because he speaks of Jesus and the resurrection, and they bring him before the Areopagus to explain himself. Paul starts from an altar dedicated “to an unknown god”. The God they do not know made everything, lives in no temple, needs nothing, and gives life and breath to all. He made every nation from one man and arranged their times and places so that people would seek him, though he is near to each of us, as their own poets said. So he cannot be represented by images of gold or stone. He has overlooked past ignorance, but now commands everyone to repent, because he has fixed a day of judgement by the man he appointed and raised from the dead. Some mock at the mention of resurrection, others want to hear more, and a few believe, including Dionysius of the council and a woman named Damaris.
verseByVerse.theology:
Natural Theology and Its Limits

Paul's Areopagus address is the New Testament's most extended engagement with natural theology — the knowledge of God available through creation. He acknowledges that God has not left himself without witness (14:17), that all nations are made from one blood and live in God-given boundaries (17:26), that the divine nature is reflected in creation sufficiently to leave humanity without excuse (Romans 1:20). But natural theology has limits: it can establish God's existence and general character; it cannot reveal the gospel of Jesus Christ. The movement from 'the God who made everything' to 'the man he has appointed' requires the Word.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Some mocked the resurrection; some said 'we will hear you again'; some believed. The three responses to the Areopagus address are the three responses to every gospel proclamation: dismissal, deferral, and faith. Now: The gospel continues to divide its hearers along these same three lines. The church's task is not to ensure the first response never comes but to preach in such a way that the third response is genuinely available to all who will receive it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now while Paul was waiting for them at Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols. So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the devout persons, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is deeply stirred by a city full of idols, and reasons in synagogue and marketplace.

Provoked. Parōxyneto: stirred, grieved, angered. The beauty of Athens did not impress Paul; its idolatry grieved him.

Full of idols. The Roman writer Petronius joked that in Athens it was easier to find a god than a man. Statues and shrines lined every street.

The marketplace. The agora, centre of public life, where Socrates had debated centuries before. Paul did the same.

On a Tuesday. What grieves you about your city? Let it move you to speak of Christ, not just to complain.
verseByVerse.note: The marketplace (agora) was the centre of public life, filled with statues and shrines.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also conversed with him. And some said, 'What does this babbler wish to say?' Others said, 'He seems to be a preacher of foreign divinities' — because he was preaching Jesus and the resurrection. And they took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, 'May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philosophers debate him, dismissing him as a babbler preaching foreign gods.

Epicureans. Followers of Epicurus (died 270 BC). The gods exist but are remote and uninterested in us; the world is made of atoms; death is the end; the goal of life is tranquil pleasure, free from fear and pain.

Stoics. Followers of Zeno (died about 262 BC), who taught in the Painted Porch (Stoa) in the agora. God is the rational principle (logos) pervading the universe; live in harmony with nature and reason; accept fate calmly.

Babbler. Spermologos: “seed-picker”, a bird that pecks up scraps; slang for someone who picks up scraps of ideas and repeats them.

Foreign gods. Perhaps they thought “Jesus” and “Anastasis” (the Greek for resurrection) were a pair of gods, male and female. Socrates had been executed for introducing new gods.

On a Tuesday. Our culture has its Epicureans (live for pleasure; nothing after death) and its Stoics (be calm; accept what happens). The gospel answers both.
verseByVerse.note: Epicureans taught that the gods were remote and the aim of life was a calm, untroubled pleasure; Stoics taught living by reason and duty. “Babbler” is literally “seed-picker” — like a bird pecking up scraps of learning. The Areopagus was the city’s ancient council, named after the Hill of Ares.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you bring some strange things to our ears. We wish to know therefore what these things mean.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They bring him to the Areopagus to explain his new teaching.

The Areopagus. The “Hill of Ares” (the Roman Mars), a rocky hill below the Acropolis, and also the name of the council that met there, which had authority over religion and education. Paul may have been examined by the council rather than simply taken to the hill.

New teaching. Novelty attracted the Athenians.

On a Tuesday. When people ask about your faith, see it as an invitation to explain.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there would spend their time in nothing except telling or hearing something new."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Athens loves novelty and talk.

Something new. A city addicted to novelty. Ancient writers, including the orator Demosthenes, mocked the Athenians for always asking “Is there any news?”

On a Tuesday. Our age is also addicted to the latest news, trend and idea. The gospel is old news that never gets old.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Paul, standing in the midst of the Areopagus, said: 'Men of Athens, I perceive that in every way you are very religious. For as I passed along and observed the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: "To the unknown god." What therefore you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins from their religiousness and their altar to an unknown god: he will make the unknown God known.

Very religious. Deisidaimonesterous: could mean “very religious” or “very superstitious”. Paul starts courteously.

An unknown god. Ancient writers mention altars in Athens “to unknown gods”. One story (in Diogenes Laertius) says that during a plague the poet Epimenides advised releasing sheep and sacrificing wherever they lay down, to whatever god was responsible, leaving altars with no name.

What you worship as unknown. Not that their worship was acceptable, but that they had an awareness of a God beyond their gods, whom they did not know.

How should we speak to unbelievers? Some read this speech as finding common ground in natural theology and Greek philosophy. Others (Cornelius Van Til) stress how sharply Paul confronts: he calls them ignorant, rejects their temples and images, and demands repentance. Verdict: both. Paul finds real points of contact, but uses them to expose the antithesis between their thinking and God’s truth.

On a Tuesday. Look for points of contact with your friends’ beliefs and longings, then lead them to the God they do not yet know.
verseByVerse.note: “Very religious” could be a compliment or mean “very superstitious.” Ancient writers mention altars at Athens dedicated to unknown gods.

verseByVerse.quote: "The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not live in temples made by man, nor is he served by human hands, as though he needed anything, since he himself gives to all mankind life and breath and everything."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God is the Creator, Lord of heaven and earth, who needs nothing and gives everything.

The Creator. Paul begins with creation, as at Lystra (14:15). Against the Epicureans: God is not remote, he made all things. Against the Stoics: God is not the world, he is its Lord.

Not in temples. Standing below the Parthenon, one of the most magnificent temples ever built, Paul says God does not live in such places. Stephen said the same of the Jerusalem temple (7:48).

Not needing anything. God is self-sufficient; we serve him not to supply his needs. Even some Greek philosophers said this.

Life and breath. Isaiah 42:5: God “gave breath to the people on it”.

On a Tuesday. Every breath you take today is God’s gift.

parallels.desc: who gives breath to the people

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he made from one man every nation of mankind to live on all the face of the earth, having determined allotted periods and the boundaries of their dwelling place, that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God made all nations from one man, set their times and places, so that they would seek him, though he is near.

From one man. Adam. All humanity is one family. The Athenians thought themselves superior, born from the soil of Attica, and despised other nations as barbarians. Paul rejects racial pride.

Against racism. This verse has been a foundation of Christian opposition to racism and ideas of superior races.

Times and boundaries. God rules history and nations (Deuteronomy 32:8, “When the Most High gave to the nations their inheritance”).

Feel their way. Like a blind person groping. Without revelation, people grope for God.

Not far. “Am I a God at hand, declares the LORD, and not a God far away?” (Jeremiah 23:23).

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV, “hath made of one blood all nations”) add “blood”. The earliest read simply “from one”.

On a Tuesday. Treat people of every race and nation as members of your own family.

parallels.desc: he fixed the borders of the peoples

verseByVerse.quote: "'for "In him we live and move and have our being"; as even some of your own poets have said, "For we are indeed his offspring."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even their own poets recognised that we live in God and are his offspring.

Your own poets. The first line is often attributed to Epimenides of Crete (sixth century BC), in a poem addressed to Zeus; Paul quotes the same poem in Titus 1:12. “We are his offspring” is from the Stoic poet Aratus of Cilicia (third century BC), who was from Paul’s home region; Cleanthes’ Hymn to Zeus has a similar line.

Using pagan sources. Paul quotes truths the Greeks had glimpsed, applying them to the true God, not to Zeus. All truth is God’s truth.

His offspring. In the sense of creation, made in his image; not that all are his children by grace (John 1:12).

On a Tuesday. Use films, songs and books your friends know to start conversations about God.
verseByVerse.note: Paul quotes Greek poets. “For we are indeed his offspring” comes from Aratus; the first line is often attributed to Epimenides.

parallels.desc: Paul quotes a Cretan prophet

verseByVerse.quote: "'Being then God's offspring, we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man. The times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he commands all people everywhere to repent,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If we are God’s offspring, idols are absurd, and God now commands everyone everywhere to repent.

The argument. If we are God’s offspring, God cannot be less than we are, a statue we make.

Idolatry. People “exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man” (Romans 1:23).

Overlooked. Not that God ignored sin, but that he held back judgement and did not send them prophets, until now (14:16; Romans 3:25).

All people everywhere. A universal command. Even philosophers must repent.

What about those who never heard? God is patient and just. But now that the gospel has come, ignorance is no longer an excuse.

On a Tuesday. Repentance is not only for “bad” people. Educated, cultured people need it too.

verseByVerse.quote: "'because he has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has fixed a day of judgment by the man he appointed, and proved it by raising him from the dead.

A fixed day. History is going somewhere: judgement. Against Epicureans, who denied judgement, and Stoics, who believed in endless cycles.

A man. Jesus, though Paul does not name him here. The judge is human, as well as divine (John 5:27).
