Assurance. Pistis: proof, guarantee. The resurrection is God’s public evidence.

On a Tuesday. Everyone you meet will stand before Jesus as judge. Let that shape how you speak with them.

parallels.desc: he will judge the world in righteousness

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this.' So Paul went out from their midst."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The resurrection divides the audience: some mock, others want to hear more.

Mocked. Most Greeks found bodily resurrection absurd. The playwright Aeschylus had written, in a play set on this very hill, that when a man dies there is no resurrection.

Three responses. Mockery, curiosity and faith (v. 34). The same today.

Did Paul fail at Athens? Some say Paul tried philosophy, failed, and went to Corinth resolved to preach only Christ crucified (1 Corinthians 2:1–2). Verdict: not really. Paul preached judgement, repentance and the resurrection here, and some believed. He adapted his starting point, not his message.

On a Tuesday. Do not be discouraged by mockery. Some will want to hear more.
verseByVerse.note: Most Greeks found bodily resurrection absurd.

verseByVerse.quote: "But some men joined him and believed, among whom also were Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris and others with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A few believe, including a member of the council and a woman named Damaris.

Dionysius. A member of the council, an important man. Tradition says he became the first bishop of Athens. (Writings under his name from the sixth century, very influential in the Middle Ages, were not by him.)

Damaris. Named alongside him, perhaps a woman of standing, since ordinary women would not usually attend such a meeting.

A few. A small harvest, but real.

For worship. Thank God that the gospel reaches even the proud and learned, and pray for universities and intellectuals today.
verseByVerse.note: Dionysius was a member of the Areopagus council.

17.theology: General Revelation and the Necessity of the Gospel. Acts 17 contains the New Testament’s most developed account of what theologians call general revelation: the knowledge of God available to all humanity through creation and conscience (Romans 1:18–20). Paul acknowledges the Athenians’ religious instinct as genuine — they are groping toward God. But groping is not finding. General revelation creates the question; the gospel alone provides the answer. The God who made all nations from one man, who determined their times and boundaries, who is not far from any of us — this God has now spoken definitively in a man he raised from the dead. The times of ignorance are over. The command is universal: all people everywhere must repent. General revelation without the gospel leaves no one saved; it only leaves everyone without excuse.
17.examples:
Then: Paul in Athens, spirit provoked, standing before the intellectual elite of the ancient world with nothing but the story of a crucified and risen Jew. Some mock. Some believe. He moves on. The church in Athens is small, but Dionysius and Damaris are there — and the gospel is in Europe to stay.

Now: The contemporary West is increasingly like Athens: intellectually sophisticated, spiritually restless, full of altars to unnamed gods, suspicious of exclusive truth claims. The Areopagus sermon is the model for engagement: begin where people are, affirm what is true in their searching, and then announce the resurrection without apology. The resurrection is still the scandal. It is also still the only answer to the altar inscribed “To the unknown god.”

18.title: Corinth
18.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. <sup>2</sup>And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them, <sup>3</sup>and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade. <sup>4</sup>And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. <sup>5</sup>When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” <sup>7</sup>And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue. <sup>8</sup>Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized. <sup>9</sup>And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, <sup>10</sup>for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.” <sup>11</sup>And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them. <sup>12</sup>But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, <sup>13</sup>saying, “This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.” <sup>14</sup>But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. <sup>15</sup>But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things.” <sup>16</sup>And he drove them from the tribunal. <sup>17</sup>And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. <sup>18</sup>After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow. <sup>19</sup>And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. <sup>20</sup>When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined. <sup>21</sup>But on taking leave of them he said, “I will return to you if God wills,” and he set sail from Ephesus. <sup>22</sup>When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch. <sup>23</sup>After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. <sup>24</sup>Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. <sup>25</sup>He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. <sup>26</sup>He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately. <sup>27</sup>And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, <sup>28</sup>for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus.
18.overview:
From Athens Paul goes to Corinth, the wealthy, proud commercial city on the isthmus, capital of the province of Achaia (see the introduction to 1 Corinthians). He finds Aquila and Priscilla, a Jewish couple recently expelled from Rome by the emperor Claudius, and works with them making tents. The Roman historian Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews because of riots “at the instigation of Chrestus”, probably disputes about Christ in the Jewish community, around AD 49. When Silas and Timothy arrive with support from Macedonia, Paul devotes himself fully to preaching. Opposed in the synagogue, he moves next door to the house of a God-fearer, Titius Justus; the synagogue ruler Crispus believes with his household, and many Corinthians are baptised. In a night vision the Lord tells Paul not to be afraid, because he has many people in this city, and Paul stays eighteen months.

When Jewish opponents bring Paul before the new proconsul, Gallio, he dismisses the case as a quarrel about Jewish words and names, not a Roman crime, a ruling that gave the church breathing space. An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio’s year in office to about AD 51–52, one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life. Paul then sails with Priscilla and Aquila to Ephesus, leaves them there, and returns via Caesarea and Jerusalem to Antioch, completing his second journey. The third journey begins with a tour of the Galatian churches. Meanwhile an eloquent, learned Jew from Alexandria, Apollos, arrives in Ephesus, preaching accurately about Jesus but knowing only John’s baptism. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately, and he goes on to Corinth, where he powerfully refutes the Jews in public, showing from the Scriptures that the Messiah is Jesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Corinth and the Return to Antioch
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul leaves Athens for Corinth, where he lodges and works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla, Jews recently expelled from Rome. He reasons in the synagogue every Sabbath, and when Silas and Timothy arrive he gives himself fully to preaching that Jesus is the Messiah. When the Jews oppose and abuse him, he shakes out his clothes and declares their blood is on their own heads; from now on he will go to the Gentiles. He moves next door to the house of Titius Justus, a God-fearer. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his household believe, and many Corinthians believe and are baptised. In a night vision the Lord tells Paul to keep speaking without fear, for no one will harm him, and he has many people in this city. Paul stays a year and a half, teaching God’s word. Under the proconsul Gallio, the Jews bring Paul to court, accusing him of persuading people to worship God against the law, but Gallio refuses to judge questions of words, names and Jewish law and throws them out. The crowd beats Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, in front of the court, and Gallio does not care. After many days Paul sails for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, having had his hair cut at Cenchreae because of a vow. At Ephesus he reasons in the synagogue, but declines to stay longer, promising to return if God wills. He lands at Caesarea, greets the church in Jerusalem and goes down to Antioch.
verseByVerse.theology:
Tent-Making Ministry and the Support of Proclamation

Paul's tent-making partnership with Aquila and Priscilla is the first explicit mention of Paul's manual labor as a means of supporting his missionary work. Reformed theology has often discussed whether 'tentmaker ministry' (self-supported missionary work) is a normative apostolic pattern or a situational adaptation. Paul's own letters suggest the latter: he worked with his hands to avoid being a burden on new churches and to model the dignity of labor, but he accepted support from established communities (Philippians 4:15–16). The Corinthian mission itself was eventually supported by the arrival of Silas and Timothy from Macedonia (v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples: Then: The Gallio decision — the Roman proconsul's dismissal of the Jewish charge against Paul — protected Paul's preaching at Corinth by treating it as an internal Jewish dispute. Now: God continues to use civil authorities and legal processes to protect the gospel's proclamation, even when those authorities have no understanding of or sympathy with the gospel. Providence works through the decisions of those who know nothing of its purposes.

verseByVerse.quote: "After this Paul left Athens and went to Corinth. And he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had commanded all the Jews to leave Rome. And he went to see them,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In proud, wealthy Corinth God provides Paul with friends and fellow workers in Aquila and Priscilla, recently expelled from Rome.

Corinth. About 50 miles from Athens. A Roman colony, capital of Achaia, with two ports and a reputation for wealth and immorality. Paul arrived “in weakness and in fear and much trembling” (1 Corinthians 2:3).

Aquila and Priscilla. A married couple, always named together; Priscilla (Prisca) is usually named first, perhaps because she was of higher social status or more prominent in ministry. Probably already believers when Paul met them.

Pontus. A region on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor (2:9).

Claudius’s decree. The Roman historian Suetonius writes that Claudius “expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly making disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus”, usually dated AD 49. “Chrestus” was probably a misunderstanding of “Christus”: disputes over Christ in Rome’s synagogues. The Jews returned after Claudius died in AD 54 (Romans 16:3).

On a Tuesday. God can turn an expulsion into a new ministry. If you have had to move unwillingly, look for what God may be doing.
verseByVerse.note: Corinth, the capital of the province of Achaia, was a busy, wealthy trading city with a reputation for immorality. The Roman historian Suetonius mentions Claudius expelling Jews from Rome over disturbances, around AD 49.

verseByVerse.quote: "and because he was of the same trade he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul supports himself by his trade, working alongside them.

Tentmaking. Working with leather or with cilicium, a goat-hair cloth from Paul’s home province of Cilicia. Tents and awnings were in demand in Corinth, especially at the Isthmian Games.

A trade. Jewish teachers commonly learned a trade; a rabbinic saying held that whoever does not teach his son a trade teaches him to steal. Paul supported himself so as not to burden anyone (1 Thessalonians 2:9, “we worked night and day, that we might not be a burden”; 2 Thessalonians 3:8).

Bivocational ministry. “Tentmaking” is now used for Christians who support themselves in secular jobs while doing ministry, especially in countries closed to missionaries.

On a Tuesday. Your workplace can be your mission field, as Paul’s workshop was.
verseByVerse.note: Tentmakers worked with leather and cloth. Jewish teachers commonly had a trade; Paul supported himself so as not to burden the churches.

verseByVerse.quote: And he reasoned in the synagogue every Sabbath, and tried to persuade Jews and Greeks. When Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was occupied with the word, testifying to the Jews that the Christ was Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reasons every Sabbath, and when his colleagues arrive he gives himself fully to preaching that Jesus is the Christ.

Persuade. Reasoning, not manipulation.

Silas and Timothy. They brought news from Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 3:6) and a gift from Philippi (2 Corinthians 11:9; Philippians 4:15), which freed Paul to preach full time.

Occupied with the word. Literally “held fast by the word”: wholly absorbed.

On a Tuesday. Supporting missionaries financially frees them to give themselves to the word.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they opposed and reviled him, he shook out his garments and said to them, 'Your blood be on your own heads! I am innocent. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.' And he left there and went to the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God. His house was next door to the synagogue."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the synagogue rejects him, Paul declares himself clear of their blood and moves next door.

Shook out his garments. A gesture of breaking off responsibility, like shaking dust from the feet (13:51).

Your blood on your heads. Echoing Ezekiel the watchman: if the watchman warns and the people do not listen, “his blood shall be upon his own head” (Ezekiel 33:4). Paul has done his duty.

Next door. A bold move: the new congregation met right beside the synagogue.

Titius Justus. A Roman name. Some identify him with Gaius, Paul’s host in Corinth (Romans 16:23), whose full name might have been Gaius Titius Justus.

On a Tuesday. When people reject the gospel, you are not responsible for their choice, if you have faithfully told them.
verseByVerse.note: Shaking out one’s garments was a gesture of breaking off responsibility.

parallels.desc: his blood shall be on his own head

verseByVerse.quote: "Crispus, the ruler of the synagogue, believed in the Lord, together with his entire household. And many of the Corinthians hearing Paul believed and were baptized."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the synagogue leader believes with his household, and many Corinthians are baptised.

Crispus. Head of the synagogue, a major conversion. Paul baptised him personally (1 Corinthians 1:14).

Heard, believed, baptised. The pattern of conversion in Acts.

On a Tuesday. Pray for community leaders. Their conversion can influence many.

parallels.desc: I baptized none of you except Crispus and Gaius

verseByVerse.quote: "And the Lord said to Paul one night in a vision, 'Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord encourages Paul not to fear but to keep speaking, for he has many people in this city.

Do not be afraid. Paul was afraid (1 Corinthians 2:3). The great apostle needed encouragement.

I am with you. The promise to Joshua (Joshua 1:9), Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:8) and the apostles (Matthew 28:20).

Many people. Not yet converted, yet already “my people”. God had chosen them, and they would come to faith through Paul’s preaching. Jesus said the same: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold” (John 10:16). Election does not make evangelism unnecessary; it guarantees its success.

On a Tuesday. God has people in your town who do not yet know him. Keep speaking.

parallels.desc: do not be afraid, for I am with you

verseByVerse.quote: "And he stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stays eighteen months, teaching the word of God.

Eighteen months. His longest stay so far. During it he probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians.

Teaching. Grounding the new church.

On a Tuesday. Lasting churches need patient teaching, not just evangelism.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth during this stay.

verseByVerse.quote: "But when Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews made a united attack on Paul and brought him before the tribunal, saying, 'This man is persuading people to worship God contrary to the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Under a new proconsul, opponents bring Paul to court for teaching unlawful worship.

Gallio. Lucius Junius Gallio, brother of the philosopher Seneca, known as a charming man. An inscription at Delphi, quoting a letter of Claudius, names Gallio as proconsul and dates his term to AD 51–52. This allows us to date Paul’s stay in Corinth and anchor the chronology of his life.

The tribunal. The bēma, a raised stone platform in Corinth’s forum, still visible today (2 Corinthians 5:10).

Contrary to the law. Which law? Probably they hoped Gallio would rule that Christianity was not Judaism, and so not a legal religion.

On a Tuesday. Pray for judges and courts in matters affecting religious freedom.
verseByVerse.note: An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio’s term as proconsul to about AD 51–52 — one of the fixed points for dating Paul’s life. The tribunal (bema) still stands in the Corinthian marketplace.

parallels.desc: the judgment seat of Christ

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, "If it were a matter of wrongdoing or vicious crime, O Jews, I would have reason to accept your complaint. But since it is a matter of questions about words and names and your own law, see to it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gallio refuses to judge a dispute about Jewish words and names, a ruling that protects the church.

Before Paul spoke. Paul did not need to defend himself.

Words and names. Gallio treated it as an internal Jewish theological dispute.

The significance. By refusing to rule, Gallio treated Christianity as a form of Judaism, which was legal. This precedent protected the church for years.

On a Tuesday. God can use the indifference of rulers to protect his church.
verseByVerse.note: Gallio treated the dispute as an internal Jewish matter, not a Roman crime.

verseByVerse.quote: And he drove them from the tribunal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gallio throws the case out.

Dismissed. The case thrown out.

On a Tuesday. Not every attack on the church succeeds.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all seized Sosthenes, the ruler of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the tribunal. But Gallio paid no attention to any of this. After this, Paul stayed many days longer and then took leave of the brothers and set sail for Syria, and with him Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchreae he had cut his hair, for he was under a vow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gallio ignores the beating of Sosthenes, and Paul eventually sails for Syria after a vow at Cenchreae.

Sosthenes. Crispus’s successor as synagogue leader. Beaten by Greek bystanders, perhaps venting anti-Jewish feeling, or by the Jews for failing. Perhaps the Sosthenes who later co-wrote 1 Corinthians (1 Corinthians 1:1).

Gallio did not care. Roman indifference to Jewish affairs.

Cenchreae. Corinth’s eastern port, where there was a church served by Phoebe (Romans 16:1).

A vow. Probably a Nazirite-type vow, a Jewish practice of special devotion to God, during which one did not cut the hair: “All the days of his vow of separation, no razor shall touch his head” (Numbers 6:5). Paul, free from the law, still chose Jewish practices as an expression of devotion.

On a Tuesday. Christian freedom allows us to keep traditions that help our devotion, as long as we do not make them conditions of salvation.
verseByVerse.note: A Sosthenes later appears with Paul as a believer. Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern port. Cutting the hair marked the end of a vow of special devotion.

parallels.desc: the Nazirite vow
Phoebe of Cenchreae

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to Ephesus, and he left them there, but he himself went into the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews. When they asked him to stay for a longer period, he declined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At Ephesus Paul leaves Priscilla and Aquila and reasons briefly in the synagogue.

Ephesus. Capital of the province of Asia, a city of perhaps 200,000, with the great temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Paul would return for nearly three years (chapter 19).

Left them there. Priscilla and Aquila prepared the ground.

On a Tuesday. Sometimes the best thing a church planter can do is leave faithful lay people behind to continue.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia.

verseByVerse.quote: But on taking leave of them he said, "I will return to you if God wills," and he set sail from Ephesus. When he had landed at Caesarea, he went up and greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul promises to return if God wills, and completes his journey via Jerusalem to Antioch.

If God wills. Paul’s constant attitude (James 4:15).

Went up. To Jerusalem, on high ground; “greeted the church” there. The second journey ends at Antioch.

A textual note. Later manuscripts (followed by the KJV) add: “I must by all means keep this feast that cometh in Jerusalem.” The earliest lack it.

On a Tuesday. Hold your plans with “if God wills”.

parallels.desc: if the Lord wills

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After some time in Antioch, Paul set out on his third journey and travelled from place to place through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples. Meanwhile a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was a learned man with a thorough knowledge of the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord and spoke with great fervour, teaching accurately about Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John. He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they invited him to their home and explained to him the way of God more adequately. When Apollos wanted to go to Achaia, the believers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there to welcome him. On arriving, he was a great help to those who by grace had believed, for he vigorously refuted his Jewish opponents in public debate, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Messiah.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Importance of Thorough Gospel Formation

Apollos's incomplete knowledge — accurate as far as it went but stopping short of the full apostolic message — is the permanent challenge of theological formation. Every generation needs to receive not just the part of the gospel that resonates with its existing categories but the complete gospel that the Scriptures teach. Priscilla and Aquila model the ministry of theological completion: receiving those who are partially formed, honoring what is genuine, and filling in what is absent. This is the ministry of discipleship.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Apollos went to Achaia and was of great help to those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus. Now: The church continues to be built by ministers whose gifts complement each other — some plant (Paul in Corinth), some water (Apollos in Corinth, 1 Corinthians 3:6), and God gives the growth.

verseByVerse.quote: "After spending some time there, he departed and went from one place to the next through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins his third journey by strengthening the disciples in Galatia and Phrygia.

The third journey. Begins with pastoral visits.

Strengthening. Paul cared for existing churches as much as planting new ones.

On a Tuesday. Strengthen the believers you know: a visit, a call, an encouraging word.
verseByVerse.note: Here begins Paul’s third missionary journey.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now a Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, competent in the Scriptures. He had been instructed in the way of the Lord. And being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only the baptism of John."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apollos, a learned and fervent Jew from Alexandria, teaches accurately about Jesus but knows only John’s baptism.

Alexandria. In Egypt, the second city of the empire, with its great library, a centre of learning and the largest Jewish community outside Judea. The Jewish philosopher Philo lived there and read Scripture allegorically. The Greek Old Testament was translated there.

Eloquent. Logios: learned, eloquent. Some Corinthians later preferred him to Paul (1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4–6).

Competent in the Scriptures. Mighty in the Old Testament.

Fervent in spirit. Literally “boiling in spirit”: enthusiastic.

Only John’s baptism. He knew about Jesus, perhaps through followers of John the Baptist, but not fully about Pentecost and Christian baptism.

On a Tuesday. Zeal and eloquence need accurate knowledge.
verseByVerse.note: Alexandria in Egypt was a great centre of learning with a large Jewish community.

verseByVerse.quote: "He began to speak boldly in the synagogue, but when Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately.

Took him aside. Privately, not publicly correcting him. A model of gracious correction.

More accurately. Filling in what he lacked.

Priscilla first. She is named first, and took part in teaching a man. Egalitarians cite this as evidence that women taught men in the early church. Complementarians note that this was private instruction, alongside her husband, in their home, not the authoritative teaching office of an elder in the church (1 Timothy 2:12). Verdict: the complementarian reading is right, but this verse should encourage women to share their knowledge of God’s word, and men like Apollos to receive it humbly.

Was Apollos rebaptised? Luke does not say so, in contrast to the disciples of 19:1–7. Perhaps his earlier baptism was accepted, as the apostles’ was.

On a Tuesday. If a gifted preacher gets something wrong, speak to them privately and kindly. And if someone corrects you, listen like Apollos.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. When he arrived, he greatly helped those who through grace had believed, for he powerfully refuted the Jews in public, showing by the Scriptures that the Christ was Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Apollos goes to Achaia and greatly helps the believers, proving from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

A letter. A letter of recommendation (compare 2 Corinthians 3:1).

Through grace had believed. Faith is the gift of grace. A small phrase, a big truth (Ephesians 2:8).

Powerfully refuted. Apollos’s training in Scripture and rhetoric was used for the gospel. Paul later said, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6).

For worship. Thank God for gifted teachers who show from the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ, and for humble people like Priscilla and Aquila who help them.
verseByVerse.note: Achaia is southern Greece, including Corinth.

parallels.desc: I planted, Apollos watered

18.theology: Election as the Ground of Courage in Mission. “I have many in this city who are my people” (v. 10) is the doctrine of election functioning as a promise to a frightened missionary. Paul is afraid — he says so later. And God’s answer to his fear is not “it will go well” or “people will respond positively” — it is “I have my people here.” The ground of missionary perseverance is not optimism about human receptivity; it is confidence in divine election. God has sheep in every city, in every culture, in every hostile context — sheep who will hear the shepherd’s voice when it is proclaimed through his servants. This is not a reason for laziness; it is a reason for courage. Preach. His people will come.
18.examples:
Then: Paul in Corinth, afraid, working as a tentmaker, preaching every Sabbath, sustained by a vision and a promise, staying eighteen months because God told him to stay. The church that emerged from that eighteen months will cause him more trouble than any other — and will receive his most profound letters about the cross, the resurrection, and love.

Now: Every city has people who are God’s — people the Spirit is already preparing, already drawing, already making ready to hear. The task of the church is to be in the city, to preach the word, to stay when the Lord says stay, and to trust that the harvest belongs to him. The missionary who preaches in the hardest city is not alone. God is already there, and his people are waiting.

19.title: Ephesus and the Power of the Word
19.text: <sup>1</sup>And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. <sup>2</sup>And he said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” And they said, “No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.” <sup>3</sup>And he said, “Into what then were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.” <sup>4</sup>And Paul said, “John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.” <sup>5</sup>On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. <sup>6</sup>And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. <sup>7</sup>There were about twelve men in all. <sup>8</sup>And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. <sup>9</sup>But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus. <sup>10</sup>This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks. <sup>11</sup>And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, <sup>12</sup>so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them. <sup>13</sup>Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.” <sup>14</sup>Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this. <sup>15</sup>But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?” <sup>16</sup>And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded. <sup>17</sup>And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. <sup>18</sup>Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices. <sup>19</sup>And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. <sup>20</sup>So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily. <sup>21</sup>Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.” <sup>22</sup>And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while. <sup>23</sup>About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. <sup>24</sup>For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen. <sup>25</sup>These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, “Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth. <sup>26</sup>And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. <sup>27</sup>And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship.” <sup>28</sup>When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>29</sup>So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul’s companions in travel. <sup>30</sup>But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. <sup>31</sup>And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater. <sup>32</sup>Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. <sup>33</sup>Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd. <sup>34</sup>But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” <sup>35</sup>And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, “Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? <sup>36</sup>Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash. <sup>37</sup>For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. <sup>38</sup>If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another. <sup>39</sup>But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. <sup>40</sup>For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion.” <sup>41</sup>And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly.
19.overview:
Ephesus is the climax of Paul’s free ministry. It was the capital of the province of Asia, a port of perhaps a quarter of a million people, home of the vast temple of Artemis and famous across the empire for magic. Paul stays nearly three years (20:31), longer than anywhere else. He first meets a dozen men who know only John’s baptism; taught about Jesus, they are baptised in his name and receive the Spirit. Three months in the synagogue are followed by two years of daily teaching in a hired hall, and the word spreads through the whole province: the churches of the Lycus valley and the seven churches of Revelation 2–3 probably date from these years.

The gospel then collides with the city’s religion. God works unusual miracles through Paul; seven Jewish exorcists who use Jesus’ name as a spell are overpowered; and new believers burn their magic books, worth a fortune. Paul plans to go through Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem and then to Rome, the plan the rest of Acts follows. Finally the silversmith Demetrius, whose trade depends on the goddess, stirs up a riot that fills the great theatre for two hours, until the town clerk calms the crowd: the Christians have committed no crime, and the courts are open. Luke’s summary is the key: the word of the Lord kept growing and prevailing (v. 20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul reaches Ephesus and finds about twelve disciples who know only John’s baptism and have not heard of the Holy Spirit. He explains that John pointed to Jesus; they are baptised in Jesus’ name, Paul lays hands on them, and the Spirit comes, with tongues and prophecy. Paul teaches in the synagogue for three months; when some harden and slander the Way, he moves the disciples to the lecture hall of Tyrannus and teaches daily for two years, so that the whole province hears the word. God does unusual miracles through him. Seven sons of a Jewish chief priest, Sceva, try to drive out a spirit in the name of “the Jesus whom Paul proclaims”, and the possessed man overpowers them. Fear falls on the city, believers confess their practices, and magicians burn books worth fifty thousand silver coins. Paul resolves to go to Jerusalem and then to Rome. Demetrius the silversmith rallies the craftsmen whose shrines of Artemis are losing trade, and the city rushes into the theatre, dragging two of Paul’s companions. Paul is kept from going in. For two hours the crowd chants “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians”, until the town clerk quiets them, points out that these men have committed no crime, sends complaints to the courts or a lawful assembly, warns of Roman displeasure, and dismisses the crowd.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Word of the Lord Prevailing Over Magic and Idolatry

The burning of the magical books — fifty thousand pieces of silver worth — is one of the most dramatic acts of new-believer repentance in Acts. The magicians do not gradually reduce their practice; they make a clean, costly, public break. Reformed theology sees in this the pattern of genuine repentance: the thoroughgoing abandonment of what the gospel has displaced, at whatever cost. The summary in v. 20 ('So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily') is the theological verdict on the entire Ephesian episode: the word wins, over magic, over economics, over riot.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Demetrius the silversmith's complaint — 'there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing' — is the most honest statement of why people oppose the gospel: it costs them something they value. Now: The gospel continues to threaten economic arrangements built on idolatry, and the opposition it meets is often economic before it is theological.

verseByVerse.quote: "And it happened that while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the inland country and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. And he said to them, 'Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?' And they said, 'No, we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul meets disciples whose faith stopped at John the Baptist, and his question shows that receiving the Spirit is the normal mark of believing.

Who they were. Probably followers of John the Baptist’s movement, like Apollos before Priscilla and Aquila taught him (18:25). They had repented and looked for the coming one, but had not heard that he had come, died, risen and poured out the Spirit. “Not heard that there is a Holy Spirit” probably means not heard that the Spirit has been given (compare John 7:39, literally “the Spirit was not yet”): any Jew who listened to John knew the Spirit existed (Luke 3:16).

Paul’s question assumes the normal case. He takes it for granted that a believer receives the Spirit on believing, and that it is something you would know (Romans 8:9; Galatians 3:2). His question exposes that their faith is incomplete, not that their Christian experience lacks a second stage.

On a Tuesday. Paul listened closely enough to notice what was missing. Good pastoral care asks gentle, direct questions rather than assuming everyone in the room has understood the gospel.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was the chief city of the province of Asia, a great port and centre of the worship of Artemis. These “disciples” knew only John’s baptism.

parallels.desc: Apollos, who knew only the baptism of John

verseByVerse.quote: "And he said, 'Into what then were you baptized?' They said, 'Into John's baptism.' And Paul said, 'John baptized with the baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the one who was to come after him, that is, Jesus.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
John’s baptism pointed beyond itself to Jesus; to stop at John is to stop short of Christ.

Baptism and belief go together. Paul moves straight from the Spirit to baptism: in the apostolic church, believing, being baptised and receiving the Spirit belonged to one conversion (2:38).

John pointed away from himself. His whole ministry was a signpost (John 1:29–30; 3:30). To stop at John is to read the signpost and never travel the road.

On a Tuesday. It is possible to be sincere, religious and repentant and still not to have heard clearly of Christ crucified and risen. Ask yourself, and those you teach, not only “are you sorry for sin?” but “whom are you trusting?”

verseByVerse.quote: "On hearing this, they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
These men are baptised into Jesus for the first time: a change of era, not a rebaptism.

Not a rebaptism. This is the only case in the New Testament of people baptised after an earlier rite, and it is not a second Christian baptism. John’s baptism looked forward; these men had never received baptism into Christ. Apollos, who probably had, is not rebaptised (18:26).

Where Christians differ: rebaptism. Some groups use this verse to rebaptise anyone whose earlier baptism they judge defective. Others, especially those who baptise infants, hold that a baptism with water in the triune name is never repeated, though they recognise this case as the passing from John to Christ. Credobaptists hold that baptism belongs to those who profess faith, and so regard a baptism given before faith as not yet the baptism the New Testament describes; many therefore baptise believers baptised as infants, while honouring paedobaptist brothers and sisters as fellow believers. Verdict: the app’s credobaptist view sees here baptism following faith at once, while insisting that Acts 19 is about the change of era from John to Christ, not a licence to rebaptise over secondary defects.

No delay. As everywhere in Acts, baptism follows hearing and believing without a waiting period (2:41; 8:38; 16:33).

For worship. John’s baptism was into a hope; this one is into a person. Thank God that you belong, by name, to the Lord Jesus.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when Paul had laid his hands on them, the Holy Spirit came on them, and they began speaking in tongues and prophesying. There were about twelve men in all."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit comes visibly on the last followers of John, joining them to the one church.

A small Pentecost. Acts marks each new frontier with a visible coming of the Spirit: Jerusalem (2:4), Samaria (8:17), the Gentiles (10:44–46), and now the last followers of John. Each confirms that the group belongs to the one church, under the apostles’ teaching. Twelve may echo Israel’s twelve tribes, though Luke says only “about”.

Where Christians differ: the Spirit after conversion. Pentecostal and charismatic Christians often read this passage as showing a baptism in the Spirit after conversion, marked by tongues. Reformed and most evangelical interpreters answer that these men were not yet Christians in the full sense: they had not believed in Jesus as having come, and they receive the Spirit at the moment their faith becomes faith in him. Elsewhere Paul says every believer has the Spirit (Romans 8:9) and all were baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Verdict: the gift of the Spirit belongs to conversion; this is a transitional case, not a pattern of two stages. Christians may and should seek to be filled again and again (Ephesians 5:18), but that is growth, not a second entry.

Laying on of hands. Not a sacrament every believer must receive, but here an apostolic sign that joined these men to the church.

For worship. Thank God that the Spirit is not reserved for an élite: he is the birthright of everyone who trusts in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he entered the synagogue and for three months spoke boldly, reasoning and persuading them about the kingdom of God. But when some became stubborn and continued in unbelief, speaking evil of the Way before the congregation, he withdrew from them and took the disciples with him, reasoning daily in the hall of Tyrannus."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reasons about the kingdom until hardened opposition leads him to teach daily in a hired hall.

Three months. His longest stay in any synagogue in Acts: Ephesus had first invited him (18:20).

The kingdom of God. Paul’s message is the reign of God come in Jesus the Messiah (28:23, 31). Kingdom and gospel are not two subjects.

Hardening. The verb is used of Pharaoh in the Greek Old Testament (Exodus 7:3). Unbelief here is not a lack of information but a settled refusal.

The hall of Tyrannus. A lecture hall, named after its owner or a teacher who used it. Textual note. The Western text adds that Paul taught “from the fifth hour to the tenth”, about 11 a.m. to 4 p.m., the hours of the midday rest. It is probably not original, but may preserve a true memory: Paul worked his trade in the mornings (20:34) and taught when the hall was free. Verdict: follow the shorter text; the detail is plausible but not Scripture.

On a Tuesday. Paul gave up his lunch break and afternoon rest, daily, for two years. Faithful ministry is mostly unglamorous, repeated work. What hours could you give?
verseByVerse.note: The hall of Tyrannus was probably a lecture hall. “The Way” was an early name for the Christian faith.

verseByVerse.quote: "This continued for two years, so that all the residents of Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through patient daily teaching the word reaches the whole province.

All Asia. Not that every person met Paul, but that the word reached the whole province through those he trained. Epaphras probably took the gospel to Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 1:7; 4:13), cities Paul himself had not visited (Colossians 2:1).

A training centre. Ephesus was a hub of roads and shipping; people came for business, heard the gospel, and carried it home. The seven churches of Revelation 2–3 are all within reach of the city.

On a Tuesday. Paul multiplied himself by teaching others who could teach others (2 Timothy 2:2). If you lead a group, train someone to lead after you.

For worship. The word of the Lord does not depend on one man’s travels. Praise God that it runs (2 Thessalonians 3:1).
verseByVerse.note: Churches such as those at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis probably began in this period through Paul’s co-workers.

parallels.desc: three years

verseByVerse.quote: And God was doing extraordinary miracles by the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons that had touched his skin were carried away to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits came out of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God works unusual miracles through Paul, pointing a city of charms to the Lord, not to objects.

Extraordinary. Literally “not the ordinary ones”: unusual even by the standards of Acts. Luke marks them as exceptional, not as a pattern.

Working clothes. Probably the sweat-band and work apron of a leatherworker. They were not relics or blessed objects; people simply took them from his workplace.

God is the subject. Luke says God did these things. Compare Peter’s shadow (5:15) and the woman who touched Jesus’ garment, whom Jesus told that her faith, not the cloth, had healed her (Luke 8:48). In a city of charms, God met people where they were and pointed them to the Lord, not to the cloth.

What it does not mean. It gives no warrant for selling “prayer cloths”, for relics or for a ministry built on objects. Paul never sent them out himself, and the very next story shows that using Jesus’ power as a technique is dangerous.

Where Christians differ: miracles today. Continuationists expect such signs whenever the gospel breaks new ground; cessationists hold that sign-gifts confirmed the apostles (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4), while God still heals in answer to prayer (James 5:14–15). Verdict: the app’s cessationist reading, held charitably: these were marks of an apostle, and Luke himself calls them unusual. God remains free to heal, and we should pray.
verseByVerse.note: The handkerchiefs and aprons were probably the cloths Paul used while working at his trade.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then some of the itinerant Jewish exorcists undertook to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, 'I adjure you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.' Seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva were doing this."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Exorcists try to use Jesus’ name as a spell, knowing him only secondhand.

Exorcism as trade. Magical papyri from this period string together powerful names, including Hebrew names of God and even Jesus, as spells. Jewish exorcists had a reputation for this. They treat Jesus’ name as a stronger password.

Sceva. No Jewish high priest of this name is known. He may have belonged to a high-priestly family, or taken the title to impress clients. Textual note. The Western text has “a priest” and adds details about the scene; the shorter reading is original.

Secondhand faith. “The Jesus whom Paul proclaims”: they know Jesus only as Paul’s Jesus. Compare Matthew 7:22–23, those who did works in his name but whom he never knew.

On a Tuesday. Praying “in Jesus’ name” is not a formula that obliges God. It means coming as one who belongs to him, asking what he wills (John 14:13–14; 1 John 5:14).
verseByVerse.note: Exorcists often called on the names of powerful beings in their spells. No high priest named Sceva is known; he may have been from a high-priestly family, or used the title for show.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the evil spirit answered them, 'Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?' And the man in whom was the evil spirit leaped on them, mastered all of them and overpowered them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ name is not a formula: the spirit overpowers those who borrow it without belonging to him.

Known in the unseen world. The spirit knows Jesus (Mark 1:24; James 2:19) and knows Paul as his servant. The verbs differ slightly, but the point is plain: authority belongs to Jesus and to those who are his, not to those who borrow his name.

A comic, sobering scene. Seven professionals are routed by one man. Luke enjoys the irony, but the lesson is serious: the occult is not a toy.

Where Christians differ: spiritual warfare. Some modern “deliverance” ministries build elaborate techniques of naming and binding spirits. Others, including most Reformed teachers, see the believer’s defence in the armour of truth, righteousness, the gospel, faith, the word and prayer (Ephesians 6:10–18), written to this same city. Verdict: take the evil one seriously, but fight with the means Scripture gives, not with formulas; Christ has already disarmed the powers (Colossians 2:15).

For worship. The demons know who Jesus is and tremble. Let his people know him and rejoice.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this became known to all the residents of Ephesus, both Jews and Greeks. And fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was extolled. Also many of those who were now believers came, confessing and divulging their practices."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fear of the Lord leads believers to bring their hidden practices into the open.

Fear, then honour. The failed exorcism shows that Jesus’ name cannot be used: it can only be trusted. The result is reverence, as after Ananias and Sapphira (5:11).

Believers confessing. These are people who had already believed but had kept their magic on the side. “Practices” probably means their spells; in magic, a spell disclosed lost its power. Telling them was itself a renunciation.

On a Tuesday. Conversion is often followed by a later, painful honesty about habits we kept hidden. Horoscopes, lucky charms, “just in case” rituals, or any secret we keep back from Christ: bring it into the light (1 John 1:7–9).

verseByVerse.quote: And a number of those who had practiced magic arts brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted the value of them and found it came to fifty thousand pieces of silver. So the word of the Lord continued to increase and prevail mightily.
verseByVerse.commentary:
New believers burn their costly magic books, and the word of the Lord prevails.

“Ephesian letters”. Ancient writers used this phrase for magical formulas, and Ephesus was renowned for them. The books were scrolls of spells and charms, valuable and secret.

The cost. If the silver pieces were drachmas, roughly a labourer’s daily wage, the total was some 50,000 days’ wages: a fortune. They burned the books rather than sell them, so that no one else would be harmed.

The word prevailed. Luke’s summary (compare 6:7; 12:24) credits the word, not Paul or the miracles. The gospel defeats the occult not by greater magic but by truth that sets people free.

What it does not mean. This is not a licence for Christians to burn other people’s books or to riot against error: these people burned their own property, freely.

On a Tuesday. Repentance sometimes costs money: a subscription cancelled, a stock sold, a collection thrown away. Do not sell to others what has harmed you.

For worship. Praise the Lord whose word is stronger than every spell and every fear.
verseByVerse.note: Ephesus was famous for magic spells. A piece of silver was probably a drachma, about a day’s wage: fifty thousand was a fortune.

verseByVerse.quote: Now after these events Paul resolved in the Spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, "After I have been there, I must also see Rome." And having sent into Macedonia two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, he himself stayed in Asia for a while.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul plans the route that the rest of Acts will follow: Jerusalem, then Rome.

The plan of the rest of Acts. Macedonia and Achaia (chapter 20), Jerusalem (chapter 21), Rome (chapter 28). Every stage happens, but not as Paul imagined: he reaches Rome as a prisoner.

In the Spirit. The phrase could mean Paul’s own spirit, but probably refers to the Holy Spirit guiding his resolve (20:22).

Must. Luke’s word for divine necessity, used of the cross (Luke 24:26). The Lord later confirms it (23:11).

The collection. Paul’s letters show the purpose of this trip: to bring the gift of the Gentile churches to the poor in Jerusalem (Romans 15:25–28; 1 Corinthians 16:1–4). 1 Corinthians was written from Ephesus at this time (1 Corinthians 16:8).

Erastus. Possibly the Corinthian city treasurer (Romans 16:23); an inscription at Corinth names an Erastus who paved a street at his own expense.

On a Tuesday. Make plans prayerfully, and hold them humbly (James 4:13–15). God may keep your plan and change its route.
verseByVerse.note: Erastus may be the city official of Corinth whose name appears on an inscription there.

verseByVerse.quote: About that time there arose no little disturbance concerning the Way. For a man named Demetrius, a silversmith, who made silver shrines of Artemis, brought no little business to the craftsmen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gospel threatens the trade and pride bound up with the goddess Artemis.

Artemis of Ephesus. Not the slim huntress of Greek myth but an ancient mother-goddess of fertility, shown in statues with many breast-like or egg-like ornaments. Her temple, four times the size of the Parthenon, was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. It was also a bank and a place of asylum, and the city’s pride and economy were bound up with it.

Silver shrines. Miniature temples or images, bought by pilgrims as souvenirs and charms. Terracotta examples survive; silver ones have not been found, but inscriptions mention silver images given to the goddess.

Two kinds of opposition. In Philippi the gospel threatened profit (16:19); here, profit and religion together.

On a Tuesday. When the gospel makes progress, expect some of the resistance to come from people whose income depends on things staying as they are. Ask honestly whether your own livelihood ever makes you deaf to truth.
verseByVerse.note: The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. Artemis of Ephesus was a mother-goddess of fertility, not the huntress of Greek myth.

parallels.desc: a wide door, and many adversaries

verseByVerse.quote: These he gathered together, with the workmen in similar trades, and said, "Men, you know that from this business we have our wealth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Demetrius rallies the craftsmen with an appeal to their income.

He begins with money. His speech opens with wages and only later turns to the goddess. Luke lets the order speak.

A guild. Trade associations in Greek cities were social and religious clubs as well as businesses, each with its patron deity. Becoming a Christian could mean leaving your guild’s feasts (1 Corinthians 8–10; Revelation 2:14, 20).

On a Tuesday. Christians in business will sometimes find that faithfulness costs trade. A firm that will not mislead customers or exploit staff may lose to one that does. Count that cost in advance, and trust God with it (Hebrews 13:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "And you see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a great many people, saying that gods made with hands are not gods. And there is danger not only that this trade of ours may come into disrepute but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis may be counted as nothing, and that she may even be deposed from her magnificence, she whom all Asia and the world worship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An opponent confirms how far the gospel has spread, and that idols are losing their grip.

An enemy’s testimony. Demetrius confirms Luke’s claim (v. 10): the gospel had spread across the province and was hurting the idol trade. Pliny the Younger later reports the same in nearby Bithynia: temples deserted and sacrificial meat unsold.

Gods made with hands. Paul’s message (17:24–29; Isaiah 44:9–20; Psalm 115:4–8). He did not attack the temple or blaspheme the goddess (v. 37); he preached the living God, and idols lost their hold.

For worship. The God we worship is not made by human hands; he made us. Adore him who needs no shrine.

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard this they were enraged and were crying out, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" So the city was filled with the confusion, and they rushed together into the theater, dragging with them Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who were Paul's companions in travel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city fills the theatre in a frenzy, chanting for its goddess.

The chant. Inscriptions show “Great is Artemis” was a standard acclamation. A slogan repeated by a crowd is not an argument.

The theatre. Its ruins still stand, seating around 25,000. It was the natural place for a city assembly.

Gaius and Aristarchus. Aristarchus of Thessalonica later sails with Paul to Rome and shares his imprisonment (20:4; 27:2; Colossians 4:10).

Textual note. The Western text adds that they ran into the street; the shorter reading is original.
verseByVerse.note: The theatre at Ephesus seated about 25,000 people. Gaius and Aristarchus were Paul’s travelling companions.

verseByVerse.quote: But when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him. And even some of the Asiarchs, who were friends of his, sent to him and were urging him not to venture into the theater.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is willing to face the mob, but the disciples and friendly officials restrain him.

Courage restrained. Paul is willing to face the mob for his friends. Wisdom, through the church, holds him back. Courage and prudence are both gifts, and he listens.

The Asiarchs. Wealthy leading men of the province, associated with the cult of the emperor and the provincial games. That some were Paul’s friends shows the gospel was not seen by the ruling class as subversive, a point Luke often makes.

On a Tuesday. Let others counsel you when you are about to do something brave but unwise. Christian zeal is not proved by walking into every fire.
verseByVerse.note: The Asiarchs were wealthy leading men of the province associated with the provincial cult of the emperor.

verseByVerse.quote: Now some cried out one thing, some another, for the assembly was in confusion, and most of them did not know why they had come together. Some of the crowd prompted Alexander, whom the Jews had put forward. And Alexander, motioning with his hand, wanted to make a defense to the crowd.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The so-called assembly is a confused crowd that does not know why it has met.

Luke’s irony. The word for the gathering is ekklēsia, “assembly”, the same word used for the church. This assembly is a confused mob; the church is the people called together by the word.

Alexander. The Jewish community probably wanted to make clear that they had nothing to do with Paul, since Jews also rejected idols and might be blamed. Whether he is the Alexander of 2 Timothy 4:14 is uncertain.

On a Tuesday. Crowds, online or in the street, often do not know why they are angry. Before you join a public outrage, ask what it is actually about.
verseByVerse.note: Alexander may have been put forward to show that the Jews had no part in the Christians’ activity.

verseByVerse.quote: But when they recognized that he was a Jew, for about two hours they all cried out with one voice, "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
For two hours the crowd shouts the same slogan, refusing to hear a Jew.

Prejudice. They will not hear him because of who he is. Anti-Jewish feeling was common in Greek cities of Asia.

Two hours. Repetition as a substitute for thought. Compare the prophets of Baal crying from morning till noon (1 Kings 18:26) and Jesus’ warning against empty phrases (Matthew 6:7).

For worship. An idol needs its worshippers to shout for it. The living God hears a whisper. Pray to him quietly today.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the town clerk had quieted the crowd, he said, 'Men of Ephesus, who is there who does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple keeper of the great Artemis, and of the sacred stone that fell from the sky? Seeing then that these things cannot be denied, you ought to be quiet and do nothing rash.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The town clerk calms the crowd by appealing to the city’s secure reputation.

The town clerk. The chief civic official, who published the decisions of the assembly and was answerable to the Roman governor for public order.

Temple keeper. Neōkoros, an honorific title Ephesus proudly used on coins and inscriptions.

The sacred stone. Probably a meteorite venerated as an image “not made by hands”, a neat answer to Paul’s charge (v. 26).

On a Tuesday. God uses unbelievers to protect his people (Proverbs 21:1; Romans 13:3–4). Pray for those in civic office, that we may live quiet lives (1 Timothy 2:1–2), a letter written to Timothy in Ephesus.
verseByVerse.note: The town clerk was the chief civic official, answerable to Rome for public order. The “sacred stone” was probably a meteorite venerated as an image of the goddess.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For you have brought these men here who are neither sacrilegious nor blasphemers of our goddess. If therefore Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open, and there are proconsuls. Let them bring charges against one another.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Christians have committed no crime, and the courts are open for any real complaint.

A testimony to Paul’s method. In three years at the centre of Artemis worship, the Christians had not desecrated the temple or insulted the goddess. They had preached Christ, and the idols lost worshippers.

Proconsuls. The plural may be general (“there is such a thing as proconsuls”), or may reflect the gap after the murder of the proconsul Junius Silanus in AD 54, when his affairs were in the hands of imperial agents.

What it does not mean. Christian witness against idolatry is not mockery or vandalism. Speak the truth, gently and plainly (1 Peter 3:15–16).

verseByVerse.quote: "But if you seek anything further, it shall be settled in the regular assembly. For we really are in danger of being charged with rioting today, since there is no cause that we can give to justify this commotion."
verseByVerse.commentary:
An unlawful riot endangers the city before Rome.

The regular assembly. The lawful assembly met on fixed days; this one was unlawful.

Rome’s displeasure. Rome tolerated local freedoms only while order was kept. A riot could cost the city its privileges.

Luke’s theme. Again Roman law, through a civic official, finds no case against the Christians (compare Gallio, 18:14–15). Luke is showing his readers that the faith is not a threat to public order.
verseByVerse.note: Rome could punish a city for unlawful rioting.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he dismissed the assembly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The riot dissolves at a word, and the word of the Lord goes on prevailing.

A quiet ending. The goddess’s mob melts away at a clerk’s word. Artemis is great in the chant, but cannot protect her own business; the word of the Lord grows and prevails (v. 20). Within a few centuries her temple was in ruins, while the church at Ephesus continued, warned and loved by Christ (Revelation 2:1–7).

On a Tuesday. Opposition that seems overwhelming can end suddenly. Keep doing faithful work; God governs the outcome.

For worship. “Great is Artemis” has fallen silent. “Great is the LORD, and greatly to be praised” (Psalm 48:1) is still sung. Join it.

19.theology: The Word of God as the Power of Mission. Ephesus is Luke’s great exhibit of what the Word of God, given time and sustained proclamation, can do. Two years in a lecture hall, and all of Asia hears. The mechanism is not apostolic travel or institutional strategy — it is daily teaching, received by hearers who carry it wherever they go. The Reformation insight that the Word creates the church (“verbum Dei creat ecclesiam”) is visible in Ephesus: the Word goes out, conversions happen, the old life is burned, fear of God falls on the city, new communities form. The Word is not one tool among many; it is the engine of the whole enterprise. This is why Paul will later write to Timothy: “preach the word; be ready in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:2). There is no substitute.
19.examples:
Then: All of Asia hears the word from a lecture hall in Ephesus. A bonfire worth more than a century’s wages lights the night. A silversmith’s trade is threatened by a theological truth. The word of the Lord prevails mightily — not with weapons, not with political power, not with cultural cachet, but with the truth about the living God and the risen Christ.

Now: The church in every generation must resist the temptation to replace sustained Word-ministry with more immediately impressive alternatives — spectacle, experience, technique, programme. Ephesus was not won by any of these. It was won by a man who reasoned daily from the Scriptures for two years. The Word still has this power. It has not diminished. The question is whether we are willing to give it the time and the centrality it requires.

20.title: Farewell to Ephesus
20.text: <sup>1</sup>After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. <sup>2</sup>When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece. <sup>3</sup>There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia. <sup>4</sup>Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. <sup>5</sup>These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas, <sup>6</sup>but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days. <sup>7</sup>On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. <sup>8</sup>There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered. <sup>9</sup>And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead. <sup>10</sup>But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” <sup>11</sup>And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed. <sup>12</sup>And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted. <sup>13</sup>But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. <sup>14</sup>And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene. <sup>15</sup>And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. <sup>16</sup>For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost. <sup>17</sup>Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him. <sup>18</sup>And when they came to him, he said to them: “You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, <sup>19</sup>serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews; <sup>20</sup>how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, <sup>21</sup>testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. <sup>22</sup>And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, <sup>23</sup>except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me. <sup>24</sup>But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God. <sup>25</sup>And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. <sup>26</sup>Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all, <sup>27</sup>for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God. <sup>28</sup>Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. <sup>29</sup>I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock; <sup>30</sup>and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. <sup>31</sup>Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears. <sup>32</sup>And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. <sup>33</sup>I coveted no one’s silver or gold or apparel. <sup>34</sup>You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. <sup>35</sup>In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ <sup>36</sup>And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. <sup>37</sup>And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him, <sup>38</sup>being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship.
20.overview:
After the riot Paul leaves Ephesus, strengthens the churches of Macedonia and spends three winter months in Corinth, where he almost certainly wrote Romans. A plot against him at sea makes him go back overland. He travels with representatives of the Gentile churches, who are carrying the collection for the poor in Jerusalem, and Luke rejoins him at Philippi (“we”). At Troas, at an evening gathering on the first day of the week, Paul teaches until midnight; a young man named Eutychus falls asleep, drops from a third-storey window and is picked up dead, and Paul restores him. The church breaks bread and talks until dawn.

Hurrying to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost, Paul sails past Ephesus and summons its elders to Miletus. His farewell is the only speech in Acts addressed to Christian leaders, and the nearest thing in Acts to one of his letters. He reviews his ministry: humble, tearful, open, teaching the whole counsel of God, supporting himself. He tells them he goes to Jerusalem bound by the Spirit and expecting chains, counting his life worth nothing beside finishing his course. He charges them to guard themselves and the flock that God bought with his own blood, warns of wolves from outside and false teachers from within, and commends them to God and the word of his grace. They kneel, pray, weep and see him to the ship.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When the uproar is over, Paul encourages the disciples and leaves for Macedonia, then spends three months in Greece. A plot by his opponents as he is about to sail for Syria makes him return through Macedonia. Seven companions from the churches go ahead to Troas, and after the Feast of Unleavened Bread Paul and Luke sail from Philippi to join them. On the first day of the week the church meets to break bread, and Paul, leaving the next day, talks until midnight in a lamp-lit upper room. Eutychus, sitting in a window, sinks into sleep and falls three storeys, and is picked up dead. Paul goes down, embraces him and says his life is in him. Back upstairs they break bread and talk till dawn, and the young man is taken home alive, to their great comfort. The party sails down the coast while Paul walks to Assos and joins them there; they pass Ephesus because Paul is hurrying to be in Jerusalem for Pentecost.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Lord's Supper as the Community's Center

The gathering at Troas 'on the first day of the week' to 'break bread' (v. 7) is the earliest explicit reference in Acts to the Christian practice of Sunday worship centered on the Lord's Supper. The resurrection day becomes the day of communal gathering; the bread broken in homes is the continuation of what Jesus instituted at the Last Supper. Reformed theology sees here the established pattern of Christian worship: Word and Table together, on the Lord's Day, as the community's defining weekly practice.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul walked from Troas to Assos (about 20 miles) while the others sailed — perhaps choosing the solitary walk for prayer and reflection as he moved toward Jerusalem and the suffering that awaited him. Now: The disciplines of solitude and prayer that prepare for costly obedience are as necessary for Christ's servants today as they were for Paul on the road to Assos.

verseByVerse.quote: "After the uproar ceased, Paul sent for the disciples, and after encouraging them, he said farewell and departed for Macedonia. When he had gone through those regions and had given them much encouragement, he came to Greece."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul leaves the shaken church stronger, and travels on strengthening the churches of Macedonia and Greece.

Encouragement first. Paul does not leave a shaken church without strengthening it. “Encourage” (parakaleō) combines comfort and exhortation.

The letters fill in the gaps. On this journey Paul waited anxiously for Titus at Troas, met him in Macedonia with good news from Corinth, and wrote 2 Corinthians (2 Corinthians 2:12–13; 7:5–7). He may also have gone as far as Illyricum, modern Albania (Romans 15:19).
