Greece. Luke’s only use of the name: here it means the province of Achaia, chiefly Corinth.

On a Tuesday. When you leave a job, a home or a church, leave people stronger. A good goodbye is part of faithful ministry.
verseByVerse.note: Greece here means Achaia, including Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "There he spent three months, and when a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to set sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A plot at sea makes Paul change his route; providence does not rule out prudence.

Romans. These winter months in Corinth are when Paul almost certainly wrote his letter to the Romans, hosted by Gaius (Romans 16:1, 23).

The plot. A pilgrim ship bound for Passover would be full of Jews; it would have been easy to kill Paul at sea. He changes his route.

On a Tuesday. Trust in God’s providence does not rule out taking sensible precautions. Paul avoids danger when he can and faces it when he must.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably wrote Romans during these three months in Corinth.

verseByVerse.quote: "Sopater the Berean, son of Pyrrhus, accompanied him; and of the Thessalonians, Aristarchus and Secundus; and Gaius of Derbe, and Timothy; and the Asians, Tychicus and Trophimus. These went on ahead and were waiting for us at Troas,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Representatives of the Gentile churches travel with Paul, carrying the collection openly together.

The collection party. These men almost certainly represented the churches that gave to the poor in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:3–4; 2 Corinthians 8:19–21). Paul wanted the gift handled openly, with witnesses.

A picture of the church. Macedonians, Galatians and Asians, Jews and Gentiles, carry a gift to Jewish believers. The collection was a sign that Gentiles and Jews are one body (Romans 15:26–27).

Textual note. Some Western manuscripts read “Doberius” for “of Derbe”, perhaps to make this Gaius the Macedonian of 19:29. The usual reading is better. Verdict: Gaius of Derbe.

On a Tuesday. If you handle money for others, be transparent: let others check, count and travel with it (2 Corinthians 8:21).
verseByVerse.note: These men probably represented the churches sending money for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "but we sailed away from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread, and in five days we came to them at Troas, where we stayed for seven days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Luke rejoins Paul, and the party gathers at Troas.

“We” again. Luke left the story at Philippi (16:17) and now rejoins it there, staying with Paul to Jerusalem and on to Rome.

The calendar. Paul keeps time by the Jewish feasts. The crossing took five days this time (compare two days in 16:11), perhaps against the wind.

A week. Probably to be with the church on the first day of the week (v. 7).
verseByVerse.note: “We” resumes: Luke rejoins Paul at Philippi.

verseByVerse.quote: "On the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread, Paul talked with them, intending to depart on the next day, and he prolonged his speech until midnight. There were many lamps in the upper room where we were gathered."
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the first day of the week the church gathers to break bread, and Paul teaches late into the night.

The first day of the week. One of the earliest signs that Christians met on Sunday, the day of the resurrection (Luke 24:1; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10, “the Lord’s day”). Probably Sunday evening, after work; slaves and labourers had no day off.

To break bread. The Lord’s Supper, probably with a shared meal (1 Corinthians 11:20–26). The gathering’s purpose is named as the Supper, and the word is preached at length.

Where Christians differ: how often the Supper. Some churches (many Brethren, Reformed and Anglican congregations, and Calvin’s own preference) hold that the Supper should be weekly, citing this verse and 2:42. Others celebrate monthly or quarterly, pointing out that Scripture commands no frequency (1 Corinthians 11:26, “as often as”). Verdict: Acts suggests a weekly pattern, and frequent communion is wise; but frequency is not commanded, and churches should not divide over it.

Where Christians differ: Sabbath and Sunday. Some see the Lord’s Day as the Christian Sabbath; others as a new day of worship without Sabbath rules. Verdict: the app holds that the Sabbath is fulfilled in Christ (Colossians 2:16–17; Hebrews 4:9–10), and the Lord’s Day is a privilege to keep gladly, not a burden.

Many lamps. Luke’s eyewitness detail: oil lamps make the crowded room hot and stuffy, which explains what follows.
verseByVerse.note: The first day of the week is Sunday; this meeting was held in the evening, probably after the working day.

verseByVerse.quote: "And a young man named Eutychus, sitting at the window, sank into a deep sleep as Paul talked still longer. And being overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was taken up dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A young man overcome by sleep falls from a window and is taken up dead.

Eutychus. A common slave name meaning “lucky”. A “young man” (neanias, v. 9; pais, “boy”, v. 12), perhaps a slave tired from a day’s work.

Dead. Luke the physician says “picked up dead”, not “as if dead” (compare 14:19, “supposing that he was dead”). He means a real death.

What it does not mean. The story is not mainly a warning against long sermons, nor a licence for them. Nor is it a rebuke of Eutychus, who is not blamed.

On a Tuesday. Church can be tiring for those who have worked all day. Make room for the weary, and do not despise them.
verseByVerse.note: Eutychus means “fortunate.” Oil lamps in a crowded upper room would have made the air close.

verseByVerse.quote: But Paul went down and bent over him, and taking him in his arms, said, "Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him." And when Paul had gone up and had broken bread and eaten, he conversed with them a long while, until daybreak, and so departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like Elijah and Elisha, Paul embraces the dead boy, and life returns; then the church goes back to the meal and the word.

Elijah and Elisha. Paul’s action echoes the prophets stretching themselves over dead boys (1 Kings 17:21; 2 Kings 4:34). As Peter raised Tabitha (9:40), Paul raises Eutychus: the apostles share in the prophetic ministry of Jesus.

His life is in him. Paul’s words could be read as “he is not dead after all”, but in context he announces that life has returned.

Back to the meal. The miracle does not end the meeting. The church breaks bread and keeps listening until daybreak. Resurrection and the Lord’s Supper sit together at the heart of Sunday worship.

For worship. On the day of resurrection, in a room of resurrection people, a dead boy rises. Christ’s victory over death is the reason the church gathers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took the youth away alive, and were not a little comforted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The young man is taken home alive, to the church’s great comfort.

Not a little. Luke’s favourite understatement: they are hugely comforted.

On a Tuesday. Comfort in the church is not only words. Sometimes God gives a visible mercy; always he gives the hope of resurrection (1 Thessalonians 4:18).

verseByVerse.quote: But going ahead to the ship, we set sail for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for so he had arranged, intending himself to go by land. And when he met us at Assos, we took him on board and went to Mitylene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul walks alone to Assos while the ship goes round, and rejoins them there.

Paul walks. About 20 miles overland, while the ship rounds the cape. Luke does not say why: perhaps for solitude and prayer before the farewells ahead, perhaps to stay a little longer with the Troas church.

The route. Assos, Mitylene on Lesbos, Chios, Samos, Miletus: a coasting voyage, anchoring each night. Luke’s log is precise, the record of someone who was there.

On a Tuesday. Even in a busy schedule, Paul makes time alone. A walk can be a place of prayer.
verseByVerse.note: Assos, Mitylene, Chios, Samos and Miletus were ports down the coast of Asia Minor and its islands.

verseByVerse.quote: And sailing from there we came the following day opposite Chios; the next day we touched at Samos; and the day after that we went to Miletus. For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus, so that he might not have to spend time in Asia, for he was hastening to be at Jerusalem, if possible, on the day of Pentecost.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul passes Ephesus to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost.

Why not Ephesus? A visit would mean days of meetings and perhaps danger after the riot. Miletus, about 30 miles south, lets him see the elders without delay.

Pentecost. Fifty days after Passover. Arriving with the Gentile gift at the feast of firstfruits, when the Spirit was first given, would have been a powerful sign (Romans 15:16).

On a Tuesday. Saying no to good things is sometimes the only way to do the best thing. Plan your priorities.
verseByVerse.note: Miletus lay about 30 miles south of Ephesus. Pentecost fell fifty days after Passover.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–38 — The Miletus Farewell to the Ephesian Elders
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From Miletus Paul calls the Ephesian elders. He reminds them how he lived among them: serving the Lord humbly, with tears and trials, holding back nothing helpful, teaching publicly and house to house, calling Jews and Greeks to repent and trust the Lord Jesus. Now the Spirit compels him to Jerusalem, and the Spirit warns him in every city of prison and hardship, but his life matters to him only so that he may finish the race and the task Jesus gave him, to testify to the gospel of God’s grace. They will not see him again, and he is clear of everyone’s blood, for he has declared the whole purpose of God. They must keep watch over themselves and the flock the Spirit has entrusted to them, shepherding God’s church, bought with his own blood. Savage wolves will come, and some of their own number will distort the truth to win followers, so they must stay alert, remembering his three years of tearful warning. He commits them to God and to the word of his grace, which can build them up and give them an inheritance. He has wanted nobody’s money, but worked with his own hands to support himself and others, to show that the weak must be helped, remembering Jesus’ words that giving is more blessed than receiving. Then he kneels and prays with them all. They weep, embrace him and kiss him, grieving most that they will not see him again, and they go with him to the ship.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Elder as Shepherd and Overseer

Paul's address to the Ephesian 'elders' (v. 17) whom he calls 'overseers' (episkopous, v. 28) and instructs to 'shepherd' (poimainein) the flock establishes the threefold nature of the pastoral office: elder (dignity of character), overseer (responsibility of governance), shepherd (work of care). The Reformed tradition has consistently seen in this passage the defining description of the ordained ministry: those who guard, feed, and care for the people whom the Holy Spirit has placed under their oversight.
verseByVerse.examples: Then: Paul warned the Ephesian elders that 'fierce wolves' would come from outside and that 'men speaking twisted things' would arise from within the community itself. Both dangers materialized: the letter to Ephesus in Revelation (2:1–7) shows a community that had resisted external pressure but had lost its first love. Now: The threats Paul named are the threats every congregation faces in every generation: external persecution and internal doctrinal corruption. The antidote is the same: the word of God's grace, committed to Spirit-filled leadership whose lives embody what they preach.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now from Miletus he sent to Ephesus and called the elders of the church to come to him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul summons the Ephesian elders to Miletus for his farewell charge.

Elders. Presbyteroi: the leaders Paul appointed in each church (14:23). In verse 28 he calls the same men “overseers” (episkopoi) and tells them to “shepherd”: elder, overseer and pastor are one office (Titus 1:5–7; 1 Peter 5:1–2).

A speech to leaders. The only speech in Acts to Christians, and the most like Paul’s letters in its vocabulary. It is a manual of pastoral ministry.

On a Tuesday. A two-day journey each way to hear one talk: the elders valued Paul’s counsel. Leaders need to be taught too.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they came to him, he said to them: 'You yourselves know how I lived among you the whole time from the first day that I set foot in Asia, serving the Lord with all humility and with tears and with trials that happened to me through the plots of the Jews.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul appeals to his life among them: humble service, tears and trials.

His life as evidence. Paul appeals first to what they had seen (1 Thessalonians 2:1–12). Character is the first qualification for ministry (1 Timothy 3:1–7).

Serving. Literally “serving as a slave” (douleuō). Paul’s favourite title for himself is slave of Christ (Romans 1:1).

Tears. Mentioned three times in this speech (vv. 19, 31, 37). Paul’s ministry was not detached (2 Corinthians 2:4; Philippians 3:18).

On a Tuesday. The best sermon a leader preaches is their life. Would those who work with you say you served them humbly?

verseByVerse.quote: how I did not shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, and teaching you in public and from house to house, testifying both to Jews and to Greeks of repentance toward God and of faith in our Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He held back nothing helpful, teaching publicly and from house to house repentance and faith in Jesus.

Did not shrink. A word for drawing back in fear, used again in verse 27. The temptation to leave out unwelcome truths is real.

Public and private. The hall of Tyrannus and the household. Teaching and pastoral visiting belong together.

Repentance and faith. The two sides of conversion: turning from sin to God, and trusting Christ (Mark 1:15; 1 Thessalonians 1:9). Neither is a work that earns salvation; both are gifts (5:31; Ephesians 2:8).

On a Tuesday. Ask what you avoid saying because it might be unwelcome, and whether it would help.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I am going to Jerusalem, constrained by the Spirit, not knowing what will happen to me there, except that the Holy Spirit testifies to me in every city that imprisonment and afflictions await me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bound by the Spirit, Paul goes to Jerusalem knowing only that suffering awaits.

Constrained by the Spirit. Literally “bound”: Paul is already a prisoner of the Spirit before he is a prisoner of Rome. The Spirit both sends him and warns him (21:4, 11).

Where Christians differ: did Paul disobey? In 21:4 believers “through the Spirit” tell Paul not to go. Some conclude Paul went against God’s guidance. Most interpreters answer that the Spirit revealed the suffering, and the disciples drew the conclusion that he should avoid it; Paul knew that the Spirit was sending him into it. Verdict: Paul obeyed. Luke presents the journey as Jesus’ own road to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), and the Lord later commends him (23:11).

On a Tuesday. Knowing God’s will does not always mean knowing what will happen. Often we see only the next step and the cost.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself, if only I may finish my course and the ministry that I received from the Lord Jesus, to testify to the gospel of the grace of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul values his life only for finishing the task Jesus gave him: to testify to the gospel of God’s grace.

Finishing. The image of the runner (2 Timothy 4:7; Philippians 3:12–14). Paul’s aim is not to live long but to finish well.

The gospel of the grace of God. A perfect summary of his message: good news of a gift, not advice for achievers (Ephesians 2:8–9).

What it does not mean. Paul does not despise life or seek death; he values it, but not above Christ (Philippians 1:21–24).

On a Tuesday. What would it mean to value your career, comfort or reputation as nothing compared with the task Christ has given you? Start by naming that task.

For worship. Praise God for grace that is worth a life.

parallels.desc: I have finished the race

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now, behold, I know that none of you among whom I have gone about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again. Therefore I testify to you this day that I am innocent of the blood of all,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Expecting never to see them again, Paul declares himself innocent of anyone’s blood.

Will not see my face. Paul expects never to return. The Pastoral Letters may suggest he later revisited the region after release from Rome (1 Timothy 1:3; 2 Timothy 4:20), but he speaks here from what he knows.

Innocent of blood. The language of the watchman (Ezekiel 3:17–21; 33:1–9). A watchman who warns has done his duty, whether or not people listen (compare 18:6).

On a Tuesday. You are not responsible for how others respond to the gospel, but you are responsible to tell them.

parallels.desc: the watchman

verseByVerse.quote: "'for I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has declared the whole counsel of God.

The whole counsel. God’s whole plan of salvation in Christ, from creation to new creation, and all that Scripture teaches for life. Paul taught Ephesus not only the basics but the whole sweep, as the letter to the Ephesians shows (Ephesians 1:3–14).

What it does not mean. Not that every pastor must cover every doctrine in every sermon, but that over time nothing God has revealed should be avoided because it is hard or unpopular: sin, judgment, election, holiness, as well as love and grace.

On a Tuesday. Read the whole Bible, not just favourite parts. Expository preaching through books helps a church hear the whole counsel.

verseByVerse.quote: "Pay careful attention to yourselves and to all the flock, in which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers, to care for the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood. I know that after my departure fierce wolves will come in among you, not sparing the flock;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders must guard themselves and the flock that God bought with his own blood, for wolves are coming.

Yourselves first. A leader who neglects his own soul will fail the flock (1 Timothy 4:16).

The Spirit made you. Elders are chosen by the church and appointed by apostles (14:23), but the Spirit is the one who makes them overseers. Their authority is delegated and accountable.

Where Christians differ: church government. Episcopal churches see bishops as a separate order above presbyters; Presbyterians see elders governing together in a church and in wider courts; Congregationalists and Baptists stress the local church under its elders. All can learn from this verse that elder and overseer are one office here, plural, and pastoral. Verdict: the New Testament pattern is a plurality of elder-overseers in each church; wider fellowship between churches is wise, but a separate order of bishop develops later.

Bought with his own blood. The church is costly: God purchased it at the price of the blood of his Son. Definite atonement finds a pointer here: Christ died to acquire a people (Ephesians 5:25; Titus 2:14).

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “church of the Lord”, probably to avoid speaking of God’s blood. The best early witnesses read “church of God”. The phrase translated “his own blood” can also mean “the blood of his own [Son]” (ESV margin). Verdict: “church of God” is original; the blood is that of God’s own Son, who is himself God (John 1:1, 14).

Wolves. False teachers (Matthew 7:15). 1 Timothy and Revelation 2:2 show this came true in Ephesus.

For worship. You are part of a church bought with blood. Love what Christ loved enough to die for.
verseByVerse.note: Paul calls the same men elders (v. 17) and overseers — two names for one office. “With his own blood” — the blood of God’s own Son. Some manuscripts read “church of the Lord”; “his own blood” may also be rendered “the blood of his Own” (ESV notes).

parallels.desc: shepherds who feed themselves

verseByVerse.quote: "and from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things, to draw away the disciples after them. Therefore be alert, remembering that for three years I did not cease night or day to admonish every one with tears."
verseByVerse.commentary:
False teachers will rise from within, so the elders must stay alert.

From within. The greater danger is not wolves outside but leaders inside. Hymenaeus and Alexander (1 Timothy 1:20) and Phygelus and Hermogenes (2 Timothy 1:15) may be examples.

Twisted things. Distortions of the truth, not open denials. Error usually comes looking like a version of the gospel.

After them. The mark of a false teacher: drawing disciples to himself rather than to Christ.

Each one. Paul warned not only the crowd but every individual. Pastoral care is personal.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of any teacher who wants your loyalty for himself. Test teaching by Scripture (17:11; 1 John 4:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I commend you to God and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up and to give you the inheritance among all those who are sanctified. I coveted no one's silver or gold or apparel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul entrusts them to God and the word of his grace, and reminds them that he coveted no one’s wealth.

Not to a successor. Paul does not commend them to a new apostle, an institution or a tradition, but to God and his word. The Reformation principle of Scripture’s sufficiency is here (2 Timothy 3:15–17).

Able to build you up. The word of grace is not only the message that converts; it is the means God uses to grow and keep his people.

The inheritance. The future possession of God’s people in Christ (Ephesians 1:14, 18; 1 Peter 1:4).

Not covetous. Silver, gold and clothing were the wealth of the ancient world. Paul’s refusal contrasts with the money-loving false teachers he warns about (1 Timothy 6:5).

For worship. Commit yourself, your family and your church to God and his word. They are enough.

parallels.desc: whose ox have I taken?

verseByVerse.quote: "'You yourselves know that these hands ministered to my necessities and to those who were with me. In all things I have shown you that by working hard in this way we must help the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he himself said, "It is more blessed to give than to receive."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He worked with his own hands to help the weak, remembering that giving is more blessed than receiving.

These hands. Perhaps Paul holds up hands roughened by leatherwork. He had a right to support but often did not use it, to avoid hindering the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12–18; 2 Thessalonians 3:7–9).

What it does not mean. This is not a rule that pastors must not be paid. Paul defends paying elders (1 Timothy 5:17–18; Galatians 6:6). His own practice was a choice for the gospel’s sake.

The weak. The sick and the poor who cannot work. Christian work aims at generosity, not just self-support (Ephesians 4:28, written to this church).

A saying of Jesus. These words are not in the Gospels; the church remembered more of Jesus’ teaching than was written down (John 21:25). It is the only such saying quoted in Acts, and it sums up the Gospels’ teaching (Luke 6:38).

On a Tuesday. Work hard not only to pay the bills but to have something to give. Set aside generosity before spending.
verseByVerse.note: This saying of Jesus is not recorded in the Gospels; it was remembered and passed on.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he knelt down and prayed with them all. And there was much weeping on the part of all; they embraced Paul and kissed him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul kneels and prays with them all, and they weep and embrace him.

Kneeling. Prayer standing was common, but kneeling marks humility and earnestness (7:60; 21:5; Luke 22:41).

Tears. Gospel friendship is deep. Men weep and embrace openly.

On a Tuesday. When you part from fellow believers, pray together. A shared prayer at a doorway can be remembered for years.

verseByVerse.quote: "being sorrowful most of all because of the word he had spoken, that they would not see his face again. And they accompanied him to the ship."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Their deepest grief is that they will not see him again.

Grief and hope. They will not see him in this life, but they will meet again at the resurrection (1 Thessalonians 4:13–17).

For worship. Thank God for the leaders who taught you, and for the day when the whole church will be gathered and no one will say goodbye.

20.theology: The Whole Counsel of God and Pastoral Faithfulness. Acts 20:27 gives the church its standard for preaching: the whole counsel of God, without shrinking. This phrase has defined the Reformed tradition’s commitment to expository, systematic, comprehensive proclamation of Scripture — preaching through whole books, teaching the full range of doctrine, refusing to select only the comfortable and suppress the challenging. The shepherd who preaches the whole counsel will declare both the tenderness of the Father and the terror of the Judge, both the free grace of justification and the necessary fruit of sanctification, both the comfort of election and the urgency of repentance. Paul could stand before his people at Miletus and say “I am innocent of your blood” because he had given them everything. That is the standard every preacher must aspire to.
20.examples:
Then: A beach at Miletus, a group of weeping elders on their knees, a man who knew he was going to chains and possibly death — and who spent his last hours with these people not arranging his escape but commending them to God and declaring his conscience clear. The tears on the beach are the overflow of three years of tears in the houses of Ephesus. Ministry that produces this kind of grief at parting has been ministry that produced this kind of love in the doing.

Now: Paul’s farewell is the standard against which every pastoral ministry will be measured. Did we shrink? Did we select? Did we give them the comfortable Christ without the demanding Lord, the free grace without the costly discipleship, the promise without the warning? The whole counsel of God. Nothing less. The flock that has been given the whole counsel will be able to stand when the wolves come — because they will recognise the deviation when they hear it.

21.title: Bound for Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. <sup>2</sup>And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail. <sup>3</sup>When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo. <sup>4</sup>And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. <sup>5</sup>When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed <sup>6</sup>and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home. <sup>7</sup>When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. <sup>8</sup>On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him. <sup>9</sup>He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied. <sup>10</sup>While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. <sup>11</sup>And coming to us, he took Paul’s belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit, ‘This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles.’” <sup>12</sup>When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem. <sup>13</sup>Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.” <sup>14</sup>And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, “Let the will of the Lord be done.” <sup>15</sup>After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. <sup>16</sup>And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge. <sup>17</sup>When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. <sup>18</sup>On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present. <sup>19</sup>After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. <sup>20</sup>And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, “You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law, <sup>21</sup>And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. <sup>22</sup>What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come. <sup>23</sup>Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; <sup>24</sup>take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law. <sup>25</sup>But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality.” <sup>26</sup>Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them. <sup>27</sup>When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, <sup>28</sup>crying out, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.” <sup>29</sup>For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. <sup>30</sup>Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut. <sup>31</sup>And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. <sup>32</sup>He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul. <sup>33</sup>Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done. <sup>34</sup>Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. <sup>35</sup>And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd, <sup>36</sup>for the mob of the people followed, crying out, “Away with him!” <sup>37</sup>As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” And he said, “Do you know Greek? <sup>38</sup>Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?” <sup>39</sup>Paul replied, “I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.” <sup>40</sup>And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:
21.overview:
Paul’s road to Jerusalem deliberately echoes Jesus’ own (Luke 9:51). At Tyre, disciples moved by the Spirit urge him not to go; at Caesarea, in the house of Philip the evangelist, the prophet Agabus binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt and foretells that the Jews will hand Paul over to the Gentiles. The church weeps and pleads; Paul answers that he is ready not only to be bound but to die for the name of the Lord Jesus, and they say, “Let the will of the Lord be done.”

In Jerusalem James and the elders welcome Paul and praise God for the Gentile mission, but warn him that thousands of zealous Jewish believers have heard he teaches Jews to abandon Moses. To show the rumour is false, he joins four men completing a vow and pays their temple costs. Near the end of the week, Jews from Asia see him in the temple, accuse him of bringing a Gentile inside, and the city erupts. The Roman tribune rescues Paul from a beating, chains him, and mistakes him for an Egyptian rebel; Paul replies in polished Greek that he is a citizen of Tarsus, and asks to address the crowd. The prophecy is fulfilled to the letter: bound, and in Gentile hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Journey to Jerusalem and the Warnings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Tearing themselves away from the Ephesian elders, Paul’s party sails by Cos, Rhodes and Patara, then crosses on a larger ship to Tyre. There they find the disciples and stay a week; prompted by the Spirit, these believers urge Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. When the week is over the whole church, wives and children too, walks them to the shore, where they kneel and pray before parting. From Ptolemais they reach Caesarea and stay with Philip the evangelist, whose four unmarried daughters prophesy. The prophet Agabus arrives from Judea, ties his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt, and announces that the Spirit says the Jews in Jerusalem will bind its owner and hand him to the Gentiles. Everyone begs Paul not to go. He asks why they are weeping and breaking his heart; he is ready to be bound and even to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. When he cannot be persuaded, they give up, saying, “The Lord’s will be done.” They go up to Jerusalem with some Caesarean disciples, who take them to lodge with Mnason of Cyprus, a believer from the early days.
verseByVerse.theology:
Guidance, and the Difference Between a Revelation and an Inference

This passage is the clearest case in Scripture of sincere, Spirit-filled Christians getting guidance wrong, and it is wonderfully instructive because nobody in it is a villain. The Spirit really did reveal what was waiting in Jerusalem; he revealed it at Tyre, at Caesarea, and in every city (20:23). What the Spirit did not say was do not go. That was added by people who loved Paul and could not bear the arithmetic. Agabus, a true prophet, models the discipline exactly: he announces the outcome and issues no instruction.

The Reformed doctrine of providence is what makes the distinction bearable. Because God ordains the end and the means together, a warning of suffering is not a detour sign; it is often the itinerary. Paul is not being tricked into a cell — he is being told the cost in advance so that he can pay it with his eyes open. And when the church cannot change his mind, its submission is not fatalism but faith with a name attached: not the will of fate, but the will of the Lord, prayed by people who know whose will it is because they have watched him keep his promises for years. It is Gethsemane repeated in a front room, and it is the sentence every Christian eventually needs.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A whole congregation at Tyre — men, women, children — walking a man they had known for seven days out of the city gate and kneeling in the wet sand of a working harbour to pray for him, in public, in front of dockers. Then going home to supper while he sailed toward chains. Their names are not recorded. Nothing they said survives. It is in the Bible anyway.

Now: Most of us are Tyre. The great work of God in our generation will pass through our town for about a week, and our share in it will be a spare bed, a meal, and a prayer on the way out — and that is not the reduced version of the Christian life, it is the thing itself. And when someone we love is walking toward a costly obedience we cannot talk them out of, we will need what that church found on the beach: the grace to stop arguing without going cold, to lose the argument and keep the love, and to say with them, let the will of the Lord be done.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had parted from them and set sail, we came by a straight course to Cos, and the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara. And having found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, we went aboard and set sail."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s road to Jerusalem begins with a painful parting and an eyewitness’s careful voyage.

Parted. Literally “torn away”: the farewell was painful (20:37–38).

The route. Coasting ships hugged the shore; at Patara, on the Lycian coast, they change to a larger vessel for the open-sea crossing of some 400 miles, using the steady north-west winds of early summer.

Textual note. The Western text adds “and Myra” after Patara, perhaps from 27:5. Verdict: the shorter text is original.

On a Tuesday. Luke writes even a sailing log with care. Ordinary details of travel and work are part of the story God is writing.
verseByVerse.note: Cos, Rhodes and Patara were ports along the south-west coast of Asia Minor; from Patara they crossed the open sea east toward Phoenicia.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come in sight of Cyprus, leaving it on the left we sailed to Syria and landed at Tyre, for there the ship was to unload its cargo."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ship lands at Tyre, a city of the prophets’ judgments that now has a church.

Cyprus on the left. Sailing south of the island, direct to the coast. Paul had first preached in Cyprus with Barnabas (13:4–12); now he passes it by.

Tyre. The great Phoenician port, long denounced by the prophets for pride (Ezekiel 26–28), and the city Jesus said would have repented at his miracles (Matthew 11:21–22). Now it has a church.

For worship. The cities of the prophets’ judgment have become places of welcome for the gospel. Praise God for his mercy to the nations.
verseByVerse.note: Tyre was a major port of Phoenicia, north of Galilee.

verseByVerse.quote: "And having sought out the disciples, we stayed there for seven days. And through the Spirit they were telling Paul not to go on to Jerusalem. When our days there were ended, we departed and went on our journey, and they all, with wives and children, accompanied us until we were outside the city. And kneeling down on the beach, we prayed"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Spirit reveals suffering ahead, and loving believers conclude Paul should not go; the whole church prays with him on the beach.

Sought out. Paul had not founded this church; it probably began with those scattered after Stephen’s death (11:19). Wherever Christians travel, they look for the family.

Through the Spirit. The Spirit revealed what awaited Paul (20:23), and out of love they concluded he should not go. Revelation and inference are not the same: the Spirit had already bound Paul to go (20:22). See the note on 20:22–23.

Where Christians differ: prophecy that can err. Some (notably Wayne Grudem) argue that New Testament prophecy, unlike Old Testament prophecy, can contain mistakes, citing this verse and Agabus (v. 11). Others answer that the Spirit’s message was true and the error lay in what people inferred from it. Verdict: the second view is better: Scripture never treats a word from the Spirit as mistaken. With the app’s cessationism, held charitably, it means prophecy today is not to be expected, and every claimed word must be tested by Scripture (1 Thessalonians 5:20–21).

A family on the beach. Wives and children kneel in the sand to pray. Luke loves to show the whole church, children included.

On a Tuesday. Bring children to the farewells and the prayers. They will remember a church on its knees.
verseByVerse.note: The Spirit revealed the danger ahead; the disciples concluded that he should not go.

verseByVerse.quote: "and said farewell to one another. Then we went on board the ship, and they returned home."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A week’s fellowship makes friends for life.

Goodbye. A week was long enough to make friends for life. Christian fellowship can be deep very quickly because it rests on a shared Lord.

On a Tuesday. Show hospitality to Christians passing through. A week’s welcome can strengthen a traveller for the trials ahead.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had finished the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, and we greeted the brothers and stayed with them for one day. On the next day we departed and came to Caesarea, and we entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul stays with Philip the evangelist, once driven out of Jerusalem by Paul himself.

Ptolemais. Modern Acre (Akko), about 30 miles south of Tyre. From there the party probably goes on foot to Caesarea.

Philip. One of the seven chosen in 6:5, who preached in Samaria and baptised the Ethiopian (8:5–40), and settled in Caesarea (8:40). Some twenty years later he is still there, known as “the evangelist”. Once Paul had helped drive Philip from Jerusalem; now he is his guest.

On a Tuesday. Grace turns enemies into hosts. Is there a broken relationship that the gospel could heal?
verseByVerse.note: Ptolemais is modern Acre. Philip was one of the seven chosen in Acts 6.

verseByVerse.quote: "He had four unmarried daughters, who prophesied."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Philip’s daughters prophesy, a sign of the Spirit given to sons and daughters alike.

Joel fulfilled. “Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy” (2:17). Luke mentions the daughters as a mark of the Spirit’s gift to women.

Where Christians differ: women and ministry. Egalitarians cite this verse as evidence that women may hold any office. Complementarians answer that prophecy and teaching-office are distinct: women prophesied in the church (1 Corinthians 11:5), but the office of elder and authoritative teaching in the assembly is given to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–7). Verdict: the app’s complementarian view, held gladly and charitably: women’s gifts are real and to be honoured, while the elder’s office belongs to men.

Unmarried. Literally “virgins”. Their singleness is noted without comment, and later tradition remembered them as important sources for the early church in Asia.

On a Tuesday. Ask how your church honours and uses the gifts of its women, single and married.

parallels.desc: your sons and your daughters shall prophesy

verseByVerse.quote: "While we were staying for many days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. And coming to us, he took Paul's belt and bound his own feet and hands and said, 'Thus says the Holy Spirit, "This is how the Jews at Jerusalem will bind the man who owns this belt and deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agabus acts out the binding that awaits Paul in Jerusalem.

Agabus. The prophet who foretold the famine (11:28). His word was fulfilled then and is fulfilled now.

An acted prophecy. Like Isaiah walking barefoot (Isaiah 20), Jeremiah’s belt (Jeremiah 13:1–11) and Ezekiel’s signs (Ezekiel 4–5). “Thus says the Holy Spirit” replaces the prophets’ “Thus says the LORD”: the Spirit is God.

Accurate in substance. Strictly, the Romans bound Paul (v. 33), but the Jews seized him and their actions delivered him into Gentile hands (28:17). Prophecy, like ordinary speech, describes the effect of actions. Jesus too was “delivered over to the Gentiles” by his own people (Luke 18:32).

For worship. Jesus walked this road first, knowing what awaited him. Praise him who went up to Jerusalem to be bound for us.
verseByVerse.note: Agabus acts out his prophecy as the Old Testament prophets often did.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we heard this, we and the people there urged him not to go up to Jerusalem."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Luke, out of love, pleads with Paul not to go.

“We”. Luke includes himself. Even the faithful companion got it wrong for a moment, out of love.

On a Tuesday. Love sometimes wants to protect people from the costly obedience God is calling them to. Pray before you advise a friend to take the safe road.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Paul answered, "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be imprisoned but even to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus." And since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, "Let the will of the Lord be done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is ready to die for Jesus’ name, and the church entrusts him to the Lord’s will.

Breaking my heart. Literally “crushing”. Their tears weaken his resolve; he needs their support, not their fear.

Ready to die. Paul is not reckless; he is resolved. Compare Peter’s boast (Luke 22:33), which failed; Paul’s resolve rests on the Spirit’s leading.

The Lord’s will. The words echo Gethsemane (Luke 22:42). The church accepts what it cannot change and entrusts Paul to God.

On a Tuesday. When a fellow believer is called into danger, missionary work or costly service, your part may be to stop pleading and start praying.

For worship. Pray “your will be done” today about something you would rather control.

parallels.desc: not my will, but yours

verseByVerse.quote: After these days we got ready and went up to Jerusalem. And some of the disciples from Caesarea went with us, bringing us to the house of Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we should lodge.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul goes up to Jerusalem and lodges with an early disciple who welcomes a mixed company.

Got ready. The word may mean saddling horses: a 65-mile journey inland and uphill.

Mnason. A disciple “from the beginning”, perhaps from Pentecost. A Hellenist Jew with a house large enough for a mixed party including Gentiles, a kindness not every Jerusalem believer would show.

On a Tuesday. Hospitality is a ministry (Romans 12:13; 1 Peter 4:9). Mnason appears once in Scripture, for opening his home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The believers in Jerusalem welcome Paul warmly. Next day he visits James with all the elders and reports in detail what God has done among the Gentiles, and they praise God. But they tell him that many thousands of Jewish believers, all zealous for the law, have heard that he teaches Jews abroad to give up Moses and not circumcise their children. They advise him to join four men who have taken a vow, go through the purification rites with them and pay for their offerings, so that everyone will see he keeps the law. As for Gentile believers, the earlier letter stands. Paul does so. When the seven days are nearly over, Jews from Asia spot him in the temple and seize him, shouting that he teaches against the people, the law and the temple, and has defiled it by bringing Greeks in; they had seen him in the city with Trophimus of Ephesus. The whole city is in uproar; Paul is dragged out and the gates are shut. As they try to kill him, the commander of the Roman garrison rushes down with troops, and the beating stops. He arrests Paul, binds him with two chains and asks who he is, but cannot get a clear answer through the shouting, and orders him taken to the barracks. The crowd is so violent that soldiers have to carry Paul up the steps while the mob yells, “Away with him!” At the door Paul asks in Greek to speak. Surprised, the commander asks if he is the Egyptian rebel who recently led four thousand terrorists into the desert. Paul says he is a Jew of Tarsus, citizen of an important city, and asks to address the people. Given permission, he stands on the steps, signals for silence, and speaks to them in Aramaic.
verseByVerse.theology:
Liberty, Accommodation, and the Line That Does Not Move

Paul in the temple, paying for sacrifices, is the most severely tested case of Christian liberty in the New Testament, and it is not a contradiction of Galatians but its application. The gospel had freed him from the law as a way of standing before God; that freedom is precisely what allowed him to keep the customs without fear. A man who needed the ritual could not have afforded to perform it. Only a justified man can shave a head, pay for a lamb, and mean nothing by it before God while meaning a great deal by it before his brothers. To the Jews I became as a Jew, in order to win Jews (1 Cor. 9:20).

The line, then, is not drawn at the act. The same razor and the same offering can be innocent or fatal, and what settles it is what the act is made to mean. When men demanded Titus be circumcised as a condition of fellowship, Paul did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel might be preserved (Gal. 2:5). Here nothing is required of any Gentile, and James says so out loud before anyone can misread the week. That is the discipline Reformed churches inherit: bend as far as love can bend on matters of culture and conscience, and not one inch on the ground of acceptance with God — and say plainly, in advance, which one you are doing.

And then the harder lesson, which is that this wise and humble course failed. The plan is what put Paul in the temple to be seen and seized. Faithfulness is not a technique for producing outcomes; it is obedience, and the outcomes belong to God, who used this failure as the road to Rome (23:11).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An apostle with a Roman citizenship in his pocket that could have ended the whole ordeal, standing chained at the door of a fortress, spending his one request not on rescue but on permission to preach to the mob that had just beaten him. And a pagan officer, who bought his citizenship for a large sum and had no idea whom he was serving, ordering the soldiers to hold the stairs so the prisoner could speak.

Now: Two things to take home. First, God's rescues rarely arrive in the uniform we were watching for; the church of tens of thousands is nowhere in this scene, and a Roman cohort is everything. Second, the platform we are given is almost never the platform we asked for. Paul wanted an unmolested week in the temple and a cleared name; he got a beating, a chain and a staircase — and from that staircase he preached to a larger Jewish crowd than he had faced in years. What has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel (Phil. 1:12) was written by a man remembering days exactly like this one.

verseByVerse.quote: "When we had come to Jerusalem, the brothers received us gladly. On the following day Paul went in with us to James, and all the elders were present."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Jerusalem believers welcome Paul, and he meets James and the elders.

James. The Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church (12:17; 15:13; Galatians 1:19). The apostles are no longer mentioned; they had probably left Jerusalem.

A formal meeting. Paul probably presented the collection here, though Luke mentions it only later (24:17). Paul had feared it might not be accepted (Romans 15:31).

The last “we”. Luke’s presence ends at verse 18 and resumes at 27:1. He was probably in Judea during Paul’s two years in Caesarea, a good time to gather material for his Gospel (Luke 1:1–3).
verseByVerse.note: James is the Lord’s brother, leader of the Jerusalem church.

verseByVerse.quote: "After greeting them, he related one by one the things that God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry. And when they heard it, they glorified God. And they said to him, 'You see, brother, how many thousands there are among the Jews of those who have believed. They are all zealous for the law,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul reports what God has done among the Gentiles, and the elders tell of thousands of Jewish believers zealous for the law.

God had done. Paul reports God’s work, not his own (14:27; 15:12). The elders glorify God, not Paul.

Thousands. Literally “tens of thousands” (myriads). The Jewish church had grown greatly since Pentecost.

Zealous for the law. They are true believers who still keep the law of Moses as Jews. Zeal was rising in Judea in the 50s, with growing nationalist tension against Rome. A Jewish leader seen as disloyal to the law was in danger, and so were Jewish Christians associated with him.

On a Tuesday. Rejoice at what God does in other churches and cultures, even when it looks different from yours.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And they have been told about you that you teach all the Jews who are among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk according to our customs. What then is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A false rumour says Paul teaches Jews to abandon Moses.

The rumour was false. Paul circumcised Timothy (16:3) and kept Jewish customs when among Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). What he opposed was imposing the law on Gentiles, or treating it as a way to be right with God (Galatians 5:2–4). He taught that circumcision counts for nothing either way (1 Corinthians 7:18–19).

A real tension. Paul’s gospel did relativise the law: if a Jew is justified by faith and eats with Gentiles, the law’s boundary markers no longer define God’s people (Galatians 2:11–16). The rumour was a distortion of something true.

On a Tuesday. When misrepresented, Christians should be willing to correct the record patiently, as Paul does here.
verseByVerse.note: The rumour was false; Paul opposed circumcision only when it was treated as necessary for salvation, especially for Gentiles.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Do therefore what we tell you. We have four men who are under a vow; take these men and purify yourself along with them and pay their expenses, so that they may shave their heads. Thus all will know that there is nothing in what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also live in observance of the law.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The elders propose that Paul pay for the vows of four men to show he keeps the law.

A Nazirite vow. Its completion required a costly set of sacrifices (Numbers 6:13–20). Paying for poor Nazirites was a recognised act of piety; Josephus says Herod Agrippa I did it.

Purification. Paul, back from Gentile lands, would need a seven-day purification to enter the inner temple courts (Numbers 19:12).

Where Christians differ: did Paul compromise? Some think Paul betrayed his own gospel by offering sacrifices after Christ’s once-for-all death (Hebrews 10:10–18). Others argue that he acted consistently: the rites were not for atonement but for vows and ritual purity, and he became “as a Jew” to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20). Verdict: Paul did not compromise the gospel. He did not trust the rites for righteousness, nor did he impose them on Gentiles, and in that transitional generation, before the temple fell, Jewish believers could keep customs as a matter of freedom and love.

On a Tuesday. In secondary matters, give up your preferences for the sake of others (Romans 14:13–21). In the gospel itself, give up nothing (Galatians 2:5).
verseByVerse.note: These men were ending a Nazirite vow, which required costly offerings; paying for them was a recognised act of piety.

parallels.desc: the offerings when the days of separation are complete

verseByVerse.quote: "But as for the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent a letter with our judgment that they should abstain from what has been sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from sexual immorality." Then Paul took the men, and the next day he purified himself along with them and went into the temple, giving notice when the days of purification would be fulfilled and the offering presented for each one of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Gentile believers remain free of the law, and Paul humbly accepts the elders’ advice.

The decree confirmed. The council’s letter (15:20, 29) stands: Gentiles are not required to keep the law, only to avoid what would most offend Jewish fellow believers and what is plainly wrong.

Paul complies. He who wrote that love “does not insist on its own way” (1 Corinthians 13:5) accepts the elders’ advice humbly. It does not work out as planned, but God uses it.

On a Tuesday. Submit to wise leaders even when you could argue. Unity is worth some personal cost (Ephesians 4:3).

verseByVerse.quote: "When the seven days were almost completed, the Jews from Asia, seeing him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd and laid hands on him, crying out, 'Men of Israel, help! This is the man who is teaching everyone everywhere against the people and the law and this place. Moreover, he even brought Greeks into the temple and has defiled this holy place.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jews from Asia seize Paul in the temple on the same false charges once brought against Stephen.

From Asia. Pilgrims from Ephesus, in Jerusalem for Pentecost, who knew Paul from home.

The charges. The same as against Stephen (6:13): against the people, the law and the temple. Paul, once Stephen’s accuser, now stands where he stood.

The barrier. A stone balustrade separated the Court of the Gentiles from the inner courts. Two Greek inscriptions from it have been found, warning that any foreigner who passes it will have himself to blame for his death. Paul later writes that Christ has broken down “the dividing wall of hostility” (Ephesians 2:14).

On a Tuesday. Expect to be misrepresented if you follow Christ (Matthew 5:11–12). Do not repay it in kind.
verseByVerse.note: Inscriptions have been found from the temple’s barrier, warning Gentiles not to go beyond it on pain of death.

parallels.desc: the dividing wall of hostility

verseByVerse.quote: "For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Then all the city was stirred up, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him out of the temple, and at once the gates were shut."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mistaken assumption sets the whole city in uproar, and the temple gates are shut.

An assumption. They saw Paul with a Gentile in the city and supposed he had taken him into the temple. Rumour and supposition did more damage than any fact.

The gates shut. Probably by the temple police, to prevent bloodshed in the sacred courts. Luke may also mean it as a symbol: the temple closes its doors on the gospel, and the story moves from Jerusalem to Rome.

On a Tuesday. Before you repeat a story about someone, ask whether you saw it or supposed it (Proverbs 18:17).

verseByVerse.quote: "And as they were seeking to kill him, word came to the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion. He at once took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. And when they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Roman commander rescues Paul from the mob.

The tribune. Claudius Lysias (23:26), commander of a cohort of up to a thousand men in the Antonia Fortress, which overlooked the temple courts at the north-west corner. Troops were on alert at festivals.

Centurions. Plural: at least two hundred men. The riot was serious.

Providence through Rome. God uses a pagan soldier to save his apostle (compare 18:12–17; 19:35–41).

For worship. Psalm 124: if the Lord had not been on our side, they would have swallowed us alive. Thank him for rescues you never saw coming.
verseByVerse.note: The tribune commanded the cohort of Roman soldiers stationed in the Antonia Fortress, which overlooked the temple courts.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the tribune came up and arrested him and ordered him to be bound with two chains. He inquired who he was and what he had done."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is bound with chains, as Agabus foretold.

Two chains. Probably chained to a soldier on each side (12:6). Agabus’s prophecy is fulfilled (v. 11).

On a Tuesday. Paul’s chains begin a four-year imprisonment that will produce testimony before governors and kings, and probably several of his letters (Ephesians 6:20; Philippians 1:12–14). God can use your restrictions.

verseByVerse.quote: "Some in the crowd were shouting one thing, some another. And as he could not learn the facts because of the uproar, he ordered him to be brought into the barracks. And when he came to the steps, he was actually carried by the soldiers because of the violence of the crowd,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd is so violent that soldiers carry Paul up the steps.

The steps. Two flights of steps led up from the temple court into the Antonia (Josephus describes them).

Carried. The mob is surging; the soldiers lift Paul off his feet to get him away.

On a Tuesday. A crowd that cannot agree on a charge can still agree on a target (compare 19:32). Be slow to join a mob, however righteous it feels.
verseByVerse.note: Steps led from the temple courts up into the fortress.

verseByVerse.quote: "for the mob of the people followed, crying out, 'Away with him!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd shouts the same words once shouted against Jesus.

The same cry. The crowd shouted these words about Jesus (Luke 23:18; John 19:15). Paul shares the fellowship of Christ’s sufferings (Philippians 3:10).

For worship. Jesus was rejected so that we would be received. Thank him.

verseByVerse.quote: "As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, 'May I say something to you?' And he said, 'Do you know Greek? Are you not the Egyptian, then, who recently stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Assassins out into the wilderness?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commander mistakes Paul for an Egyptian rebel until Paul speaks in educated Greek.

Polite Greek. Paul’s cultured Greek startles the officer. He had assumed the cause of a riot must be a rebel.

The Egyptian. Josephus tells of an Egyptian false prophet, around AD 54, who gathered followers on the Mount of Olives, promising that Jerusalem’s walls would fall at his command. The governor Felix attacked; many were killed, but the Egyptian escaped. Josephus gives larger numbers; Luke’s four thousand is probably nearer the truth.

The Assassins. Sicarii, “dagger-men”: extremists who hid short daggers in their clothes and stabbed opponents in festival crowds.

What it does not mean. Christianity was not a revolutionary movement. Luke repeatedly shows Roman officials discovering that the Christians are not rebels.
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus describes an Egyptian false prophet who led followers to the Mount of Olives a few years earlier and escaped when the Romans attacked. The “Assassins” were extremists who stabbed opponents with hidden daggers in crowds.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul replied, 'I am a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city. I beg you, permit me to speak to the people.' And when he had given him permission, Paul, standing on the steps, motioned with his hand to the people. And when there was a great hush, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bound and beaten, Paul asks to speak to the crowd that tried to kill him.

No obscure city. Tarsus was a university city, rich and proud. A citizen of Tarsus belonged to its elite. Paul does not yet mention Roman citizenship (22:25).

Courage. Beaten, chained and carried by soldiers, Paul’s first thought is to speak to the crowd that wanted to kill him. Compare Romans 9:1–3: his heart for his people.

The Hebrew language. Probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Judea, though it may mean Hebrew itself. Speaking their own language gains a hush (22:2).

On a Tuesday. When people have treated you badly, look for the chance to tell them the gospel. Speak their language, culturally as well as literally.

For worship. Praise God for grace that makes a beaten man plead with his attackers.
verseByVerse.note: Tarsus was a proud and prosperous city, known for learning. The “Hebrew language” was probably Aramaic, the everyday language of Jews in Judea.

21.theology: The Will of God and the Path of Suffering. Acts 21 presents with unusual clarity the Reformed conviction that the will of God is not always comfortable, and that knowing it does not mean avoiding what it contains. Paul knows chains await. He goes anyway. His companions know Paul knows. They submit anyway. “Let the will of the Lord be done” is not fatalism — it is the active, willing submission of people who have learned that God’s purposes are worked out through suffering, not around it. This is the theology of Romans 8:28 embodied in a house in Caesarea: all things — including imprisonment, beatings, and the howling of a mob — work together for good for those who love God and are called according to his purpose. Paul’s chains will take him to Rome. God knew this. Paul submitted to it. Rome receives the gospel.
21.examples:
Then: A man walking knowingly toward chains, accompanied by weeping friends who have said everything they can say and now can only pray. A church in Jerusalem that receives the Gentile mission report with joy and then watches its guest arrested in the temple court. The will of the Lord, being done — at great cost, with great grief, toward a great purpose that none of them can yet see fully.

Now: The church in every age must learn the grammar of “let the will of the Lord be done.” It is learned most deeply in the moments when the will of the Lord leads into what we would not choose — illness, loss, rejection, persecution. Paul goes to Jerusalem not because it is easy or because he can see the outcome, but because the Spirit has said go and the Lord has said trust. This is the faith that follows a Lord who himself prayed “not my will, but yours.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul addresses the crowd as brothers and fathers, and when they hear him speak in their own tongue they grow quieter. He tells them he is a Jew born in Tarsus, raised in Jerusalem and trained precisely in the ancestral law under Gamaliel, as zealous for God as they are. He hunted the Way to the death, arresting men and women, with the authority of the high priest and the council. On the road to Damascus at midday a blinding light flashed round him; he fell and heard a voice asking why he was persecuting him. He asked who was speaking, and the voice answered that it was Jesus of Nazareth. His companions saw the light but did not grasp the voice. Told to go into Damascus to learn what he must do, he was led there blind. Ananias, a devout and respected keeper of the law, came and restored his sight, and told him the God of their fathers had chosen him to know his will, see the Righteous One and be his witness to all people. He urged him to be baptised and have his sins washed away, calling on his name. Later, praying in the temple in Jerusalem, Paul fell into a trance and saw the Lord, who told him to leave quickly because they would not accept his testimony. Paul protested that they knew how he had persecuted believers and had approved Stephen’s death. But the Lord replied that he was sending him far away to the Gentiles.
verseByVerse.theology:
Sovereign Grace, and a Commission Older Than the Convert

Ananias's word for what God did to Saul is appointed — chosen and designated (22:14) — and Paul never forgot it, writing later that God had set me apart before I was born (Gal. 1:15). The light at noon was not God changing his mind about Saul of Tarsus. It was God keeping an appointment made before Saul existed. Nothing in the account belongs to the convert: Christ sought him, struck him down, named him in his mother tongue, blinded him, and told him what he would do. Paul did not find Jesus; Jesus took Paul.

Two guards keep this from being abstract. First, on the timing of the new birth Scripture is deliberately reticent, and we should be too — regeneration is the Spirit's secret work, known by its fruits and not by a stopwatch (see the note at vv. 9–10). Second, on wash away your sins (v. 16), the sign is spoken of in the language of the thing signified, as Scripture habitually does; the blood of Christ does the washing and baptism seals and publishes it, which is exactly how Paul afterwards handled circumcision as a seal of a righteousness already had by faith (Rom. 4:11).

And the chapter's summit is what grace does with a specific, named, unforgettable sin. The man who guarded the garments at Stephen's stoning is sent to the ends of the earth with Stephen's message. That is not grace overlooking a small thing. It is the blood of the Righteous One proving stronger than the blood that was shed.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A frightened disciple in Damascus was given the address of the man holding warrants for his arrest, and went. He knew his own name was probably on the list. He knocked, walked into the one house in the city where a Christian could be seized on the spot, and said two words before anything had been proved about the blind man sitting there: Brother Saul.

Now: Picture the person whose arrival in your church on Sunday would be hardest to absorb — not a stranger, but someone with a history, and a history with you. Somebody who did real damage and knew what they were doing. Now suppose the Lord has laid hold of them. How long, in practice, before anyone says brother, and means it, and stops watching the door? Ananias managed it in three days, before any evidence of change had been produced, because he understood that the church does not decide who its family is. It recognises whom the Lord has already taken in.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.' And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul addresses his attackers courteously as family, in their own language.

Brothers and fathers. The same courteous opening Stephen used (7:2). Paul speaks to his attackers as family.

Defence. Apologia: a reasoned answer, the word behind “apologetics” (1 Peter 3:15). Paul’s defence is his testimony.

On a Tuesday. Courtesy disarms. When you face hostility, speak respectfully and in terms people understand.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s first defence, to the Jerusalem crowd.

parallels.desc: Stephen’s same opening

verseByVerse.quote: "'I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s testimony begins with an honest account of his strict Judaism and his violent persecution of the Way.

Brought up in this city. Paul came to Jerusalem young; his sister’s family lived there (23:16). His Judaism was not provincial.

Gamaliel. The leading Pharisee teacher of his generation (5:34–39). Students literally sat at their teacher’s feet.

As you are. Paul identifies with their zeal, generously: he was once where they stand. Compare Romans 10:2, zeal without knowledge.

To the death. Paul does not soften his past (1 Timothy 1:13–15).

On a Tuesday. A testimony begins with honesty about who we were. Do not exaggerate your past for drama, or hide it for pride.
verseByVerse.note: Gamaliel was the most respected Pharisee teacher of the day; students sat at their teacher’s feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "'as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
His past is a matter of public record, and on the road to Damascus a light brighter than noon stopped him.

Witnesses. Paul appeals to public record. His conversion was not a private feeling but an event with consequences known to the authorities.

Noon. A detail added here (and in 26:13): a light brighter than the midday sun. This was no trick of the dark.

To the brothers. Paul still calls the Jews of Damascus his brothers.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?" And I answered, "Who are you, Lord?" And he said to me, "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus identifies himself with the people Paul was persecuting.

Me. To persecute Christians is to persecute Christ, for they are his body (1 Corinthians 12:27; Matthew 25:40).

Of Nazareth. Added only in this account: for this audience, Jesus of the despised town is the risen Lord.

For worship. Christ counts his people’s sufferings as his own. Bring your troubles to him who feels them.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. And I said, "What shall I do, Lord?" And the Lord said to me, "Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul alone understood the voice, and he surrendered: what shall I do, Lord?

A supposed contradiction. In 9:7 the companions “hearing the voice but seeing no one”; here they “did not understand the voice”. The Greek verb “hear” can mean either perceive a sound or understand words, and Luke’s grammar marks the difference. They heard a sound; they did not make out the message. Compare John 12:29, where some thought it thundered.

What shall I do? The first question of a converted man (2:37; 16:30). Surrender follows recognition.

Appointed. Paul’s life was planned for him by God before he was born (Galatians 1:15).

On a Tuesday. Ask the Lord daily, “What shall I do?” and then do the next thing he has shown you.
verseByVerse.note: His companions saw the light and heard a sound but could not make out the words.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The proud persecutor was led blind into Damascus, where a devout Jew came to him.

Led by the hand. The persecutor arrives not as a commander but as a blind man needing help.

Ananias described for this audience. In chapter 9 he is “a disciple”; here “a devout man according to the law”. Both are true. Paul chooses what will help his hearers see that following Jesus is not betraying Israel.

On a Tuesday. In telling the gospel, it is right to stress what your hearers can recognise, without hiding or changing the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: "'came to me, and standing by me said to me, "Brother Saul, receive your sight." And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ananias greets Paul as a brother, and his sight returns.

Brother. The first word Paul hears from a Christian is a word of family. Ananias had been afraid of him (9:13–14), but grace overcomes fear.

On a Tuesday. Welcome new believers warmly, especially those with a frightening past.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And he said, "The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The God of their fathers appointed Paul to see the Righteous One and be his witness.

The God of our fathers. The God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the same God the crowd worships (3:13; 5:30). Paul has not changed God; he has met God’s Messiah.

Appointed. Paul’s calling is God’s choice, not his own decision (Galatians 1:15–16). Effectual calling: the Lord who summoned Paul also gave him the will to come.

The Righteous One. A title of the Messiah (3:14; 7:52; Isaiah 53:11). Paul saw the risen Christ, which qualified him as an apostle (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8).

To everyone. Paul does not yet say “Gentiles”, but the hint is there.

For worship. Thank God that he chose you to know his will (Ephesians 1:9).
verseByVerse.note: “The Righteous One” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.' When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ananias urges immediate baptism, calling on Jesus’ name for the washing away of sins.

Why wait? Baptism followed conversion immediately.

Where Christians differ: does baptism wash away sin? Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Churches of Christ traditions read this as baptism being the means by which sins are forgiven. Reformed and Baptist interpreters note that the washing is tied to “calling on his name”, that is, faith (2:21; Romans 10:13); that Paul had already met the Lord and been called “brother”; and that baptism is the outward sign and seal of a washing that Christ does inwardly (1 Peter 3:21; Titus 3:5). Verdict: baptism pictures and publicly seals the cleansing received by faith; sins are washed away by Christ, through faith, signified in water. The sign and the thing signified belong together and must not be separated lightly, but the sign does not work on its own.

In the temple. For this audience Paul stresses that his call to the Gentiles came while he was praying in the temple. He did not despise it.

On a Tuesday. If you have trusted Christ but never been baptised, ask Ananias’s question: why wait?

verseByVerse.quote: "'and saw him saying to me, "Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me." And I said, "Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a temple vision the Lord told Paul to leave Jerusalem, though Paul thought his past made him the ideal witness there.

A vision in the temple. Like Isaiah, called in the temple (Isaiah 6), Paul is sent from the temple.

Paul’s objection. He thought his past made him the ideal witness to Jerusalem: who could doubt a converted persecutor? The Lord knew better. Our reasoning about where we will be most effective is not always God’s.

Harmony with chapter 9. In 9:29–30 the believers send Paul away because of a plot. Both are true: the Lord warned him and the church acted.
