verseByVerse.quote: "'And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.' And he said to me, "Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord sent Paul far away to the Gentiles.

Your witness. Martys, a witness; Stephen’s death helped give the word its later sense of “martyr”.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “to his death” after “approving” (hence the KJV “consenting unto his death”), probably from 8:1. Verdict: the shorter text is original; the meaning is the same.

Far away to the Gentiles. The word that triggers the riot (v. 22). For the crowd, God’s grace to the Gentiles without the law was the unbearable part.

For worship. If the gospel had stayed in Jerusalem, most of us would never have heard it. Thank God he sent Paul far away, to us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–30 — The Roman Custody and Paul's Citizenship
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the word “Gentiles” the crowd erupts, shouting that such a man should be wiped off the earth, tearing off their cloaks and throwing dust into the air. The commander orders Paul into the barracks to be flogged and questioned, to discover why they are shouting against him. As they stretch him out for the lash, Paul asks the centurion whether it is lawful to flog a Roman citizen who has not been condemned. The centurion warns the commander, who comes and asks Paul directly whether he is a citizen. Paul says yes. The commander says that his own citizenship cost him a great deal; Paul answers that he was born a citizen. Those about to interrogate him withdraw at once, and the commander is alarmed at having put a citizen in chains. Next day, wanting to know exactly what the Jews accuse him of, he releases Paul and orders the chief priests and the whole council to assemble, and brings Paul before them.
verseByVerse.theology:
Rights as Tools, Not Shields

Paul's Roman citizenship is one of the clearest case studies in Scripture of how a Christian may handle a legitimate privilege. He does not renounce it, and he does not hide behind it. At Philippi he took the beating with the card in his pocket and produced it only the next morning (16:37), because that beating served the gospel and produced a jailer's household. On the barracks steps one chapter ago he deliberately withheld it, because he wanted a pulpit and not a rescue (21:39). Here he plays it, seconds before the whip falls, because a scourging would have ended a man who has been told he must testify at Rome.

The deciding question is never what will hurt least. It is what will serve most. That is a harder rule than either renouncing rights or clinging to them, because it has to be asked fresh every time and it cannot be settled in advance by policy.

Underneath it lies the Reformed conviction about the civil magistrate. God gave the sword to the state (Rom. 13:4), and he uses it — often through officials with no interest in him at all. A centurion protecting his own career, a commander doing the arithmetic on his pension, an empire enforcing its own statutes: none of them knows he is keeping the apostle to the Gentiles alive and moving him toward Rome. God's providence does not require the cooperation of the people it employs.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Four officials in turn — Lysias, Felix, Festus and Agrippa — examined the case against Paul, and not one of them could name a crime. The tribune could not learn the facts in the uproar, and wrote that he found nothing deserving death or imprisonment (23:29). Festus said the accusers brought no charge of the sort he had expected (25:18) and finally admitted it was unreasonable to send on a prisoner without indicating the charges (25:27). Luke records all four without a word of editorial.

Now: Where the church is opposed, it is worth being clear about which thing is happening. Sometimes Christians are disciplined for genuine wrongdoing, and the right response is repentance, not a persecution narrative. But when the file keeps coming back empty — when the offence turns out to be the message itself, and no one can state a charge — that is the pattern of this chapter, and the answer is not outrage. It is to keep doing exactly what the empty file says you were doing, and to go on asking, as Paul did with his back to a whipping post, for permission to speak.

verseByVerse.quote: "Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, 'Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.' And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The word Gentiles enrages the crowd: grace to outsiders is the offence.

The offence. Not Jesus’ name, not the resurrection, but God sending a Jew to Gentiles, as equals, without first making them Jews. Jesus met the same fury at Nazareth for the same reason (Luke 4:25–29).

Dust and cloaks. Gestures of rage and of horror at blasphemy, perhaps also preparing to throw stones.

On a Tuesday. Grace to outsiders still offends religious people. Ask whether there are people you would rather God did not save.
verseByVerse.note: Throwing dust in the air and tearing off cloaks were gestures of outrage.

verseByVerse.quote: "the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, 'Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul claims his citizen’s right not to be flogged without trial.

The scourge. The Roman flagellum was a whip of leather thongs with bone or metal, used to extract confessions from slaves and non-citizens. Some died under it. It was far worse than the synagogue’s thirty-nine lashes (2 Corinthians 11:24).

Roman law. The Porcian and Julian laws forbade binding, beating or scourging a citizen without trial. To claim citizenship falsely was punishable by death, so the claim was usually believed.

Why now? At Philippi Paul spoke up only after the beating (16:37). Here he speaks before it, perhaps because he must survive to bear witness in Rome (23:11).

What it does not mean. Christians are not forbidden to use their legal rights. Paul uses them, not for comfort, but for the gospel.

On a Tuesday. It is right to use lawful protections, a lawyer, a complaint, a vote, when it serves justice and the gospel (Romans 13:1–4).
verseByVerse.note: Roman interrogation of non-citizens often used the scourge; flogging an uncondemned Roman citizen was illegal.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, 'What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.' So the tribune came and said to him, 'Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?' And he said, 'Yes.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion warns the commander, and Paul confirms his citizenship.

The centurion. Once again a centurion shows sense (Luke 7:2–10; 23:47; Acts 10; 27:43).

A simple yes. Paul makes no speech. Let your yes be yes (Matthew 5:37).

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune answered, 'I bought this citizenship for a large sum.' Paul said, 'But I am a citizen by birth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s citizenship by birth outranks the commander’s bought one.

Bought citizenship. Under Claudius, citizenship could be obtained through bribes to officials; the commander’s name, Claudius Lysias (23:26), suggests he took the emperor’s name when he received it.

Born a citizen. Paul’s father or grandfather was granted citizenship, perhaps for service to a Roman general. A citizen by birth outranked one who bought it.

Two citizenships. Paul held Roman citizenship, but wrote that “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). That one cannot be bought: it is a gift, by new birth (John 3:3–5).

For worship. Thank God for a citizenship purchased not with silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ (1 Peter 1:18–19).
verseByVerse.note: Citizenship could be bought through bribes under Claudius. Paul was born a citizen, probably because his father or grandfather had been granted it.

verseByVerse.quote: "So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Alarmed, the commander releases Paul’s chains and brings him before the Sanhedrin.

Afraid. The commander had broken the law by binding a citizen without charge; Paul could make trouble for him.

The Sanhedrin. The Jewish supreme council of seventy-one, under the high priest. Jesus, Peter, John and Stephen had all stood before it (Luke 22:66; Acts 4:5–7; 6:12). Now Paul, once its agent, stands there as the accused.

On a Tuesday. God sets the stage. Paul’s imprisonment brings him, one by one, before every audience Jesus promised: councils, governors and kings (Luke 21:12–13).
verseByVerse.note: The council is the Sanhedrin.

22.title: Paul's Defence Before the Crowd
22.text: <sup>1</sup>“Brothers and fathers, hear the defense that I now make before you.” <sup>2</sup>And when they heard that he was addressing them in the Hebrew language, they became even more quiet. And he said: <sup>3</sup>“I am a Jew, born in Tarsus in Cilicia, but brought up in this city, educated at the feet of Gamaliel according to the strict manner of the law of our fathers, being zealous for God as all of you are this day. <sup>4</sup>I persecuted this Way to the death, binding and delivering to prison both men and women, <sup>5</sup>as the high priest and the whole council of elders can bear me witness. From them I received letters to the brothers, and I journeyed toward Damascus to take those also who were there and bring them in bonds to Jerusalem to be punished. <sup>6</sup>“As I was on my way and drew near to Damascus, about noon a great light from heaven suddenly shone around me. <sup>7</sup>And I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ <sup>8</sup>And I answered, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And he said to me, ‘I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting.’ <sup>9</sup>Now those who were with me saw the light but did not understand the voice of the one who was speaking to me. <sup>10</sup>And I said, ‘What shall I do, Lord?’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Rise, and go into Damascus, and there you will be told all that is appointed for you to do.’ <sup>11</sup>And since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those who were with me, and came into Damascus. <sup>12</sup>“And one Ananias, a devout man according to the law, well spoken of by all the Jews who lived there, <sup>13</sup>came to me, and standing by me said to me, ‘Brother Saul, receive your sight.’ And at that very hour I received my sight and saw him. <sup>14</sup>And he said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know his will, to see the Righteous One and to hear a voice from his mouth; <sup>15</sup>for you will be a witness for him to everyone of what you have seen and heard. <sup>16</sup>And now why do you wait? Rise and be baptized and wash away your sins, calling on his name.’ <sup>17</sup>“When I had returned to Jerusalem and was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance <sup>18</sup>and saw him saying to me, ‘Make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because they will not accept your testimony about me.’ <sup>19</sup>And I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that in one synagogue after another I imprisoned and beat those who believed in you. <sup>20</sup>And when the blood of Stephen your witness was being shed, I myself was standing by and approving and watching over the garments of those who killed him.’ <sup>21</sup>And he said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’” <sup>22</sup>Up to this word they listened to him. Then they raised their voices and said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth! For he should not be allowed to live.” <sup>23</sup>And as they were shouting and throwing off their cloaks and flinging dust into the air, <sup>24</sup>the tribune ordered him to be brought into the barracks, saying that he should be examined by flogging, to find out why they were shouting against him like this. <sup>25</sup>But when they had stretched him out for the whips, Paul said to the centurion who was standing by, “Is it lawful for you to flog a man who is a Roman citizen and uncondemned?” <sup>26</sup>When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and said to him, “What are you about to do? For this man is a Roman citizen.” <sup>27</sup>So the tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” And he said, “Yes.” <sup>28</sup>The tribune answered, “I bought this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I am a citizen by birth.” <sup>29</sup>So those who were about to examine him withdrew from him immediately, and the tribune also was afraid, for he realized that Paul was a Roman citizen and that he had bound him. <sup>30</sup>But on the next day, desiring to know the real reason why he was being accused by the Jews, he unbound him and commanded the chief priests and all the council to meet, and he brought Paul down and set him before them.
22.overview:
From the steps of the Antonia Fortress Paul speaks to the crowd that has just tried to kill him. This is the second of three accounts of his conversion in Acts (9:1–19; 26:9–18), each shaped for its audience. Here, before a Jewish crowd and in their own language, he stresses how Jewish he is: trained under Gamaliel, zealous for the law, a persecutor of the Way; Ananias is a devout law-keeper; the God who called him is “the God of our fathers”; and his commission came in a vision in the temple itself.

The crowd listens until he says that the Lord sent him to the Gentiles. Then they explode. The tribune orders him to be examined under the lash, but as they stretch him out Paul asks whether it is legal to flog an uncondemned Roman citizen. The tribune, who bought his own citizenship, learns that Paul was born a citizen, and is alarmed. To find out the real charge, he summons the Sanhedrin the next day. Luke shows again that the real offence of Paul’s gospel is grace to the Gentiles, and that Roman law protects the messenger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Before the Sanhedrin and the Plot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul looks steadily at the council and says he has lived before God with a wholly clear conscience. The high priest Ananias orders those near him to hit him on the mouth. Paul retorts that God will strike him, the whitewashed wall: he sits to judge by the law, yet breaks the law by ordering him struck. When bystanders protest that he is insulting God’s high priest, Paul says he did not realise it was the high priest, for Scripture forbids speaking evil of a ruler of the people. Knowing that the council includes Sadducees and Pharisees, Paul calls out that he is a Pharisee, son of Pharisees, on trial over the hope of the resurrection. This splits the assembly, since Sadducees deny resurrection, angels and spirits, while Pharisees accept them. In the uproar some Pharisee scribes declare him innocent: perhaps a spirit or angel has spoken to him. The dispute turns so violent that the commander, fearing Paul will be torn apart, has soldiers snatch him back into the barracks. The following night the Lord stands beside Paul and tells him to take heart: as he has testified in Jerusalem, so he must testify in Rome. In the morning over forty men vow not to eat or drink until they have killed Paul. They ask the chief priests to request another hearing so they can ambush him on the way. Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and tells Paul, who has a centurion take the young man to the commander. Taken aside, the nephew explains the plan, and the commander sends him away with orders to tell no one.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Promise That Does Not Remove the Danger

Acts 23:11 is the hinge of the second half of the book, and what makes it pastorally useful is as much what it withholds as what it gives. The Lord does not tell Paul he will be released, or comfortable, or vindicated. He does not mention the two years in Caesarea, the storm, or the shipwreck — all of which are still coming, and none of which is cancelled. He gives an assignment and guarantees its completion: you must testify also in Rome. The word is dei, Luke's word for divine necessity, the same word he uses for the sufferings of the Son of Man. Paul's arrival in Rome is now as fixed as the cross.

That is the Reformed doctrine of providence at work, and this chapter shows both halves of it. God ordains the end, and he ordains the means — and the means are startlingly ordinary: a boy who overhears something, an officer protecting his career, a duty roster. Paul believes the promise absolutely and immediately calls a centurion, exactly as he will later believe an angel's word that all aboard will live and then warn that unless the sailors stayed in the ship no one could be saved (27:31). Certainty about the outcome does not make action unnecessary; it makes action possible without panic.

And the instruments need not be godly, or even willing. Claudius Lysias is a self-serving man who falsifies his own report. The Lord uses him unimproved, and he goes off shift with no idea what he has just done.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A conspiracy of more than forty men, sworn under a self-curse, endorsed by the chief priests and elders, with the machinery of the Sanhedrin ready to supply the pretext — defeated by an unnamed young man who happened to hear something and had the nerve to walk across a city and say it out loud. He is never named, never mentioned again, and there is no tradition about him at all. Every consequence of Paul's Roman years runs through his afternoon.

Now: Very few Christians are given a Paul-sized life, and almost every Christian is at some point given the nephew's. You know something. You noticed something. You are standing near enough to do something, and you have about a minute to decide whether it is really your business. The thing that makes this hard is not courage in the heroic sense; it is that the action looks far too small to matter and you will almost certainly never be told how it turned out. He was ordered to keep quiet and sent home. Do it anyway. The size of the outcome has never been the measure of the obedience, and it is not usually visible from where you are standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "And looking intently at the council, Paul said, 'Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.' And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul claims a clear conscience before the council, and the corrupt high priest has him struck.

A good conscience. Paul means that he acted sincerely, even as a persecutor (26:9; 1 Timothy 1:13), and since his conversion has had nothing to hide (24:16; 2 Corinthians 1:12). It is not a claim to be sinless.

Ananias. High priest about AD 47–58, notorious for greed: Josephus says his servants seized the tithes owed to ordinary priests, some of whom starved. He was later murdered by Jewish rebels in AD 66.

Struck. Jesus was struck before the high priest too (John 18:22).

What it does not mean. A clear conscience is not proof of being right: Paul had one while persecuting the church. Conscience must be taught by Scripture (1 Corinthians 4:4).
verseByVerse.note: Ananias was high priest from about AD 47 to 58; Josephus describes him as greedy and violent.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Paul said to him, 'God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?' Those who stood by said, 'Would you revile God's high priest?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul rightly exposes the high priest’s hypocrisy, but in a manner that falls short of his Lord’s.

Whitewashed wall. A crumbling wall made to look sound (Ezekiel 13:10–15; compare Matthew 23:27, “whitewashed tombs”). Ananias claims the law and breaks it (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 25:1–2).

A prophecy? “God is going to strike you” came true when Ananias was killed. Paul may be pronouncing judgment, or simply stating that God judges injustice.

Where Christians differ: did Paul sin here? Some, as early as Jerome, think Paul lost his temper, unlike Jesus, who answered calmly (John 18:23), and that his apology admits a fault. Others defend him as speaking prophetically against injustice. Verdict: Paul’s rebuke was true, but his manner fell short of his Lord’s, as his own quick apology shows. Even apostles were sinners saved by grace; Scripture records it honestly.

On a Tuesday. When you are treated unjustly, it is right to name the injustice, but watch your tongue (James 1:19–20). Be quick to apologise.
verseByVerse.note: A whitewashed wall looks solid but hides the crumbling beneath.

parallels.desc: you shall do no injustice in court

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, "You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul at once submits to Scripture’s command to respect the office.

Did not know? Several explanations: Paul had been away for years; the high priest may not have been in robes at an informal meeting; Paul’s eyesight may have been poor (Galatians 4:15; 6:11); or Paul is ironic, “I did not recognise such a man as high priest.” The simplest reading is that he genuinely did not know who spoke.

The law quoted. Exodus 22:28. Paul submits to Scripture even when it rebukes him. Respect for an office does not depend on the worthiness of the person holding it (Romans 13:7; 1 Peter 2:17).

On a Tuesday. Speak respectfully of those in authority, even when you disagree with them, including politicians, employers and church leaders.

parallels.desc: nor curse a ruler of your people

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, 'Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.' And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul brings the trial back to its real issue, the hope of the resurrection, and the council divides.

Still a Pharisee? In belief about resurrection, angels and the hope of Israel, yes (26:5–8; Philippians 3:5). He has given up Pharisaic confidence in law-keeping (Philippians 3:7–9), not the hope.

The real issue. The resurrection is the heart of the matter: if Jesus rose, he is the Messiah, and Israel’s hope is fulfilled (26:6–8; 1 Corinthians 15:12–20).

Where Christians differ: clever tactic or honest witness? Some see Paul cleverly dividing his enemies to escape. Others answer that he states the true centre of his case, and the division follows. Verdict: both: Paul is shrewd, but what he says is true and central. Wise as serpents, innocent as doves (Matthew 10:16).

For worship. “The hope and the resurrection”: our whole faith hangs on an empty tomb. Rejoice in it.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees' party stood up and contended sharply, 'We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pharisees and Sadducees fall out, and some Pharisees even defend Paul.

The Sadducees. The aristocratic priestly party, who controlled the temple. They denied resurrection because they did not find it in the five books of Moses (Luke 20:27–38, where Jesus answers them from Exodus 3:6).

No angel nor spirit. Perhaps they denied the developed belief in angels and spirits of the dead, not angels altogether, since angels appear in the books of Moses.

The Pharisees’ defence. They half-accept Paul’s vision of Christ, as Gamaliel once urged caution (5:38–39). Partisanship can make people fair for the wrong reasons.

On a Tuesday. Do not join a side just because it defends you. Truth, not tribe, is the test.
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and probably held the five books of Moses above the rest of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The supreme council cannot conduct a hearing, and Rome rescues Paul again.

The council’s failure. The supreme court of Israel cannot conduct a hearing. Luke shows the leaders unable to judge rightly about Jesus or his witnesses.

Third rescue. Rome has saved Paul three times in three days (21:32; 22:24–29; 23:10). God governs pagan powers for his people’s good.

verseByVerse.quote: "The following night the Lord stood by him and said, 'Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.' When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At his lowest point the Lord stands by Paul and promises he will testify in Rome, while forty men swear to kill him.

The Lord stood by him. At his lowest point, alone in a barracks after a failed hearing, Paul receives a visit from Jesus himself (18:9–10; 27:23–24; 2 Timothy 4:17).

Must. God’s necessity again (19:21). Paul’s journey to Rome is now guaranteed. Everything that follows, plots, trials, storm and snake, cannot stop it.

Juxtaposition. Luke sets the Lord’s promise and the men’s oath side by side. The plotters swear an oath; the Lord has already sworn a better one.

On a Tuesday. When you are discouraged after doing your best and it seems to have failed, remember that Christ stands by his servants. Take heart (John 16:33).

For worship. Thank Jesus that he does not only send us; he comes to us.

verseByVerse.quote: "There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. They went to the chief priests and elders and said, 'We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The conspirators bind themselves with a curse.

A curse-oath. Literally they “anathematised” themselves: calling down God’s curse if they failed. Religious zeal turned murderous (John 16:2).

What happened to them? Rabbinic law allowed release from vows that could not be fulfilled. They probably did not starve.

Rash vows. Compare Jephthah (Judges 11:30–31) and Saul (1 Samuel 14:24). God does not honour oaths to do evil.

parallels.desc: Saul’s rash oath

verseByVerse.quote: "'Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.' Now the son of Paul's sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The chief priests join the murder plot, but Paul’s nephew overhears it.

The leaders complicit. The chief priests, keepers of the law, agree to a plan of murder.

Paul’s nephew. The only glimpse of Paul’s family in the New Testament. His sister lived in Jerusalem; whether they were believers we do not know. Paul may have been disowned by his family for following Christ (Philippians 3:8), but a nephew still cares.

Access. As an unconvicted Roman citizen, Paul could receive visitors.

On a Tuesday. God’s providence often works through small, ordinary people: a boy overhearing a conversation. Do not underestimate the part you can play.
verseByVerse.note: This is the only mention of Paul’s family in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul called one of the centurions and said, 'Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.' So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, 'Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Trusting the promise, Paul still uses sensible means to foil the plot.

Faith and means. Paul has the Lord’s promise that he will reach Rome, but he still acts sensibly to avoid the plot. God’s sovereignty does not make human action pointless; it works through it.

Paul the prisoner. A title Paul later takes for himself: “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 3:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "The tribune took him by the hand and going aside asked him privately, 'What is it that you have to tell me?' And he said, 'The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commander kindly hears the young man in private.

By the hand. A kind gesture: the commander puts a nervous young man at ease. Luke notices small kindnesses.

The Jews. The nephew means the plotters, not all Jews. Luke’s phrase refers to particular opponents.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.' So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, 'Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commander acts on the warning and keeps it secret.

Secrecy. The commander protects both the informant and his plan.

On a Tuesday. If you learn of a plan to harm someone, tell those who can stop it. Speaking up can save a life (Proverbs 24:11–12).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The commander calls two centurions and orders two hundred soldiers, seventy cavalry and two hundred spearmen to be ready to leave for Caesarea at nine that night, with horses for Paul, to bring him safely to Governor Felix. He writes a letter: Claudius Lysias greets His Excellency Felix. The Jews had seized this man and were about to kill him when he rescued him with his troops, having learned he was a Roman. Wanting to know the charge, he brought him before their council and found it concerned disputes about their law, nothing deserving death or prison. Told of a plot against the man, he has sent him at once and instructed his accusers to bring their case to Felix. The soldiers take Paul overnight as far as Antipatris; next day the cavalry go on with him while the rest return. In Caesarea they deliver the letter and hand Paul over. Felix reads it, asks his province, and on hearing Cilicia says he will hear the case when the accusers arrive. He orders Paul kept under guard in Herod’s palace.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Wearing a Uniform

Nothing in this section is miraculous, and that is the theological point. The God who opened the Philippian jail with an earthquake here uses a boy's ears, an officer's fear of a court-martial, a standard troop deployment, and a piece of self-serving correspondence. Scripture is entirely comfortable with both, and Christians who will only recognise God's hand in the spectacular will miss most of what he does.

Two guards keep this from turning into fatalism. First, providence does not excuse the wickedness it employs: the chief priests who agreed to supply the pretext for a murder are guilty of it, and Lysias's falsified report is a lie, and Luke's silence is not approval. Second, providence does not promise comfort. This chapter's happy ending is a two-year detention under a governor angling for a bribe. God's certain purposes and a believer's real losses run down the same road, at the same time, and Scripture never asks anyone to pretend otherwise.

The pattern is Joseph's: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen. 50:20). The forty men were, without knowing it, working for the One they were trying to thwart — and so was the empire, which spent a great deal of money that night keeping alive a man it would one day execute.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The tribune's letter told the governor a true story arranged to flatter its author. He did not invent a single fact. He moved one clause — putting the discovery of Paul's citizenship before the rescue instead of after it — and let his superior draw a generous conclusion. Luke set the letter down beside the events of the previous chapter and left it there.

Now: Take the story you tell most often about a hard episode — why the job ended, why the friendship cooled, how the argument went. You have told it enough times that it runs smoothly now. Every detail in it probably happened. Then lay it beside a transcript, the way Luke lays this letter beside chapter 22, and ask the narrower question: is the sequence right, and is the motive you imply the motive you actually had? Most of us are not liars. Most of us are editors, and the edit is nearly always in our own favour.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he called two of the centurions and said, 'Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God keeps his promise through a Roman army of 470 men.

470 men. Nearly half the garrison, for one prisoner. The commander takes no chances: if a Roman citizen were killed in his custody, he would answer for it. The ambush of forty is now hopeless.

Spearmen. The Greek word is rare; it may mean light-armed troops or slingers.

Felix. Antonius Felix, a former slave freed by the imperial family, governor about AD 52–59. The historian Tacitus said he exercised the power of a king with the mind of a slave.

Textual note. The Western text adds that the commander was afraid the Jews would seize and kill Paul and that he would then be accused of having taken a bribe. It is a vivid explanation, but not original.

For worship. The Lord promised Paul Rome (v. 11); within a day he gives him a Roman army. Praise him who keeps his word through unlikely means.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the third hour of the night was about 9 p.m. Felix, a former slave, was governor of Judea from about AD 52 to 59.

verseByVerse.quote: "And he wrote a letter to this effect: 'Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commander writes to the governor in proper form.

A real letter form. Name of sender, recipient, greeting, as in Paul’s letters and countless papyri. “To this effect” suggests Luke gives the gist.

His Excellency. Kratistos, “most excellent”, the title Luke gives Theophilus (Luke 1:3).
verseByVerse.note: Claudius Lysias probably took the emperor’s name when he bought his citizenship.

parallels.desc: “most excellent”

verseByVerse.quote: "'This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter puts the commander’s own conduct in the best light.

Spin. Lysias rearranges the order: he learned of Paul’s citizenship only after nearly flogging him (22:25–29). He omits that he chained and almost scourged a citizen. Luke lets us see the official version beside the truth.

On a Tuesday. Be honest in reports, references and emails, even when the truth does not flatter you (Ephesians 4:25).
verseByVerse.note: Lysias leaves out that he had nearly flogged a Roman citizen.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rome finds nothing in Paul deserving death or prison.

Not guilty. The first of several Roman verdicts in Paul’s favour (25:25; 26:31–32), like Pilate’s over Jesus (Luke 23:4, 14–15, 22). Luke’s readers learn that Christianity is not a crime under Roman law.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commander passes the case to the governor.

Passing the case on. The commander is relieved to hand a political problem to a higher authority.

Textual note. Later manuscripts add “Farewell” at the end (hence the KJV). Verdict: probably a scribal addition matching letter form.

verseByVerse.quote: "So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is taken safely by night beyond the reach of the plotters.

Antipatris. About 35 to 40 miles from Jerusalem, built by Herod the Great and named after his father Antipater. A hard night’s march.

Beyond danger. Past Antipatris lay mainly Gentile country, so the infantry could return while cavalry escorted Paul the remaining 25 miles.
verseByVerse.note: Antipatris was about 35 miles from Jerusalem; the road beyond was safer, running through mostly Gentile country.

verseByVerse.quote: "When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul arrives in Caesarea, where he will spend two years.

Caesarea. The Roman capital of Judea, built by Herod on the coast. Paul had passed through it before (9:30; 18:22; 21:8). Now he will spend two years there (24:27).

On a Tuesday. Paul did not choose Caesarea; he was taken there. Places we do not choose can become places of fruitful ministry (24:24–26).
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea, on the coast, was the Roman capital of Judea.

verseByVerse.quote: "On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, he said, 'I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.' And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod's praetorium."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Felix agrees to hear the case and keeps Paul in Herod’s palace.

Which province? To decide jurisdiction. Cilicia was then administered with Syria, under the same legate as Judea; Felix can try the case.

Herod’s praetorium. The palace Herod the Great built, now the governor’s headquarters. Paul is held in reasonable comfort, as a citizen awaiting trial.

For worship. The plotters fasted; the Lord kept his servant. Psalm 121:7–8: the LORD will keep your going out and your coming in.
verseByVerse.note: Herod’s praetorium was the palace Herod the Great had built at Caesarea, used as the governor’s residence.

23.title: The Plot and the Providence
23.text: <sup>1</sup>And looking intently at the council, Paul said, “Brothers, I have lived my life before God in all good conscience up to this day.” <sup>2</sup>And the high priest Ananias commanded those who stood by him to strike him on the mouth. <sup>3</sup>Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, you whitewashed wall! Are you sitting to judge me according to the law, and yet contrary to the law you order me to be struck?” <sup>4</sup>Those who stood by said, “Would you revile God’s high priest?” <sup>5</sup>And Paul said, “I did not know, brothers, that he was the high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’” <sup>6</sup>Now when Paul perceived that one part were Sadducees and the other Pharisees, he cried out in the council, “Brothers, I am a Pharisee, a son of Pharisees. It is with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial.” <sup>7</sup>And when he had said this, a dissension arose between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided. <sup>8</sup>For the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit, but the Pharisees acknowledge them all. <sup>9</sup>Then a great clamor arose, and some of the scribes of the Pharisees’ party stood up and contended sharply, “We find nothing wrong in this man. What if a spirit or an angel spoke to him?” <sup>10</sup>And when the dissension became violent, the tribune, afraid that Paul would be torn to pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him away from among them by force and bring him into the barracks. <sup>11</sup>The following night the Lord stood by him and said, “Take courage, for as you have testified to the facts about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.” <sup>12</sup>When it was day, the Jews made a plot and bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they had killed Paul. <sup>13</sup>There were more than forty who made this conspiracy. <sup>14</sup>They went to the chief priests and elders and said, “We have strictly bound ourselves by an oath to taste no food till we have killed Paul.” <sup>15</sup>Now therefore you, along with the council, give notice to the tribune to bring him down to you, as though you were going to determine his case more exactly. And we are ready to kill him before he comes near.” <sup>16</sup>Now the son of Paul’s sister heard of their ambush, so he went and entered the barracks and told Paul. <sup>17</sup>Paul called one of the centurions and said, “Take this young man to the tribune, for he has something to tell him.” <sup>18</sup>So he took him and brought him to the tribune and said, “Paul the prisoner called me and asked me to bring this young man to you, as he has something to say to you.” <sup>19</sup>The tribune took him by the hand, and going aside asked him privately, “What is it that you have to tell me?” <sup>20</sup>And he said, “The Jews have agreed to ask you to bring Paul down to the council tomorrow, as though they were going to inquire somewhat more closely about him. <sup>21</sup>But do not be persuaded by them, for more than forty of their men are lying in ambush for him, who have bound themselves by an oath neither to eat nor drink till they have killed him. And now they are ready, waiting for your consent.” <sup>22</sup>So the tribune dismissed the young man, charging him, “Tell no one that you have informed me of these things.” <sup>23</sup>Then he called two of the centurions and said, “Get ready two hundred soldiers, with seventy horsemen and two hundred spearmen to go as far as Caesarea at the third hour of the night. <sup>24</sup>Also provide mounts for Paul to ride and bring him safely to Felix the governor.” <sup>25</sup>And he wrote a letter to this effect: <sup>26</sup>“Claudius Lysias, to his Excellency the governor Felix, greetings. <sup>27</sup>This man was seized by the Jews and was about to be killed by them when I came upon them with the soldiers and rescued him, having learned that he was a Roman citizen. <sup>28</sup>And desiring to know the charge for which they were accusing him, I brought him down to their council. <sup>29</sup>I found that he was being accused about questions of their law, but charged with nothing deserving death or imprisonment. <sup>30</sup>And when it was disclosed to me that there would be a plot against the man, I sent him to you at once, ordering his accusers also to state before you what they have against him.” <sup>31</sup>So the soldiers, according to their instructions, took Paul and brought him by night to Antipatris. <sup>32</sup>And on the next day they returned to the barracks, letting the horsemen go on with him. <sup>33</sup>When they had come to Caesarea and delivered the letter to the governor, they presented Paul also before him. <sup>34</sup>On reading the letter, he asked what province he was from. And when he learned that he was from Cilicia, <sup>35</sup>he said, “I will give you a hearing when your accusers arrive.” And he commanded him to be guarded in Herod’s praetorium.
23.overview:
Paul stands before the Sanhedrin, the council he once served. The hearing is a disaster as a trial and a triumph of providence. The high priest Ananias, a notoriously greedy and violent man, has Paul struck for claiming a clear conscience; Paul flares up, then apologises when told who gave the order, citing the law. Seeing the council split between Sadducees and Pharisees, he declares that he is on trial for the hope of the resurrection, and the council dissolves into a shouting match, some Pharisees even defending him. The tribune has to rescue him a second time.

That night the Lord stands by Paul: he must testify in Rome as he has in Jerusalem. Next morning more than forty men swear not to eat or drink until they have killed him, but Paul’s nephew hears of the plot and warns him, and the tribune sends Paul by night under an escort of 470 soldiers to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter that states Paul has done nothing deserving death or chains. God’s promise is kept through a boy’s ears, a centurion’s errand and a Roman army. Paul is now in Roman custody, which will last more than four years and bring him, as promised, to Rome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Five days later the high priest comes down with elders and a lawyer, Tertullus. After flattering Felix, Tertullus charges Paul with being a troublemaker who stirs up Jews everywhere, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and one who tried to desecrate the temple. The Jews back him up. Paul replies calmly: he went up to worship only twelve days ago and started no disturbance anywhere, and they cannot prove their claims. He admits that he worships the God of their fathers as a follower of the Way, believing the Law and the Prophets and sharing their hope that God will raise both righteous and wicked; so he strives for a clear conscience. He came bringing gifts for the poor and was found in the temple ritually pure; the Asian Jews who caused the trouble are not even here, and the council found nothing except his cry about the resurrection. Felix, who knows about the Way, adjourns the case and keeps Paul under guard with some freedom. Later he and his wife Drusilla hear Paul on faith in Christ; when Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control and judgment, Felix grows afraid and sends him away until a convenient time. Hoping for a bribe, he often sends for him. After two years Festus succeeds Felix, who leaves Paul in prison to please the Jews.
verseByVerse.theology:
Almost Persuaded: the Sin of the Postponed Decision

Felix is the most quietly terrifying figure in Acts, because nothing about him is dramatic. He does not oppose the gospel. He is interested in it. He understands it accurately (v. 22), he sends for the preacher repeatedly (v. 26), and on the first hearing it frightens him badly enough to end the meeting. He is the nearest thing in this book to a man under conviction — and he dies outside of Christ, so far as Scripture records, with nothing standing between him and the kingdom except a word: later.

Scripture never treats delay as neutral ground. Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts (Heb. 3:15); behold, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2). The reason is visible in this very chapter: Felix felt more at the first conversation than at any of the many that followed. Repeated exposure without submission does not keep the heart tender; it callouses it. The second hearing of a truth is always easier to survive than the first.

This is why the Reformed tradition has insisted that conviction is not conversion. Felix's fear was real and it was the Spirit's work on his conscience — and a frightened conscience saves nobody. What God requires is not to be moved but to be surrendered. Grace is sovereign and grace is free, and the same doctrine that says no one comes unless the Father draws him says also that whoever comes will never be cast out (John 6:37, 44). The only sane response to a conviction you can feel is to act on it while you can still feel it.

Alongside Felix stands Paul, and the contrast is the chapter's argument. One man is free and cannot decide; the other is in chains and settled to the point of cheerfulness (v. 10). One postpones; the other has already been told he must testify at Rome and simply waits. Circumstance is a poor guide to who in a room is actually at liberty.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul was asked, by the man who could have freed him with a sentence, to speak about faith in Christ Jesus. He was a prisoner, entirely in that man's power, and the governor's known weaknesses were a court that could be bought and a wife he had taken from another man. Paul chose righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment. He did not trim one of the three, and he stayed in prison for two more years.

Now: Most Christians will never address a governor, and nearly all of us will at some point have something true to say to somebody who holds an advantage over us — an employer, a relative whose goodwill we need, a friend whose reaction we fear. The pressure is not usually to lie. It is to select: to say the two things that will land well and leave out the third, and to call the omission tact. Ask what your version leaves out, and then ask why it is always the same one. Paul's three subjects took ten seconds to choose and cost him two years, and Luke thought them worth recording precisely because he did not shorten the list to two.

verseByVerse.quote: "And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: 'Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A hired advocate opens the prosecution with flattery of a corrupt governor.

A hired advocate. Tertullus was a professional orator, perhaps a Hellenistic Jew, skilled in Roman court procedure.

Flattery. A captatio benevolentiae, the standard opening to win the judge’s favour. It was also false: Felix had crushed revolts brutally, and his rule increased unrest. Tacitus and Josephus both remember him badly.

On a Tuesday. Flattery is a form of lying (Psalm 12:2–3; Proverbs 26:28). Encourage people truthfully, but do not butter up the powerful.
verseByVerse.note: Tertullus was a professional advocate hired to present the case. Opening with flattery of the judge was standard courtroom style; Roman historians remember Felix’s rule as harsh and corrupt.

verseByVerse.quote: "'in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tertullus promises brevity because his case is thin.

Brief. A conventional promise, often broken. Here the speech is short because the case is thin.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charges are sedition, sect leadership and sacrilege, designed to alarm a Roman judge.

Three charges. Political (sedition, a capital crime under Rome), religious (leading an unrecognised sect), and sacrilege (the temple). The first is designed to frighten a Roman governor: Claudius had written to Alexandria about Jews “fomenting a general plague throughout the world”.

The Nazarenes. An early name for Jesus’ followers, still used for Christians in Hebrew and Arabic today. It links them to a despised village (John 1:46).

Textual note. The Byzantine text and the KJV add (vv. 6b–8a) that the Jews wanted to judge him by their law but Lysias took him away by force. It is missing from the earliest manuscripts and probably not original. Verdict: follow the shorter text; “him” in verse 8 then refers to Paul.

On a Tuesday. Christians may be called a menace to society. Make sure that if the charge is false, our lives prove it (1 Peter 2:12).
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add at the end of verse 6 and in verse 7 a complaint that Lysias had taken Paul away by force. “Nazarenes” was a name for Jesus’ followers.

verseByVerse.quote: "'By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Tertullus offers no evidence, only an invitation to cross-examine.

Bluff. Tertullus offers no witnesses or evidence, only an invitation to cross-examine the prisoner.

verseByVerse.quote: "The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repeated assertion is presented as proof.

Assertion is not evidence. Several voices repeating a charge do not make it true (Deuteronomy 19:15–19; compare Mark 14:56).

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: 'Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul answers respectfully and with facts: he came to worship only twelve days ago.

Respect without flattery. Paul’s opening is true: Felix had long experience of Jewish affairs. Compare Tertullus’s gushing.

Twelve days. Too short a time to organise a sedition, and much of it spent in custody.

To worship. Paul came as a pilgrim, not an agitator.
verseByVerse.note: Felix had been in office for several years.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one saw him causing trouble, and they cannot prove their claims.

The burden of proof. Paul rightly insists the accusers must prove their case. Roman law, like ours, required evidence.

On a Tuesday. When accused, answer calmly with facts, not counter-accusations.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul confesses that he worships the God of his fathers in the Way, believing the Scriptures and hoping in the resurrection of all.

Not a new religion. The Way is the fulfilment of Israel’s faith, not a departure from it (26:22–23; Romans 3:21). Under Rome, Judaism was a recognised religion; Paul argues that the Way belongs within it.

The just and the unjust. Daniel 12:2; John 5:28–29. Paul’s hope includes judgment.

Where Christians differ: one resurrection or two? Premillennialists distinguish a resurrection of believers before a thousand-year reign from that of the wicked after it (Revelation 20:4–6). Amillennialists read Scripture as teaching one general resurrection of all at Christ’s return (John 5:28–29; Matthew 25:31–46), and the “first resurrection” of Revelation 20 as the reign of believers’ souls with Christ now. Verdict: the app’s amillennial view: one general resurrection, at the last day, of both just and unjust.

Where Christians differ: the end of the unjust. Annihilationists hold the wicked are raised to be judged and then destroyed. The traditional view holds that their punishment is conscious and everlasting (Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11). Verdict: the traditional view, held soberly and with tears.

For worship. The same God who raised Jesus will raise us. Live in that hope.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, and some to shame

verseByVerse.quote: "'So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
That hope makes him careful to keep a clear conscience, and he came to Jerusalem bringing gifts for his nation.

Hope shapes conduct. Because there will be a judgment, Paul lives carefully (2 Corinthians 5:9–10; 1 John 3:3).

Alms. The collection from the Gentile churches (Romans 15:25–28), Luke’s only mention of it. Far from attacking his nation, Paul brought it a gift.

On a Tuesday. A clear conscience takes effort: “I take pains”. Keep short accounts with God and people. Put things right quickly.
verseByVerse.note: The alms were the collection from the Gentile churches for the poor believers in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: "'While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia — they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He was found purified in the temple, and his original accusers are not even present.

The missing witnesses. Roman law penalised accusers who abandoned a charge. The original accusers are absent, which seriously weakens the case.

Purified. Paul was keeping the law, not breaking it (21:26).
verseByVerse.note: Roman law expected accusers to appear in person.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: "It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The council found nothing against him except his cry about the resurrection.

A pointed challenge. The council itself had descended into argument and found nothing (23:9).

The resurrection again. Paul brings everything back to the central issue. A theological dispute is not a crime.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, 'When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.' Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Felix, well informed about the Way, delays the case and gives Paul some freedom.

Rather accurate knowledge. Perhaps through Drusilla, or through the church in Caesarea (Philip, Cornelius). Felix knows the Christians are not rebels.

Delay. Felix should have released Paul. He postpones to avoid offending the Jewish leaders. Lysias never seems to come.

Liberty and friends. Prisoners relied on friends for food and care. The church in Caesarea, and Luke, probably looked after Paul for two years (compare Philippians 2:25; 2 Timothy 1:16–17).

On a Tuesday. Visit Christians in prison and those suffering for the faith (Hebrews 13:3; Matthew 25:36).

verseByVerse.quote: "After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, 'Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearing Paul on righteousness, self-control and judgment, Felix is afraid but puts off a response.

Drusilla. Youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I (12:1–23), sister of Agrippa II and Bernice. Still a teenager, she had left her husband, the king of Emesa, to marry Felix, his third wife. Her family history was full of the gospel: her great-grandfather tried to kill the infant Jesus, her great-uncle beheaded John the Baptist, her father killed James.

Righteousness, self-control, judgment. Paul preaches to the conscience of an unjust, self-indulgent man. Faith in Christ is not presented as a comfort without repentance.

Alarmed. The word of God reached him. But fear without faith produced only postponement.

A convenient time. The KJV’s “a convenient season” has become proverbial. There is no record that it came. “Now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

On a Tuesday. Do not put off responding to God until it is convenient. If his word troubles you today, answer it today (Hebrews 3:15).
verseByVerse.note: Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I; she had left her first husband to marry Felix.

verseByVerse.quote: "At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hoping for a bribe, Felix hears the gospel often and never believes, and leaves Paul in prison to please the leaders.

A bribe. Paul had spoken of bringing alms (v. 17); Felix assumed money was available. Bribery was illegal but common. Paul did not pay: justice was not for sale.

Often. Felix heard the gospel many times, from the apostle himself, and apparently never believed. Familiarity can harden.

Two years. About AD 57–59. Felix was recalled after a violent clash between Jews and Gentiles in Caesarea. Paul’s two years were not wasted: Luke likely researched his Gospel, and Paul’s witness continued.

A favour. Felix needed goodwill with the Jewish leaders, who were complaining about him to Rome. Paul is a pawn in politics.

On a Tuesday. Waiting years for justice is hard. Paul’s example: keep a clear conscience, refuse to bribe, and keep witnessing. God’s timetable for Rome stands (23:11).

For worship. Two years of waiting were in God’s hands. Commit your own waiting to him (Psalm 31:15).
verseByVerse.note: Porcius Festus governed Judea from about AD 59 until his death in 62. Paul had been in custody at Caesarea for two years.

24.title: Paul Before Felix
24.text: <sup>1</sup>And after five days the high priest Ananias came down with some elders and a spokesman, one Tertullus. They laid before the governor their case against Paul. <sup>2</sup>And when he had been summoned, Tertullus began to accuse him, saying: “Since through you we enjoy much peace, and since by your foresight, most excellent Felix, reforms are being made for this nation, <sup>3</sup>in every way and everywhere we accept this with all gratitude. <sup>4</sup>But, to detain you no further, I beg you in your kindness to hear us briefly. <sup>5</sup>For we have found this man a plague, one who stirs up riots among all the Jews throughout the world and is a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes. <sup>6</sup>He even tried to profane the temple, but we seized him. <sup>8</sup>By examining him yourself you will be able to find out from him about everything of which we accuse him.” <sup>9</sup>The Jews also joined in the charge, affirming that all these things were so. <sup>10</sup>And when the governor had nodded to him to speak, Paul replied: “Knowing that for many years you have been a judge over this nation, I cheerfully make my defense. <sup>11</sup>You can verify that it is not more than twelve days since I went up to worship in Jerusalem, <sup>12</sup>and they did not find me disputing with anyone or stirring up a crowd, either in the temple or in the synagogues or in the city. <sup>13</sup>Neither can they prove to you what they now bring up against me. <sup>14</sup>But this I confess to you, that according to the Way, which they call a sect, I worship the God of our fathers, believing everything laid down by the Law and written in the Prophets, <sup>15</sup>having a hope in God, which these men themselves accept, that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust. <sup>16</sup>So I always take pains to have a clear conscience toward both God and man. <sup>17</sup>Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation and to present offerings. <sup>18</sup>While I was doing this, they found me purified in the temple, without any crowd or tumult. But some Jews from Asia— <sup>19</sup>they ought to be here before you and to make an accusation, should they have anything against me. <sup>20</sup>Or else let these men themselves say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the council, <sup>21</sup>other than this one thing that I cried out while standing among them: ‘It is with respect to the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you this day.’” <sup>22</sup>But Felix, having a rather accurate knowledge of the Way, put them off, saying, “When Lysias the tribune comes down, I will decide your case.” <sup>23</sup>Then he gave orders to the centurion that he should be kept in custody but have some liberty, and that none of his friends should be prevented from attending to his needs. <sup>24</sup>After some days Felix came with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish, and he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. <sup>25</sup>And as he reasoned about righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment, Felix was alarmed and said, “Go away for the present. When I get an opportunity I will summon you.” <sup>26</sup>At the same time he hoped that money would be given him by Paul. So he sent for him often and conversed with him. <sup>27</sup>When two years had elapsed, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus. And desiring to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in prison.
24.overview:
Five days after Paul reaches Caesarea, the high priest arrives with elders and a hired advocate, Tertullus, who opens with lavish flattery of Felix and then brings three charges: Paul is a public menace who stirs up Jews across the empire, a ringleader of the Nazarene sect, and a would-be desecrator of the temple. Paul answers calmly, point by point. He went to Jerusalem to worship only twelve days ago and caused no disturbance anywhere; the accusers cannot prove their claims. He admits only that he worships the God of the fathers according to the Way, believing the Law and the Prophets and hoping, as they do, for the resurrection of both righteous and wicked. He came bringing alms, was found ritually pure in the temple, and the Asian Jews who started the trouble are not even present.

Felix, who knows a good deal about the Way, adjourns the case. Over the following two years he and his Jewish wife Drusilla summon Paul repeatedly. When Paul speaks of righteousness, self-control and judgment to come, the governor, notorious for cruelty and for taking another man’s wife, becomes afraid and sends him away until a convenient time. He also hopes for a bribe. When he is recalled, he leaves Paul in prison to please the Jewish leaders. The chapter is a portrait of a man who heard the gospel often and put it off.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Festus and the Appeal to Caesar
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days after arriving in his province, Festus goes up from Caesarea to Jerusalem. The chief priests and Jewish leaders present their charges against Paul and press him, as a favour, to transfer Paul to Jerusalem, planning to kill him on the way. Festus answers that Paul is held at Caesarea and he himself will soon return there; their leaders can come and accuse him if he has done wrong. After about ten days he goes back, takes his seat in court the next day and has Paul brought in. The Jews from Jerusalem surround him with many serious charges they cannot prove. Paul declares he has done nothing wrong against the Jewish law, the temple or Caesar. Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asks Paul whether he will go to Jerusalem for trial. Paul answers that he is standing before Caesar’s court, where he should be tried, and he has done the Jews no wrong, as Festus well knows. If he deserves death he will not refuse to die, but if the charges are empty, no one may hand him over to them: he appeals to Caesar. After consulting his advisers, Festus replies that to Caesar he shall go. Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrive to welcome Festus, who tells the king about the prisoner Felix left behind. The Jewish leaders wanted him condemned, but Roman custom requires that the accused face his accusers and defend himself. When they came, their charges were not the crimes he expected, but disputes about their religion and about a dead man named Jesus whom Paul claims is alive. Unsure how to investigate, Festus offered a trial in Jerusalem, but Paul appealed to the emperor. Agrippa says he would like to hear the man, and Festus promises he shall, tomorrow.
verseByVerse.theology:
Lawful Means and the God Who Uses Them

Paul's appeal to Caesar settles a question Christians still raise: may a believer use the legal protections available to him, or is that a failure of faith? Acts answers plainly. Paul had a promise from the risen Christ that he would testify at Rome (23:11), and he used a statutory right to get there. Faith in the promise did not make the appeal unnecessary; it made the appeal obvious. The same man who was told every soul aboard the ship would survive still warned that unless the sailors stayed in the ship no one could be saved (27:31).

Providence does not bypass means. It employs them, and it is content to employ thoroughly unspiritual ones — a citizenship registry, a governor's ambition, an emperor's court, and a bureaucrat's need to fill in a form correctly. God ordains the end and he ordains the road, and the road here runs through Roman administrative procedure.

Two guards. First, the lawfulness of the means does not sanctify the motives of those who supply them: Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, is doing what Felix did, and Luke uses the identical phrase so the reader will not miss it. Second, God's certain purpose does not cancel real injustice. Four officials find no crime and Paul stays in chains. Scripture never asks anyone to pretend that the second fact is softened by the first. They are simply both true, and the Christian lives in the overlap.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Festus described the Christian faith to a king with complete accuracy and total detachment — a dispute about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. He had identified the hinge of the entire religion. He could have passed an examination on it. And it never crossed his mind that if it were true it might concern him personally; it was a fact about somebody else's people.

Now: This is the particular danger of a life spent near the things of God. Anyone raised in a believing home, or twenty years in a pew, or halfway through a theology course, can state the resurrection more accurately than Festus did. The question the governor puts to such a reader is not whether the doctrine is held correctly. It is whether it has ever once been allowed to be about him. Say the sentence out loud — a certain Jesus, who was dead, and who is alive — and notice honestly whether anything in you moves. Festus said it in passing and moved on.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A new governor arrives, and Paul’s enemies, two years on, renew their attack at once.

Festus. Porcius Festus, governor about AD 59–62. Josephus presents him as more just and energetic than Felix; he died in office.

Three days. A conscientious new governor quickly visits the religious capital of his province.

Two years on. A new high priest, Ishmael son of Phiabi, now held office, but the hatred of Paul had not cooled.

verseByVerse.quote: "asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem — because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They ask for a favour that hides a murder plot.

Same plot, new governor. They hope a newcomer, keen to win local goodwill, will agree before he understands the case (compare 23:12–15).

On a Tuesday. Unforgiveness can last years. Ask God to show you any grudge you have nursed, and let it go (Ephesians 4:31–32).

verseByVerse.quote: "Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. 'So,' said he, 'let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God protects Paul through Festus’s preference for proper procedure.

Providence through procedure. Festus, whether from caution or fairness, refuses. God protects Paul through a governor’s preference for correct process.

verseByVerse.quote: "After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The accusers bring many serious charges they cannot prove.

The tribunal. The bēma, the judge’s seat; the hearing is now formal.

Could not prove. Two years have produced no new evidence.

For worship. Jesus too was faced with many charges that did not agree (Mark 14:55–59). Praise him who stood silent so that we might be acquitted.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul argued in his defense, 'Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul denies any offence against the law, the temple or Caesar.

Three denials. Answering the three areas of accusation: religion, holy place and state (compare 24:5–6).

Against Caesar. The political charge is the most dangerous before a Roman judge. Christians are loyal subjects who pray for rulers (1 Timothy 2:1–2), though they will not worship them.

verseByVerse.quote: "But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, 'Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?' But Paul said, 'I am standing before Caesar's tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Wanting to please the Jews, Festus proposes a trial in Jerusalem, and Paul refuses.

A favour. The same weakness as Felix (24:27). Festus hopes to make a good start with the local leadership.

Paul’s insight. A trial in Jerusalem would mean ambush, or a court under Jewish pressure. Two years of delay have taught him that he will not get justice from local governors.

As you know. Paul speaks plainly, even to a governor.

verseByVerse.quote: "'If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.' Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, 'To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul appeals to Caesar, the route by which the Lord’s promise of Rome will be kept.

The appeal. A Roman citizen could appeal (provocatio) to the emperor against a provincial magistrate’s decision. The emperor was Nero, at this point still in the relatively good early years of his reign, before the persecution of AD 64.

Not escaping death. Paul is not trying to escape justice, only injustice.

Where Christians differ: capital punishment. Some Christians argue that the death penalty is incompatible with the gospel of mercy. Others note that Paul here accepts that some crimes deserve death, and that the state bears the sword as God’s servant (Romans 13:4; Genesis 9:6). Verdict: Scripture grants the state the right to punish the gravest crimes with death, but does not require it; Christians may differ on whether a particular nation should use it, given the risk of error and injustice.

The Lord’s plan. This appeal is how the promise of 23:11 is fulfilled: Paul will testify in Rome.

On a Tuesday. Use proper channels to seek justice, not cunning or force. And trust that God can work through ordinary legal processes.
verseByVerse.note: A Roman citizen could appeal to be tried by the emperor himself — at this time Nero.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul's case before the king, saying, 'There is a man left prisoner by Felix,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
King Agrippa and Bernice visit, and Festus lays the puzzling case before them.

Agrippa II. Son of the Herod who killed James and died struck down by an angel (12:1–23). Raised in Rome, he ruled territories north-east of Galilee and had the right to appoint the high priest and oversee the temple treasury. He was expert in Jewish customs (26:3).

Bernice. His sister, a widow, who lived with him; Roman writers gossiped about their relationship. She later became the mistress of the future emperor Titus.

Courtesy. A client king welcomes the new governor. Festus seizes the chance to consult an expert.
verseByVerse.note: King Agrippa (Herod Agrippa II) was the son of Herod Agrippa I and ruled territories to the north-east. Bernice was his sister.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus insisted that Roman law requires the accused to face his accusers.

Roman justice. Festus presents himself, a little flatteringly, as a model of fair procedure. The principle is right and biblical (Deuteronomy 1:16–17; Proverbs 18:17; John 7:51).

On a Tuesday. In church discipline, workplace disputes and family arguments, hear both sides before judging.

verseByVerse.quote: "'So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus acted promptly, unlike Felix.

Prompt. In contrast with Felix’s two years of delay.

verseByVerse.quote: "'When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The real dispute, Festus says, is about a dead man named Jesus whom Paul says is alive.

Religion. Deisidaimonia, the word Paul used at Athens (17:22); here, addressing a Jewish king, Festus probably means it neutrally, though it can carry a hint of “superstition”.

The heart of the matter. A pagan governor sums up the whole case accurately: is Jesus dead or alive? Everything depends on that (1 Corinthians 15:14–17).

For worship. “A certain Jesus, who was dead”, yet alive. Worship the one who was dead and is alive for evermore (Revelation 1:18).
