verseByVerse.quote: "'Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unable to judge such questions, Festus offered Jerusalem, and Paul appealed to the emperor.

At a loss. A Roman official does not know how to judge claims about resurrection. Festus’s honesty is to his credit, though he omits his wish to please the Jews (v. 9).

The emperor. Literally “the Augustus”, the emperor’s title, “the revered one”.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then Agrippa said to Festus, 'I would like to hear the man myself.' 'Tomorrow,' said he, 'you will hear him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agrippa, curious, wants to hear Paul himself.

Echoes. His great-uncle Herod Antipas had wanted to see Jesus (Luke 9:9; 23:8). Curiosity is not faith, but God can use it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Next day Agrippa and Bernice arrive with great ceremony and enter the audience hall with the senior officers and leading citizens, and Paul is brought in. Festus introduces him: the whole Jewish community, in Jerusalem and here, has petitioned against this man, crying that he must not live. But Festus has found that he has done nothing deserving death, and since Paul has appealed to the emperor, he has decided to send him. The trouble is that he has nothing definite to write to his lord. So he has brought Paul before them, and above all before King Agrippa, so that after this hearing he may have something to write; it seems absurd to send a prisoner without stating the charges.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Platform the World Cannot Help Providing

Jesus told his disciples that they would be dragged before kings and governors for his name's sake, and then said something startling about it: this will be your opportunity to bear witness (Luke 21:12–13). Not your ordeal — your opportunity. Acts 25 is that promise arriving in a form nobody would have designed. The hostility of the Sanhedrin, the ambition of two governors, the curiosity of a king, and an administrative problem with a covering letter combine to assemble the entire ruling class of a Roman province in one room and sit them down in front of a preacher.

Note who did the assembling. Not the church, which had no power to convene such a gathering and no money to hire the hall. The opposition built the platform, paid for it, filled it with the most important people available, and then handed the prisoner the floor.

The Reformed instinct here is neither triumphalism nor passivity. God is not obliged to use worldly power, and he frequently works through nobodies in obscurity. But when he does use the machinery of the age, he does not ask its permission and he does not need its cooperation to be willing. Festus wanted a charge sheet. What he arranged was an evangelistic meeting for the aristocracy of Judea.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Everything visible in that hall belonged to the other side. The king had the title, Bernice had the jewels, the tribunes had the swords, the leading men had the money, and Festus had the authority to decide what happened next. Paul had a chain and the floor. Within a day the man with the chain had spoken so directly to the king that Agrippa had to deflect him with a joke.

Now: Most Christians will never address a governor, and the principle does not require it. It shows up in smaller rooms — the meeting where you are plainly the least senior person present, the family table where your faith is the eccentric position, the conversation where everyone else has the confidence and the vocabulary and the standing. The instinct is to wait for a better platform, one where you are taken more seriously. Paul never got a better platform than the one his enemies built for him, and he did not ask for one. He used the floor he was given, in the clothes he was wearing, with the chain on.

verseByVerse.quote: "So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. And Festus said, 'King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
In a hall full of pomp, the chained apostle is presented to king and city.

Pomp. Phantasia, show. Luke contrasts the glittering hall with the chained apostle. Which of them would history remember?

Military tribunes. Five cohorts were stationed in Caesarea, each under a tribune.

The whole people. An exaggeration, but it shows the depth of hostility.

On a Tuesday. Do not be impressed by status or overawed by power. The chained man in the room was the one with eternal words (2 Corinthians 4:7).

parallels.desc: I will speak of your testimonies before kings

verseByVerse.quote: "'But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Festus has found Paul innocent but has nothing to write to the emperor.

Innocent. Another official verdict of innocence (23:29), like Pilate’s over Jesus (Luke 23:4).

My lord. Kyrios, a title emperors increasingly claimed. Christians confessed that Jesus is Lord (Romans 10:9), a claim that would cost many their lives under later emperors.

For worship. Caesar is called lord; Christ is Lord. Confess him gladly today.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sending a prisoner without charges is absurd: there is no case.

Festus’s embarrassment. Sending Nero an innocent man would make him look foolish. The real situation is clear: there is no case.

On a Tuesday. When you cannot state a charge against someone, do not keep holding it against them.

25.title: Paul Before Festus
25.text: <sup>1</sup>Now three days after Festus had arrived in the province, he went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea. <sup>2</sup>And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid out their case against Paul, and they urged him, <sup>3</sup>asking as a favor against Paul that he summon him to Jerusalem—because they were planning an ambush to kill him on the way. <sup>4</sup>Festus replied that Paul was being kept at Caesarea and that he himself intended to go there shortly. <sup>5</sup>“So,” said he, “let the men of authority among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong about the man, let them bring charges against him.” <sup>6</sup>After he stayed among them not more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea. And the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and ordered Paul to be brought. <sup>7</sup>When he had arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many and serious charges against him that they could not prove. <sup>8</sup>Paul argued in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.” <sup>9</sup>But Festus, wishing to do the Jews a favor, said to Paul, “Do you wish to go up to Jerusalem and there be tried on these charges before me?” <sup>10</sup>But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where I ought to be tried. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you yourself know very well. <sup>11</sup>If then I am a wrongdoer and have committed anything for which I deserve to die, I do not seek to escape death. But if there is nothing to their charges against me, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar.” <sup>12</sup>Then Festus, when he had conferred with his council, answered, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.” <sup>13</sup>Now when some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus. <sup>14</sup>And as they stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left prisoner by Felix, <sup>15</sup>and when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews laid out their case against him, asking for a sentence of condemnation against him. <sup>16</sup>I answered them that it was not the custom of the Romans to give up anyone before the accused met the accusers face to face and had opportunity to make his defense concerning the charge laid against him. <sup>17</sup>So when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day took my seat on the tribunal and ordered the man to be brought. <sup>18</sup>When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge in his case of such evils as I supposed. <sup>19</sup>Rather they had certain points of dispute with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive. <sup>20</sup>Being at a loss how to investigate these questions, I asked whether he wanted to go to Jerusalem and be tried there regarding them. <sup>21</sup>But when Paul had appealed to be kept in custody for the decision of the emperor, I ordered him to be held until I could send him to Caesar.” <sup>22</sup>Then Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” said he, “you will hear him.” <sup>23</sup>So on the next day Agrippa and Bernice came with great pomp, and they entered the audience hall with the military tribunes and the prominent men of the city. Then, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in. <sup>24</sup>And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all who are present with us, you see this man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, shouting that he ought not to live any longer. <sup>25</sup>But I found that he had done nothing deserving death. And as he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to go ahead and send him. <sup>26</sup>But I have nothing definite to write to my lord about him. Therefore I have brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that, after we have examined him, I may have something to write. <sup>27</sup>For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to indicate the charges against him.”
25.overview:
A new governor, Porcius Festus, arrives about AD 59. Within days the Jerusalem leaders ask him to bring Paul to Jerusalem, intending to ambush him on the road, as their predecessors had tried two years earlier. Festus insists they come to Caesarea instead. They bring many serious charges they cannot prove, and Paul denies any offence against the law, the temple or Caesar. When Festus, wanting to please the Jews, proposes a trial in Jerusalem, Paul sees the danger and uses his right as a citizen: “I appeal to Caesar.” Festus has no choice but to send him to Nero.

The appeal leaves Festus with a problem: he must send a report to the emperor, and he can find no crime. When King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice pay a courtesy visit, Festus explains the case: the dispute concerned the Jews’ religion and “a certain Jesus, who was dead, but whom Paul asserted to be alive.” Agrippa wants to hear Paul, and the next day, in a hall full of pomp, Festus presents the prisoner. Jesus had promised that his followers would stand before kings and governors for his name’s sake (Luke 21:12); this chapter sets the scene for the greatest of Paul’s defences.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Given leave to speak, Paul tells King Agrippa he is glad to defend himself before one who knows Jewish customs so well. All his people know he lived as a strict Pharisee; now he is on trial for hoping in God’s promise to the fathers, the hope that God raises the dead. Once he was sure he must oppose Jesus’ name: he jailed believers, voted for their deaths and hunted them abroad. On the way to Damascus at noon a light brighter than the sun struck him and his companions down, and a voice in Aramaic asked why he persecuted him: it was hard to kick against the goads. It was Jesus, who appointed him servant and witness, to open the eyes of Jews and Gentiles and turn them from darkness to light and from Satan to God, to receive forgiveness and a place among the sanctified by faith. Paul obeyed, preaching repentance and its fruits everywhere; for this he was seized and nearly killed, but God has helped him. He says only what Moses and the prophets foretold: the Messiah would suffer, rise first from the dead and bring light to Israel and the nations. Festus shouts that Paul’s learning has made him mad. Paul answers that he speaks sober truth: the king knows, for this was not done in a corner. Does Agrippa believe the prophets? Agrippa asks if Paul thinks he can make him a Christian so quickly. Paul replies that he prays all his hearers may become as he is, apart from the chains. Leaving, the officials agree he has done nothing deserving death or prison; he could have been freed if he had not appealed to Caesar.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Gospel as Israel's Hope, Not Israel's Rival

The theological spine of this speech is that Christianity is not a new religion. Paul stakes everything on continuity: he is on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers (v. 6), he says nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass (v. 22), and he asks the king the one question that would settle it — do you believe the prophets? The charge is innovation; his answer is that he is the conservative in the room and his accusers have stopped believing their own Scriptures.

That claim rests on three things the Old Testament had promised and Paul insists are now fulfilled: a Messiah who must suffer (Isa. 53; Luke 24:26), a resurrection that opens the age to come (Dan. 12:2), and light reaching the nations (Isa. 42:6; 49:6). Take away the third and the first two become a private Jewish settlement; that is precisely what his opponents wanted, and precisely what he would not give them.

Underneath it lies the doctrine this whole chapter is a case study in: grace that is entirely from God's side. Nothing in Paul's account belongs to Paul. He was not seeking, dissatisfied, or badly taught; he was convinced, exactingly trained, and in a raging fury, riding hard in the opposite direction — and he was stopped, blinded, named, and commissioned. He did not find Christ. Christ appeared to him. Every clause of the commission in vv. 17–18 is something done to people, not by them: eyes opened, a realm changed, a dominion broken, sins forgiven, a place given.

And the chapter guards that against cheapness in the same breath. Repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance (v. 20). The works are never the root; they are the fruit, exactly as Paul argued at length elsewhere (Eph. 2:8–10). A sovereign work of grace produces a visibly different life, and a life with no fruit on it after several seasons invites an honest question about the root.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Agrippa heard the finest presentation of the gospel any ruler in the New Testament ever received, delivered by the ablest preacher of the age, in his own theological vocabulary, by a man who prayed for him out loud in open court. He did not argue with it. He did not refute a single point. He made a joke, stood up, walked out, and remarked in the corridor that the prisoner had done nothing wrong.

Now: Notice how the refusal was actually shaped, because almost nobody declines Christ the way we imagine. There was no debate, no crisis, no considered rejection. There was wit, and then there was standing up, and the standing up was the answer. That is how it usually goes — a subject changed with a light remark, an evening that ran late, a genuine intention to come back to it. If you have been near this for years, the question is not whether you have objections; Agrippa had none worth stating. It is whether the conversation has quietly been allowed to end the same way five or six times, and whether anything is actually going to be different about the sixth. Paul's one request at the start of the speech was that the king would not become impatient before he had finished. It is still the only thing being asked.

verseByVerse.quote: "So Agrippa said to Paul, 'You have permission to speak for yourself.' Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: 'I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul makes his fullest defence, glad to speak before a judge who understands the issues.

The orator’s gesture. An outstretched hand, the classic pose of a speaker; perhaps also lifting the chain on his wrist (v. 29).

Fortunate. Not flattery but truth: at last a judge who understands the issues.

Third account. Each telling of Paul’s conversion (chapters 9, 22, 26) is fitted to its hearers. Here, before a king, it is fullest on Paul’s commission to the Gentiles.

On a Tuesday. Your own story of how Christ found you is a powerful witness. Learn to tell it briefly and truthfully, adapting it to the hearer.
verseByVerse.note: This is the third account of Paul’s conversion in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: "'especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Agrippa’s expert knowledge of Jewish affairs makes him the right hearer.

An informed judge. Agrippa controlled the temple treasury and appointed high priests. He could understand the case.

Patiently. Paul expects to speak at length; the gospel needs explaining.

verseByVerse.quote: "'My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s strict Pharisaic life is public knowledge.

Public record. Paul’s life was lived in the open (compare v. 26).

Strictest. The Pharisees were the most exacting interpreters of the law (Philippians 3:5–6; Galatians 1:14).

If they are willing. They could, but they will not, because it would help his case.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is on trial for the hope God promised Israel, the hope of resurrection.

The promise. God’s promise to Abraham, David and the prophets of a coming kingdom and resurrection life (13:32–33; Romans 4:13–25). The resurrection of Jesus is that hope begun.

Twelve tribes. Israel as a whole, all tribes, not just Judah; the twelve tribes were never “lost” to God (James 1:1; Luke 2:36, Anna of the tribe of Asher).

The irony. Jews accuse him for believing what Judaism hopes. To Paul, Christianity is the fulfilment of Israel’s faith (28:20, “the hope of Israel”).

For worship. Worship the God who keeps promises across centuries (2 Corinthians 1:20).

parallels.desc: because of the hope of Israel

verseByVerse.quote: "'Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If God is God, raising the dead is not incredible, and Paul himself once resisted Jesus with all his might.

Incredible? If God is the Creator, raising the dead is not beyond him (Romans 4:17; Mark 12:24). The question turns from the king to everyone in the hall.

Paul’s own unbelief. He admits he once thought as they do. He knows how resistance feels.

What it does not mean. Believing in the resurrection is not credulity. Paul offers witnesses and Scripture (1 Corinthians 15:3–8), not blind faith.

On a Tuesday. When friends find the resurrection unbelievable, start where Paul does: is anything too hard for God (Genesis 18:14)?

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul describes honestly his violent persecution of the saints.

The saints. Paul now calls those he persecuted by their true name, God’s holy ones.

Cast my vote. Literally “cast down my pebble”, the stone used in voting. It may mean he was a member of a court, even the Sanhedrin, or simply that he approved (8:1). Some infer from this that Paul was married, since Sanhedrin members were expected to be, but this is uncertain.

Make them blaspheme. To curse Jesus’ name (compare Pliny’s later test for Christians). The tense suggests he tried, not that he succeeded.

On a Tuesday. No one is beyond God’s reach. Pray for the fiercest opponents of the gospel (1 Timothy 1:15–16).
verseByVerse.note: “Cast my vote” may mean he voted as a member of a council, or simply that he approved of the executions.

verseByVerse.quote: "'In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
At noon on the Damascus road the glory of the risen Christ outshone the sun.

Brighter than the sun. The glory of the risen Christ (Matthew 17:2; Revelation 1:16). Noon makes it unmistakable.

Around me and those with me. An objective event, not a private dream.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, "Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells Paul that resisting him is as useless as an ox kicking against the goad.

The goads. A goad was a pointed stick used to drive oxen; a beast that kicks against it only hurts itself. It was a Greek proverb for useless resistance to a god (it appears in Euripides). Jesus speaks in terms an educated Greek audience would understand.

What goads? Perhaps Paul’s uneasy conscience: Stephen’s face and words (7:55–60), the law’s exposure of his covetousness (Romans 7:7–11). Or simply that resisting Christ is futile.

Where Christians differ: can grace be resisted? Arminians say God’s grace may be finally resisted, and point to such pressures. Reformed theology answers that people do resist the Spirit (7:51), but when God effectually calls, he overcomes resistance by making the unwilling willing. Paul is the clearest example: he kicked, and God conquered. Verdict: effectual calling; grace is resisted before it prevails, and it prevails without violence to the will (John 6:37, 44; Philippians 2:13).

For worship. Thank God that he did not let you go on kicking.
verseByVerse.note: A goad was a pointed stick for driving oxen; kicking against it only hurt the ox. It was a Greek proverb for resisting fate — or here, God.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And I said, "Who are you, Lord?" And the Lord said, "I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus commissioned Paul as his servant and witness.

Rise and stand. The words of God to Ezekiel when calling him as a prophet (Ezekiel 2:1–3). Paul’s call is prophetic.

Servant and witness. Hypēretēs, an assistant or attendant (Luke 1:2, “ministers of the word”), and martys, witness. Paul is commissioned directly by Christ, an apostle not from men (Galatians 1:1).

Compressed. Here Paul combines what Jesus said on the road with what Ananias told him (9:15–16; 22:14–15). He gives the substance of the commission, not every stage.

verseByVerse.quote: "'delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles — to whom I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s mission is the Servant’s: to open eyes and turn people from darkness to light and from Satan to God, for forgiveness through faith in Jesus.

The Servant’s task. Isaiah 42:6–7, 16: the Servant is a light for the nations, to open blind eyes and bring prisoners from darkness. Paul shares the mission of Christ, the true Servant (13:47).

Conversion described. Eyes opened (illumination), turning (repentance and faith), from Satan’s power to God (transfer of kingdom, Colossians 1:13), forgiveness (justification), and a place among the sanctified (inheritance, 20:32).

By faith in me. The final phrase governs all of it: these blessings come through faith in Jesus, not works.

Who opens eyes? Paul is sent to open them, but only God can (2 Corinthians 4:4–6; compare Lydia, 16:14). The messenger speaks; God gives sight.

For worship. Praise God who has delivered us from the domain of darkness into the kingdom of his beloved Son.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus’ commission echoes the calling of Isaiah’s Servant.

parallels.desc: to open the eyes that are blind

verseByVerse.quote: "'Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul obeyed the heavenly vision, preaching repentance shown in deeds.

Not disobedient. A modest way of saying he obeyed wholeheartedly. God’s call and Paul’s response go together.

Judea. Galatians 1:22 says the churches of Judea did not know him by sight, so this may summarise his later ministry, or mean visits rather than an extended campaign.

Deeds in keeping with repentance. The language of John the Baptist (Luke 3:8). Works do not earn forgiveness, but real repentance shows itself in changed life.

Where Christians differ: faith and works. Roman Catholics hold that faith formed by love and works justifies. Some evangelicals have suggested that a person may receive Christ as Saviour without submitting to him as Lord. Verdict: the Reformed position avoids both: we are justified by faith alone, but saving faith is never alone; it always brings repentance and good works (Ephesians 2:8–10; James 2:17).

On a Tuesday. What would a deed in keeping with repentance look like for you this week? An apology, a repayment, a habit broken?

verseByVerse.quote: "'For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass:'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has helped him, and he says only what Moses and the prophets foretold.

Help from God. Paul credits survival to God, not to Rome. Lysias, Felix and Festus were God’s instruments.

Small and great. Slaves and kings hear the same message (compare 1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

Nothing new. The gospel is the fulfilment of the Old Testament (Luke 24:25–27, 44–47). Christianity is not a novelty.

verseByVerse.quote: "'that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.' And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, 'Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Messiah must suffer and rise first from the dead, bringing light to all, and Festus thinks Paul is mad.

The gospel in brief. Suffering Messiah (Isaiah 53), resurrection (Psalm 16:10), light to the nations (Isaiah 49:6).

The first to rise. Others had been raised and died again; Christ is the first to rise to undying life, the “firstfruits” of the harvest (1 Corinthians 15:20; Colossians 1:18).

Festus’s outburst. To an educated Roman, bodily resurrection was absurd (17:32). Festus perhaps saw Paul surrounded by scrolls during his imprisonment (2 Timothy 4:13). Jesus too was called mad (Mark 3:21; John 10:20).

On a Tuesday. If you are thought foolish for believing the resurrection, you are in good company (1 Corinthians 1:18–25).
verseByVerse.note: Most educated Greeks and Romans found bodily resurrection absurd.

parallels.desc: a light for the nations

verseByVerse.quote: "But Paul said, 'I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s words are true and sober, and the events were public and checkable.

Courtesy under insult. “Most excellent”, even after being called mad.

True and rational. Christianity makes claims that are both true (corresponding to fact) and reasonable (sober-minded). Faith is not opposed to reason.

Not in a corner. A classical phrase. Jesus’ ministry, death and the empty tomb were public events, in a public city, at a festival (Luke 24:18). They could be checked.

On a Tuesday. Christianity invites investigation. Encourage enquirers to read the Gospels and weigh the evidence (Luke 1:1–4).

verseByVerse.quote: "'King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.' And Agrippa said to Paul, 'In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul presses Agrippa personally, and the king deflects with a wry question.

A direct appeal. Paul turns the trial into an evangelistic conversation. A king in public cannot easily say he disbelieves the prophets, nor admit that they point to Jesus.

Agrippa’s answer. Probably wry and evasive: “Do you think you can make me a Christian so quickly?” The KJV’s “Almost thou persuadest me” makes him sound nearly converted, but the Greek more likely means “in a short time”, and the tone is ironic.

Textual note. Later manuscripts read “to become” a Christian (hence the KJV). The earliest read “to make”, which may mean “make me a Christian” or “make me play the Christian” (ESV margin, “act like a Christian”). Verdict: the harder reading, “to make”, is original; either way, Agrippa sidesteps.

Christian. One of only three uses in the New Testament (11:26; 1 Peter 4:16), a name used by outsiders.

On a Tuesday. People often deflect a personal question with a joke. Do not be put off; answer graciously, as Paul does.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the question can also be read “In a short time would you persuade me to act like a Christian?” “Christian” was still a nickname used by outsiders.

verseByVerse.quote: "And Paul said, 'Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — except for these chains.' Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul longs for every hearer to become a Christian like him, apart from his chains.

Paul’s prayer. In chains, before a glittering court, Paul pities them. He is the free man in the room (John 8:36).

Except for these chains. A touch of humour and grace: he wants their salvation, not their suffering.

The king rises. The hearing ends when the king chooses. He has heard enough. There is no record that he believed.

On a Tuesday. Pray for everyone you speak to about Christ, that they may become as you are, forgiven and free.

For worship. Thank God that you are not almost but altogether his.

parallels.desc: an ambassador in chains

verseByVerse.quote: "And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, 'This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.' And Agrippa said to Festus, 'This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The officials agree that Paul is innocent and could have been freed but for his appeal.

Innocent again. Agrippa, the expert, agrees with Festus. Luke records this for any Roman reader: the apostle was a law-abiding man.

Could have been freed. Legally, once an appeal was made it had to be heard. Humanly, the appeal looks like a mistake. But it was the Lord’s route to Rome (23:11). Paul’s chains bring the gospel to Caesar’s household (Philippians 4:22).

On a Tuesday. A decision that looks like a mistake in hindsight may be the very means God uses. Trust his providence over your regrets (Romans 8:28).
verseByVerse.note: Luke repeatedly shows Roman officials finding Paul innocent.

26.title: Paul Before Agrippa
26.text: <sup>1</sup>So Agrippa said to Paul, “You have permission to speak for yourself.” Then Paul stretched out his hand and made his defense: <sup>2</sup>“I consider myself fortunate that it is before you, King Agrippa, I am going to make my defense today against all the accusations of the Jews, <sup>3</sup>especially because you are familiar with all the customs and controversies of the Jews. Therefore I beg you to listen to me patiently. <sup>4</sup>My manner of life from my youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and in Jerusalem, is known by all the Jews. <sup>5</sup>They have known for a long time, if they are willing to testify, that according to the strictest party of our religion I have lived as a Pharisee. <sup>6</sup>And now I stand here on trial because of my hope in the promise made by God to our fathers, <sup>7</sup>to which our twelve tribes hope to attain, as they earnestly worship night and day. And for this hope I am accused by Jews, O king! <sup>8</sup>Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead? <sup>9</sup>I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth. <sup>10</sup>And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them. <sup>11</sup>And I punished them often in all the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, and in raging fury against them I persecuted them even to foreign cities. <sup>12</sup>In this connection I journeyed to Damascus with the authority and commission of the chief priests. <sup>13</sup>At midday, O king, I saw on the way a light from heaven, brighter than the sun, that shone around me and those who journeyed with me. <sup>14</sup>And when we had all fallen to the ground, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’ <sup>15</sup>And I said, ‘Who are you, Lord?’ And the Lord said, ‘I am Jesus whom you are persecuting. <sup>16</sup>But rise and stand upon your feet, for I have appeared to you for this purpose, to appoint you as a servant and witness to the things in which you have seen me and to those in which I will appear to you, <sup>17</sup>delivering you from your people and from the Gentiles—to whom I am sending you <sup>18</sup>to open their eyes, so that they may turn from darkness to light and from the power of Satan to God, that they may receive forgiveness of sins and a place among those who are sanctified by faith in me.’ <sup>19</sup>Therefore, O King Agrippa, I was not disobedient to the heavenly vision, <sup>20</sup>but declared first to those in Damascus, then in Jerusalem and throughout all the region of Judea, and also to the Gentiles, that they should repent and turn to God, performing deeds in keeping with their repentance. <sup>21</sup>For this reason the Jews seized me in the temple and tried to kill me. <sup>22</sup>To this day I have had the help that comes from God, and so I stand here testifying both to small and great, saying nothing but what the prophets and Moses said would come to pass: <sup>23</sup>that the Christ must suffer and that, by being the first to rise from the dead, he would proclaim light both to our people and to the Gentiles.” <sup>24</sup>And as he was saying these things in his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “Paul, you are out of your mind; your great learning is driving you out of your mind.” <sup>25</sup>But Paul said, “I am not out of my mind, most excellent Festus, but I am speaking true and rational words. <sup>26</sup>For the king knows about these things, and to him I speak boldly. For I am persuaded that none of these things has escaped his notice, for this has not been done in a corner. <sup>27</sup>King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.” <sup>28</sup>And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” <sup>29</sup>And Paul said, “Whether short or long, I would to God that not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am—except for these chains.” <sup>30</sup>Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice and those who were sitting with them. <sup>31</sup>And when they had withdrawn, they said to one another, “This man is doing nothing to deserve death or imprisonment.” <sup>32</sup>And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.”
26.overview:
This is Paul’s fullest and most polished defence, given before King Agrippa II, Bernice, the governor Festus and the leading men of Caesarea. It is the third account of his conversion in Acts, now shaped for an audience that includes a Jewish king expert in the Scriptures. Paul presents his whole life as one story of Israel’s hope. He was a strict Pharisee; he is on trial for believing God’s promise to the fathers, the hope of resurrection. He once thought he must oppose Jesus’ name with all his strength, imprisoning and voting against believers. Then on the Damascus road, at noon, a light brighter than the sun stopped him, and the risen Jesus commissioned him as servant and witness, to open the eyes of Jews and Gentiles, to turn them from darkness to light and from Satan to God, that they might receive forgiveness and a place among the sanctified by faith in him.

Paul obeyed, preaching repentance and its fruits everywhere, and he says nothing beyond what Moses and the prophets foretold: that the Messiah would suffer, rise first from the dead and bring light to Israel and the nations. Festus interrupts, shouting that Paul’s learning has driven him mad. Paul replies that his words are true and sober, and appeals directly to the king: do you believe the prophets? Agrippa deflects with a wry question; Paul answers that he wishes everyone listening would become what he is, except for the chains. The officials agree that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. In Luke’s design, the gospel has now been heard before a king.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–26 — Setting Sail and the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul and other prisoners are handed to Julius, a centurion of the Augustan Cohort, and sail with Luke and Aristarchus on a coastal ship. At Sidon Julius kindly lets Paul see friends. Contrary winds take them past Cyprus to Myra, where they board an Alexandrian grain ship for Italy. Progress is slow, and they reach Fair Havens on Crete. It is now after the autumn Fast, and sailing is dangerous; Paul warns of disaster. But the centurion follows the pilot and the owner, and the majority vote to try for a better winter harbour at Phoenix. A gentle south wind tempts them out, then a violent northeaster rushes down from the island and drives them helplessly before it. Behind the island of Cauda they haul in the boat, brace the hull with cables, and, fearing the Syrtis sandbanks, lower the sea anchor. They throw cargo and tackle overboard. For many days there is no sun or stars, and all hope is lost. Then Paul stands up: they should have listened, but now they must take heart. An angel of the God he belongs to and serves has told him that he must stand before Caesar, and that God has given him the lives of all on board. They will lose only the ship and must run aground on an island.
verseByVerse.theology:
What God Actually Promised

The theology of this section turns on a distinction most Christians need more than they need another verse about victory: the difference between what God promises and what we assume he promises.

The angel's word was precise, and it had two halves. There will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship (v. 22), and then we must run aground on some island (v. 26). God guaranteed every person. He explicitly did not guarantee the vessel, the cargo, the owner's fortune, the crew's wages, or a safe arrival at a chosen port — and he said so in advance. Every one of those was lost, and the promise was kept in full.

That is the pattern of the promises Scripture actually makes. Nothing will separate his people from his love (Rom. 8:38–39); he works all things together for their good (Rom. 8:28); he will never leave them (Heb. 13:5). Read the list and notice what is not on it. Comfort is not on it. Property is not on it. The preservation of your circumstances is not on it. A believer standing in the surf watching his ship break up is not watching God fail; he may well be watching God keep his word exactly as given.

Alongside that runs the chapter's second theme: providence works through means, and never around them. God decreed that all 276 would live, and he decreed the whole chain that delivered it — the frapping cables, the four stern anchors, the sailors kept aboard, the meal at dawn, the swimmers going first. Paul's absolute confidence in the angel's word and his urgent practical interventions are not in tension; they are the same faith, and the sharpest expression of it is his own sentence at v. 31: unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.

And note the instruments God employs. Not one of them is a believer. A centurion's professional kindness, a crew's seamanship, an officer's fear for his own career — the Lord uses them all, unimproved and unconsulted, and they go off duty with no idea what they have been part of.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The disaster began with a harbour that was perfectly safe and thoroughly boring. Fair Havens would have kept 276 people alive all winter. It was small, it sat beside an unremarkable village, it had no facilities, and staying there meant four idle months with a valuable cargo earning nothing. So the professionals took a vote and ran for somewhere better, forty miles down the coast, on one day's easy sail — and a gentle south wind came up that morning and seemed to confirm it.

Now: Most people can spot the obviously ruinous choice and avoid it. Far fewer notice the other moment — when something safe and unglamorous was working, and the only real argument against it was that it was dull. The job that was steady. The church that was ordinary. The routine that was quietly keeping you upright. The stretch of life that felt like stagnation and was actually shelter. And when you moved, the circumstances seemed to agree with you, because a following wind on the morning of a decision feels overwhelmingly like a green light and is very often just the weather. Before the northeaster, every soul on that ship would have told you they had made a sensible call. Afterwards, every one of them would have given everything they owned to be back in the boring harbour.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul begins his voyage to Rome as a prisoner, with Luke and Aristarchus at his side.

“We” again. Luke rejoins the story and stays to the end. The detail that follows is an eyewitness’s.

The Augustan Cohort. An imperial unit; an inscription mentions a “Cohort Augusta” in the region. Julius may have been on courier duty.

Aristarchus. Perhaps travelling as Paul’s attendant, even registered as his slave, to be allowed to accompany him. He later shares Paul’s imprisonment (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24).

On a Tuesday. Faithful friends travel with us into hard places. Who could you accompany through a trial?
verseByVerse.note: “We” returns: Luke sails with Paul. Adramyttium was a port in north-west Asia Minor. Aristarchus later shared Paul’s imprisonment.

parallels.desc: Aristarchus my fellow prisoner

verseByVerse.quote: "The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. And putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion Julius treats Paul kindly, letting him visit friends at Sidon.

Kindness. Julius treats Paul humanely throughout, and in the end saves his life (v. 43). God gives his servants favour (Genesis 39:21; Daniel 1:9).

His friends. Literally “the friends”, perhaps a name Christians used for one another (3 John 15).

Under the lee. In summer the prevailing wind is from the west and north-west, so they pass to the east and north of Cyprus, sheltered by the island, then use land breezes along the coast.
verseByVerse.note: Sidon was a Phoenician port north of Tyre. “Under the lee” means sheltered from the wind by the island.

verseByVerse.quote: "And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Contrary winds force a long route along the coast to Myra.

Myra. A major harbour for the Egyptian grain fleet, which often sailed north to Asia Minor and then west because of the winds. Paul sails past his home province of Cilicia.

Textual note. The Western text says the crossing took fifteen days, an addition probably based on sailing experience.
verseByVerse.note: Myra, on the south coast of Asia Minor, was a major stop for the grain ships from Egypt to Rome.

verseByVerse.quote: "There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They transfer to an Alexandrian grain ship and make slow progress to Crete.

A grain ship. Egypt supplied about a third of Rome’s grain. These ships were large, with state backing, and could carry hundreds of passengers.

Against the wind. Ancient square-rigged ships could not sail close to the wind. A north-westerly forced them south of Crete.
verseByVerse.note: Ships from Alexandria carried Egypt’s grain to feed Rome. Cnidus lay at the south-western tip of Asia Minor; they turned south to shelter behind Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They reach Fair Havens, a poor harbour for winter.

Fair Havens. A small bay on the south coast of Crete, still called Kaloi Limenes. It offered protection from north-west winds but was exposed to others, not a good place to winter.
verseByVerse.note: Fair Havens was a small bay on the south coast of Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, saying, 'Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Experienced in shipwreck, Paul warns that sailing on will bring disaster.

The Fast. The Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:29–31), in late September or October. Ancient writers considered sailing dangerous after mid-September and closed from November to March.

Paul’s advice. Not a prophecy but the counsel of an experienced traveller who had already been shipwrecked three times (2 Corinthians 11:25). Later God reveals more (v. 22), and the loss of life is averted.

On a Tuesday. A Christian’s common sense and experience can be a gift to unbelieving colleagues. Speak up when you see danger, respectfully.
verseByVerse.note: “The Fast” is the Day of Atonement, in late September or October. Sailing became dangerous from mid-September and stopped altogether in winter.

verseByVerse.quote: "But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion trusts the experts and the majority, against Paul’s advice.

Experts and majorities. The centurion naturally trusts professionals; the owner has money at stake. The majority decide. But experts can be wrong, and majorities are not always wise (Exodus 23:2).

Phoenix. Probably modern Loutro or nearby, about 40 miles west, a much better harbour.

On a Tuesday. In business decisions, beware when financial interest drives risk-taking. Listen to the cautious voice.
verseByVerse.note: Phoenix was a better harbour farther west along Crete.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A gentle south wind tempts them out, then a violent north-easter strikes.

Supposing. A gentle breeze tempts them out. Circumstances that seem favourable can deceive.

Euraquilo. A sailors’ hybrid name, from the Greek Euros (east wind) and Latin Aquilo (north wind). Sudden north-easterly gales still sweep down from Crete’s mountains.

What it does not mean. A good feeling about a decision is not proof of God’s guidance (Proverbs 14:12).
verseByVerse.note: The northeaster (Euraquilo) was a violent wind sweeping down from the mountains of Crete.

parallels.desc: he raised the stormy wind

verseByVerse.quote: "And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ship is helpless and runs before the storm.

Helpless. Seasoned sailors can do nothing but run before the storm. Human expertise reaches its limit.

On a Tuesday. There are storms in life you cannot steer through, only endure. Psalm 107:23–30: the LORD brings sailors to their wits’ end, and then to the haven they desire.

verseByVerse.quote: "Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship's boat. After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crew does everything possible to save the ship from breaking up or running onto the sandbanks.

Cauda. Modern Gavdos, about 23 miles south of Crete. Textual note. Some manuscripts spell it “Clauda”; both forms are found in ancient writers.

Undergirding. Passing ropes or chains under or around the hull to stop the planks working loose, a technique known from ancient sources.

Syrtis. The notorious quicksands and shoals off Libya, the graveyard of ships, far to the south-west.

Lowered the gear. Probably a sea anchor dragged to slow the drift, or the mainsail lowered. Either way, they are doing all they can.
verseByVerse.note: The ship’s boat was a dinghy towed behind. Cables were passed under the hull to hold it together. The Syrtis were dangerous sandbanks off the coast of North Africa.

verseByVerse.quote: "Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. And on the third day they threw the ship's tackle overboard with their own hands."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They throw cargo and gear overboard.

Jettisoning. Like Jonah’s sailors (Jonah 1:5). Some grain is kept as food and ballast until later (v. 38).

Their own hands. Everyone, passengers included, helps throw spare gear overboard. Luke may include himself in the labour.

On a Tuesday. In a crisis, possessions quickly lose their value. What would you throw overboard to save a life? What are you holding that is weighing you down (Hebrews 12:1)?

parallels.desc: the mariners hurled the cargo into the sea

verseByVerse.quote: "When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, 'Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
With no sun or stars, all hope is lost, and Paul reminds them that he warned them.

No sun or stars. Without them, ancient navigators could not fix their position. They were lost.

All hope abandoned. Including, it seems, Luke’s. The darkest moment comes just before God’s word.

Without food. Seasickness, fear and the difficulty of cooking in a storm.

I told you so? Paul is not gloating but establishing credibility: his first warning proved true, so they should trust his next word.
verseByVerse.note: Without sun or stars, ancient sailors had no way to navigate.

verseByVerse.quote: "'Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship,'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul encourages them: the God he belongs to and serves has promised no lives will be lost.

Take heart. The prisoner becomes the encourager. Faith gives courage in the dark (Psalm 46:1–3).

The God whose I am. A beautiful confession before pagans: Paul belongs to God, and serves him. Belonging comes before serving.

For worship. Say it today: I belong to God, and I worship him. Nothing in the storm changes that.

verseByVerse.quote: "'and he said, "Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you." So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has granted Paul the lives of all aboard, for he must stand before Caesar, and Paul trusts God’s word.

Must. God’s plan for Paul guarantees the safety of everyone else on board. They are saved because of him.

Granted you. Perhaps Paul had been praying for them. God gives the lives of pagans to his servant, as he spared Sodom for Abraham’s intercession (Genesis 18:22–33).

Faith. “I have faith in God”: faith takes God at his word before the outcome is seen (Hebrews 11:1; Romans 4:20–21).

On a Tuesday. Christians in a workplace, family or nation can be a blessing to everyone around them. Pray for those who share your ship.

verseByVerse.quote: "'But we must run aground on some island.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rescue will come through shipwreck on an island.

Specific and humbling. Rescue, but not comfort: the ship will be wrecked. God’s promises often include hardship on the way.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the fourteenth night, drifting across the Adriatic, the sailors sense land near. Soundings show the water growing shallower, so they drop four anchors from the stern and pray for daylight. When the sailors try to escape in the boat, pretending to lay anchors from the bow, Paul tells the centurion that unless they stay, the rest cannot be saved, and the soldiers cut the boat loose. Before dawn Paul urges everyone to eat after two weeks of fasting: they need strength, and not a hair of their heads will be lost. He takes bread, gives thanks to God in front of them all, breaks it and eats, and they are all encouraged and eat. There are 276 on board. After eating they lighten the ship by throwing the grain into the sea. At daybreak they see an unfamiliar coast with a beach and decide to run the ship ashore. They cut the anchors, loosen the steering oars, raise the foresail and head for the beach, but strike a sandbar. The bow sticks fast and the stern is broken up by the waves. The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners to prevent escape, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. He orders those who can swim to jump first and the rest to follow on planks and wreckage. And so everyone reaches land safely.
verseByVerse.theology:
Certainty and Effort Are the Same Faith

Verse 31 is the hinge, and it is one of the clearest answers in Scripture to the oldest bad question about providence: if God has already decided, why bother?

Nine verses after announcing an unconditional promise — not one life will be lost — Paul says something that sounds like its opposite: unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved. Both are true, because God does not merely decree ends; he decrees the means that bring them about. The sailors staying aboard was not an alternative to the promise. It was the promise arriving. The same logic governs the meal at dawn: eat, because God has guaranteed you will live and you will need the strength.

So Paul's serenity and Paul's urgency are not in tension. A man who thinks everything hangs on his own vigilance is too frightened to act well; a man who thinks nothing depends on him does not act at all. Paul is neither, and the doctrine he lived by he also wrote down: work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Phil. 2:12–13). The for in that sentence carries the whole argument.

The section also shows how God's promises are typically fulfilled — not by suspending the ordinary world but by working through the wreckage of it. There is no calmed sea here, no parting of the waters, no angel carrying anyone ashore. There are exhausted people swimming, and non-swimmers clinging to splintered planks off the ship that has just been destroyed beneath them. The debris of the disaster is the means of the rescue, and the promise is kept down to the last person on the roll.

And one thing more, quietly at the centre: the prisoners live because the centurion wanted Paul. Condemned men, under a sentence they had earned, spared entirely on account of the worth of another. Luke does not press the point. He does not have to.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: An hour before the ship broke apart, with an unknown shore ahead and no boat left, Paul took a piece of bread and thanked God for it out loud where everyone could hear. He had nothing. He had not eaten in two weeks, he was in chains, the vessel was doomed, and he was about to swim for his life. And a shipful of frightened people watched a man be visibly grateful to God, and something in them changed — Luke says they were encouraged, and they ate.

Now: Notice what actually moved that ship's company. Not Paul's argument; he had made his case at Fair Havens and been outvoted. Not his warning; they had ignored it. What reached them was watching one man's confidence in God hold steady when there was no visible reason for it, and do something ordinary and cheerful in front of them. People around you are far better at reading that than at following reasoning. They will discount what you say about God when things are going well, and they will not forget what you did with a piece of bread on the worst morning of your life. Courage is contagious in a way that argument is not — and the place it becomes contagious is almost always the small, practical, unembarrassed act done in front of witnesses.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After two weeks adrift, the sailors sense land and take soundings.

The Adriatic. In ancient usage the name covered the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy and Sicily, not just today’s Adriatic.

Sensing land. Probably the sound of breakers. At St Paul’s Bay in Malta the approach passes the point of Koura, where surf can be heard at night.

The accuracy of Luke. James Smith calculated that a ship drifting from Cauda at the likely rate would take about thirteen to fourteen days to reach Malta, and that the soundings match the approach to St Paul’s Bay.
verseByVerse.note: In ancient usage the Adriatic Sea included the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy and Sicily. The ESV notes that twenty fathoms is about 120 feet and fifteen about 90 feet.

verseByVerse.quote: "And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the ship's boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
They anchor and pray for daylight, and the sailors try to abandon ship.

Stern anchors. To keep the bow pointing towards the shore, ready to run aground when daylight shows a beach.

Prayed. Literally “wished”, but the word is often used of prayer. Pagan sailors cry out in the dark (Jonah 1:5–6).

Desertion. The sailors try to save themselves and leave the passengers to die. Fear makes people selfish.
verseByVerse.note: Anchors from the stern kept the bow pointing toward land, ready for beaching.

verseByVerse.quote: "Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, 'Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.' Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship's boat and let it go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s promise includes the means: the sailors must stay if all are to be saved.

Sovereignty and means. God has promised that all will live (v. 24); yet Paul says that unless the sailors stay, they cannot be saved. Both are true. God’s decree includes the means: the sailors’ skill is needed to beach the ship.

Where Christians differ: God’s decree and human action. Fatalism says that if God has decided, what we do does not matter. Some Arminians conclude that because human action matters, God’s promise must be conditional. Reformed theology holds both: God ordains the end and the means, and works through human responsibility (Philippians 2:12–13; Westminster Confession 5.3). Verdict: God’s sovereignty does not make our choices pointless; it makes them meaningful. We pray, act, preach and stay at our posts because God has promised.

The soldiers act. Now the centurion listens to Paul (contrast v. 11).

On a Tuesday. Trust God’s promises and use every sensible means: take the medicine, study for the exam, save for the future, and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: "As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, 'Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, For not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul urges everyone to eat, for not a hair of their heads will perish.

Practical care. They will need strength to swim. Faith does not ignore the body (1 Kings 19:5–8).

Not a hair. Jesus’ own words of protection (Luke 21:18; 12:7).

On a Tuesday. When someone is in crisis, sometimes the most spiritual thing is to get them to eat.

parallels.desc: not one hair of his head shall fall

verseByVerse.quote: "And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul gives thanks to God before them all, and everyone is encouraged.

Giving thanks. Before 275 frightened pagans, Paul prays. A public testimony that God is the giver of food and life.

Where Christians differ: the Lord’s Supper? The words take, give thanks, break and eat echo the Supper (Luke 22:19). Some think Paul celebrated it on board. Most interpreters answer that this was an ordinary meal, eaten with unbelievers, with the grace said as any devout Jew would. Verdict: an ordinary meal, but Luke’s wording hints that every meal received with thanks points to the Lord who provides and saves (Luke 24:30).

Encouraged. One man’s calm faith steadies a whole ship.

For worship. Give thanks before your next meal deliberately, as a confession of faith.
verseByVerse.note: Paul gives thanks as the head of a Jewish household did before a meal.

verseByVerse.quote: "(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary:
All 276 eat, and throw the grain overboard.

276. Luke counts individuals: each life saved matters (v. 44). Textual note. One early manuscript (Vaticanus) reads “about seventy-six”, perhaps from a copying slip of Greek numerals. Verdict: 276 is better attested and fits a large grain ship; Josephus sailed on one with 600 aboard.

The grain thrown out. The whole purpose of the voyage, the cargo, is sacrificed so that the ship will ride higher and run further up the beach.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts read seventy-six. A large grain ship could carry several hundred people.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach."
verseByVerse.commentary:
At dawn they head for a beach in an unknown bay.

Unrecognised. Malta was off the usual route. St Paul’s Bay on the north-east coast fits the description: a bay with a sandy beach.

The rudders. Two large steering oars at the stern, lashed up during the storm, now lowered for the run in.

The foresail. A small sail at the bow (artemōn), to give steerage.
verseByVerse.note: Ancient ships were steered by two large oars (rudders) at the stern.

verseByVerse.quote: "But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The ship strikes a sandbar and breaks up, as God said.

A place between two seas. Literally; perhaps a shoal where two currents meet, as at the channel between Malta and the islet of Salmonetta in St Paul’s Bay.

The bow stuck. The bed of the bay there is of thick clay, which would grip a bow firmly.

As Paul said. The ship is lost (v. 22), just as God foretold.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that the reef is literally “a place between two seas” — perhaps a sandbar where currents met.

verseByVerse.quote: "The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The centurion saves Paul, and all the prisoners with him, from the soldiers’ plan to kill them.

The soldiers’ logic. Guards who let prisoners escape could suffer their punishment (12:19; 16:27).

Saved for Paul’s sake. The other prisoners owe their lives to Paul’s presence. The centurion who ignored Paul’s advice (v. 11) now risks his career for him.

On a Tuesday. Your integrity can win the trust of unbelievers over time, and that trust may protect others.
verseByVerse.note: Guards who let prisoners escape could face their punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: "and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
By swimming and clinging to wreckage, everyone reaches land safely, just as God promised.

All brought safely. The word is the verb “save”. Every one of the 276 is saved, as God promised. Not one lost (John 6:39; 17:12).

Through ordinary means. Swimming, planks, wreckage, a centurion’s order. Providence is not usually spectacular, but it is always sure.

A picture. Many have seen here a parable of salvation: the ship of human effort breaks up, but God’s word holds, and all whom he has given are brought home.

For worship. Praise the God who keeps every promise and loses none whom he has given to his Son.

parallels.desc: three times I was shipwrecked

27.title: Storm, Shipwreck, and Sovereignty
27.text: <sup>1</sup>And when it was decided that we should sail for Italy, they delivered Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion of the Augustan Cohort named Julius. <sup>2</sup>And embarking in a ship of Adramyttium, which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, accompanied by Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica. <sup>3</sup>The next day we put in at Sidon. And Julius treated Paul kindly and gave him leave to go to his friends and be cared for. <sup>4</sup>And putting out to sea from there we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us. <sup>5</sup>And when we had sailed across the open sea along the coast of Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia. <sup>6</sup>There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy and put us on board. <sup>7</sup>We sailed slowly for a number of days and arrived with difficulty off Cnidus, and as the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the lee of Crete off Salmone. <sup>8</sup>Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea. <sup>9</sup>Since much time had passed, and the voyage was now dangerous because even the Fast was already over, Paul advised them, <sup>10</sup>saying, “Sirs, I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and the ship, but also of our lives.” <sup>11</sup>But the centurion paid more attention to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to what Paul said. <sup>12</sup>And because the harbor was not suitable to spend the winter in, the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete, facing both southwest and northwest, and spend the winter there. <sup>13</sup>Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, close to the shore. <sup>14</sup>But soon a tempestuous wind, called the northeaster, struck down from the land. <sup>15</sup>And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along. <sup>16</sup>Running under the lee of a small island called Cauda, we managed with difficulty to secure the ship’s boat. <sup>17</sup>After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. Then, fearing that they would run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear, and thus they were driven along. <sup>18</sup>Since we were violently storm-tossed, they began the next day to jettison the cargo. <sup>19</sup>And on the third day they threw the ship’s tackle overboard with their own hands. <sup>20</sup>When neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay on us, all hope of our being saved was at last abandoned. <sup>21</sup>Since they had been without food for a long time, Paul stood up among them and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not have set sail from Crete and incurred this injury and loss. <sup>22</sup>Yet now I urge you to take heart, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship. <sup>23</sup>For this very night there stood before me an angel of the God to whom I belong and whom I worship, <sup>24</sup>and he said, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And behold, God has granted you all those who sail with you.’ <sup>25</sup>So take heart, men, for I have faith in God that it will be exactly as I have been told. <sup>26</sup>But we must run aground on some island.” <sup>27</sup>When the fourteenth night had come, as we were being driven across the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors suspected that they were nearing land. <sup>28</sup>So they took a sounding and found twenty fathoms. A little farther on they took a sounding again and found fifteen fathoms. <sup>29</sup>And fearing that we might run on the rocks, they let down four anchors from the stern and prayed for day to come. <sup>30</sup>And as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship, and had lowered the ship’s boat into the sea under pretense of laying out anchors from the bow, <sup>31</sup>Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men stay in the ship, you cannot be saved.” <sup>32</sup>Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the ship’s boat and let it go. <sup>33</sup>As day was about to dawn, Paul urged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing. <sup>34</sup>Therefore I urge you to take some food. For it will give you strength, for not a hair is to perish from the head of any of you.” <sup>35</sup>And when he had said these things, he took bread, and giving thanks to God in the presence of all he broke it and began to eat. <sup>36</sup>Then they all were encouraged and ate some food themselves. <sup>37</sup>(We were in all 276 persons in the ship.) <sup>38</sup>And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea. <sup>39</sup>Now when it was day, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore. <sup>40</sup>So they cast off the anchors and left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the ropes that tied the rudders. Then hoisting the foresail to the wind they made for the beach. <sup>41</sup>But striking a reef, they ran the vessel aground. The bow stuck and remained immovable, and the stern was being broken up by the surf. <sup>42</sup>The soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. <sup>43</sup>But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan. He ordered those who could swim to jump overboard first and make for the land, <sup>44</sup>and the rest on planks or on pieces of the ship. And so it was that all were brought safely to land.
27.overview:
Luke’s account of the voyage to Rome is one of the most detailed descriptions of ancient seafaring that survives. In 1848 James Smith, a Scottish yachtsman who sailed these waters, showed that its winds, depths, distances and manoeuvres fit the conditions exactly: this is the log of an eyewitness. Paul, a prisoner under the centurion Julius, sails with Luke and Aristarchus up the coast to Myra, then on an Alexandrian grain ship towards Italy. Late in the season, against Paul’s warning, the ship leaves Fair Havens on Crete for a better harbour, and is caught by a violent north-easterly gale. For two weeks it is driven helplessly west, without sun or stars, cargo and tackle thrown overboard, until all hope is gone.

Then the prisoner takes charge. An angel has told Paul that he must stand before Caesar and that God has given him the lives of everyone aboard; they will lose the ship but not one life. When land is near, Paul stops the sailors abandoning ship, urges everyone to eat, gives thanks and breaks bread. At dawn they run the ship onto a sandbar off Malta; the stern breaks up, the soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them, and all 276 reach land. The chapter is a parable of providence: God’s promise is certain, and he keeps it through ordinary means, sailors, anchors, food, a centurion’s decision, and planks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Malta and the Journey to Rome
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Safe ashore, the travellers learn the island is Malta. The islanders show unusual kindness, lighting a fire and welcoming everyone, for it is raining and cold. As Paul puts a bundle of sticks on the fire, a viper driven out by the heat fastens on his hand. The islanders conclude he must be a murderer whom Justice will not let live, even though he escaped the sea. But Paul shakes the snake into the fire and is unharmed. They wait for him to swell up or drop dead, and when nothing happens, they change their minds and say he is a god. Publius, the island’s chief official, has an estate nearby and welcomes them generously for three days. His father is ill with fever and dysentery; Paul visits him, prays, lays hands on him and heals him. Then the rest of the sick on the island come and are cured. The islanders honour them in many ways and, when they sail, supply what they need. After three months they leave on an Alexandrian ship that had wintered there, with the twin gods as its emblem. They stop at Syracuse for three days, then Rhegium, and with a south wind reach Puteoli, where they find believers and stay a week. And so they come to Rome. Believers there hear of them and travel out as far as the Forum of Appius and Three Taverns to meet them; seeing them, Paul thanks God and is encouraged. In Rome Paul is allowed to live on his own, with a soldier guarding him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Providence Through People Who Never Know

Everything Paul needs in this section is supplied, and hardly any of it comes from a believer. A fire lit by islanders who worship other gods. Three days' hospitality from a Roman official. A winter's provisions loaded aboard by people who thought Paul was a deity. A ship dedicated to Castor and Pollux. A favourable wind. God furnishes the last stage of his apostle's journey almost entirely out of pagan hands, and not one of those hands knows what it is doing.

That is the same doctrine the storm chapter taught, arriving now in a gentler key. There God used a centurion's fear and a crew's seamanship; here he uses simple human decency. The Reformed conviction that God governs all things through secondary causes is not an abstraction in Acts — it is a bonfire on a wet beach.

The viper episode adds the other half. The Maltese read Paul's circumstances and drew a confident conclusion about his standing with God, and they were as wrong as it is possible to be — twice, in opposite directions, within one evening. Scripture is consistent about this: you cannot read a person's standing before God off the surface of their life. Job's friends could not, the disciples could not at the blind man (John 9:2–3), and neither can we, in a sickroom or anywhere else.

And the section's tenderest theology is in v. 15. Paul took courage, which means he needed to.
